q: In neutral organic molecules, how many covalent bonds do C, N, O and Cl usually form, in that order?
h: Count the valence electrons each atom needs to reach an octet; each bond supplies one electron.
w: C needs 4 more electrons, N needs 3, O needs 2 and Cl needs 1, so the usual bond counts are 4, 3, 2, 1. Hydrogen also forms just one bond.
x: This swaps N and O. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more for an octet, while oxygen has 6 and needs only 2.
Chlorine has 7 valence electrons, so it needs just one more electron to reach an octet. That means one bond, like hydrogen.
This swaps C and O. Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more, while oxygen needs only 2.

q: What is the approximate H–C–H bond angle in ethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Each carbon has four single bonds (four electron groups). Which shape spreads four groups as far apart as possible?
w: Four bonded groups around carbon give a tetrahedral shape with angles of about 109.5°. 120° goes with a C=C double bond and 180° with a triple bond.
x: 120° goes with a carbon that has three electron groups, like a C=C carbon. Each carbon in ethane has four single bonds.
180° is the linear angle for two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Ethane's carbons have four groups each.
90° angles would crowd four groups together. Four groups spread out in 3-D, not in a flat square.

q: What is the shape around each carbon atom in ethene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>?
h: A double bond counts as one electron group. How many groups surround each carbon?
w: Each carbon has three groups (two H and the double bond to the other C), so it is trigonal planar with ~120° angles. Tetrahedral is for carbons with four single bonds.
x: Tetrahedral goes with four electron groups, like a carbon with four single bonds. In ethene the double bond counts as one group.
Linear goes with two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Count the groups around each ethene carbon.
Bent, about 105°, describes an atom like the O in water, with two bonds and two lone pairs. Carbon in ethene has no lone pairs.

q: Which of these molecules is polar?
h: Look for an electronegative atom (F, N, O) whose bond dipole is not canceled by symmetry.
w: Methanol's polar O–H and C–O bonds do not cancel, so CH3OH is polar. CCl4 and CO2 have polar bonds arranged symmetrically, so their dipoles cancel; propane has only nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds.
x: CCl<sub>4</sub> has polar C–Cl bonds, but they point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar.
Propane has only C–C and C–H bonds, which are essentially nonpolar, so the molecule is nonpolar.
CO<sub>2</sub> has polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

q: Compared with sodium chloride, the organic compound hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>, would be expected to
c: melt at a much lower temperature
h: Think about covalent molecules held together by weak attractions versus an ionic lattice.
w: Hexane is a nonpolar covalent compound with weak attractions between molecules, so it melts at a much lower temperature than ionic NaCl. It has no ions to conduct and is insoluble in water.
x: Conducting when melted needs ions that can move. Hexane is a covalent molecule with no ions.
Hexane is nonpolar, with only C–C and C–H bonds, so it does not mix with polar water. "Like dissolves like."
Hexane contains only covalent C–C and C–H bonds. Ionic bonds hold compounds like NaCl together.

q: Which functional group is present in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Where is the oxygen? Is it bonded to H, to a C=O, or between two carbon groups?
w: An oxygen bonded to two carbon groups, R–O–R, is an ether (this one is diethyl ether, an old anesthetic). An alcohol needs an –OH group.
x: An alcohol has an –OH group. In this compound the oxygen has no H; it sits between two carbon groups.
That group needs a C=O next to the oxygen (–COO–). This molecule has no C=O at all.
A ketone has a C=O bonded to two carbons. This molecule has no double bond to oxygen.

q: Which functional group is present in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Write out –COO–: is the second oxygen bonded to H or to a carbon?
w: The C=O carbon is bonded to an –O–CH3 group, so it is an ester (methyl propanoate). A carboxylic acid would be –COOH, with H on the oxygen.
x: A carboxylic acid is –COOH, with H on the second oxygen. Here that oxygen is bonded to a CH<sub>3</sub> instead.
That group has an O between two carbons with no C=O next to it. Here one of the carbons on the O is a C=O carbon.
An aldehyde has a C=O at the end of a chain bonded to H (–CHO). Here the C=O carbon is bonded to another oxygen.

q: The compound CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> contains which functional group?
h: Is the nitrogen attached directly to a carbonyl (C=O) carbon?
w: The –NH2 is bonded to a C=O carbon, which makes an amide (ethanamide). An amine has nitrogen bonded only to carbons or H, with no C=O next to it.
x: In an amine, N is bonded only to carbons or H with no C=O next to it. Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is on a C=O carbon.
A ketone has a C=O bonded to two carbons. Here the C=O carbon is bonded to a nitrogen.
That group has –COO–, an oxygen on the C=O carbon. Here the C=O carbon carries an –NH<sub>2</sub> instead.

q: Which condensed formula is NOT a possible structure?
h: Count the bonds on every carbon. Carbon must have exactly four.
w: In CH3CH2=CH2 the middle carbon has a bond to CH3, two H atoms and a double bond, which is 5 bonds, so it is impossible. In CH3CH=CH2 the middle carbon has 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 bonds.
x: This one is fine: the middle carbon has a bond to CH<sub>3</sub>, one H and a double bond, for 4 bonds. Look for a carbon with 5.
This is ethanol, a real compound. Every carbon has four bonds and O has two. Check the other formulas carbon by carbon.
This is propyne, a real compound. The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has 4 bonds, and each triple-bonded carbon has 3 + 1 = 4.

q: In a skeletal (line-angle) formula, each corner and each line end represents
c: a carbon atom plus enough H atoms for four bonds
a hydrogen atom bonded to a carbon atom
a carbon atom with no hydrogen atoms attached
an oxygen or nitrogen atom with its H atoms
h: Skeletal formulas leave out some atoms to save time. Which atoms are not drawn?
w: Corners and ends are carbon atoms; the H atoms on carbon are not drawn but are understood to fill each carbon to four bonds. Heteroatoms such as O and N are always written in.
x: Hydrogen atoms on carbon are the ones left out of a skeletal formula, not shown by corners. Each corner stands for a heavier atom.
Corners and ends do carry hydrogens; they are just not drawn. You add enough H to give each of those atoms four bonds.
O and N are always written out in a skeletal formula. Unlabeled corners and ends stand for a different element.

q: What is the molecular formula of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH?
h: Count every C, every H (including the one on oxygen) and every O.
w: C: 3. H: 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8. O: 1. The formula is C3H8O. Forgetting the H on the –OH gives the C3H7O distractor.
x: This misses the H on the –OH. Count every H, including the one on oxygen.
This has two H too few, which would need a C=O or C=C. CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH has only single bonds.
Count the carbons again: CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub> are three carbon groups.

q: Which bond is the most polar?
h: Bond polarity grows with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms.
w: O (3.5) and H (2.1) differ by 1.4, more than N–H (0.9) or C–H (0.4); C–C is nonpolar. So O–H is the most polar.
x: N–H is polar, but N (3.0) and H (2.1) differ by only 0.9. Look for a bigger electronegativity difference.
C (2.5) and H (2.1) differ by only 0.4, so C–H is nearly nonpolar.
Two identical atoms share electrons equally, so C–C is nonpolar.

q: What is the shape around the nitrogen atom in trimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N?
h: Count the electron groups on N, including its lone pair, then name the shape from the bonded atoms only.
w: N has three bonded C atoms and one lone pair: four electron groups, but only three are atoms, so the shape is trigonal pyramidal (like NH3). Trigonal planar would need no lone pair.
x: Trigonal planar needs three groups and no lone pair. The N in an amine still has a lone pair, which pushes the bonds down.
Four electron groups are arranged tetrahedrally, but the shape is named from atoms only. N here has three atoms and a lone pair.
Bent is for two bonded atoms plus lone pairs, like water. This N has three bonded carbons.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Find the longest chain first, then name the branch on it. Is the branch attached at its end carbon or its middle carbon?
w: The longest chain has 7 carbons (heptane). The branch –CH(CH3)2 is attached through its middle carbon, so it is isopropyl, on C4: 4-isopropylheptane. A propyl branch would be –CH2CH2CH3.
x: A propyl branch is a straight –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> attached through its end carbon. Here the branch is attached through its middle carbon, which has a different name.
Recount the longest chain. Running through the branch never gives more than 7 carbons, so the parent is not octane.
A tert-butyl group has four carbons, C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>. Count the carbons in this branch: there are only three.

q: How many primary (1°) carbons are in 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: A primary carbon is bonded to exactly one other carbon. That means every CH<sub>3</sub> group here.
w: There are three CH3 groups on the quaternary carbon and two on the CH carbon: 5 primary carbons. Answering 2 counts only the two end carbons of the pentane chain and forgets that every branch CH3 is also a 1° carbon. The molecule also has one 2° (CH2), one 3° (CH) and one 4° carbon.
x: 4 misses one CH<sub>3</sub>. Every CH<sub>3</sub> group, whether at a chain end or on a branch, is bonded to just one carbon and counts as 1°.
3 counts only the methyls on the quaternary carbon. The CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the CH carbon are also bonded to only one carbon each.
2 counts only the two ends of the pentane chain. Branch CH<sub>3</sub> groups are also bonded to just one carbon, so they are 1° too.

q: Which compound is a constitutional isomer of hexane?
h: Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) but a different connection of atoms.
w: 2,2-Dimethylbutane has 6 C and 14 H, the same as hexane, with a different skeleton, so it is an isomer. Cyclohexane is C6H12; 2-methylhexane is C7H16; 2,2-dimethylpropane is C5H12.
x: Cyclohexane is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>: closing the ring removes 2 H. Isomers must have exactly the same formula as hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>.
2-Methylhexane has a six-carbon chain plus a methyl: 7 carbons, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. An isomer of hexane must have 6 carbons in total.
2,2-Dimethylpropane has only 5 carbons in total (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>). An isomer of hexane needs 6 carbons and 14 H.

q: Which alkene can exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Each carbon of the double bond must carry two different groups.
w: In 2-pentene each double-bond carbon has an H and a different alkyl group, so CH3CH=CHCH2CH3 has cis and trans forms. The others each have a double-bond carbon with two identical groups (two H or two CH3).
x: The end carbon of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH– carries two H atoms. When one double-bond carbon has two identical groups, swapping sides gives the same molecule.
The left double-bond carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Two identical groups on one C=C carbon rule out cis and trans forms.
Here one C=C carbon has two CH<sub>3</sub> groups and the other has two H atoms, so neither carbon has two different groups.

q: A six-carbon ring has a methyl group on each of two neighboring ring carbons. What is its name?
h: Name the ring by its number of carbons, then number the substituents with the lowest possible numbers.
w: A six-carbon ring is cyclohexane, and neighboring positions are numbered 1 and 2: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane. 1,3 would skip a carbon; 1,1 would put both methyls on the same carbon.
x: 1,3 would leave one ring carbon between the two methyl groups. Here the methyls are on neighboring carbons.
Cyclopentane is a five-carbon ring. Count the ring carbons in the description again.
1,1 puts both methyl groups on the same ring carbon. Here each methyl is on a different, neighboring carbon.

q: Which alkane has the highest boiling point?
h: Boiling point rises with more carbons and falls with more branching.
w: Hexane has the most carbons and is unbranched, giving the largest surface area and strongest dispersion forces. 2,2-Dimethylbutane has the same formula but is compact, so it boils lower.
x: 2,2-Dimethylbutane has six carbons, but it is compact and highly branched, so it has less surface contact and weaker dispersion forces than an unbranched isomer.
Pentane is unbranched but has only five carbons. A larger molecule here has more electrons and stronger dispersion forces.
2-Methylbutane is small (five carbons) and branched, which both lower the boiling point.

q: Propane burns completely in a gas grill. When the equation below is balanced, what is the coefficient of O<sub>2</sub>?
h: Balance C first, then H, then count the oxygen atoms on the product side.
w: C3H8 + 5 O2 → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. Products have 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 O atoms, so 5 O2. Choosing 4 copies the water coefficient, 3 copies the CO2 coefficient, and 2 counts only the four O atoms in the water and forgets the six in CO2.
x: 3 copies the CO<sub>2</sub> coefficient. Count all the O atoms in the products: 3 CO<sub>2</sub> plus 4 H<sub>2</sub>O, then divide by 2.
4 copies the H<sub>2</sub>O coefficient. Add up every O atom on the product side, from both CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, then divide by 2.
2 O<sub>2</sub> supplies only 4 O atoms, enough for the water alone. The CO<sub>2</sub> molecules need oxygen too.

q: Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of light to form a monochlorinated product. What are the products?
h: In halogenation, one halogen atom replaces one H atom. Where does the removed H go?
w: Substitution swaps one H for one Cl: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. The H that leaves combines with the other Cl atom, not with another H.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl is right, but H<sub>2</sub> is not the by-product. The H removed from carbon pairs with the other Cl atom of Cl<sub>2</sub>.
CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> has two H replaced, but the question asks for a monochlorinated product. Also, the removed H leaves with Cl, not as H<sub>2</sub>.
Carbon can form only four bonds, so CH<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> cannot exist. Alkanes have no double bond to add to; a Cl swaps places with an H instead.

q: What is the product when 2-butene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, reacts with H<sub>2</sub> over a platinum catalyst?
h: Hydrogenation adds one H to each carbon of the double bond.
w: Adding H2 across the C=C gives CH3CH2CH2CH3, butane. Adding water (hydration) would give 2-butanol instead.
x: 1-Butene is still an alkene: it just moves the C=C. Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> and removes the double bond entirely.
2-Butanol contains an OH, which would come from adding water (hydration). H<sub>2</sub> supplies only hydrogen atoms.
2-Butyne has a triple bond and fewer H atoms than 2-butene. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen, so the product has more H, not fewer.

q: Propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the major product?
h: Use Markovnikov's rule to decide where the H and the OH go.
w: The H adds to the end CH2 carbon (which already has more H), and the OH adds to the middle carbon, giving 2-propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3. 1-Propanol would be the anti-Markovnikov product.
x: This puts the OH on the end carbon, which is the anti-Markovnikov product. The H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
Propane is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Adding water puts an OH group into the product.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is an aldehyde with a C=O. Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C, giving an alcohol, not a carbonyl compound.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with HBr?
h: HBr adds H and Br, one to each double-bond carbon. Which carbon gets the H?
w: By Markovnikov's rule, H goes to the CH2 carbon and Br to the carbon bearing the two methyls: (CH3)3CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide). A dibromo product would come from Br2, not HBr.
x: Br on the CH<sub>2</sub> end is the anti-Markovnikov product. The H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
Two Br atoms would come from Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.
2-Bromobutane has an unbranched four-carbon chain. Addition to the C=C never changes the branched carbon skeleton of 2-methylpropene.

q: Markovnikov's rule states that when HX or H<sub>2</sub>O adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H atom adds to the double-bond carbon that
c: is bonded to more carbon atoms
is at the center of the chain
h: Markovnikov's rule is sometimes called “the rich get richer.” Compare how many H atoms are already on each of the two double-bond carbons.
w: The H goes to the carbon that already has more H atoms, and the X or OH goes to the more substituted carbon. Picking “fewer H” reverses the rule.
x: That reverses the rule. The carbon with fewer H atoms is where the X or OH ends up.
The carbon bonded to more carbons usually has fewer H atoms; that is where X or OH goes, not the H.
Position in the chain does not matter. The rule compares the number of H atoms already on each double-bond carbon.

q: Poly(vinyl chloride), PVC, is used in IV bags and medical tubing. Which monomer is used to make it?
h: An addition polymer is built from an alkene monomer; the name tells you which atom it carries.
w: Vinyl chloride is chloroethene, CH2=CHCl. Ethene makes polyethylene, propene makes polypropylene, and CF2=CF2 makes Teflon.
x: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> (ethene) makes polyethylene, which has no chlorine. The name vinyl chloride tells you the monomer carries a Cl.
CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>3</sub> (propene) makes polypropylene. The monomer for PVC must contain chlorine.
CF<sub>2</sub>=CF<sub>2</sub> makes Teflon, a fluorine polymer. The monomer for PVC carries chlorine, not fluorine.

q: How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> are needed to completely hydrogenate 1 mole of HC≡C–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>?
h: Each H<sub>2</sub> adds across one pi bond. How many pi bonds are in a C=C, and how many in a C≡C?
w: The triple bond needs 2 mol H2 and the double bond needs 1 mol H2: 2 + 1 = 3 mol H2, giving butane. Counting each multiple bond as one gives the tempting answer 2.
x: 2 counts each multiple bond once. A triple bond takes up two H<sub>2</sub> to become a single bond.
1 H<sub>2</sub> would saturate only one pi bond. This molecule has both a C≡C and a C=C to fill.
4 is too many. A triple bond takes two H<sub>2</sub> and a double bond takes one; there is nothing else to add to.

q: Which compound has the molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>?
h: Each ring or double bond removes 2 H from the alkane formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>.
w: Cyclohexene has a ring plus a C=C: 14 − 2 − 2 = 10 H, so C6H10. Cyclohexane and 1-hexene each have only one ring or one double bond (C6H12); hexane is C6H14.
x: Cyclohexane has a ring but no double bond: 14 − 2 = 12 H, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. Look for a compound with two features that each remove 2 H.
1-Hexene has one C=C and no ring: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. You need a compound missing 4 H from the alkane formula.
Hexane is the saturated open-chain alkane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>. It has no ring or double bond to remove H atoms.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Number the chain from the end that gives the double bond the lower number.
w: Five carbons with the double bond between C2 and C3 when numbered from the right: 2-pentene. “3-Pentene” comes from numbering from the wrong end.
x: 3-Pentene numbers the chain from the wrong end. Number from the end nearer the double bond so it gets the lowest number.
Count the carbons: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> has five, so the parent is pentene, not hexene.
1-Pentene has the C=C at the end of the chain. Here the double bond is between two inner carbons.

q: Which statement about benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, is true?
c: All six C–C bonds are the same length.
It has three short double bonds and three long single bonds.
It reacts readily with Br<sub>2</sub> by addition, like an alkene.
Each carbon is bonded to two hydrogen atoms.
h: Think about what the circle drawn inside the benzene ring represents.
w: The pi electrons are spread evenly around the ring, so all six C–C bonds are identical, between a single and a double bond in length. That stability is why benzene resists addition reactions; each C has only one H.
x: That describes one drawing of benzene, but its pi electrons are spread over the whole ring. Measured C–C bond lengths do not alternate between short and long.
Alkenes add Br<sub>2</sub> quickly, but benzene does not: addition would break up its stable ring of pi electrons.
Two H on every carbon would be C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> (cyclohexane). Benzene is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: six H for six carbons.

q: A benzene ring has a –CH<sub>3</sub> group and a –Cl atom on adjacent carbons. Which name is correct?
h: Use toluene as the parent (the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon is C1), then number to the Cl.
w: With the methyl carbon as C1, an adjacent Cl is on C2: 2-chlorotoluene (ortho-chlorotoluene). 3- and 4- would be meta and para; phenol needs an –OH group.
x: 3- means one ring carbon sits between the –CH<sub>3</sub> and the –Cl (meta). Here the two groups are on neighboring carbons.
4- puts the –Cl directly across the ring from the –CH<sub>3</sub> (para). Here the two groups are on neighboring carbons.
Phenol is the parent name for a ring with an –OH group. This ring has a –CH<sub>3</sub> group instead, which sets a different parent name.

q: Two substituents on a benzene ring are on carbons 1 and 3. This arrangement is called
h: Ortho = neighbors, para = opposite. What is in between?
w: 1,2 is ortho, 1,3 is meta, and 1,4 is para.
x: Ortho means neighboring carbons, 1,2. On carbons 1 and 3 one ring carbon sits between the two substituents.
Para means directly across the ring, 1,4. Carbons 1 and 3 are not opposite each other.
Alpha is not used for positions on a benzene ring. Two groups on a benzene ring are described as ortho, meta or para.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: When a benzene ring is a substituent on a carbon chain, it is called phenyl. Count the chain carbons.
w: The chain has 5 carbons and the C6H5 group sits on C3: 3-phenylpentane. Benzyl would be C6H5CH2–, which is not present here.
x: Benzyl is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–, a ring plus an extra CH<sub>2</sub>. Here the ring is bonded directly to a chain carbon, with no CH<sub>2</sub> in between.
Count from either end: CH<sub>3</sub>, then CH<sub>2</sub>, then the CH that holds the ring. That carbon is not C2.

Count the chain again: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has five carbons, not six. The C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> carbons belong to the ring substituent, not the main chain.

q: Naphthalene, used in some mothballs, is best described as
c: a benzene ring with a methyl group
a benzene ring with two –OH groups
h: Naphthalene is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon. What does polycyclic mean?
w: Naphthalene (C10H8) is two benzene rings sharing one side. Larger fused-ring aromatics, such as benzo[a]pyrene in cigarette smoke, are carcinogens.
x: A benzene ring with a methyl group is toluene, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. Naphthalene is C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, and all ten carbons are in rings.
A six-carbon cycloalkane (cyclohexane) is saturated and not aromatic. Naphthalene is aromatic and has ten carbons.
A benzene ring with two –OH groups is a phenol such as hydroquinone. Naphthalene is a hydrocarbon, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, with no oxygen.

q: Benzene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> in the presence of FeCl<sub>3</sub>. What are the products?
h: Benzene keeps its stable ring: does it add atoms across a double bond or swap an H?
w: Benzene undergoes substitution: one H is replaced by Cl, giving chlorobenzene + HCl. Addition products such as dichlorocyclohexane would destroy the aromatic ring.
x: 1,2-Dichlorocyclohexane has no double bonds left, so the aromatic ring would be gone. Benzene resists losing its ring of pi electrons and does not add Cl<sub>2</sub> the way an alkene does.
Chlorocyclohexane is a saturated ring: all three double bonds would have disappeared. The product of this reaction is still aromatic.
Only one Cl from each Cl<sub>2</sub> ends up on the ring; the other Cl leaves with the H that was displaced. H<sub>2</sub> is not a product.

q: What is the common name of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, a benzene ring with an amino group?
h: Each common aromatic parent has its own name: –OH, –CH<sub>3</sub> and –NH<sub>2</sub> each have one.
w: C6H5NH2 is aniline. Phenol is C6H5OH, toluene is C6H5CH3 and benzamide is C6H5CONH2.
x: Phenol is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, a ring with an –OH group, not an –NH<sub>2</sub> group.
Toluene is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, a ring with a methyl group. It has no nitrogen.
Benzamide is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>: its N is attached to a C=O, which makes an amide. Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is bonded straight to the ring.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH?
h: Find the longest chain that includes the carbon bonded to –OH, then number from the end nearer the –OH.
w: The longest chain through the C–OH carbon has 3 carbons, with –OH and a methyl both on C2: 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol). 2-Methyl-1-propanol is a different isomer, (CH3)2CHCH2OH.
x: 2-Methyl-1-propanol is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH, with the –OH on an end carbon. Here the –OH is on the central carbon that holds the three CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
2-Butanol needs a four-carbon chain. The longest chain through the C–OH carbon here has only three carbons; the fourth carbon is a branch.
1-Butanol is a straight four-carbon chain with –OH on the end. This molecule is branched, with the –OH on a central carbon.

q: Which is a secondary (2°) alcohol?
h: Classify by how many carbons are bonded to the carbon that holds the –OH, not by branching elsewhere.
w: In 2-butanol (sec-butyl alcohol) the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is 2°. (CH3)2CHCH2OH is branched but its –OH carbon has only one C neighbor, so it is 1°; (CH3)3COH is 3°.
x: The C–OH carbon here is bonded to three carbons, so this alcohol is tertiary.
The –OH is on an end carbon bonded to only one other carbon, so this alcohol is primary.
This one is branched, but the branch is not on the C–OH carbon. The –CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon has just one carbon neighbor, so it is primary.

q: What is the common name of CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Name the two groups on the oxygen alphabetically, then add “ether.”
w: The groups are methyl (CH3–) and propyl (–CH2CH2CH3): methyl propyl ether. Isopropyl would be attached through its middle carbon, –CH(CH3)2.
x: Ethyl is two carbons. The chain on the right side of the O, –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, has three.
Dipropyl would mean a three-carbon group on both sides of the O. One side here is only CH<sub>3</sub>.
Isopropyl is attached through its middle carbon, –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Here the three-carbon group is a straight chain attached at its end.

q: What is the name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH?
h: An –SH group is a thiol; keep the full alkane name and add “-thiol.”
w: Two carbons plus –SH gives ethanethiol. Small thiols smell strongly; ethanethiol is added to natural gas so leaks can be detected.
x: Ethanol has an –OH group. This compound has –SH, with sulfur in place of oxygen.
The meth- prefix means one carbon (CH<sub>3</sub>SH). Count the carbons in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH again.
A sulfide has S between two carbon groups, with no H on S. Here the S carries an H.

q: Eugenol, the clove-oil compound dentists use as a mild pain reliever, has an –OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring. Eugenol is classified as a(n)
h: An –OH on an aromatic ring carbon gets its own family name.
w: An –OH bonded directly to a benzene ring makes a phenol. An alcohol has –OH on a carbon that is not part of an aromatic ring.
x: In an alcohol the –OH sits on a carbon that is not part of an aromatic ring. An –OH directly on a benzene ring gets its own family name.
A ketone has a C=O between two carbons. The key group described here is an –OH, not a C=O.
An aldehyde has a –CHO group. The key group described here is an –OH on a ring.

q: Which statement correctly compares phenol and ethanol in water?
c: Phenol is a weak acid; ethanol is essentially neutral.
Ethanol is a weak acid; phenol is essentially neutral.
Both are strong acids that ionize completely.
Both are weak bases that accept H<sup>+</sup> ions.
h: Which compound can lose H<sup>+</sup> from its –OH and form a stabilized negative ion?
w: Phenol partly ionizes to phenoxide and H3O+, so phenol is a weak acid; ethanol does not ionize appreciably.
x: This reverses them. Ethanol's O–H barely ionizes, while the other compound can form a negative ion stabilized by its ring.
Neither ionizes completely; strong acids are things like HCl. These compounds are at most weakly acidic.
Neither is a base that accepts H<sup>+</sup> in water. Think about whether either –OH can give up an H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
h: Which molecule can form hydrogen bonds with its own kind?
w: Only 1-propanol has an O–H that can hydrogen bond between molecules, so CH3CH2CH2OH boils highest (97 °C). The ether has O but no O–H, so it can't H-bond to itself.
x: This ether has an O but no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
Butane is a nonpolar hydrocarbon held together only by dispersion forces, so it has a very low boiling point.
Propane is a small nonpolar hydrocarbon with only weak dispersion forces. It boils far below room temperature.

q: Which alcohol is the least soluble in water?
h: The –OH is polar, but the hydrocarbon part is nonpolar. Which molecule has the largest nonpolar part?
w: As the carbon chain grows, the nonpolar part takes over; 1-hexanol, with six carbons, is only slightly soluble. Alcohols with 1–3 carbons mix completely with water.
x: Methanol has the smallest nonpolar part and mixes completely with water. Look for the alcohol with the longest carbon chain.
Ethanol mixes completely with water, as in alcoholic drinks. Its two-carbon chain is too small to keep it out of water.
1-Propanol's three-carbon chain is still short enough for it to mix completely with water. A longer chain dissolves less.

q: 2-Butanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is heated with an acid catalyst. What is the major product?
h: Dehydration removes H and OH to form C=C. Zaitsev's rule picks which H is removed.
w: Zaitsev's rule: the H is removed from the neighboring carbon that has fewer H atoms, giving the more substituted alkene, 2-butene (CH3CH=CHCH3). 1-Butene forms only as the minor product; butanone would be an oxidation product.
x: 1-Butene does form, but only as the minor product. Zaitsev's rule favors the alkene with more carbon groups on the C=C.
Butanone is a ketone, which comes from oxidizing 2-butanol. Heating with an acid catalyst removes water instead.
Butane has no C=C and no O, so it would require adding H<sub>2</sub>. Losing water from an alcohol forms a C=C.

q: Rubbing alcohol, 2-propanol, is oxidized with K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. What is the product?
h: A secondary alcohol is oxidized once. What carbonyl compound does that give?
w: Oxidizing a 2° alcohol removes 2 H and gives a ketone: CH3COCH3, propanone (acetone). Aldehydes and carboxylic acids come from 1° alcohols.
x: An aldehyde comes from oxidizing a primary alcohol. In 2-propanol the –OH is on the middle carbon, which has two carbon neighbors.
A carboxylic acid needs the C=O at the end of a chain, which comes only from a primary alcohol. 2-Propanol has its –OH on the middle carbon.
Propene is made by dehydration (loss of water), not by oxidation with K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.

q: Which alcohol is NOT oxidized by an oxidizing agent such as K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?
h: Oxidation needs an H atom on the carbon that holds the –OH.
w: In tert-butyl alcohol, 2-methyl-2-propanol, the –OH carbon is bonded to three carbons and has no H, so it is not oxidized. 1° and 2° alcohols are oxidized; 2-methyl-1-propanol is 1° despite its similar name.
x: Despite the similar name, this is a primary alcohol: the –OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub>, which still has H atoms to lose.
2-Propanol is secondary; its C–OH carbon still has one H, so it is oxidized to a ketone.
1-Butanol is primary, with two H atoms on the C–OH carbon, so it is readily oxidized.

q: In the liver, ethanol from alcoholic drinks is first oxidized to
h: Ethanol is a primary alcohol. What does the first oxidation step give?
w: A 1° alcohol is oxidized first to an aldehyde: ethanol → ethanal, which is then oxidized further to acetic acid. Acetaldehyde buildup causes many hangover symptoms.
x: Acetic acid is formed, but in a second oxidation step. Ethanol is a primary alcohol, so its first oxidation product is one step earlier.
Ethene forms by dehydration (loss of water), not oxidation. The liver's enzymes oxidize ethanol.
Dimethyl ether is an isomer of ethanol, not an oxidation product. Oxidation forms a C=O.

q: When two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized, as happens when permanent-wave solution reshapes hair keratin, the product contains a(n)
c: sulfide bond (–S–) with loss of S
h: Oxidation removes an H from each –SH. What forms between the two sulfur atoms?
w: 2 R–SH → R–S–S–R + 2 H: a disulfide bond. In hair, disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains are broken and re-formed in new positions.
x: No sulfur atom is lost. Oxidation removes only an H from each –SH, and the two sulfur atoms then bond to each other.
An ether has an oxygen between two carbons. No oxygen is added; the bond forms between the two sulfur atoms.
A sulfonic acid needs oxygen atoms added to one sulfur. Oxidizing two –SH groups together just links them.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO?
h: –CHO at the end of the chain is an aldehyde. Count all the carbons, including the CHO carbon.
w: Four carbons with a terminal –CHO: butanal. The CHO carbon counts in the chain, so propanal is wrong; butanone would have the C=O in the middle.
x: Butanone is a ketone, with the C=O inside the chain. A –CHO group sits at the end of the chain.
1-Butanol is an alcohol with –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. This formula has a C=O (–CHO), not an –OH.
Propanal has three carbons. The –CHO carbon counts as part of the chain, so count it too.

q: Methyl ethyl ketone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is a solvent. What is its IUPAC name?
h: Count the carbons (both sides of the C=O). Ketones end in “-one.”
w: Four carbons with a C=O inside the chain: butanone (2-butanone). Butanal is the aldehyde isomer; propanone has only 3 carbons.
x: Butanal is an aldehyde with the C=O at the end of the chain. Here the C=O carbon has a carbon on both sides.
2-Butanol is an alcohol, with –OH instead of C=O. This compound keeps its carbonyl group.
Propanone has only three carbons. Count the carbons on both sides of the C=O.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Number the six-carbon chain from the end that gives the C=O carbon the lower number.
w: Six carbons; numbering from the left puts C=O at C3: 3-hexanone. Numbering from the right gives 4, which is not the lowest number.
x: 4 comes from numbering from the right end. Number from the end that gives the C=O carbon the lower number.
The -al ending is for aldehydes, where the C=O is at the end (always C1). Here the C=O is in the middle of the chain.
3-Pentanone has five carbons. Count every carbon on both sides of the C=O.

q: Acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, mixes completely with water. The best explanation is that
c: water molecules hydrogen bond to acetone's carbonyl oxygen
acetone molecules hydrogen bond to one another
acetone ionizes completely into ions in water
acetone and water are both nonpolar molecules
h: Does acetone have an O–H? If not, can its oxygen still take part in hydrogen bonding with water?
w: Acetone has no O–H, so it cannot H-bond to itself, but its polar C=O oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water. That is why small aldehydes and ketones dissolve well yet boil lower than alcohols.
x: Acetone has no O–H (or N–H), so it cannot hydrogen bond to other acetone molecules. Think about what water can supply.
Acetone is a neutral molecule that does not ionize in water. Its solubility comes from attractions between whole molecules.
Water is very polar, and acetone's C=O is polar too. Nonpolar molecules would not mix with water.

q: Which compound is oxidized to propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, by a mild oxidizing agent?
h: Which carbonyl compound has an H on its C=O carbon that can be replaced by OH?
w: An aldehyde oxidizes easily to the carboxylic acid with the same carbon count: propanal → propanoic acid. Propanone (a ketone) and 2-propanol (which gives a ketone) cannot give a carboxylic acid.
x: Propanone is a ketone: its C=O carbon has no H to replace, so mild oxidation does not affect it.
2-Propanol is a 2° alcohol; oxidation gives a ketone, not a carboxylic acid.
Propane is an alkane with no oxygen. A mild oxidizing agent does not convert it to an acid.

q: Which compound gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
h: Tollens' test detects compounds that are easily oxidized: which family?
w: Tollens' reagent (Ag+) oxidizes aldehydes and is reduced to Ag metal (the mirror). Only propanal, CH3CH2CHO, is an aldehyde; ketones such as acetone give no reaction.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> is a ketone (acetone). Ketones are not oxidized by Tollens' reagent, so no silver forms.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> is an alcohol. Tollens' reagent detects a more easily oxidized functional group.
CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> is an ether, which is not oxidized by Tollens' reagent.

q: In a positive Benedict's test for glucose in urine, the blue solution forms a brick-red precipitate of
h: The sugar is oxidized, so the copper(II) ion in the blue reagent is reduced. Work out the charge on copper in each copper compound.
w: Cu2+ (blue) is reduced to copper(I) oxide, Cu2O, the brick-red solid. Silver metal is the product of the Tollens' test, not Benedict's.
x: Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> still contains copper(II), which is not reduced. In a positive test the copper ion gains an electron.
CuSO<sub>4</sub> is a blue copper(II) compound that stays dissolved. The red solid forms when copper(II) is reduced.
Silver metal is the mirror from Tollens' test. Benedict's reagent contains copper, not silver.

q: What is formed when butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is reduced with [H] (a reducing agent)?
h: Reduction adds H to each atom of the C=O. Which class of alcohol does a ketone give?
w: Adding H atoms across the C=O gives CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, 2-butanol, a 2° alcohol. Reducing a ketone never gives a 1° alcohol, and butanoic acid would be an oxidation product.
x: 1-Butanol has the OH on the end carbon, but in butanone the C=O is on carbon 2. Reduction puts the OH on the former C=O carbon.
Butanal is an aldehyde isomer, not a reduction product. Reduction ([H]) converts the C=O into C–OH.
Butanoic acid would be an oxidation product, and a ketone cannot form it. [H] is a reducing agent.

q: A carbon atom bonded to one –OH group and one –OR group (formed when an aldehyde adds one alcohol molecule) is part of a(n)
h: “Hemi” means half: only one alcohol has added.
w: One alcohol adding to the C=O gives a carbon with –OH and –OR: a hemiacetal. An acetal has two –OR groups and no –OH; an ester has a C=O; a hemiketal forms from a ketone, not an aldehyde.
x: An acetal has two –OR groups and no –OH; it forms after a second alcohol adds. Here only one alcohol has added.
An ester has a C=O and an –OR on the same carbon. This carbon has no C=O.
A hemiketal forms from a ketone. The question says the carbonyl compound was an aldehyde.

q: Ethanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, reacts with two molecules of methanol in the presence of acid. What is the organic product?
h: The first methanol gives a hemiacetal; the second replaces the –OH and releases water.
w: With two alcohol molecules and acid, the aldehyde carbon ends up with two –OCH3 groups: CH3CH(OCH3)2, an acetal, plus H2O. The hemiacetal is only the intermediate after one methanol.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)OCH<sub>3</sub> is what forms after only one methanol adds. The question uses two molecules of methanol.
An ester has a C=O, and it forms from a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde. Here the C=O is used up as alcohols add.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> has only one oxygen, but two methanol molecules were used. Each methanol adds its own –OCH<sub>3</sub> group to the former carbonyl carbon.

q: Formalin, used to preserve tissue specimens, is an aqueous solution of
h: The “form-” prefix means one carbon, which rules out one choice. Then think about which one-carbon compound is used to preserve tissue.
w: Formalin is about 37% methanal, HCHO, in water. Methanol is the alcohol; methanoic acid is formic acid.
x: Methanol is an alcohol, and "formalin" is not named for it. Formalin comes from a one-carbon carbonyl compound.
Methanoic (formic) acid is a carboxylic acid, found in ant stings. Formalin is a solution of a different one-carbon compound.
Acetone (propanone) has three carbons. The "form-" root means one carbon.

q: Which compound contains a chiral carbon?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups attached. Check each C bonded to –OH.
w: In 2-butanol the C–OH carbon carries H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3, all different, so CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 is chiral. 3-Pentanol is not: its C–OH carbon has two identical ethyl groups.
x: This is 2-propanol. Its C–OH carbon carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it does not have four different groups.
This is 3-pentanol. Its C–OH carbon carries two identical ethyl groups (CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), so it is not chiral.
The C–OH carbon here holds three identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups and no H, so it cannot have four different groups.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the open-chain form of glucose, CH<sub>2</sub>OH(CHOH)<sub>4</sub>CHO?
h: Check each carbon: the CHO carbon and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon cannot have four different groups.
w: C1 (CHO) and C6 (CH2OH) are not chiral; C2, C3, C4 and C5 each have four different groups: 4 chiral carbons. Counting C6 or all CHOH and end carbons gives 5 or 6.
x: That count includes an end carbon. C6 is a CH<sub>2</sub>OH with two identical H atoms, and the CHO carbon has a C=O double bond.
That counts every carbon. The CHO carbon has a double bond (only three groups), and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon has two identical H atoms.
Too few. Go through the chain carbon by carbon: each CH(OH) carbon in the middle has H, OH and two different chain pieces.

q: Which statement about a pair of enantiomers is true?
c: They rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.
They have different melting and boiling points.
They are superimposable mirror images of each other.
They have different molecular formulas and masses.
h: Enantiomers are mirror images made of the same atoms joined by the same bonds. Which properties could still differ between them?
w: Enantiomers have the same melting point, boiling point and formula, but rotate polarized light equally in opposite directions. They are NON-superimposable mirror images.
x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties such as melting and boiling points. They differ only in how they interact with polarized light and other chiral things.
Enantiomers are mirror images that can NOT be superimposed, like your left and right hands. Superimposable mirror images are the same compound.
Enantiomers are stereoisomers: same atoms, same bonds, same formula and mass. Only the 3-D arrangement differs.

q: Only one enantiomer of many drugs (for example, ibuprofen) is responsible for the drug's effect. Why can enantiomers act differently in the body?
c: Enzymes and receptors are chiral and fit only one enantiomer well.
The two enantiomers have different molecular formulas and masses.
One enantiomer of any chiral drug is always toxic to the body.
Only one enantiomer is soluble enough to dissolve in blood plasma.
h: Think of a right hand fitting into a right-handed glove.
w: Proteins are built from L-amino acids, so their binding sites are chiral and fit one enantiomer better than the other. Enantiomers have the same formula and solubility; one is not automatically toxic.
x: Enantiomers have exactly the same atoms, so their formulas and masses are identical. The difference is only in 3-D shape.
There is no such rule. Often the other enantiomer is simply less active, and many racemic drugs like ibuprofen are safe.
Enantiomers have the same solubility in water and plasma. Think instead about what in the body could tell a left hand from a right hand.

q: In a Fischer projection, the horizontal lines at a chiral carbon represent bonds that
c: lie in the plane of the page
h: Picture the molecule as a bow tie with the arms reaching out at you.
w: Horizontal bonds come toward the viewer and vertical bonds go back, away from the viewer. The chiral carbon is the intersection of the cross.
x: In a Fischer projection the vertical bonds are the ones that go back, away from you. The horizontal bonds do the opposite.
A Fischer projection is a flat code for 3-D shape: neither the horizontal nor the vertical bonds lie in the page. Picture the bow tie.
The lines of a Fischer cross are all single bonds to the chiral carbon. They show direction in space, not bond order.

q: In the Fischer projection of D-glyceraldehyde, CHO–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>OH, with CHO at the top, the –OH on the chiral carbon is
h: D and L tell which side of the Fischer projection the –OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O points to.
w: In D-glyceraldehyde the –OH points to the right; in L-glyceraldehyde it points to the left.
x: An –OH on the left of the chiral carbon is the L form of glyceraldehyde, the mirror image of the D form.
The top position holds the CHO group. The –OH on the chiral carbon sits on a horizontal bond, to one side.
The bottom position holds the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group. The –OH on the chiral carbon sits on a horizontal bond, to one side.

q: D-Erythrose and D-threose are aldotetroses that differ only in the position of the –OH on carbon 2. These two compounds are
h: They are stereoisomers. Are they mirror images of each other?
w: Only one of two chiral carbons differs, so they are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers. Enantiomers would differ at every chiral carbon; constitutional isomers have different bonding.
x: Enantiomers are opposite at every chiral carbon. These two sugars have two chiral carbons but differ at only one.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. These sugars have the same bonding; only the 3-D arrangement at one carbon differs.
They are different compounds: switching the –OH on carbon 2 changes the 3-D arrangement, and the two cannot be superimposed.

q: Starting from the Fischer projection of D-glucose, which change gives its enantiomer, L-glucose?
c: Switch the –H and –OH at every chiral carbon.
Switch the –H and –OH at carbon 5 only.
Switch the –H and –OH at carbon 2 only.
Switch the –H and –OH at carbons 2 and 3 only.
h: An enantiomer is the full mirror image. How many chiral centers must change?
w: The mirror image inverts every chiral carbon (C2–C5). Changing only C5 gives a different D/L diastereomer (L-idose), not L-glucose, and changing only C2 gives D-mannose; changing only C2 and C3 gives D-altrose.
x: Changing only C5 flips D to L, but the other chiral carbons stay the same, so the result is not a mirror image. It is a different sugar (L-idose).
Changing only C2 inverts one of several chiral carbons, giving a diastereomer (D-mannose), not the mirror image.
Changing C2 and C3 leaves C4 and C5 untouched, so the product is still a D sugar and a diastereomer (D-altrose), not the mirror image.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, the compound responsible for the smell of rancid butter?
h: Count every carbon, including the –COOH carbon, and use the ending “-oic acid.”
w: Four carbons including the carboxyl carbon: butanoic acid (butyric acid). Forgetting to count the COOH carbon gives propanoic acid.
x: Propanoic acid has only three carbons. Did you leave out the –COOH carbon? It counts as part of the parent chain.
Pentanoic acid would need five carbons. Count the carbons in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH again, one per C.
The ending -al names an aldehyde (–CHO). This compound has a –COOH group, which takes a different ending.

q: Ethyl acetate, CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is a solvent in nail-polish remover. What is its IUPAC name?
h: The alkyl group on the single-bonded O is named first; the part containing C=O becomes “-oate.”
w: The acid part is CH3CO– (ethanoate) and the alcohol part is ethyl: ethyl ethanoate. Methyl propanoate is an isomer, CH3CH2COOCH3.
x: Methyl propanoate is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>, an isomer. Here the C=O side has only two carbons, and the group on the single-bonded O is two carbons too.
Propanoate would mean three carbons on the C=O side. In CH<sub>3</sub>COO– the acid part has just two carbons.
The alkyl group on the single-bonded O is –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, which has two carbons, not three.

q: Propanoic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the organic product?
h: Esterification: the –OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol leave as water.
w: CH3CH2COOH + HOCH3 → CH3CH2COOCH3 (methyl propanoate) + H2O. Ethyl ethanoate has the same formula but comes from acetic acid and ethanol.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is ethyl ethanoate, made from acetic acid and ethanol. Propanoic acid has three carbons, so its C=O side must keep all three.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> is an ether with no C=O. Esterification keeps the acid's carbonyl group.
C(=O)NH is an amide, which needs an amine as a reactant. Methanol supplies an –O–, not an –NH–.

q: Which species are present in an aqueous solution of acetic acid (vinegar), besides water and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH molecules?
h: A carboxylic acid is a weak acid. Which H does it donate to water?
w: The –COOH donates its H to water: CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO− + H3O+. Only a small fraction ionizes, so most of the acid stays as molecules.
x: Weak acids do not break C–C bonds when they ionize. Only the acidic H on the –COOH group is given to water.
That would mean acetic acid accepted an H<sup>+</sup> from water, acting as a base. In water a carboxylic acid donates its H<sup>+</sup> instead.
Acetic acid does not lose OH<sup>−</sup> in water; it is an acid, not a base. Think about which H atom it gives away.

q: What are the products of the neutralization of acetic acid with sodium hydroxide?
h: Acid + base → salt + water. Which ion replaces the acidic H?
w: CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COO−Na+ (sodium ethanoate, sodium acetate) + H2O. The carbon count of the acid does not change, so it is not a methanoate.
x: Neutralization does not turn an acid into an alcohol, and no sodium oxide forms. Acid + base gives a salt and water.
Methanoate means a one-carbon acid (formic acid). Acetic acid has two carbons, and neutralization does not change the carbon count.
Neutralization does not make an anhydride or NaH. The OH<sup>−</sup> of the base picks up the acid's H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative instead of benzoic acid mainly because sodium benzoate
c: is ionic and more soluble in water
is a stronger acid than benzoic acid
has a higher molar mass than benzoic acid
is nonpolar and dissolves in fats
h: Compare a neutral carboxylic acid with its carboxylate salt.
w: Carboxylate salts are ionic, so they dissolve far better in water than the acids, which have a large nonpolar ring. The same idea is used to make many drugs water-soluble.
x: Sodium benzoate is the salt of benzoic acid (its conjugate base), so it is not a stronger acid. Think about how ions interact with water.
A slightly higher molar mass does not make a preservative work better. Think about how well each form dissolves in watery foods and drinks.
Sodium benzoate is ionic, not nonpolar, and sodas and liquid medicines are mostly water. What does an ionic compound do in water?

q: Propyl ethanoate (the odor of pears) is hydrolyzed in acid. What are the products?
h: Hydrolysis reverses esterification. The “-oate” part becomes the acid; the alkyl part becomes the alcohol.
w: CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 + H2O → CH3COOH (ethanoic acid) + CH3CH2CH2OH (1-propanol). Swapping the parts gives propanoic acid and ethanol, the hydrolysis products of a different ester.
x: Those are the products of ethyl propanoate, a different ester. In propyl ethanoate the C=O side has two carbons and the O–alkyl group has three.
Hydrolysis gives one acid and one alcohol. The C=O side of the ester becomes a carboxylic acid, not a second alcohol.
Propane is an alkane with no –OH. The propyl group on the ester oxygen leaves with that O as an alcohol.

q: Methyl butanoate is heated with aqueous NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
h: In base, the carboxylic acid formed is neutralized immediately.
w: Base hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt, sodium butanoate, and the alcohol, methanol. The free acid forms only in acid hydrolysis or after acidifying.
x: Butanoic acid forms in acid hydrolysis. In NaOH the acid cannot stay as –COOH; the base neutralizes it.
This swaps the two sides. The C=O side of methyl butanoate has four carbons and the O–alkyl group is methyl.
Butanoic acid and sodium methoxide cannot exist together in water: the base would grab the acid's H<sup>+</sup>. Which product actually carries the Na<sup>+</sup>?

q: These compounds all have molar mass 74 g mol⁻¹. Which has the highest boiling point?
h: Count the hydrogen-bonding sites. Carboxylic acids can pair up through two hydrogen bonds.
w: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers (two H bonds per pair), so propanoic acid (141 °C) boils above 1-butanol (118 °C). Esters and ethers have no O–H and boil much lower.
x: 1-Butanol hydrogen bonds and boils high (118 °C), but one compound here can form two hydrogen bonds per pair of molecules.
An ester has no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. It boils much lower than compounds with O–H groups.
An ether has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself and has a low boiling point (about 35 °C).

q: Aspirin, acetylsalicylic acid, contains which two functional groups?
c: a carboxylic acid and an ester
h: Aspirin is made by reacting the phenol –OH of salicylic acid with an acetyl group. What group forms when an acid joins an –OH?
w: The original –COOH remains, and the phenol –OH becomes an acetyl ester, so aspirin has a carboxylic acid and an ester. Salicylic acid itself has the phenol group.
x: Aspirin has no aldehyde (–CHO). The phenol –OH of salicylic acid was converted to another group when aspirin was made.
Aspirin has no alcohol –OH and no ketone. Look at what the acetyl group is attached to and what is left of the original acid.
Aspirin has no nitrogen, so it cannot contain an amide. Its O–C=O groups belong to other families.

q: Lactic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH, is a carboxylic acid (a weak acid). In blood at pH 7.4, lactic acid exists mainly as
h: At body pH, does a carboxylic acid keep its H<sup>+</sup> or lose it?
w: Carboxylic acids are weak acids that give up their H+ at body pH (7.4), so lactic acid is present as the carboxylate ion, lactate. That is why we say “lactate” in physiology.
x: At pH 7.4 a carboxylic acid does not keep its H<sup>+</sup>. Blood is far more basic than the pH where –COOH stays neutral.
A carboxylic acid gives up H<sup>+</sup>; it does not gain extra H<sup>+</sup> at body pH. A positive ion like this would need very acidic conditions.
Esters form when an acid reacts with an alcohol, not simply by dissolving in blood. Think about acid–base behavior at pH 7.4.

q: Dimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, is classified as a
h: Count the carbon groups bonded directly to the nitrogen.
w: Nitrogen carries two methyl groups and one H, so it is a 2° amine. It has no C=O, so it is not an amide.
x: A primary amine has only one carbon group on N. Here the nitrogen carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
A tertiary amine has three carbon groups on N and no N–H. This nitrogen still has one H.
An amide needs a C=O carbon bonded to the nitrogen. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH has no carbonyl group at all.

q: sec-Butylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>, is classified as a
h: For amines, count the carbons on the nitrogen, not on the carbon that holds the N.
w: The N is bonded to only one carbon (and two H), so it is a 1° amine. The “sec” describes the alkyl group's carbon, not the amine class; that is the trap behind the 2° answer.
x: The "sec" describes the carbon holding the N, not the nitrogen itself. For amines, count only the carbons bonded directly to N.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on N and no N–H. Look at the –NH<sub>2</sub>: how many carbons does that N actually touch?
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons on a positively charged N. This compound is neutral and its N still holds H atoms.

q: What is the common name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>?
h: Name the alkyl group attached to N, then add “amine.”
w: The straight three-carbon group on N is propyl: propylamine. Isopropylamine is (CH3)2CHNH2; propanamide would have a C=O.
x: Isopropyl means the N is on the middle carbon, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–. In this formula the N sits on the end carbon of a straight chain.
An amide name (-amide) requires a C=O on the carbon bonded to N. This formula has no carbonyl group.
"Di" would mean two propyl groups on the nitrogen. This N carries only one carbon group and two H.

q: Which condensed formula is tert-butylamine?
h: A tert-butyl group is attached through a carbon that bears three methyl groups.
w: tert-Butyl is (CH3)3C–, so tert-butylamine is (CH3)3CNH2. The others are sec-butylamine, butylamine and isobutylamine.
x: This is sec-butylamine: the N is on a carbon bonded to two other carbons. A tert-butyl carbon is bonded to three CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
This is butylamine: a straight chain with N on the end carbon. The tert-butyl group is highly branched.
This is isobutylamine: the N is on a CH<sub>2</sub> next to the branch. In tert-butyl, the N carbon itself carries the branches.

q: Methylamine is a weak base. Which ions form when it dissolves in water?
h: The lone pair on nitrogen accepts an H<sup>+</sup> from water.
w: CH3NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3NH+3 + OH−. The amine is the proton acceptor, so hydroxide ions form and the solution is basic.
x: An amine acts as a base, so its nitrogen gains an H<sup>+</sup>; it does not lose one. Producing H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> would make it an acid.
Dissolving in water does not break the C–N bond. The amine stays intact and only its nitrogen lone pair reacts.
If the amine takes H<sup>+</sup> from water, what is left of the water molecule? It cannot also form H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.

q: Many amine drugs, such as diphenhydramine, are sold as hydrochloride salts. Why?
c: The ionic salt is more soluble in water and body fluids.
The salt is a stronger base than the free amine.
The salt is more volatile, so it is absorbed faster.
HCl converts the amine into a more stable amide.
h: What happens to an amine's nitrogen when it reacts with HCl?
w: Amine + HCl → ammonium chloride salt. The ionic salt dissolves well in water and is a stable, odorless solid. It is not an amide, and salts are less volatile, not more.
x: The salt is the protonated (conjugate acid) form, so it is no longer a base at all. Its advantage is about how it behaves in water.
Ionic salts are less volatile than free amines; they are odorless solids. Think about what ionic compounds do in water.
HCl just transfers H<sup>+</sup> to the N, making an ammonium salt. Forming an amide would require a carboxylic acid and heat.

q: Which isomer of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N has the lowest boiling point?
h: Which amine has no N–H bond for hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
w: A 3° amine has no H on nitrogen, so it cannot H-bond to itself; trimethylamine boils at only ~3 °C. The 1° and 2° isomers have N–H bonds, so they hydrogen bond and boil higher (about 32–48 °C).
x: Propylamine is a 1° amine with two N–H bonds, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other. That raises its boiling point (about 48 °C).
Ethylmethylamine is a 2° amine; its N–H still lets molecules hydrogen bond to each other, raising the boiling point.
Isopropylamine is a 1° amine with two N–H bonds, so it can hydrogen bond to itself. Look for the isomer with no N–H.

q: Propanoic acid is heated with methylamine. What is the organic product of this amidation?
h: The –OH of the acid and an H from the amine leave as water; N attaches to the C=O carbon.
w: CH3CH2COOH + H2NCH3 → CH3CH2CONHCH3 + H2O: N-methylpropanamide. Methyl propanoate would come from methanol, not methylamine.
x: That name puts the C=O on a one-carbon (methanoic) piece and a propyl on N, which swaps the two parts. The C=O stays with the acid's three-carbon chain.
An ester like methyl propanoate forms from an acid and an alcohol (methanol). Here the partner is an amine, so the new bond is C–N.
An amine has no C=O, but the acid's carbonyl stays in the product. Amidation keeps the C=O and forms a new C–N bond.

q: N-Ethylethanamide, CH<sub>3</sub>CONHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is heated with aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
h: Base hydrolysis of an amide gives the carboxylate salt and the free amine.
w: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond; in NaOH the acid becomes sodium ethanoate and the N part is released as ethylamine. Acid hydrolysis would instead give the free acid and the ammonium salt; ammonia would come only from an unsubstituted amide.
x: These are acid hydrolysis products. In NaOH the acid cannot stay neutral and the amine cannot stay protonated.
Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond of the amide, not a bond elsewhere. No alcohol forms, and the C=O carbon cannot keep its N.
Ammonia comes only from an amide with an unsubstituted –NH<sub>2</sub>. Here the N carries an ethyl group, which stays attached when it is released.

q: Nicotine, caffeine and morphine are physiologically active nitrogen-containing compounds from plants. They are called
h: The name hints that these compounds are basic, like alkalis.
w: Plant-derived, biologically active amines are alkaloids. Many medicines (codeine, quinine, atropine) come from this group.
x: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, with both –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH groups. These plant compounds are a different, basic group.
Steroids are lipids built on a four-ring carbon skeleton, often with no nitrogen. These compounds are defined by their basic nitrogen.
Terpenes are plant compounds built from isoprene units and usually contain no nitrogen. The key feature here is a basic N.

q: Nylon 6,6, used in sutures, is a polyamide made from hexanedioic acid and 1,6-hexanediamine. What linkage joins the monomers?
h: A carboxylic acid reacting with an amine forms which bond?
w: Each –COOH reacts with an –NH2 to form an amide bond, releasing water; that is why nylon is a polyamide. Polyesters such as PET use ester linkages.
x: An ester linkage forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Nylon's monomers are an acid and an amine, which react differently.
An ether linkage is C–O–C with no C=O, formed between alcohols. Neither monomer here reacts that way.
Glycosidic bonds link sugar units in carbohydrates. Nylon is made from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine, not sugars.

q: Fructose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has its carbonyl group on carbon 2. Fructose is classified as a(n)
h: Aldose or ketose depends on where the C=O is; the suffix depends on the number of carbons.
w: A C=O on C2 (not the end) makes a ketone, and six carbons make a hexose: ketohexose. Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses.
x: An aldose has its C=O at the end of the chain, on carbon 1, as an aldehyde. Fructose's C=O is on carbon 2, inside the chain.
The "pent-" part means five carbons, but fructose has six carbons (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>).
This gets both parts wrong: a C=O on carbon 2 is not an aldehyde, and fructose has six carbons, not five.

q: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucose, the –OH group on carbon 1 is
c: below the ring, opposite the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group
above the ring, on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group
in the plane of the ring
h: In a D-sugar Haworth projection the CH<sub>2</sub>OH on C5 points up. Recall how the α and β anomers differ at C1.
w: In a D-sugar the CH2OH points up; in the α anomer the C1 –OH points down, opposite it. The β anomer has the C1 –OH up.
x: An –OH on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group describes the β anomer. Recall which anomer is "trans" and which is "cis."
In a Haworth projection, groups on ring carbons are drawn above or below the ring, not in its plane.
The ring oxygen comes from the C5 –OH, not the C1 –OH. Carbon 1 keeps an –OH after the ring closes.

q: When pure α-D-glucose is dissolved in water, the solution soon contains α-D-glucose, β-D-glucose and a little open-chain glucose. This process is called
h: The ring opens at the hemiacetal and closes again with the –OH on either side.
w: Interconversion of the α and β anomers through the open-chain form is mutarotation; no bonds to other molecules are broken, so it is not hydrolysis.
x: Hydrolysis uses water to break a bond between two units, such as a glycosidic bond. Here a single glucose ring just opens and recloses.
Fermentation is the conversion of glucose to ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub> by yeast. The glucose here stays glucose; only its C1 –OH changes position.
The solution still contains only glucose forms. Nothing here changes the aldose into a ketose; only the anomeric –OH flips between up and down.

q: D-Galactose differs from D-glucose only in the position of the –OH group on carbon
h: Glucose and galactose are epimers: they differ at just one chiral carbon.
w: Galactose is the C-4 epimer of glucose. Changing C2 gives mannose; changing C5 would change D to L.
x: Changing the –OH on carbon 2 of glucose gives mannose, not galactose.
Glucose and galactose have the same –OH position on carbon 3. Compare their Fischer projections carbon by carbon to find the one that differs.
Carbon 5 sets D or L, and both sugars here are D. Flipping C5 would change the D/L label, not turn glucose into galactose.

q: Which sugar is NOT a reducing sugar?
h: A reducing sugar needs a free hemiacetal (a ring that can open to give an aldehyde).
w: In sucrose, both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it cannot open and gives a negative Benedict's test. Maltose, lactose and glucose are reducing.
x: Maltose still has one glucose with a free hemiacetal C1, so its ring can open to an aldehyde. That makes it a reducing sugar.
In lactose, the glucose unit keeps a free hemiacetal at C1, so the ring can open and react in Benedict's test. Lactose is reducing.
Free glucose is a hemiacetal that opens to an aldehyde, so it gives a positive Benedict's test. It is a reducing sugar.

q: A patient with lactose intolerance lacks enough lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into
h: Lactose is milk sugar; recall which two monosaccharides it is built from.
w: Lactose → galactose + glucose. Two glucose units come from maltose; glucose + fructose comes from sucrose.
x: Two glucose units are what maltase releases from maltose. Milk sugar contains a different monosaccharide alongside glucose.
Glucose and fructose come from sucrose (table sugar) when sucrase acts on it, not from milk sugar.
Fructose is not part of lactose. It comes from sucrose (table sugar). Recall the two units that make up milk sugar.

q: Which carbohydrate consists of exactly two glucose units joined by an α(1→4)-glycosidic bond?
h: Malt sugar comes from the breakdown of starch.
w: Starch digestion produces maltose, glucose–α(1→4)–glucose. Lactose is galactose–β(1→4)–glucose, sucrose contains fructose, and amylose is a long chain of many glucose units.
x: Lactose is a disaccharide, but it contains galactose and its bond is β(1→4), not α(1→4) between two glucose units.
Sucrose contains a fructose unit, and its linkage is α,β(1→2), not α(1→4).
Amylose does use α(1→4) bonds, but it is a long polymer of many glucose units, not exactly two.

q: In sucrose, glucose and fructose are joined by which glycosidic bond?
h: The bond connects the anomeric carbon of glucose with the anomeric carbon of fructose.
w: C1 of α-glucose bonds to C2 of β-fructose: an α,β(1→2) linkage. Because both anomeric carbons are used, sucrose is not a reducing sugar.
x: α(1→4) joins C1 of one glucose to C4 of another, as in maltose. In sucrose the bond must use the anomeric carbon of fructose, so ask which carbon held fructose's C=O.
β(1→4) is the lactose and cellulose linkage. Sucrose's bond connects the anomeric carbon of each sugar, and fructose's anomeric carbon is not C4.
This gets the α,β part right, but carbon 4 of fructose is not its anomeric carbon. Which carbon held fructose's C=O?

q: Humans can digest starch but not cellulose because cellulose contains
c: fructose units in place of some glucose units
galactose units in place of glucose units
h: Both are polymers of glucose; what differs is the linkage between units.
w: Cellulose is glucose joined by β(1→4) bonds, and human amylases hydrolyze only α bonds. Starch also has α(1→6) branches, so branching is not the difference; cellulose passes through as dietary fiber.
x: Cellulose is made only of glucose, just like starch. The difference lies in how the glucose units are linked.
α(1→6) branch points are found in starch (amylopectin) and glycogen, which we digest. Cellulose is unbranched.
Cellulose contains no galactose; it is a polymer of glucose only, just like starch.

q: Which statement best describes glycogen?
c: a highly branched glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle
an unbranched glucose polymer that plants store in seeds and roots
a branched polymer of fructose stored in the liver
a structural polymer of β-glucose in plant cell walls
h: Glycogen is “animal starch.” Think about how often it branches and where it is stored.
w: Glycogen is α(1→4)-linked glucose with frequent α(1→6) branches, making it highly branched, stored in liver and muscle. Unbranched amylose is a plant starch; cellulose is the β structural polymer.
x: That describes amylose, the unbranched plant starch. Glycogen is the animal storage form and has many branch points.
Glycogen is built from glucose, not fructose, and it is stored in muscle as well as liver.
That describes cellulose, the β-linked structural polymer of plants. Glycogen is an animal energy-storage polymer with α linkages.

q: For an aldohexose drawn as a Fischer projection, which carbon's –OH position determines whether the sugar is D or L?
h: Look at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group.
w: C5 is the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O, so carbon 5 decides: an –OH on the right makes it D. C1 and C6 are not chiral at all.
x: Carbon 1 is the aldehyde carbon (–CHO). It is not a chiral carbon, so it has no –OH position to compare.
Carbon 2 is chiral, but it is the chiral carbon closest to the C=O. D/L is set by the one farthest from it.
Carbon 6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH group with two H atoms, so it is not chiral and cannot set D or L.

q: When glucose forms its six-membered ring, the –OH on carbon 5 adds to the carbonyl group on carbon 1. The ring is a cyclic
h: An alcohol adding once to an aldehyde gives which group?
w: One alcohol (the C5 –OH) adding to an aldehyde (C1) forms a hemiacetal. A glycosidic bond to a second sugar turns it into an acetal. A hemiketal would form from a ketone sugar such as fructose.
x: An acetal forms when a second alcohol (–OR) adds, as in a glycosidic bond. Ring closure adds only one alcohol to the aldehyde.
An ester forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Glucose's C1 is an aldehyde, not a carboxylic acid.
A hemiketal forms when an alcohol adds to a ketone, as in fructose. Glucose's carbon 1 is an aldehyde carbon.

q: In the five-membered ring form of fructose, the anomeric carbon (the one whose –OH can be α or β) is carbon
h: The anomeric carbon is the former carbonyl carbon. Where is the C=O in fructose?
w: Fructose's C=O is on C2, so after cyclization C2 is the anomeric carbon. C1 is the anomeric carbon only in aldoses such as glucose.
x: Carbon 1 is the anomeric carbon in aldoses like glucose. In fructose, C1 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH group outside the ring.
In the five-membered ring, the C5 –OH supplies the ring oxygen. C5 is where the ring closes from, not the former carbonyl carbon.
Carbon 6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH group outside the ring; it is not chiral. Look for the carbon that was the C=O carbon.

q: These fatty acids all have 18 carbons. Which has the lowest melting point?
h: Each cis double bond puts a kink in the chain. How do kinks affect packing?
w: More cis kinks mean poorer packing and weaker dispersion forces, so linolenic acid melts lowest (about −11 °C). Saturated stearic acid packs best and melts highest; this is why oils are liquid and butter is solid.
x: Linoleic acid's two cis kinks lower its melting point, but another choice has even more kinks and packs even worse.
Oleic acid has only one cis kink, so its chains pack better than fatty acids with more double bonds.
Stearic acid has no double bonds, so its straight chains pack tightly. It has the highest melting point of the four.

q: Linolenic acid is an omega-3 fatty acid. “Omega-3” means that
c: the first double bond is 3 carbons from the CH<sub>3</sub> end
it has three C=C double bonds somewhere along its chain
the first double bond is at carbon 3 from the –COOH end
it has 3 carbons fewer than stearic acid, which has 18
h: Omega (ω) is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so count from the opposite end of the chain.
w: Omega numbering counts from the CH3 (omega) end: the first C=C starts at carbon 3 from that end. Linolenic acid happens to have three double bonds too, but that is not what ω-3 means.
x: Linolenic acid does have three double bonds, but that is a coincidence. The omega number tells you where a double bond sits, not how many there are.
Counting from the –COOH end gives the Δ-style position. Omega is the last Greek letter, so ω numbering starts from the other end of the chain.
Linolenic acid has 18 carbons, the same as stearic acid. The omega number describes the position of a double bond, not chain length.

q: A triacylglycerol (triglyceride) is formed from
c: glycerol and three fatty acids joined by ester bonds
glycerol and three fatty acids joined by amide bonds
sphingosine, a fatty acid and phosphate
h: Fatty acids are carboxylic acids and glycerol has three –OH groups. What bond do acids and alcohols form?
w: Each –OH of glycerol forms an ester with a fatty acid: glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids.
x: Amide bonds form between an acid and an amine, as in proteins. Glycerol has –OH groups, so it bonds to fatty acids a different way.
Cholesterol is a steroid with only one –OH group; it can form a cholesteryl ester, not a triacylglycerol. "Glycerol" is in the name for a reason.
Sphingosine, a fatty acid and phosphate are parts of sphingolipids such as sphingomyelin, not triacylglycerols.

q: How many moles of NaOH are needed to completely saponify 1 mole of a triacylglycerol?
h: Count the ester bonds; each one uses one hydroxide.
w: A triacylglycerol has three ester bonds, so 3 mol NaOH give glycerol and three moles of sodium fatty-acid salts (soap).
x: One mole of NaOH breaks only one ester bond. Count how many ester bonds a triacylglycerol has.
Two moles would break only two ester bonds, leaving one fatty acid still attached to glycerol.
6 uses two hydroxides for each ester bond. Each ester bond uses just one hydroxide, so count the ester bonds again.

q: A triacylglycerol contains one oleic acid (1 C=C) and two linoleic acids (2 C=C each). How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> are needed to fully hydrogenate 1 mole of it?
h: Each C=C uses one H<sub>2</sub>. Add up the double bonds in all three chains.
w: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 mol H2. Answering 3 counts the fatty acids instead of the double bonds. The ester C=O groups are not hydrogenated.
x: 3 counts the fatty acids, not the double bonds. Each C=C needs its own H<sub>2</sub>.
4 counts the two linoleic acids correctly but leaves out the oleic acid's double bond. Add up all three chains.
6 would need two C=C in every chain. Oleic acid has only one, and the ester C=O groups are not hydrogenated.

q: Beeswax and carnauba wax (used in dental impression materials and car polish) are
c: esters of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol
triacylglycerols made only from saturated fatty acids
steroids built from four fused carbon rings
phospholipids with a choline head group and two fatty acid tails
h: Waxes have only one ester bond. What is on each side of it?
w: A wax is one ester made from a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol, which makes it very water-repellent. Triacylglycerols contain glycerol.
x: Triacylglycerols contain glycerol and three ester bonds. Waxes have just one ester bond.
Steroids have four fused rings and no ester bond in their core. Waxes are long, straight-chain esters.
Phospholipids have a phosphate head group. Waxes contain no phosphate or choline.

q: Lecithin, a glycerophospholipid, contains glycerol, two fatty acids, a phosphate group and
h: Glycerophospholipids have a polar head made of phosphate plus a small nitrogen-containing alcohol.
w: Lecithin = phosphatidylcholine: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + choline. A third fatty acid would make a triacylglycerol.
x: A glycerol with three fatty acids is a triacylglycerol. In a glycerophospholipid, the third –OH holds the phosphate instead.
Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids. Lecithin already has glycerol as its backbone.
Cholesterol is a separate membrane lipid, not part of a phospholipid. The head group here is a small nitrogen-containing alcohol.
