q: Sphingomyelin, abundant in the myelin sheath around nerve cells, differs from glycerophospholipids because its backbone is
h: The name of the lipid class tells you its backbone.
w: Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine; its amino group forms an amide with one fatty acid. Glycerophospholipids are built on glycerol.
x: Glycerol is the backbone of glycerophospholipids, the very class sphingomyelin is being compared with.
Cholesterol is a steroid with no phosphate head group. Sphingomyelin is a phospholipid with a different backbone.
Sphingomyelin does contain a fatty acid, but it is attached to the backbone by an amide bond. It is not the backbone itself.

q: Cholesterol, the sex hormones and cortisone are steroids. All steroids contain
c: four fused rings: three six-membered and one five-membered
three fatty acids bonded by ester links to a glycerol backbone
a long-chain fatty acid joined by an ester bond to a long alcohol
a phosphate head group and two fatty-acid tails
h: Steroids are lipids with no fatty acids; recognize them by their ring system.
w: The steroid nucleus is four fused rings: three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring. Cholesterol adds an –OH and a hydrocarbon side chain.
x: Glycerol plus three fatty acids is a triacylglycerol. Steroids contain no fatty acids.
A long-chain fatty acid ester describes a wax or fat. Steroids are recognized by their ring system instead.
A phosphate head and two fatty-acid tails describes a glycerophospholipid. Steroids have no fatty-acid tails.

q: In the fluid-mosaic model of a cell membrane, the phospholipid bilayer is arranged with
c: polar heads facing the water and nonpolar tails inside
nonpolar tails facing the water and polar heads inside
all molecules lying flat on the cell surface
h: Like dissolves like: which part of a phospholipid should touch water?
w: The hydrophilic heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell while the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails point toward each other in the middle. Proteins float in this layer, like a mosaic.
x: Nonpolar tails are hydrophobic, so they would not face water. Which part of a phospholipid is attracted to water?
Phospholipids in a bilayer stand side by side, perpendicular to the surface, in two layers. They do not lie flat.
Proteins are embedded in or attached to the bilayer, but they do not form a layer of their own. Both layers are phospholipids.

q: Aspirin and ibuprofen reduce pain and inflammation by blocking the COX enzyme, which converts arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon fatty acid) into a family of eicosanoids. Which lipids do these drugs keep the body from making?
c: prostaglandins, which contain a five-membered ring
steroids, which contain four fused rings
triacylglycerols, which contain three ester bonds
sphingolipids, which contain a sphingosine backbone
h: “Eicosa-” means 20. Which choice is an eicosanoid made from a 20-carbon fatty acid?
w: COX converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins, the eicosanoids that cause pain, fever and inflammation; blocking COX is how NSAIDs work. Steroids are made from cholesterol, and triacylglycerols and sphingolipids are not eicosanoids.
x: Steroids are made from cholesterol, not from arachidonic acid, and the COX enzyme does not make them.
Triacylglycerols are storage fats made from glycerol and fatty acids. They are not eicosanoids.
Sphingolipids are membrane lipids built on sphingosine. They are not made from arachidonic acid by COX.

q: Partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils is a health concern mainly because it
c: converts some cis double bonds to trans
adds cholesterol to the vegetable oil
breaks the ester bonds to glycerol
makes the fatty acids more unsaturated
h: During partial hydrogenation, some double bonds remain but change shape.
w: Some remaining double bonds isomerize to the trans form; trans fats raise LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart disease. Hydrogenation makes fats less, not more, unsaturated, and plant oils contain no cholesterol.
x: Plant oils contain essentially no cholesterol, and hydrogenation adds only H<sub>2</sub> to C=C bonds; it does not add cholesterol.
Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> to C=C double bonds. It leaves the ester bonds to glycerol in place.
Adding H<sub>2</sub> removes double bonds, so hydrogenation makes fats less unsaturated, not more.

q: Which amino acid has a nonpolar side chain?
h: Look for a side chain made only of carbon and hydrogen.
w: Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group, a hydrocarbon, so valine is nonpolar. Serine is polar neutral (O), lysine is basic (N) and aspartic acid is acidic.
x: Serine's side chain has an –OH group, and the polar O–H bond makes it a polar (hydrophilic) side chain.
Lysine's side chain ends in an amino group, which picks up H<sup>+</sup> to become charged. That makes lysine a basic amino acid, not a nonpolar one.
Aspartic acid's side chain has a –COOH group, which ionizes to –COO<sup>−</sup>. That makes it an acidic amino acid, not a nonpolar one.

q: At its isoelectric point (pI), an amino acid exists mainly as
c: a zwitterion with a net charge of zero
a cation with a net charge of +1
an anion with a net charge of −1
h: The pI is the pH where positive and negative charges balance.
w: At the pI the amino acid is H3N+–CHR–COO−, a zwitterion with zero net charge, so it does not move in an electric field.
x: A +1 cation is the main form at a pH well below the pI, where both the –COOH and the amino group carry H<sup>+</sup>.
A −1 anion is the main form at a pH well above the pI, where the amino group has lost its H<sup>+</sup>.
In water, amino acids are almost never present as neutral molecules with both –COOH and –NH<sub>2</sub>. The acid group gives its H<sup>+</sup> to the basic amino group.

q: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is placed in a strongly acidic solution, at a pH far below its pI. Which form is present mainly?
h: At a pH far below the pI, extra H<sup>+</sup> is available. Which group picks it up?
w: Far below the pI the –COO− is protonated, giving H3N+CH2COOH with a net +1 charge. The zwitterion is the main form at the pI; H2NCH2COO− is the form far above the pI.
x: This is the zwitterion, the main form near the pI. Far below the pI there is plenty of H<sup>+</sup>, so ask which group would pick one up.
This form has lost the H<sup>+</sup> from the amino group. It is the main form far above the pI, in strongly basic solution.
Glycine is almost never present as this uncharged form in water. In strong acid, think about what extra H<sup>+</sup> does to each group.

q: A peptide bond is formed between
c: the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH<sub>2</sub> of the next
the side chains of two neighboring amino acids
the –NH<sub>2</sub> groups of two neighboring amino acids
the –COOH groups of two neighboring amino acids
h: A peptide bond is an amide bond, and water is released when it forms.
w: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next form an amide, –CO–NH–, releasing H2O. Side chains are not involved.
x: Side chains (R groups) are not part of the peptide bond. They hang off the backbone and stay free to interact with other groups.
Two amino groups cannot react to form an amide. An amide bond needs one acid group and one amine group.
Two carboxyl groups cannot form an amide. An amide bond needs one acid group and one amine group, with water released.

q: What is the name of the tripeptide Ala–Gly–Ser (written from the N-terminal end)?
h: Every residue except the C-terminal one gets the ending “-yl.”
w: Start at the N-terminus: alanyl, glycyl, then the C-terminal residue keeps its full name: alanylglycylserine. Reversing the order names a different peptide.
x: This names the residues starting from the C-terminal end. Peptide names start at the N-terminal residue, the one written first.
Here the last residue was also given the -yl ending. The C-terminal residue keeps its full amino acid name.
Peptide names change the ending of every residue except the last one to -yl. Simply stringing the full names together is not the naming rule.

q: How many peptide bonds are in a tetrapeptide?
h: Each bond connects two neighboring amino acids in a chain.
w: Four amino acids in a row are joined by 3 peptide bonds (n − 1).
x: That counts one bond per amino acid. A bond only forms between two neighbors, so the end residue does not need its own bond.
That is more bonds than there are amino acids. Each peptide bond links two neighboring residues; count the gaps between four beads on a string.
Two bonds would join only three amino acids, a tripeptide. Count the links needed to join four residues in a row.

q: In sickle-cell anemia, glutamic acid at position 6 of the hemoglobin β chain is replaced by valine. Which level of protein structure is changed directly?
h: Which level of structure is defined by the amino acid sequence?
w: Changing one amino acid changes the sequence, the primary structure. The new nonpolar valine then makes hemoglobin molecules clump, affecting higher levels as a consequence.
x: Secondary structure (α helix, β sheet) comes from backbone hydrogen bonds. A changed amino acid can affect it, but only as a consequence of something more basic.
The clumping of hemoglobin molecules is a downstream effect. Ask which level is defined directly by the order of amino acids.
The DNA mutation is the cause, but the protein made from it also changes: one amino acid is swapped for another in the chain.

q: The α helix and the β-pleated sheet are stabilized mainly by
c: hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains
salt bridges between acidic and basic side chains
h: Secondary structure involves only the repeating backbone atoms, not the R groups.
w: In secondary structure, the C=O of one peptide bond hydrogen bonds to the N–H of another. Disulfides and salt bridges involve side chains and belong to tertiary structure.
x: Disulfide bonds link cysteine side chains, which are R groups. They help hold the overall 3-D fold (tertiary structure), not the regular helix or sheet pattern.
Salt bridges form between charged R groups. They belong to tertiary structure; the helix and sheet come from repeating backbone atoms.
Peptide bonds join the backbone; they never link side chains. They hold the primary sequence together but do not create the helix or sheet shape.

q: A disulfide bond between two cysteine side chains in the same polypeptide chain stabilizes which level of protein structure?
h: Interactions between side chains that fold a single chain into its 3-D shape belong to which level?
w: Side-chain interactions within one chain (disulfides, salt bridges, H bonds, hydrophobic attractions) make up tertiary structure. Quaternary would require bonds between separate chains.
x: Primary structure is just the amino acid sequence held by peptide bonds. A disulfide is an extra link between side chains, not part of the sequence.
Secondary structure is the α helix and β sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups, not by side chains.
Quaternary structure involves interactions between separate polypeptide chains. Here both cysteines are in the same chain.

q: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide subunits (two α and two β) held together. This describes its
h: Which level applies only to proteins with more than one polypeptide chain?
w: The arrangement of multiple subunits in one active protein is quaternary structure. Each subunit has its own primary through tertiary structure.
x: Tertiary structure is the 3-D fold of a single polypeptide chain. Here we are describing how several chains fit together.
Secondary structure is the α helices and β sheets within a chain. It does not describe how separate subunits combine.
Primary structure is the amino acid sequence of one chain. It says nothing about how four chains are assembled.

q: A 70% isopropyl alcohol swab disinfects skin before an injection by denaturing bacterial proteins. Denaturation disrupts
c: secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, but not peptide bonds
only the covalent peptide bonds that join the amino acids together
the primary structure only, while the higher levels of structure stay intact
all levels, breaking the protein into free amino acids
h: Denaturation unfolds a protein. Does it break covalent peptide bonds?
w: Denaturing agents (heat, alcohol, acids, heavy-metal ions) break the interactions that fold the protein but leave the peptide bonds intact, so the primary structure survives. Breaking peptide bonds is hydrolysis.
x: Denaturing agents like alcohol unfold proteins; they do not break covalent peptide bonds. Breaking peptide bonds requires hydrolysis.
Primary structure is held by strong covalent peptide bonds, which survive denaturation. Unfolding affects the weaker interactions that fold the chain.
Breaking a protein into free amino acids is hydrolysis, as in digestion. An alcohol swab unfolds proteins but leaves the chain intact.

q: Which process breaks a protein's primary structure, as happens during digestion?
h: Primary structure is held together by covalent amide bonds. What reaction breaks an amide?
w: Digestive enzymes (or strong acid with heat) carry out hydrolysis, adding water across peptide bonds to free amino acids. Heat and pH changes only denature.
x: Heat denatures a protein by disrupting the interactions that fold it. The covalent bonds of the amino acid sequence stay intact.
Hydrogen bonds hold secondary and tertiary structure. Breaking them unfolds the protein but leaves the sequence of linked amino acids intact.
A small pH change can disrupt salt bridges and unfold a protein, but it does not break the covalent bonds of the primary structure.

q: In a globular protein dissolved in water, which side chain is most likely buried in the interior of the folded protein?
h: Polar and charged side chains like water. Where do nonpolar ones go?
w: Hydrophobic interactions pull nonpolar side chains such as leucine's isobutyl group into the interior, away from water. Charged lysine and glutamate and polar serine stay on the surface.
x: Lysine's side chain is positively charged, so it is attracted to water and stays on the protein surface.
Glutamate's side chain carries a negative charge, so it interacts well with water and stays on the protein surface.
Serine's –OH group hydrogen bonds with water, so this polar side chain tends to be on the surface, not hidden inside.

q: According to the induced-fit model of enzyme action,
c: the active site changes shape to fit the substrate as it binds
the active site is a rigid shape that exactly matches the substrate
the substrate changes the enzyme's primary structure
the enzyme is consumed in the reaction
h: Compare it with the older lock-and-key model, in which the active site never changes.
w: In induced fit, the flexible active site adjusts its shape around the substrate, which explains why some enzymes accept a group of similar substrates. A rigid site is the lock-and-key model; enzymes are never consumed.
x: A rigid active site that exactly matches the substrate is the older lock-and-key model. Induced fit pictures a more flexible active site.
The primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held by covalent peptide bonds. Substrate binding does not change the sequence.
Enzymes are catalysts: they come out of the reaction unchanged and can be used again and again.

q: Urease catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea and no other compound. This is an example of
h: How many different substrates does urease accept?
w: An enzyme that acts on only one substrate shows absolute specificity. Group specificity means one functional group in many compounds; linkage means one bond type.
x: Group specificity means the enzyme acts on one type of functional group in many different compounds. Urease accepts only one compound.
Linkage specificity means the enzyme acts on one kind of bond wherever it occurs. Think about how many substrates urease accepts.
Stereochemical specificity means telling apart mirror-image forms (such as D and L). Nothing here is about mirror images.

q: Hexokinase moves a phosphate group from ATP to glucose. To which enzyme class does hexokinase belong?
h: Focus on what the enzyme does: it moves a group from one molecule to another.
w: Enzymes that move a functional group (here, phosphate) between molecules are transferases; kinases are a type of transferase. Hydrolases use water to split bonds.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. Here nothing is split by water; a phosphate is moved from ATP onto glucose.
An oxidoreductase catalyzes oxidation and reduction, such as moving hydrogen to NAD<sup>+</sup>. Moving a phosphate group is not a redox change.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Here a group moves from one molecule (ATP) to a different molecule (glucose).

q: A patient has a very high fever of 42 °C. What generally happens to the activity of the patient's enzymes?
c: It decreases because the enzymes begin to denature.
It increases without limit as temperature rises.
It stays the same because enzymes are catalysts.
It decreases because substrate molecules move more slowly.
h: Most human enzymes work best near 37 °C. What happens to proteins well above that?
w: Above the optimum temperature (~37 °C), enzymes start to lose their shape (denature), so activity drops. Molecules move faster, not slower, when hot.
x: Rate rises with temperature only up to the optimum. Enzymes are proteins, so well above about 37 °C something happens to their shape.
Being a catalyst does not make an enzyme immune to heat. Enzymes are proteins, and their shape depends on temperature.
Higher temperature makes molecules move faster, not slower. The drop in activity comes from a change in the enzyme itself.

q: Pepsin works best at about pH 2 in the stomach. When pepsin enters the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity
h: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. What happens far from it?
w: pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum of 2, so the charges on its side chains change, its active site loses its shape, and its activity decreases sharply. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, takes over there.
x: Moving away from an enzyme's optimum pH lowers activity. pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum of about 2.
pH changes the charges on side chains, which affects the active site's shape. A change from pH 2 to 8 is a big one.
A higher pH is not better for every enzyme. Each enzyme has its own optimum pH, and pepsin's is very acidic.

q: With a fixed amount of enzyme, the reaction rate stops increasing at very high substrate concentration because
c: all of the active sites are occupied
the enzyme is denatured by the substrate
h: Think about a fixed number of active sites working as fast as they can.
w: Once every enzyme molecule is bound to substrate, the enzyme is saturated, so adding more substrate cannot raise the rate. Adding more enzyme could.
x: Substrate does not denature the enzyme; heat, extreme pH and heavy metals do. The leveling off happens with a healthy enzyme.
The substrate is what the enzyme acts on, not an inhibitor. Think about how many active sites are available to work.
Products are made, not used up, as the reaction runs. The limit comes from the fixed amount of enzyme.

q: Methanol poisoning can be treated with ethanol, which binds to the active site of alcohol dehydrogenase and slows the formation of toxic formaldehyde. Ethanol is acting as a(n)
h: Where does ethanol bind, and does it resemble the substrate?
w: Ethanol resembles methanol and competes for the same active site: competitive inhibition. A noncompetitive inhibitor would bind elsewhere and could not be outcompeted.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. Ethanol binds in the active site itself.
An irreversible inhibitor forms a permanent covalent bond with the enzyme. Ethanol binds reversibly and is eventually metabolized.
A coenzyme helps the enzyme do its job. Here ethanol slows the enzyme's action on methanol.

q: A noncompetitive inhibitor decreases an enzyme's activity by
c: binding at a site other than the active site and changing its shape
binding in the active site in place of the substrate
forming a covalent bond with the substrate molecule
raising the activation energy of the uncatalyzed reaction
h: Can adding more substrate overcome this type of inhibition? That tells you where it binds.
w: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site, distorting the enzyme so the active site no longer works; extra substrate does not help. Binding in the active site is competitive inhibition.
x: Binding in the active site in place of the substrate describes competitive inhibition, which can be overcome by more substrate.
Inhibitors act on the enzyme, not by bonding to the substrate molecule.
Inhibitors do not change the uncatalyzed reaction at all. They work by interfering with the enzyme itself.

q: Organophosphate insecticides and nerve agents form a covalent bond with the active site of acetylcholinesterase. This is an example of
h: Ask whether adding more substrate could push out a poison that is covalently bonded to the active site.
w: Covalent modification of the active site is irreversible inhibition; acetylcholine then builds up at nerve synapses. Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly.
x: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly and can be pushed out by more substrate. A covalent bond to the active site is permanent.
Allosteric activation speeds an enzyme up. These poisons shut acetylcholinesterase down.
Feedback control is the end product of a pathway slowing an early enzyme reversibly. These poisons are outside chemicals that bond covalently.

q: The end product of a metabolic pathway binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme of the pathway and slows it down. This is called
h: The product “talks back” to the start of the pathway when enough has been made.
w: When enough end product is present, it inhibits the first enzyme allosterically, turning off its own production: feedback control. It binds a regulatory site, not the active site, so it is not competitive inhibition.
x: A competitive inhibitor binds in the active site. Here the end product binds an allosteric (regulatory) site instead.
Zymogen activation turns an inactive precursor into an active enzyme by cutting it. This question describes slowing an enzyme down.
Induced fit describes how an active site changes shape as substrate binds. It is not a way of regulating a pathway.

q: The coenzyme NAD<sup>+</sup> is made from which vitamin?
h: The “N” in NAD<sup>+</sup> refers to nicotinamide.
w: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide comes from niacin. Riboflavin forms FAD and pantothenic acid forms coenzyme A.
x: Riboflavin (B<sub>2</sub>) is used to make FAD, a different coenzyme. Think about what the "N" in NAD<sup>+</sup> stands for.
Pantothenic acid (B<sub>5</sub>) is used to make coenzyme A, not NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant needed for collagen formation. It is not the source of NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: A nucleoside consists of
c: a nitrogenous base and a five-carbon sugar
a nitrogenous base, a sugar and a phosphate
a nitrogenous base and a phosphate
h: A nucleoTIDE has one more part than a nucleoSIDE.
w: Nucleoside = base + sugar; adding a phosphate makes a nucleotide.
x: Base + sugar + phosphate is a nucleotide. The nucleoside has one fewer part.
A sugar and phosphate alone is just a piece of the backbone. Every nucleoside contains a nitrogenous base.
A base cannot bond directly to a phosphate; the sugar connects them. Think about which two parts a nucleoside keeps.

q: Which component is found in RNA but not in DNA?
h: RNA and DNA differ in their sugar and in one of their pyrimidine bases.
w: RNA contains ribose and uracil; DNA contains deoxyribose and thymine. Both have phosphate.
x: Thymine is found in DNA. RNA uses a different pyrimidine base in its place.
Deoxyribose is the sugar of DNA. RNA contains ribose, which has an extra –OH.
Phosphate is in both DNA and RNA; it links the sugars in every nucleic acid backbone.

q: A sample of DNA is 20% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
h: A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so A = T and G = C. All four must add to 100%.
w: A = T = 20%, which leaves 100 − 40 = 60% for G + C, so G = 30%. Answering 60% stops before splitting G + C in half; answering 80% subtracts only the adenine (100 − 20) and forgets that thymine also takes 20%.
x: 80% subtracts only the adenine (100 − 20) and forgets that thymine equals adenine, so T is also 20%.
40% is A + T together. The question asks for guanine, which shares what is left with cytosine.
60% is G + C combined. Since G = C, that amount is split between the two bases.

q: What is the complementary DNA strand for 5′-ACGTTG-3′?
h: Pair A with T and G with C, and remember the two strands are antiparallel.
w: A↔T, C↔G, G↔C, T↔A gives TGCAAC, running in the opposite direction: 3′-TGCAAC-5′. Writing it 5′→3′ with the same letter order ignores the antiparallel arrangement; U appears only in RNA.
x: This just copies the original letters in reverse direction. A complementary strand pairs A with T and G with C.
U is found only in RNA. A complementary DNA strand uses T to pair with A.
The letters are paired correctly, but the ends are labeled wrong. The two strands of DNA are antiparallel, so the new strand runs the opposite way.

q: In the backbone of DNA, nucleotides are linked by
c: phosphodiester bonds joining 3′ and 5′ sugar carbons
hydrogen bonds between bases on the same strand
peptide bonds between neighboring phosphate groups
h: The backbone alternates sugar–phosphate–sugar. What links them?
w: Each phosphate forms ester bonds to the 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′ carbon of the next: a phosphodiester bond. Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together, not the backbone.
x: Hydrogen bonds form between bases on opposite strands and hold the two strands together. They are not part of the backbone.
Glycosidic bonds join each base to its sugar, not one sugar to the next.
Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins. DNA's backbone alternates sugar and phosphate, linked through the phosphate group.

q: Which base pair is held together by three hydrogen bonds?
h: One of the correct DNA base pairs is held more strongly than the other.
w: G–C forms three hydrogen bonds; A–T (and A–U in RNA) form two. G–T is not a normal base pair.
x: A–T is held by two hydrogen bonds, making it the weaker of the two DNA base pairs.
A–U, the RNA version of A–T, is held by two hydrogen bonds.
G–T is not a normal base pair. In DNA, guanine pairs only with its usual partner.

q: After DNA replication, each new double helix contains
c: one parent strand and one newly made strand
pieces of parent and new DNA mixed in each strand
h: Replication is described as semiconservative. What is conserved?
w: Each parent strand is a template for a new strand, so every daughter helix has one old and one new strand (semiconservative replication).
x: If both strands were new, the parent strands would be discarded. In fact each parent strand serves as a template.
If both strands were parental, the old helix would just re-form with no copying. Think about what each parent strand is used for.
Mixed pieces in each strand describes a dispersive model, which experiments ruled out. Each strand is either entirely old or entirely new.

q: A DNA template strand has the sequence 3′-TACGGC-5′. What is the mRNA transcribed from it?
h: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, and uses U instead of T.
w: Pairing T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C gives AUGCCG, built 5′→3′: 5′-AUGCCG-3′ (which starts with the start codon AUG). ATG contains T, which RNA does not use.
x: This sequence contains T, but RNA uses U in place of T.
The bases are right, but the ends are flipped. The mRNA is antiparallel to the template, and RNA is built 5′→3′.
This copies the template and just swaps T for U. The mRNA must be complementary to the template, pairing A with U and G with C.

q: Not counting the stop codon, how many mRNA nucleotides are needed to code for a polypeptide of 50 amino acids?
h: Each codon is a triplet of nucleotides that specifies one amino acid.
w: 50 amino acids × 3 nucleotides per codon = 150 nucleotides. Answering 50 assumes one nucleotide per amino acid; 100 uses two per codon; 17 divides 50 by 3 instead of multiplying.
x: 50 assumes one nucleotide per amino acid. Each amino acid is specified by a codon of several nucleotides.
100 uses two nucleotides per codon. Codons are triplets.
17 divides 50 by 3 instead of multiplying. Each amino acid needs its own full codon.

q: Which mutation is most likely to produce a completely nonfunctional protein?
c: deletion of one base near the start of the gene
substitution of one base in the third position of a codon
substitution that replaces leucine with isoleucine
deletion of three bases (one whole codon) near the end
h: Which change shifts the reading frame of every codon that follows?
w: Deleting one base near the start causes a frameshift, changing every codon after it. Third-position substitutions are often silent, and losing one codon or swapping similar amino acids usually has a smaller effect.
x: Third-position changes are often silent because the code is redundant; the same amino acid is usually still added.
Leucine and isoleucine are both nonpolar and similar in size, so swapping one for the other often has little effect.
Losing one whole codon removes one amino acid but keeps the reading frame. Near the end of the gene, the effect is usually small.

q: A point mutation changes the codon UGG (tryptophan) to UGA (a stop codon). What is the most likely result?
c: The protein is shorter because translation stops early.
Tryptophan is replaced by another amino acid.
The protein is longer than normal.
There is no effect because the codon still starts with UG.
h: What does a stop codon tell the ribosome to do?
w: A new stop codon ends translation early (a nonsense mutation), giving a shortened, usually nonfunctional protein. A swap of one amino acid would be a missense mutation.
x: Replacing tryptophan with another amino acid is a missense mutation. UGA does not code for an amino acid.
A stop codon ends translation; it cannot add amino acids. The protein would not be longer.
The whole codon matters, not just the first two letters. UGA has a very different meaning from UGG.

q: HIV is a retrovirus. After it infects a cell, which enzyme makes DNA from the virus's RNA genome?
h: This enzyme runs the usual DNA → RNA direction backward.
w: Reverse transcriptase builds DNA using viral RNA as the template. Nucleoside analogs such as AZT block this enzyme. RNA polymerase makes RNA from DNA.
x: RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template, the usual direction. Here the virus needs the opposite.
DNA ligase seals gaps between pieces of DNA; it does not build DNA from an RNA template.
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences. They do not make DNA.

q: In catabolic pathways, the coenzyme NAD<sup>+</sup> functions as
c: an oxidizing agent that accepts hydrogen and is reduced to NADH
a reducing agent that donates hydrogen to the substrates
an energy store that releases a phosphate group to ADP
a carrier that transfers acetyl groups into the citric acid cycle
h: In catabolism, fuels are oxidized. What must happen to the coenzyme that removes their hydrogen?
w: NAD+ accepts H (a hydride and electrons) from the oxidized substrate, so it is reduced to NADH, which makes it the oxidizing agent. Coenzyme A, not NAD+, carries acetyl groups.
x: A reducing agent donates hydrogen. In catabolism the fuel is being oxidized, so the coenzyme has to take hydrogen away from it, not give hydrogen to it.
That describes ATP, which transfers a phosphate group. NAD<sup>+</sup> is an electron and hydrogen carrier, not a phosphate donor.
That is the job of coenzyme A, which carries acetyl groups as acetyl CoA. NAD<sup>+</sup> carries hydrogen and electrons instead.

q: The digestion of which type of food begins in the mouth?
h: Saliva contains an enzyme. Which macromolecule does it attack?
w: Salivary amylase starts hydrolyzing the α-glycosidic bonds of starch in the mouth. Protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin); fat digestion mainly occurs in the small intestine with lipase and bile salts.
x: Protein digestion starts in the stomach, where HCl and pepsin act. Think about which enzyme is in saliva.
Fat digestion happens mainly in the small intestine, with bile salts and pancreatic lipase. Saliva's enzyme works on a different nutrient.
Nucleic acids are hydrolyzed by nucleases from the pancreas in the small intestine. Saliva's enzyme attacks a different polymer.

q: What is the net number of ATP produced directly in glycolysis from one glucose molecule?
h: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses some in its first (energy-investment) steps.
w: 4 ATP are formed, but 2 ATP are invested at the start, so the net yield is 2 ATP (plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate). 32 is the total for complete oxidation.
x: 4 is the gross number of ATP made in the payoff steps. Remember that ATP was spent in the first steps of glycolysis.
That is roughly the total for complete oxidation of glucose, including the citric acid cycle and electron transport. The question asks about glycolysis alone.
36 is an older total for complete oxidation of glucose, not the yield of glycolysis alone. Glycolysis by itself makes far less ATP.

q: During strenuous exercise, when oxygen is limited, muscle cells convert pyruvate to
h: Under anaerobic conditions, the cell must regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> without oxygen.
w: Reducing pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Ethanol + CO2 is the yeast pathway; acetyl CoA forms when oxygen is plentiful.
x: Acetyl CoA forms when oxygen is plentiful, because its NADH must be reoxidized by the electron transport chain. Without enough O<sub>2</sub>, the cell needs another route.
Ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub> are made by yeast during alcoholic fermentation. Human muscle uses a different anaerobic product.
Making glucose from pyruvate (gluconeogenesis) uses energy and occurs mainly in the liver, not in a working muscle short of oxygen.

q: In transamination, the amino group of an amino acid trades places with the C=O of an α-keto acid. Alanine, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)–COOH, reacts with α-ketoglutarate, HOOC–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CO–COOH. What are the products?
h: Rewrite each reactant after the swap: put a C=O where alanine's –NH<sub>2</sub> was, and an –NH<sub>2</sub> where α-ketoglutarate's keto C=O was. Then name both new compounds.
w: Alanine's –NH2 goes to α-ketoglutarate, which becomes glutamate; alanine becomes the α-keto acid pyruvate. Free NH+4 is released later, when glutamate is oxidatively deaminated, and is converted to urea in the urea cycle.
x: Lactate would require a reduction, and glutamine forms from glutamate plus NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, not by transamination. Here the amino group simply swaps places with the C=O.
In transamination the amino group is handed to the keto acid rather than released as free ammonium. Ask which compound receives alanine's –NH<sub>2</sub>.
Oxaloacetate and aspartate form when the amino acid partner is aspartate. The reactants here are alanine and α-ketoglutarate, so look at what each one becomes.

q: Cyanide is deadly because it blocks cytochrome c oxidase, the last enzyme complex of the electron transport chain. What does this block directly?
c: the transfer of electrons to O<sub>2</sub>, stopping ATP synthesis
the breakdown of glucose to pyruvate in glycolysis
the digestion of proteins by pepsin in the stomach
the release of fatty acids from adipose (fat) cells
h: Cytochrome c oxidase is the final complex. What is the final electron acceptor?
w: Cytochrome c oxidase passes electrons to O2, forming water. With it blocked, electron flow and proton pumping stop, so oxidative phosphorylation stops making ATP. Glycolysis can still run.
x: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol and does not use the electron transport chain, so it keeps running. Think about the last step of the chain.
Pepsin works in the stomach and has nothing to do with the electron transport chain in mitochondria.
Releasing fatty acids from adipose tissue is a hormone-controlled hydrolysis, not part of the electron transport chain. Think about what the final complex hands its electrons to.

q: One turn of the citric acid cycle produces the reduced coenzymes and GTP listed in the table. Using the ATP values given, how many ATP are produced from one acetyl CoA?
h: Multiply each coenzyme by its ATP yield, then add the GTP.
w: 3(2.5) + 1(1.5) + 1 = 7.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP. Forgetting the GTP gives 9; forgetting the FADH2 gives 8.5; counting only the NADH gives 7.5.
x: 7.5 counts only the 3 NADH. Add in the FADH<sub>2</sub> and the GTP from one turn too.
9 leaves out the GTP made directly in the cycle. Each GTP counts as 1 ATP.
8.5 forgets the FADH<sub>2</sub>. One turn also makes 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>, worth 1.5 ATP.

q: How many acetyl CoA molecules are produced by the complete β-oxidation of stearic acid, an 18-carbon fatty acid?
h: Each acetyl CoA contains two carbons from the fatty acid chain.
w: 18 C ÷ 2 C per acetyl CoA = 9 acetyl CoA. This takes 8 cycles of β-oxidation, because the last cycle produces two acetyl CoA; answering 8 mixes up cycles and products.
x: 8 is the number of β-oxidation cycles, not the number of acetyl CoA. The last cycle releases two acetyl CoA at once.
That counts one acetyl CoA per carbon. Each acetyl CoA carries two carbons from the chain.
6 does not match the chain length. Divide the number of carbons by the carbons in each acetyl group.

q: In uncontrolled diabetes or long fasting, the liver converts excess acetyl CoA into ketone bodies. Which group lists the ketone bodies?
h: When oxaloacetate is low, acetyl CoA from fat cannot enter the citric acid cycle. What do two acetyl CoA form?
w: Ketogenesis produces acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. Too much of these lowers blood pH (ketoacidosis), and acetone gives the fruity breath odor.
x: Pyruvate and lactate come from glycolysis, not from ketogenesis. Only acetone in this list is a ketone body.
These are the starting material and citric acid cycle compounds. Ketone bodies form when acetyl CoA cannot enter the cycle.
Glucose and glycogen are carbohydrates. Ketone bodies are made from acetyl CoA when the body is burning fat.

q: Between meals, glucagon signals the liver to break glycogen down into glucose to keep blood sugar normal. This process is called
h: Split the word: glycogen + lysis (splitting). Which name means breaking glycogen apart?
w: Breaking glycogen into glucose (via glucose-1-phosphate) is glycogenolysis. Glycogenesis is the reverse (making glycogen after a meal, stimulated by insulin), and gluconeogenesis makes new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources.
x: Glycogenesis means making glycogen from glucose, the storage process stimulated by insulin after a meal. The question describes the opposite.
Gluconeogenesis makes new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources such as lactate or amino acids. Here glucose comes from stored glycogen.
Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate. The question is about releasing glucose from a stored polymer.

q: Glycogen breakdown releases glucose-6-phosphate, which cannot leave the cell until the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase removes its phosphate. Liver and muscle both store glycogen, but only the liver releases free glucose into the blood. What is the best explanation?
c: Liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate; muscle does not
Only liver has glycogen phosphorylase to split the stored glycogen
Muscle glycogen is a polymer of fructose instead of glucose
Muscle cells lack hexokinase, so glucose cannot be trapped inside them
h: Glucose-6-phosphate cannot cross the cell membrane. Which enzyme turns it into free glucose?
w: Glycogenolysis gives glucose-6-phosphate, which is trapped inside the cell. The liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate; muscle does not, so muscle keeps its glucose-6-phosphate for its own glycolysis. Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase.
x: Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase and breaks down its own glycogen. The difference lies in what happens to glucose-6-phosphate afterward.
Muscle glycogen, like liver glycogen, is a polymer of glucose. Both tissues store the same polymer.
Muscle cells do have hexokinase. The issue is removing the phosphate so glucose can leave the cell, not adding it.

q: Gluconeogenesis builds glucose from pyruvate or from glycolysis intermediates, but the step pyruvate → acetyl CoA cannot be reversed. Which compound CANNOT be used by the liver to make a net amount of new glucose?
h: Gluconeogenesis can start only from pyruvate or a glycolysis intermediate. Trace each choice: which one cannot get back to either?
w: Lactate and alanine (→ pyruvate) and glycerol (→ dihydroxyacetone phosphate) can all become glucose. Pyruvate → acetyl CoA is irreversible, and the 2 carbons of acetyl CoA leave as 2 CO2 in the citric acid cycle, so acetyl CoA from fatty acids gives no net glucose.
x: Lactate is oxidized back to pyruvate, which gluconeogenesis can turn into glucose (the Cori cycle). Look for a molecule formed after pyruvate's irreversible step.
Glycerol is converted to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, a glycolysis intermediate, so it can be made into glucose.
Alanine is transaminated to pyruvate, which can be made into glucose. It is a glucogenic amino acid.

q: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced by hard-working muscle travels in the blood to the liver, where it is
c: converted back to glucose, which returns to the muscle
converted to urea, which is excreted by the kidneys
converted to triacylglycerol, which is stored in fat cells
oxidized to acetone, which is exhaled through the lungs
h: The Cori cycle recycles muscle lactate. What useful fuel can the liver rebuild from it?
w: The liver oxidizes lactate to pyruvate and uses gluconeogenesis to make glucose, which returns to the muscle through the blood. Urea comes from amino-acid nitrogen, not from lactate.
x: Urea is made from amino-acid nitrogen. Lactate contains no nitrogen, so it cannot become urea.
Storing the carbons as fat would not help the muscle keep working. The Cori cycle returns usable fuel to the muscle.
Acetone is a ketone body made from acetyl CoA during fasting or diabetes. Lactate is recycled into something more useful.

q: The pentose phosphate pathway is especially active in fat-forming cells and red blood cells. Its main products are
h: Fat synthesis needs a reducing coenzyme, and nucleotides need a five-carbon sugar. Which pair fits?
w: The pentose phosphate pathway oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate to give NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. NADPH supplies reducing power for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and protects red cells from oxidation; ribose is used to build nucleotides. NADH and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate belong to glycolysis.
x: NADH and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate are associated with glycolysis. Biosynthesis needs a different reducing coenzyme and a five-carbon sugar.
FADH<sub>2</sub> and acetyl CoA come from β-oxidation and pyruvate oxidation. Neither supplies the 5-carbon sugar needed for nucleotides.
ATP and lactate come from glycolysis and fermentation. This pathway's job is to supply reducing power and a pentose.

q: When bread dough rises, yeast cells growing without oxygen convert pyruvate into
h: Think fermentation. Which gas makes the dough rise, and what alcohol is in beer?
w: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde and then reduces it, giving ethanol and CO2 (the gas that raises the dough). Human muscle makes lactate instead, and acetyl CoA forms only under aerobic conditions.
x: Lactate is made by human muscle under low oxygen. Yeast uses a different fermentation, and it releases a gas that raises the dough.
Acetyl CoA forms only when oxygen is available. The question says the yeast is growing without oxygen.
Pyruvate cannot be turned into glucose and O<sub>2</sub> by yeast. Fermentation does not produce oxygen.

q: Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted to acetyl CoA. Besides acetyl CoA, this reaction produces
h: Pyruvate has 3 carbons and an acetyl group has 2. Where does the extra carbon go, and which coenzyme is reduced?
w: Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH. The 3-carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2 and is oxidized while NAD+ is reduced to NADH. O2 is consumed only later, in the electron transport chain.
x: O<sub>2</sub> is not produced here; it is consumed only later, in the electron transport chain. Ask where pyruvate's third carbon goes.
The carbon count is right, but FAD is not the coenzyme reduced in this step. FAD is used when a C=C forms, as in succinate → fumarate.
Water and ATP are not direct products of this step. The 3-carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as a gas and a coenzyme is reduced.

q: Why do muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate when oxygen is in short supply?
c: to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> so glycolysis can continue
to make extra ATP in the lactate-forming step
to make CO<sub>2</sub> for use in the citric acid cycle
to store glucose carbons as lactate for later
h: Glycolysis uses up NAD<sup>+</sup>. Without O<sub>2</sub>, NADH cannot be reoxidized by the electron transport chain. What does pyruvate → lactate do to NADH?
w: Pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD+. This step regenerates NAD+, which glycolysis needs for its oxidation step, so the cell can keep making 2 ATP per glucose. The lactate step itself makes no ATP.
x: Pyruvate → lactate makes no ATP at all. Its purpose involves the coenzyme that glycolysis keeps using up.
Converting pyruvate to lactate releases no CO<sub>2</sub>; the carbon count stays at 3. Think about the NADH made earlier in glycolysis.
Lactate is not a storage form; storage would be glycogen. The step solves a coenzyme problem so glycolysis can keep going.

q: Where in the cell do glycolysis and the citric acid cycle take place?
c: glycolysis in the cytosol; the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix
glycolysis in the mitochondrial matrix; the citric acid cycle in the cytosol
glycolysis and the citric acid cycle both in the cytosol of the cell
glycolysis and the citric acid cycle both in the inner mitochondrial membrane
h: Glycolysis works even in red blood cells, which have no mitochondria.
w: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol; pyruvate then moves into the mitochondria, where the citric acid cycle runs in the matrix. The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
x: This has the two locations reversed. Red blood cells have no mitochondria yet still carry out glycolysis.
The citric acid cycle needs pyruvate to move into an organelle first. Only one of the two pathways runs in the cytosol.
The inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, not glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.

q: After a meal with more carbohydrate than the body needs, the liver makes fatty acids from acetyl CoA (lipogenesis). This pathway
c: adds 2 carbons per cycle and uses NADPH as the reducing agent
adds 2 carbons per cycle and produces NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>
removes 2 carbons per cycle and uses NADPH as the reducing agent
adds 3 carbons per cycle and uses FAD as the oxidizing agent
h: Building a fatty acid is a reduction, the opposite of β-oxidation. Which coenzyme supplies the electrons for biosynthesis?
w: Lipogenesis builds the chain 2 carbons at a time (acetyl CoA via malonyl CoA) and uses NADPH to reduce C=O groups to CH2. Removing 2 carbons and producing NADH and FADH2 describes β-oxidation, the catabolic opposite.
x: Producing NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> is what β-oxidation does when it breaks a chain down. Building a chain needs a reducing agent instead.
Removing 2 carbons per cycle describes β-oxidation, the breakdown pathway. Lipogenesis lengthens the chain.
Fatty acids grow 2 carbons at a time, which is why most have an even number of carbons, and building them is a reduction, not an oxidation by FAD.

q: When a cell already has plenty of ATP and NADH, what happens to the rate of the citric acid cycle?
c: It slows, because ATP and NADH inhibit key enzymes of the cycle
It speeds up, because ATP activates the enzymes of the cycle
It speeds up, so the extra energy can be stored as GTP
It is unchanged, because the citric acid cycle is not regulated
h: Feedback control: if the cell already has lots of energy, should an energy-producing pathway speed up or slow down?
w: High ATP and NADH signal plenty of energy, so they inhibit key enzymes of the cycle, slowing it (feedback control). High ADP and NAD+ (low energy) speed it up.
x: ATP signals that energy is already plentiful, so it does not activate the enzymes of an energy-producing pathway.
Cells do not store extra energy as GTP. When energy is high, energy-producing pathways are turned down.
The citric acid cycle is regulated; several of its enzymes respond to the cell's energy level.

q: In the electron transport chain, the final electron acceptor is ____, which is reduced to ____.
h: Why do we need to breathe? Think about what happens to the oxygen we inhale.
w: At the end of the chain (cytochrome c oxidase), electrons combine with O2 and H+ to form H2O. NAD+ and FAD carry electrons into the chain; they are not the final acceptor.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup>/NADH carries electrons into the chain at Complex I. The final acceptor sits at the other end.
CO<sub>2</sub> is a waste product of catabolism, and making glucose from it is photosynthesis, not electron transport.
FAD/FADH<sub>2</sub> delivers electrons into the chain. Think about why we breathe in a certain gas.

q: According to the chemiosmotic model, what directly provides the energy for ATP synthase to make ATP?
c: H<sup>+</sup> flowing back into the matrix down its gradient
electrons passing from FADH<sub>2</sub> directly onto ADP
O<sub>2</sub> binding to ATP synthase inside the matrix
hydrolysis of GTP made in the citric acid cycle
h: The electron transport chain pumps H<sup>+</sup> into the intermembrane space. What happens when those ions return?
w: Electron transport pumps H+ into the intermembrane space, building a proton gradient. H+ flowing back into the matrix through ATP synthase drives the joining of ADP and Pi. Electrons never go to ADP directly.
x: Electrons never go to ADP. They travel through the chain to O<sub>2</sub>, and the energy is stored in a different form first.
O<sub>2</sub> accepts electrons at Complex IV; it does not bind ATP synthase. Think about the ions pumped across the membrane.
GTP from the cycle is made by substrate-level phosphorylation and is not what drives ATP synthase.

q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP), once sold as a diet pill, carries H<sup>+</sup> back across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. What is the result?
c: O<sub>2</sub> use continues, but energy is released as heat instead of ATP
electron transport stops, and O<sub>2</sub> use falls to zero
ATP synthesis increases because more H<sup>+</sup> enter the matrix
glycolysis stops because NAD<sup>+</sup> can no longer be regenerated
h: An uncoupler separates electron transport from ATP synthesis. Does electron flow stop, or only ATP production?
w: DNP lets the proton gradient leak away, so electron transport and O2 use continue (even speed up), but the energy is lost as heat instead of being captured as ATP, causing dangerous fever. Stopping electron transport completely is what cyanide does.
x: Stopping electron transport is what cyanide does. DNP only provides a leak for H<sup>+</sup>, so electrons still flow to O<sub>2</sub>.
The H<sup>+</sup> that leak back through DNP bypass ATP synthase, so they cannot drive ATP production. ATP synthesis falls.
Glycolysis is in the cytosol and is not directly blocked by DNP. With electron transport still running, NADH is still reoxidized.

q: Why does each FADH<sub>2</sub> produce only about 1.5 ATP, while each NADH produces about 2.5 ATP?
c: FADH<sub>2</sub> enters the chain after complex I, so fewer H<sup>+</sup> are pumped
FADH<sub>2</sub> carries only one electron, while NADH carries two
FADH<sub>2</sub> passes its electrons straight to O<sub>2</sub> at the end
FADH<sub>2</sub> is made in the cytosol and must be moved inside
h: Compare where each carrier hands its electrons to the chain and how many proton pumps the electrons pass through.
w: NADH gives its electrons to complex I, but FADH2 gives them to coenzyme Q (through complex II), skipping complex I, so fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made. Both carriers deliver 2 electrons.
x: Both FADH<sub>2</sub> and NADH carry two electrons. The difference is where in the chain they hand those electrons over.
FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons still pass through Complexes III and IV before reaching O<sub>2</sub>. Consider which earlier pump they skip.
The FADH<sub>2</sub> of the citric acid cycle is made inside the mitochondrion, at Complex II. Location is not the reason.

q: Using the ATP values in the table, how many ATP form when one pyruvate is completely oxidized to CO<sub>2</sub> (conversion to acetyl CoA plus one turn of the citric acid cycle)?
h: Count the NADH from pyruvate → acetyl CoA, then the NADH, FADH<sub>2</sub> and GTP from one turn of the cycle.
w: Pyruvate → acetyl CoA: 1 NADH = 2.5 ATP. One turn: 3 NADH × 2.5 = 7.5, 1 FADH2 × 1.5 = 1.5, 1 GTP = 1, total 10. Sum = 2.5 + 10 = 12.5 ATP. 13.5 counts the FADH2 as 2.5; 15 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2; 25 is for two pyruvates (one glucose).
x: 15 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 from the table.
13.5 counts the FADH<sub>2</sub> as 2.5 ATP, like an NADH. FADH<sub>2</sub> is worth only 1.5.
25 is the yield for two pyruvates, one whole glucose. The question asks about one pyruvate.

q: In the small intestine, bile salts help digest dietary fat by
c: emulsifying fat into small droplets that lipase can reach
hydrolyzing ester bonds to release free fatty acids
carrying fatty acids through the blood as lipoproteins
oxidizing fatty acids to acetyl CoA for quick energy
h: Bile salts act like detergents; enzymes do the actual bond breaking. What does a detergent do to a large blob of grease?
w: Bile salts (made from cholesterol) emulsify fat into tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface area so pancreatic lipase can hydrolyze the ester bonds. The hydrolysis itself is done by lipase, not by bile salts.
x: Hydrolyzing ester bonds is the job of the enzyme lipase. Bile salts are not enzymes; they act like detergents.
Lipoproteins such as chylomicrons carry fat in the blood and lymph. Bile salts work inside the intestine, before absorption.
Oxidizing fatty acids to acetyl CoA is β-oxidation, which happens in mitochondria of cells, not in the intestine.

q: Palmitic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>14</sub>COOH, is completely oxidized. Using the ATP values in the table, what is the net ATP yield?
h: A 16-carbon acid gives 8 acetyl CoA. The number of β-oxidation cycles is one less than that; each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 16 C → 8 acetyl CoA from 7 cycles. 8 × 10 = 80; 7 NADH × 2.5 = 17.5; 7 FADH2 × 1.5 = 10.5; activation −2. Net = 80 + 17.5 + 10.5 − 2 = 106 ATP. 108 forgets the activation cost; 110 uses 8 cycles instead of 7; 129 uses the older values of 12 ATP per acetyl CoA, 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH2.
x: 108 leaves out the 2-ATP cost of activating the fatty acid. Subtract it at the end.
110 uses 8 β-oxidation cycles. A 16-carbon acid needs one fewer cycle than its number of acetyl CoA.
129 uses the older values of 12 ATP per acetyl CoA, 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: Lauric acid, a 12-carbon saturated fatty acid in coconut oil, undergoes β-oxidation. How many NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> are produced by the β-oxidation cycles themselves (not counting the citric acid cycle)?
h: Each cycle cuts off 2 carbons and makes 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>. How many cuts does it take to divide a 12-carbon chain into 2-carbon pieces?
w: 12 C gives 6 acetyl CoA, which needs 6 − 1 = 5 cycles. Each cycle yields 1 NADH and 1 FADH2, so 5 NADH and 5 FADH2. 6 and 6 is the common mistake of counting one cycle per acetyl CoA.
x: This counts one cycle per acetyl CoA. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA, so there is one fewer cycle.
Each cycle makes exactly one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>, so the two numbers must be equal.
Each cycle makes exactly one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>, so the two numbers must be equal.

q: A patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes has fruity-smelling breath and a blood pH of 7.1. What best explains the low blood pH?
c: acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids made from extra acetyl CoA
acetone is a strong acid that is formed from the excess blood glucose
lactate builds up because the cells are receiving too much insulin
urea builds up because amino acids are broken down too quickly
h: Without insulin, cells burn fat and the liver is flooded with acetyl CoA. Which of its products are carboxylic acids?
w: With little insulin, fat breakdown makes more acetyl CoA than the citric acid cycle can use, so the liver makes ketone bodies. Acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid are acids that lower blood pH (diabetic ketoacidosis). Acetone causes the fruity breath but is a neutral ketone, not an acid.
x: Acetone causes the fruity breath, but it is a neutral ketone, not an acid, and it comes from acetyl CoA, not from glucose.
Too little insulin, not too much, is the problem in type 1 diabetes. Look at what the liver makes from extra acetyl CoA.
Urea is a neutral compound and does not explain the low pH. The fruity breath points to a different set of products.

q: Oxidative deamination of glutamate releases NH+4, which is toxic. In the liver, this NH+4 is
c: converted to urea in the urea cycle and excreted in urine
converted to uric acid and stored in the joints as crystals
oxidized to nitrate ions and exhaled through the lungs
stored in fat cells as a reserve of amino-acid nitrogen
h: Ammonium must be changed into a less toxic, water-soluble compound that the kidneys can remove.
w: The liver combines NH+4 with CO2 (and nitrogen from aspartate) in the urea cycle, forming urea, which the kidneys excrete. In liver failure, ammonia builds up in the blood. Uric acid comes from purine breakdown, not amino acids.
x: Uric acid comes from breaking down purines in nucleic acids, and its crystals cause gout. Ammonium from amino acids is handled another way.
Nitrogen from amino acids is not oxidized to nitrate or exhaled. It must be made into a water-soluble compound the kidneys can remove.
The body has no storage form for amino-acid nitrogen in fat cells. Excess NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> must be detoxified and excreted.

q: Which process is an example of anabolism?
c: oxidation of fatty acids to acetyl CoA
breakdown of proteins to amino acids
h: Anabolic pathways build larger molecules and use energy; catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy.
w: Making glycogen from many glucose units builds a larger molecule and requires energy (UTP), so it is anabolic. The other three break molecules into smaller ones, which is catabolism.
x: Hydrolyzing starch breaks a polymer into smaller glucose units. That is catabolism (digestion).
β-Oxidation breaks fatty acids into 2-carbon pieces and releases energy, so it is catabolic.
Breaking proteins into amino acids splits a large molecule into smaller ones, which is catabolism.

q: Type B red blood cells carry an extra galactose unit on their surface markers that type O cells lack; type A cells carry an extra amino sugar (N-acetylgalactosamine) instead. The ABO blood types therefore differ in the
c: carbohydrate chains attached to the surface of red blood cells
number of hemoglobin molecules packed inside each red blood cell
fatty acids in the phospholipids of the red cell membrane
amount of iron in the heme groups of the red blood cells
h: Antibodies recognize “identity tags” on the outer surface of the red cell membrane. Which class of biomolecule forms these surface markers?
w: All red cells carry a basic oligosaccharide (type O). Type A adds N-acetylgalactosamine, type B adds galactose, and type AB has both. So the blood types differ in the carbohydrate chains on the red blood cell surface, which is why mismatched transfusions trigger antibodies.
x: Hemoglobin is inside the cell, where antibodies cannot reach it. Blood type markers sit on the outer surface of the membrane.
The question describes extra galactose and an amino sugar on the markers. Those are not fatty acids.
Heme iron is inside the cell and is the same in all blood types. The extra units named in the question are sugars on the cell surface.

q: Which pair of polysaccharides contains α(1→6)-glycosidic bonds at branch points?
h: Unbranched chains have only one kind of glycosidic bond. Which two glucose polymers are branched?
w: All three starch-type polymers have α(1→4) chains, but only amylopectin (branch about every 25 units) and glycogen (about every 10 units) also have α(1→6) branch points. Amylose is unbranched α(1→4); cellulose is unbranched β(1→4).
x: Neither is branched: amylose is unbranched α(1→4) glucose, and cellulose is unbranched β(1→4) glucose.
Amylopectin is branched, but amylose is an unbranched α(1→4) chain with no α(1→6) bonds.
Glycogen is branched, but cellulose is an unbranched β(1→4) chain with no α(1→6) bonds.

q: An infant with galactosemia cannot convert galactose into glucose, so toxic galactose products build up. Which food must be removed from the infant's diet?
c: table sugar, because sucrose contains galactose
h: Which disaccharide is made of galactose + glucose, and where is it found?
w: Lactose (milk sugar) is galactose + glucose, so milk and other lactose-containing foods must be removed. Sucrose is glucose + fructose, and starch contains only glucose.
x: Sucrose is glucose + fructose; it contains no galactose, so table sugar is not the problem here.
Starch is built only from glucose units, so bread starch does not supply galactose.
Fructose is a monosaccharide on its own; it does not contain galactose. Look for the disaccharide that does.

q: In poorly controlled diabetes, excess glucose in the lens of the eye is converted to sorbitol, which contributes to cataracts. Sorbitol is
c: a sugar alcohol formed by reducing the aldehyde of glucose
a carboxylic acid formed by oxidizing the aldehyde of glucose
a disaccharide formed by joining two glucose molecules
a ketose formed by moving the carbonyl of glucose to C2
h: The name ends in -ol. What happens to an aldehyde group when it is reduced?
w: Reduction of the aldehyde (–CHO) on C1 of glucose gives a primary alcohol (–CH2OH), so sorbitol (glucitol) is a sugar alcohol. Oxidizing the aldehyde would give gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid. Sorbitol is also used as a sugar-free sweetener.
x: Oxidizing the aldehyde gives gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid. The "-ol" ending of sorbitol points to the opposite kind of reaction.
Sorbitol comes from a single glucose molecule; no glycosidic bond is formed. Joining two glucose units would give a disaccharide such as maltose.
Moving the C=O to C2 would give fructose, which still has a carbonyl. The "-ol" ending tells you sorbitol has no C=O left.

q: LDL carries cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues, where excess can deposit in artery walls. HDL is often called “good cholesterol” because it
c: carries cholesterol from the tissues back to the liver
carries cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues
carries more triacylglycerol than any other lipoprotein
carries only phospholipid and protein, with no cholesterol
h: Think about the direction of transport. Which direction lowers the cholesterol that can deposit in artery walls?
w: HDL picks up excess cholesterol from tissues and returns it to the liver, where it can be made into bile salts and removed. LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues, and high LDL leads to plaque (atherosclerosis). Chylomicrons carry the most triacylglycerol.
x: Carrying cholesterol from the liver out to tissues is LDL's job, which can lead to plaque in arteries.
Chylomicrons carry the most triacylglycerol. HDL's benefit has to do with where it takes cholesterol.
HDL does carry cholesterol. What makes it "good" is the direction it carries it.

q: Linoleic acid and linolenic acid are called essential fatty acids because
c: the body cannot make them, so they must come from the diet
they are the only fatty acids found in cell membranes
they are saturated and provide the most energy per gram
the body makes them from glucose when the diet lacks fat
h: “Essential” in nutrition means the same thing here as it does for essential amino acids.
w: Humans cannot put double bonds at the omega-3 and omega-6 positions, so these polyunsaturated fatty acids must be obtained from food. They are unsaturated, not saturated.
x: Cell membranes contain many kinds of fatty acids. "Essential" is about where the body must get them.
Linoleic and linolenic acids are polyunsaturated, not saturated. "Essential" has to do with where they come from.
If the body could make them from glucose, they would not be essential. In nutrition, "essential" means the opposite.

q: Butter and lard are solids at room temperature, while olive oil is a liquid. The best explanation is that the animal fats contain more
c: saturated fatty acids, whose straight chains pack closely
unsaturated fatty acids, whose cis kinks pack closely
glycerol per molecule, which raises the melting point
short-chain fatty acids, which form hydrogen bonds
h: Compare the shapes of saturated chains and cis-unsaturated chains. Which shape lets molecules pack tightly?
w: Saturated chains are straight and pack closely, giving stronger dispersion forces and higher melting points. Cis double bonds put kinks in the chains, so oils (mostly unsaturated) pack poorly and stay liquid. Every triacylglycerol has exactly one glycerol.
x: Cis kinks make chains pack poorly, not closely. That is why unsaturated fats such as olive oil are liquids.
Every triacylglycerol has exactly one glycerol, so animal fats and oils have the same amount per molecule.
Fatty acid chains are nonpolar and do not form hydrogen bonds with each other. Shorter chains would actually lower the melting point.

q: Glucose moves into red blood cells from higher to lower concentration through a specific membrane protein, without using ATP. This is
h: Ask two questions: does it use energy, and does it need a protein?
w: Movement down a concentration gradient with no energy input is passive; because it needs a protein carrier it is facilitated transport. Simple diffusion needs no protein (small nonpolar molecules such as O2), and active transport uses ATP to move against a gradient.
x: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against a gradient. Here glucose moves from higher to lower concentration with no ATP.
Simple diffusion goes straight through the bilayer with no protein. Here glucose needs a specific membrane protein.
Secondary active transport uses the energy of another ion's gradient to move a solute against its own gradient. Here glucose simply moves down its gradient.

q: Which lipid does NOT undergo saponification with NaOH?
h: Saponification is the hydrolysis of an ester bond by a base. Which lipid has no ester group?
w: Waxes, glycerophospholipids such as lecithin, and triacylglycerols all contain ester bonds that NaOH hydrolyzes. Cholesterol is a steroid alcohol with no ester group, so it is nonsaponifiable.
x: Beeswax is an ester of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol, so NaOH can hydrolyze its ester bond.
Lecithin has two fatty acids joined to glycerol by ester bonds, so NaOH can saponify it.
Glyceryl tripalmitate is a triacylglycerol with three ester bonds, the classic fat that NaOH turns into soap.

q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine is missing. Which statement about a person with PKU is correct?
c: Tyrosine becomes essential, and phenylalanine intake must be limited
Phenylalanine becomes nonessential, so it can be eaten freely
Tyrosine builds up to toxic levels, so it must be avoided
Aspartame is safe because it contains no amino acids at all
h: If the conversion step is blocked, which amino acid piles up, and which one can no longer be made in the body?
w: Phenylalanine (and phenylpyruvate) builds up and can damage the developing brain, so its intake is limited. Because the body can no longer make tyrosine from phenylalanine, tyrosine must come from the diet. Aspartame contains phenylalanine, which is why diet drinks carry a PKU warning.
x: Phenylalanine is essential for everyone; PKU does not let the body make it. In PKU it actually builds up because it cannot be converted.
With the conversion step blocked, tyrosine is not made from phenylalanine. Think about which amino acid piles up and which one runs short.
Aspartame is a dipeptide made partly from phenylalanine. That is why diet drinks carry a warning for people with PKU.

q: Which amino acid is essential for adults and must be obtained from the diet?
h: Nonessential amino acids can be made in the body, often by transamination of keto acids from glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.
w: Lysine is essential (along with His, Ile, Leu, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp and Val, plus Arg, which this course counts as the conditionally essential tenth). Alanine, glutamate and serine are made from pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate and a glycolysis intermediate. Corn is low in lysine, so corn-based diets need complementary proteins.
x: Alanine is nonessential: the body makes it from pyruvate by transamination.
Glutamate is nonessential: the body makes it from α-ketoglutarate, a citric acid cycle intermediate.
Serine is nonessential: the body makes it from an intermediate of glycolysis.

q: Collagen’s three strands are held together partly by hydrogen bonds from hydroxyproline, a proline with an extra –OH group. Vitamin C is needed by the enzyme that adds that –OH. In scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), collagen is weak because
c: fewer –OH groups are added, so the strands form fewer hydrogen bonds
the peptide bonds between glycine and proline in each strand cannot form
the disulfide bonds holding the three strands together break
glucose units can no longer be attached to the strands to hold them
h: What attraction do –OH groups on neighboring strands form? What happens if fewer –OH groups are added?
w: Without vitamin C, proline is not converted to hydroxyproline, so there are fewer –OH groups and fewer hydrogen bonds holding the triple helix together. Collagen is weak, causing bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Peptide bonds still form normally.
x: Vitamin C is not needed to form peptide bonds; collagen chains are still built normally. The problem is a later change to proline.
Vitamin C's job here is adding –OH groups to proline, not making or keeping disulfide bonds. Think about what attraction those –OH groups form.
Attaching glucose is not the vitamin C-dependent step described here. Look again at what the enzyme adds to proline and what that group does.

q: Which protein is correctly matched with its function?
c: collagen: carries oxygen in the blood
h: Recall the protein classes: transport, storage, structural, hormone, enzyme, protection and contractile.
w: Myoglobin stores O2 in muscle. Hemoglobin (not collagen) transports O2, and collagen is structural. Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose, antibodies (immunoglobulins) protect against infection, and actin and myosin contract muscle.
x: Collagen is a structural protein found in skin, tendons and bone. It does not carry oxygen.
Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose. Starch is digested by enzymes such as amylase.
Antibodies (immunoglobulins) are protective proteins that fight infection. Muscle contraction uses contractile proteins such as actin and myosin.

q: A mixture of the three amino acids in the table undergoes electrophoresis in a buffer at pH 6.0. Compare the buffer pH with each pI. Which result is expected?
c: Lys moves to the − electrode, Asp to the + electrode, Gly stays
Lys moves to the + electrode, Asp to the − electrode, Gly stays
All three move to the − electrode, but at different speeds
Gly moves to the + electrode, while Lys and Asp stay in place
h: If pH < pI the amino acid is net positive; if pH > pI it is net negative; at pH = pI the net charge is zero.
w: At pH 6.0, lysine (pH below its pI) is net positive and moves to the negative electrode; aspartic acid (pH above its pI) is net negative and moves to the positive electrode; glycine is at its pI (zwitterion) and does not move.
x: This has the electrodes reversed. A net positive amino acid is attracted to the negative electrode, and a net negative one to the positive electrode.
Only amino acids with a net positive charge move toward the − electrode. Compare pH 6.0 with each pI: they are not all net positive.
Glycine's pI is 6.0, equal to the buffer pH, so its net charge is zero. Lys and Asp have pIs far from 6.0, so they carry a charge.

q: How does an enzyme increase the rate of a reaction in the body?
c: It lowers the activation energy of the reaction
It raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
It makes the overall reaction more exothermic
It shifts the equilibrium toward the products
h: A catalyst changes the pathway, not the energies of the starting materials or products.
w: An enzyme provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed at body temperature. It does not change ΔH or the equilibrium position; it speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally.
x: Enzymes do not heat the reaction; body temperature stays about 37 °C. They change the pathway the reaction follows.
A catalyst does not change ΔH. The energies of the reactants and products stay the same.
A catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the equilibrium position.

q: Statins such as atorvastatin (Lipitor) block HMG-CoA reductase, the liver enzyme that controls the pathway making cholesterol from acetyl CoA. A statin resembles the enzyme’s normal substrate and binds reversibly in its active site. A statin is therefore a(n)
h: It looks like the substrate and binds where the substrate binds.
w: An inhibitor that resembles the substrate and competes for the active site is a competitive inhibitor. With less cholesterol made, the liver removes more LDL from the blood. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme; an irreversible inhibitor forms a covalent bond.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. The statin binds in the active site and resembles the substrate.
An irreversible inhibitor forms a covalent bond. The question says the statin binds reversibly.
An activator speeds an enzyme up. Statins slow cholesterol production.

q: Penicillin irreversibly inhibits transpeptidase, an enzyme bacteria use to build their cell walls. Why does penicillin harm bacteria but not human cells?
c: Human cells have no cell walls, so they do not use this enzyme
Human cells break down penicillin before it can reach them
Human transpeptidase has an active site that penicillin cannot fit
Human substrates outcompete penicillin for the active site
h: An inhibitor can only harm cells that actually depend on the enzyme it blocks.
w: Penicillin bonds covalently to transpeptidase, so bacteria cannot cross-link their cell walls and they burst. Animal cells have no cell walls, so the target is absent in humans. Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor, so substrate cannot outcompete it.
x: Penicillin does reach human cells; it circulates in the blood. The real question is whether human cells use this enzyme.
Humans do not have a transpeptidase for building cell walls. Ask what structure bacteria have that human cells lack.
Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor, so substrate cannot outcompete it. Think about whether human cells even use this enzyme.

q: Damaged cells leak their proteins into the blood, so blood tests can show which tissue is injured. Troponin (a muscle protein) and the enzyme CK-MB (a form of creatine kinase) are concentrated in heart muscle, lipase in the pancreas, ALT in the liver, and amylase in the pancreas and salivary glands. A few hours after chest pain, a patient’s blood troponin and CK-MB rise sharply. Which tissue is most likely damaged?
h: Match the markers that rose to the tissue where they are concentrated.
w: Troponin and CK-MB are concentrated in heart muscle, so their rise after chest pain points to a heart attack. Troponin is the main heart-attack test used today; CK-MB is an older enzyme marker. High lipase would point to the pancreas and high ALT to the liver.
x: Lipase and amylase point to the pancreas. The markers that rose here are concentrated in a different tissue.
ALT is the liver marker. The markers that rose here are not ALT.
Amylase points to the salivary glands. Match troponin and CK-MB to the tissue where they are concentrated.

q: In β-oxidation, and in the citric acid cycle step succinate → fumarate, a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group is oxidized to –CH=CH–. Which coenzyme accepts the hydrogen atoms in this type of reaction?
c: FAD, which is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
coenzyme A, which forms a thioester
NADPH, which is oxidized to NADP<sup>+</sup>
h: One oxidizing coenzyme turns C–OH into C=O; the other forms C=C double bonds. Which is which?
w: Forming a carbon–carbon double bond uses FAD → FADH2 (FAD is made from vitamin B2, riboflavin). NAD+ oxidizes C–OH groups to C=O, coenzyme A carries acyl groups, and NADPH is a reducing agent used in biosynthesis.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> is used when a C–OH is oxidized to C=O. Forming a C=C double bond uses the other oxidizing coenzyme.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups as thioesters; it does not accept hydrogen atoms in an oxidation.
NADPH is a reducing agent used in biosynthesis. This step is an oxidation, so the coenzyme must accept hydrogen, not give it.

q: Which type of RNA carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and matches it to a codon on the mRNA?
h: This RNA has an anticodon loop at one end and an amino acid attachment site at the other.
w: tRNA binds its amino acid at the 3′ end and pairs its anticodon with the mRNA codon. mRNA carries the genetic message, rRNA makes up the ribosomes, and snRNA helps remove introns.
x: mRNA carries the genetic message (the codons) from DNA to the ribosome. It does not carry amino acids.
rRNA is a structural part of the ribosome. It does not bring amino acids or read codons with an anticodon.
snRNA helps remove introns during RNA processing. It does not deliver amino acids.

q: An mRNA codon is 5′-GCU-3′. What is the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it?
h: Pair the bases antiparallel (G–C, A–U). tRNA is RNA, so it uses U, not T.
w: Reading the codon 5′→3′: G pairs with C, C with G, and U with A, giving the antiparallel anticodon 3′-CGA-5′ (the same molecule as 5′-AGC-3′). T is not found in RNA, and 3′-AGC-5′ has the bases in reverse order.
x: This contains T, but tRNA is RNA and uses U instead of T.
This just copies the codon. An anticodon is complementary: G pairs with C and U pairs with A.
These are the right bases, but in reverse order. Line up each base with its partner antiparallel to the codon.

q: A point mutation changes an mRNA codon from CUU to CUC. Both codons code for leucine. What is the effect on the protein?
