c: no change, because it is a silent mutation
leucine is replaced by another amino acid
the protein ends early at a stop codon
every amino acid after this point changes
h: Several codons can code for the same amino acid. If the amino acid stays the same, does the protein change?
w: Because the genetic code is redundant, both codons still put leucine into the chain, so the primary structure is unchanged: a silent mutation. Changing every amino acid after the mutation is a frameshift, caused by an insertion or deletion.
x: Both codons code for leucine, so leucine is still added. A swap to another amino acid would be a missense mutation.
Neither CUU nor CUC is a stop codon; both code for leucine.
Changing every amino acid after a point is a frameshift, caused by an insertion or deletion. Here one base was substituted, so the reading frame is unchanged.

q: During DNA replication, the lagging strand is made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments) because
c: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 5′→3′ direction
DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 3′→5′ direction
helicase unwinds the lagging strand only in short sections
the lagging strand contains uracil, which must be removed
h: The two parent strands are antiparallel, but every new strand must grow in the same chemical direction.
w: DNA polymerase builds new DNA only 5′→3′, adding to a free 3′–OH. The leading strand grows continuously toward the replication fork; the lagging strand must be made in short fragments away from the fork, which DNA ligase then joins.
x: DNA polymerase does not build in the 3′→5′ direction. It adds each new nucleotide to the free 3′–OH of the growing strand.
Helicase unwinds both strands continuously at the fork. The fragments come from the direction in which new DNA can grow.
DNA does not contain uracil. The short fragments are about the direction DNA polymerase works.

q: Tetracycline and streptomycin bind to bacterial ribosomes, which differ in structure from human ribosomes. Which process do these antibiotics block?
c: transcription of DNA in human cells
h: What process takes place on a ribosome?
w: Ribosomes are where mRNA is translated into protein, so these drugs block translation in bacteria (tetracycline blocks tRNA binding; streptomycin causes misreading of mRNA). Because human ribosomes differ, our protein synthesis is much less affected. Replication and transcription do not happen on ribosomes.
x: DNA replication does not happen on ribosomes. Think about which process the ribosome carries out.
Transcription occurs in the nucleus, not on ribosomes, and these drugs target bacteria, not human cells.
Reverse transcription is a viral enzyme process, not a ribosome process. These antibiotics bind bacterial ribosomes.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>?
h: Draw the 5-carbon chain, then shorten it by one carbon and by two carbons, placing branches without duplicating.
w: Pentane CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, 2-methylbutane CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 and 2,2-dimethylpropane C(CH3)4: 3. A methyl on carbon 3 of butane or on the end carbon just redraws one of these.
x: You have found two, but one skeleton is missing. Try a 3-carbon chain with two branches on the middle carbon.
One of your drawings is a repeat. A methyl on carbon 3 of butane, or on an end carbon, just redraws a structure you already have.
Some of these drawings are the same molecule. Name each one; a methyl on an end carbon only makes the chain longer.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>?
h: Longest chain 6, then 5 with one methyl, then 4 with two methyls. Rename each to catch duplicates.
w: Hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane: 5. Drawings such as 1-methylpentane or 2-ethylbutane are really hexane and 3-methylpentane, which is how students reach 6 or more.
x: One skeleton is missing. Check the 5-carbon chains (methyl on C2 or C3) and the 4-carbon chains with two methyls.
One of these is a duplicate. A drawing like 2-ethylbutane is really 3-methylpentane once you find the longest chain.
This counts many drawings that are really the same molecule. Rename each one using its longest chain to remove repeats.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O (count both alcohols and ethers)?
h: Place the –OH on each different carbon of the two C<sub>4</sub> skeletons, then place an O between carbons to make ethers.
w: Alcohols: 1-butanol, 2-butanol, 2-methyl-1-propanol (isobutyl alcohol), 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol) = 4. Ethers: diethyl ether, methyl propyl ether, isopropyl methyl ether = 3. Total 7. Choosing 4 counts only the alcohols.
x: This counts only the alcohols. The O can also sit between two carbons to make an ether.
This counts only the ethers. The O can also be part of an –OH group to make an alcohol.
One isomer is missing. Check the branched skeleton for both alcohols and the branched ether.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>?
h: Keep the 3-carbon chain. Put both Cl on the same carbon, then on different carbons; check for repeats by numbering from the other end.
w: 1,1-dichloropropane, 2,2-dichloropropane, 1,2-dichloropropane and 1,3-dichloropropane: 4. 3,3- and 2,3- are just 1,1- and 1,2- numbered from the other end.
x: One isomer is missing. Both Cl atoms can go on the same carbon in two different ways: on an end carbon or on the middle carbon.
This misses some arrangements. Try both Cl on one carbon (end or middle) as well as on two different carbons.
One of these is a repeat. Number each from the other end: 2,3- is the same as 1,2-, and 3,3- is the same as 1,1-.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Cl?
h: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has two skeletons (butane and isobutane). How many different carbons can the Cl replace an H on in each?
w: Butane skeleton: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane. Isobutane skeleton: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (isobutyl chloride) and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl chloride). Total 4. Choosing 2 forgets the branched skeleton.
x: This uses only the straight butane skeleton. C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> also has a branched skeleton.
One isomer is missing. On the branched skeleton, the Cl can go on an end CH<sub>3</sub> carbon or on the central carbon.
One of these is a repeat. 3-Chlorobutane, for example, is just 2-chlorobutane numbered from the other end.

q: Counting cis and trans forms as separate compounds, how many open-chain alkenes have the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>?
h: Find the different positions for C=C on butane and isobutane skeletons, then ask which one has two different groups on each double-bond carbon.
w: 1-Butene CH2=CHCH2CH3, 2-methylpropene CH2=C(CH3)2, and 2-butene CH3CH=CHCH3, which exists as cis and trans. 3 + 1 = 4. Choosing 3 ignores cis–trans; adding the rings cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane is wrong because they are not alkenes.
x: This counts each skeleton position once but ignores that one of these alkenes has both cis and trans forms.
One of these is a duplicate or not an alkene. 3-Butene is just 1-butene, and rings such as cyclobutane have no C=C.
This forgets the branched skeleton and the cis–trans pair. There are more alkenes than just one per straight-chain position.

q: Not counting cis–trans isomers, how many open-chain alkenes have the formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>?
h: Place the double bond in every distinct position on pentane, then on 2-methylbutane. 2,2-dimethylpropane has no room for C=C.
w: Pentane skeleton: 1-pentene, 2-pentene. 2-Methylbutane skeleton: 2-methyl-1-butene, 3-methyl-1-butene, 2-methyl-2-butene. Total 5. Answering 2 counts only the straight-chain skeleton and forgets the branched alkenes; 4 misses one of the branched ones.
x: This counts only the straight-chain skeleton. Branched skeletons such as 2-methylbutane also give alkenes.
One branched alkene is missing. On the 2-methylbutane skeleton, the C=C can go in three different places.
This misses some of the branched alkenes. On the 2-methylbutane skeleton, the C=C can go in three different places.

q: How many constitutional isomers have the formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O?
h: With one O and saturated carbons, the O can be in an –OH group or between two carbons (an ether).
w: 1-Propanol CH3CH2CH2OH, 2-propanol CH3CH(OH)CH3 and ethyl methyl ether CH3OCH2CH3: 3. Choosing 2 misses the ether.
x: This counts only the alcohols. The O can also sit between two carbons to make an ether.
One of these is a repeat. 3-Propanol, for example, is just 1-propanol numbered from the other end.
There is more than one way to connect these atoms. The –OH can go on an end carbon or the middle carbon, and the O can also form an ether.

q: What is the relationship between CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count C and H in each. If the formulas match, are the atoms connected in the same order?
w: Both are C4H10, but one is a straight chain (butane) and the other is branched (isobutane), so they are constitutional isomers. No C=C or ring is present, so cis–trans is not possible.
x: One is a straight chain and the other is branched. Different connections cannot be the same compound.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. Both of these are open-chain alkanes.
Count the atoms: both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>. Compounds with the same formula are isomers of some kind.

q: What is the relationship between CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Name both. Writing a chain from the other end does not change the molecule.
w: Both are a 4-carbon chain with a methyl on carbon 2 (2-methylbutane), written left-to-right and right-to-left: the same compound. Different-looking condensed formulas are not automatically isomers.
x: Name both: each is a 4-carbon chain with a methyl on carbon 2. Writing a chain from the other end does not change the connections.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. These are alkanes, so that type of isomer is not possible.
Count the atoms: both are C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. Ask whether the connections are actually different.

q: In one molecule of CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are on the same side of the double bond; in another they are on opposite sides. These two molecules are
h: Same formula and same connections; the only difference is the arrangement around a C=C that cannot rotate.
w: Same side = cis-2-butene, opposite sides = trans-2-butene. The atoms are connected identically, so they are cis–trans isomers, not constitutional isomers. Without free rotation around C=C they cannot interconvert, so they are not the same compound.
x: The C=C cannot rotate, so a molecule with the CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the same side cannot turn into one with them on opposite sides.
Constitutional isomers have different connections. Here every atom is bonded to the same neighbors; only the arrangement in space differs.
Both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> with the same connections, so they are isomers of some kind.

q: What is the relationship between CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Isomers must have the same molecular formula. Count the hydrogens.
w: 2-Butene is C4H8 and butane is C4H10. Different formulas, so they are unrelated (not isomers). Same number of carbons is not enough.
x: One has a C=C and the other does not, so they cannot be the same compound. Count the hydrogens in each.
Isomers must have the same molecular formula. Count the hydrogens in each.
Cis–trans isomers need the same formula and the same connections. Count the hydrogens in each.

q: Which compound can exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups.
w: In ClCH=CHCl each double-bond carbon has H and Cl, so the Cl atoms can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans): ClCH=CHCl. In the others at least one carbon has two identical groups (two H or two Cl).
x: One carbon of the C=C carries two H, and the other carries two Cl. A carbon with two identical groups cannot give cis and trans forms.
The CH<sub>2</sub>= carbon carries two identical H atoms, so swapping sides gives the same molecule.
Each carbon of the C=C carries two identical Cl atoms, so there is no same-side versus opposite-side difference.

q: Ethanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is a functional-group isomer of which compound?
h: Find the compound with the same formula, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O, but a different functional group.
w: Dimethyl ether CH3OCH3 is C2H6O, like ethanol, but is an ether instead of an alcohol: CH3OCH3. CH3OCH2CH3 is C3H8O and CH3CHO is C2H4O.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has three carbons (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O). Isomers must have exactly the same formula as ethanol.
CH<sub>3</sub>CHO is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O, two H fewer than ethanol. Isomers need the same formula.
CH<sub>3</sub>OH has only one carbon. Isomers must have the same number of each atom.

q: Which compound is a constitutional isomer of propanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO?
h: Propanal is C₃H₆O. Write the molecular formula of each choice and find the one that matches exactly.
w: Acetone (propanone) CH3COCH3 is also C3H6O, with a ketone in place of the aldehyde: CH3COCH3. 1-Propanol is C3H8O (two more H) and propanoic acid has an extra O.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH is C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O, two H more than propanal.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH has two O atoms, one more than propanal.
CH<sub>3</sub>CHO has only two carbons. Isomers need exactly the same formula, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O.

q: Propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, has the same molecular formula as which ester?
h: Write the formula of propanoic acid, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, then count the C atoms in each ester, including the alkyl group on O.
w: Methyl ethanoate CH3COOCH3 is C3H6O2, a functional-group isomer of propanoic acid: CH3COOCH3. Methyl propanoate has 4 carbons because the methyl on O counts too.
x: Methyl propanoate has 4 carbons: the methyl group on O counts too. Propanoic acid has only 3.
This ester has 5 carbons once you count the propyl group on O. Propanoic acid has only 3.
Methyl formate has only 2 carbons (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>). Propanoic acid has 3.

q: Which compound can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?
h: Molecules H-bond with each other only if an H is attached directly to F, N or O.
w: Ethylamine has N–H bonds, so it H-bonds with itself: CH3CH2NH2. In dimethyl ether, trimethylamine and fluoroethane every H is on carbon, so there is no H–F, H–N or H–O to donate.
x: Dimethyl ether has an O, but all six of its H atoms are on carbon. Without an H on O, N or F it cannot donate a hydrogen bond to itself.
Trimethylamine has an N, but its nitrogen carries three CH<sub>3</sub> groups and no H. All of its H atoms are on carbon.
Fluoroethane has an F, but the F is bonded to carbon, not to H. Every H here is on carbon, so there is nothing to donate.

q: Which compound cannot hydrogen bond with other molecules of itself but can accept hydrogen bonds from water, making it partly water-soluble?
h: Look for an O atom with lone pairs but no H on O, N or F.
w: Diethyl ether has an O that water's H can bond to, but no O–H of its own: CH3CH2OCH2CH3. 1-Butanol and propanoic acid have O–H and H-bond with themselves; pentane has no O at all.
x: 1-Butanol has an O–H, so its molecules do hydrogen bond with each other. Look for an O with lone pairs but no O–H.
Pentane has no O or N at all, so it cannot even accept a hydrogen bond from water. It is insoluble.
Propanoic acid has an O–H in its COOH group, so its molecules hydrogen bond strongly with each other.

q: Which compound has the lowest boiling point?
h: All are nonpolar alkanes. More carbons raise the boiling point; for isomers, more branching (a rounder shape) lowers it.
w: Three choices are C5H12 isomers; the most branched, nearly spherical 2,2-dimethylpropane has the least surface contact and weakest dispersion forces: C(CH3)4 (about 10 °C, vs 36 °C for pentane). Hexane is larger, so it boils highest.
x: 2-Methylbutane is a C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> isomer with only one branch. An isomer with more branching is more compact and boils lower.
Pentane is unbranched, so it has the most surface contact of the C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> isomers and boils highest among them.
Hexane has six carbons, more than the others, so its dispersion forces are strongest. It boils highest, not lowest.

q: Propane, dimethyl ether and ethanol have similar molar masses. Which ranking of boiling points is correct?
h: With similar size, rank by the strongest IMF: dispersion only < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
w: Propane is nonpolar (dispersion only), dimethyl ether is polar (dipole–dipole), and ethanol has O–H (hydrogen bonding): propane < dimethyl ether < ethanol (−42 °C, −24 °C, 78 °C).
x: This puts dimethyl ether below propane. The ether is polar (bent C–O–C), so it has dipole–dipole forces that nonpolar propane lacks.
This order is reversed. Propane has only dispersion forces, while ethanol's O–H lets it hydrogen bond.
This puts dimethyl ether above ethanol. The ether has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself the way ethanol does.

q: Which alkane has the strongest London dispersion forces and therefore the highest melting point?
h: Dispersion forces grow with molecular size (more electrons, more surface area).
w: The 20-carbon alkane is the biggest molecule, so it has the strongest dispersion forces and the highest melting point: CH3(CH2)18CH3. It is a waxy solid at room temperature, like the alkanes in petroleum jelly, while the others are liquids.
x: This is a 10-carbon alkane. Another choice is a much larger molecule with more electrons and more surface contact.
This is an 8-carbon alkane. Dispersion forces grow with size, and another choice is much larger.
This is pentane, only 5 carbons. It is the smallest choice, so its dispersion forces are the weakest.

q: Which compound is the most soluble in water?
h: More –OH groups per carbon means more hydrogen bonding with water and a smaller nonpolar part.
w: Ethylene glycol has two –OH groups on only two carbons and mixes with water in all proportions: HOCH2CH2OH. 1-Butanol and diethyl ether dissolve only slightly (about 7 g per 100 mL); pentane is nonpolar and insoluble.
x: 1-Butanol has one –OH, but its four-carbon nonpolar chain limits solubility. Look for more –OH groups on fewer carbons.
Diethyl ether has no O–H; its O can only accept hydrogen bonds from water, and its four carbons are nonpolar. It is only slightly soluble.
Pentane is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with no O or N, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water. It is insoluble.

q: What is the shape around the oxygen atom in dimethyl ether, CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>, and the approximate C–O–C bond angle?
h: Count electron groups on O: two bonds plus two lone pairs.
w: Oxygen has 2 bonding groups and 2 lone pairs = 4 electron groups (tetrahedral arrangement), so the molecular shape is bent, about 109°, like water. Because it is bent, the C–O dipoles do not cancel and the ether is polar.
x: Linear (180°) happens with only two electron groups. Oxygen here also has two lone pairs, giving four groups in all.
120° goes with three electron groups. Count again: oxygen has two bonds plus two lone pairs.
Trigonal planar needs three bonding groups and no lone pairs. Oxygen here has two bonds and two lone pairs.

q: What is the shape and approximate bond angle around the carbonyl (C=O) carbon of acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count electron groups on the carbonyl carbon; a double bond counts as one group.
w: The carbonyl carbon has three groups (two CH3 and one C=O) and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, 120°. The methyl carbons are tetrahedral, which is the tempting wrong answer.
x: Tetrahedral, 109.5° is the shape of the CH<sub>3</sub> carbons, which have four single bonds. The carbonyl carbon has a double bond, counted as one group.
Linear, 180° needs only two electron groups. The carbonyl carbon is bonded to three groups.
Trigonal pyramidal requires a lone pair, as on the N of ammonia. The carbonyl carbon has no lone pair.

q: Which molecule is nonpolar even though it contains polar bonds?
h: In a tetrahedral molecule, bond dipoles cancel only if all four atoms on carbon are identical.
w: In tetrachloromethane all four C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and cancel: CCl4. With a mix of H and Cl on carbon the dipoles do not cancel, so CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CH3Cl are polar.
x: CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> has two H and two Cl on carbon. The C–Cl and C–H dipoles differ, so they do not cancel and the molecule is polar.
CHCl<sub>3</sub> has one H among three Cl atoms. With different atoms on carbon, the dipoles do not cancel.
CH<sub>3</sub>Cl has one polar C–Cl bond that nothing balances, so the molecule is polar.

q: Acetic acid reacts with methylamine as shown below. Which statement is correct?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is the acid; CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is the base.
CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is the acid; CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is the base.
Both CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> act as acids.
Both CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> act as bases.
h: Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: the acid donates it, the base accepts it.
w: Acetic acid loses H+ (becoming acetate), and methylamine gains it (becoming methylammonium). Carboxylic acid = acid, amine = base.
x: This is reversed. Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: the carboxylic acid loses it and the amine gains it.
If both donated H<sup>+</sup>, nothing would accept it. In an acid–base reaction one partner donates and the other accepts.
If both accepted H<sup>+</sup>, nothing would donate it. One partner must give up an H<sup>+</sup>.

q: In which reaction does water act as an acid?
h: Water can act as an acid or a base. In each reaction, decide whether water gains an H⁺ or loses one.
w: With the amine (a base), water donates H+ and becomes OH−: CH3NH2 + H2O. With acids (HCl, carboxylic acids) water accepts H+ to form H3O+, so there it is a base.
x: Here water gains H<sup>+</sup> and becomes H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, so it is acting as a base. An acid gives H<sup>+</sup> away.
Water gains H⁺ from HCl to form H₃O⁺, so here it is a base. An acid gives H⁺ away.
Water accepts H<sup>+</sup> from formic acid to form H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, so here it is a base. Look for a reaction where water loses an H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Which pair contains a strong acid and a strong base?
h: A strong acid or strong base ionizes completely in water. Decide which of these compounds ionize only partly.
w: HCl and NaOH both ionize completely in water. Carboxylic acids such as acetic acid are weak acids, and amines and ammonia are weak bases.
x: NaOH is a strong base, but acetic acid is a carboxylic acid, and carboxylic acids are weak acids.
HCl is a strong acid, but CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is an amine, and amines are weak bases.
Both are weak: acetic acid is a weak organic acid and ammonia is a weak base.

q: Acetaminophen, the pain reliever in Tylenol, has the formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>. What is its molar mass?
h: Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript and add: C 12.01, H 1.008, N 14.01, O 16.00.
w: 8(12.01) + 9(1.008) + 1(14.01) + 2(16.00) = 96.08 + 9.072 + 14.01 + 32.00 = 151.16 g mol⁻¹. 43.03 comes from adding one of each atom without the subscripts; 135.16 uses only one O; 137.15 leaves out the nitrogen.
x: 135.16 counts only one O. The formula has O<sub>2</sub>, so multiply 16.00 by 2.
43.03 adds one of each atom and ignores the subscripts. Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript first.
137.15 leaves out the nitrogen. Include 14.01 for the one N atom.

q: Lactic acid, which builds up in muscles during hard exercise, is CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH. What is its molar mass?
h: First write the molecular formula, counting every H (including those on O) and every O, then add atomic masses.
w: Formula C3H6O3: 3(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 36.03 + 6.048 + 48.00 = 90.08 g mol⁻¹. Missing one H on an –OH gives 89.07; dropping one O (C3H6O2) gives 74.08.
x: 89.07 is one H short. Count every H in the formula, including the ones bonded to O.
88.06 is two H short, as if the H atoms on the O atoms were skipped. Count every H in CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH.
74.08 counts only two O atoms. The –OH and the –COOH together contain three O.

q: Heating 1-propanol with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives propene, as shown below. This elimination is called
h: Name the small molecule removed: H<sub>2</sub>, HX, H<sub>2</sub>O or X<sub>2</sub>.
w: An H and an –OH are removed from neighboring carbons as H2O, forming C=C: dehydration. Hydration is the reverse (adding water to an alkene).
x: Dehydrogenation removes H<sub>2</sub>. Here an alcohol loses its –OH along with an H, so the small molecule removed contains oxygen.
Dehydrohalogenation removes H and a halogen (HX). 1-Propanol has no halogen atom.
Hydration adds water to an alkene. This reaction goes the other way: water is removed from an alcohol to make an alkene.

q: Propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with HBr to give 2-bromopropane, CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub>. Why is this classified as an addition reaction?
c: The H and Br add across the C=C, and no atoms are lost: two reactants give one product
A Br atom replaces an H atom, and HBr is released
Atoms are removed from neighboring carbons to form a C=C
The alkene reacts with O<sub>2</sub> to give CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Compare the reactants and products. Did the C=C form, break, or stay? Was anything left over?
w: In an addition reaction the parts of a reagent add to the two carbons of a C=C, which becomes a single bond. Here H and Br add across the C=C and nothing is lost, so two reactants give one product. (Markovnikov's rule puts the H on CH2 and the Br on the middle carbon.)
x: That describes a substitution, such as the halogenation of an alkane in light. Here no H atom is replaced and no HBr is released; HBr is used up.
That describes an elimination, which forms a C=C. Here the C=C is used up.
That describes combustion. This reaction uses HBr, not O<sub>2</sub>.

q: Which reactant gives propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, when it is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (dehydration)?
h: Dehydration removes H<sub>2</sub>O, so the reactant needs an –OH group.
w: Dehydration removes an –OH and an H from neighboring carbons as H2O, forming a C=C. 2-Propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3, loses water to give propene. This elimination is the reverse of the hydration of propene.
x: This compound has no –OH group, so it cannot lose H<sub>2</sub>O.
Propane has no –OH group to lose as water. Alkanes do not undergo dehydration.
Propanal is an aldehyde. Its oxygen is in a C=O, not an –OH, so it does not lose water to form an alkene.

q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and gives ethene, as shown below. What is removed, and what is the reaction called?
h: Compare formulas: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>. What is missing?
w: C2H6O minus C2H4 leaves H2O, so water is removed and a C=C forms: dehydration, an elimination reaction. Hydration is the reverse addition of water to an alkene.
x: Removing only H<sub>2</sub> would leave the oxygen behind in the product. The product, ethene, has no oxygen.
Hydration adds water to an alkene. Here water is removed from an alcohol, so the name needs a prefix meaning removal.
In a substitution one group replaces another and no C=C forms. Here a C=C forms and a water molecule leaves.

q: Which condensed structure is the isobutyl group?
h: Iso- names a chain ending in a carbon with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Where is the attachment point relative to that branch?
w: Isobutyl is attached through a CH2 to a Y-shaped CH(CH3)2: –CH2CH(CH3)2. The others are sec-butyl, tert-butyl and butyl.
x: This is sec-butyl: it attaches through a CH that carries a CH<sub>3</sub> and an ethyl. In iso- groups the Y-shaped CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is at the far end.
This is tert-butyl: it attaches through a carbon bonded to three CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
This is the unbranched butyl group. Iso- groups end in a branch with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.

q: What is the common name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Find the carbon bonded to Cl. How many other carbons is it bonded to?
w: Cl is on carbon 2 of a straight 4-carbon chain; that carbon is bonded to two carbons (secondary): sec-butyl chloride (2-chlorobutane). Butyl chloride has Cl on the end carbon; isobutyl and tert-butyl are branched.
x: Isobutyl compounds have a branched chain, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>–. This four-carbon chain is unbranched.
In tert-butyl chloride the Cl carbon is bonded to three other carbons. Here the Cl carbon is bonded to only two.
Butyl chloride has Cl on the end carbon of the chain. Here the Cl is on an inner carbon.

q: Propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>, decolorizing the red-brown bromine. What is the product?
h: Halogenation opens the double bond and adds one halogen atom to each of the two double-bond carbons.
w: One Br adds to each former C=C carbon: CH3CHBrCH2Br (1,2-dibromopropane). The single-Br products come from HBr (hydrohalogenation), not Br2.
x: This has only one Br, on the end carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> supplies two Br atoms, one for each double-bond carbon.
This has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds a Br to each of the two double-bond carbons.
Both Br atoms are on the same carbon here. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Br.

q: Which compound is a hemiketal?
h: Find the carbon bonded to two O atoms. Hemi = one –OH and one –OR. Ketal-type carbons have two carbon groups and no H.
w: The carbon in (CH3)2C(OH)OCH3 has one –OH, one –OCH3 and two CH3 groups (it came from acetone + methanol): hemiketal. CH3CH(OH)OCH3 has an H on that carbon (hemiacetal); the two –OCH3 compounds are a ketal and an acetal.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)OCH<sub>3</sub> has an H on the carbon bearing both oxygens, so it came from an aldehyde: that is a hemiacetal.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> and no –OH, so it is a full ketal, not a hemi- compound.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has two –OR groups and an H on that carbon: a full acetal from an aldehyde.

q: A carbon atom is bonded to two –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> groups and two carbon groups (no H, no –OH). This carbon is part of a(n)
h: Two –OR groups means the full product (no hemi). Two carbon groups on that carbon point back to which carbonyl compound?
w: Two –OR groups and no –OH = the second alcohol has added. Two carbon groups (no H) on that carbon means the original carbonyl was a ketone: ketal, formed from a ketone. An acetal's carbon keeps the aldehyde H.
x: An acetal carbon keeps the aldehyde's H. This carbon has two carbon groups and no H.
A hemiketal has one –OH and one –OR. This carbon has two –OR groups and no –OH.
A hemiacetal has an –OH, and its carbon keeps an H. This carbon has neither.

q: Which compound is reduced to 2-pentanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Reduction runs oxidation backward. A secondary alcohol comes from a ketone with C=O on the same carbon.
w: Adding H atoms across the C=O of 2-pentanone puts –OH on carbon 2: CH3COCH2CH2CH3. 3-Pentanone gives 3-pentanol, and pentanal or pentanoic acid give the primary alcohol 1-pentanol.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is an aldehyde; reduction gives a primary alcohol with OH on the end carbon (1-pentanol).
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has its C=O on carbon 3, so reduction gives 3-pentanol. The OH must end up on carbon 2.
A carboxylic acid has its C=O at the end of the chain, so reducing it gives a primary alcohol. The target has OH on carbon 2.

q: Which compound is oxidized to propanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, by a mild oxidizing agent and reduced to 1-propanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, by [H] (a reducing agent)?
h: Which compound sits between a 1° alcohol and a carboxylic acid on the oxidation line?
w: An aldehyde sits in the middle of the oxidation line: 1° alcohol ⇌ aldehyde → carboxylic acid. Propanal is oxidized to propanoic acid and reduced to 1-propanol, with the C=O staying on the end carbon.
x: Propanone is a ketone. It is not oxidized by mild oxidizing agents, and its reduction gives 2-propanol, not 1-propanol.
2-Propanol is a 2° alcohol. Oxidizing it gives propanone, a ketone, not propanoic acid.
Propane is an alkane with no oxygen. It is neither oxidized to an acid by a mild oxidizing agent nor reduced by [H].

q: Ibuprofen is sold as a racemic mixture. What does this mean?
c: It contains equal amounts of two enantiomers.
It contains only the active enantiomer.
It contains equal amounts of two diastereomers.
It contains equal amounts of cis and trans isomers.
h: "Racemic" describes a 50:50 mixture of a particular pair of stereoisomers that are mirror images.
w: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of a pair of enantiomers, so it contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Their opposite rotations cancel, so it does not rotate plane-polarized light. Diastereomers are not mirror images.
x: A single-enantiomer drug is the opposite of racemic. Racemic means both mirror-image forms are present.
Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. A racemic mixture is made from a pair of mirror-image forms.
Cis and trans isomers come from restricted rotation around a double bond or ring. Racemic refers to a 50:50 mix of chiral mirror-image forms.

q: How many chiral carbons are in CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Check each carbon for four different groups. CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub> carbons cannot be chiral.
w: C2 has H, OH, CH3 and the rest of the chain; C3 has H, NH2, CH2CH3 and CH(OH)CH3. Both have four different groups: 2. The CH3 and CH2 carbons have at least two H atoms.
x: Too few. Check both CH carbons: the one with –OH and the one with –NH<sub>2</sub>. Does each have four different groups?
Too many. The CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub> carbons have two or three identical H atoms, so they cannot be chiral.
Look again at the CH carbons bearing –OH and –NH<sub>2</sub>. List the four groups on each and compare them.

q: How many chiral carbons are in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: A CH bonded to two CH<sub>3</sub> groups cannot be chiral. Check the carbon bearing –OH carefully.
w: Only the C–OH carbon has four different groups (H, OH, isopropyl, isobutyl): 1. Each CH(CH3)2 carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so it is not chiral, which is the trap behind 3.
x: That count likely includes one of the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> carbons. Each of those carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not chiral.
That counts both CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> carbons, but each one has two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Check which CH carbon has four truly different groups.
Look at the carbon bearing –OH. Compare the two carbon groups on each side of it: are they identical or different?

q: Which compound is a thiol?
h: A thiol is the sulfur version of an alcohol: an –SH group on a carbon.
w: 1-Propanethiol has an –SH group: CH3CH2CH2SH. CH3CH2SCH3 has S between two carbons (a sulfide), CH3SSCH3 is a disulfide, and the –OH compound is an alcohol.
x: Here the S is between two carbons with no H on it, so this is a sulfide, the sulfur version of an ether.
This has an –OH group, so it is an alcohol. A thiol has sulfur in place of that oxygen.
This has two sulfur atoms bonded to each other, so it is a disulfide. Neither S carries an H.

q: Acetic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, and ethanethiol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH, combine by condensation (water is lost). What is the organic product?
h: Treat it like making an ester: –OH from the acid and H from –SH leave as water. Which side keeps the C=O?
w: The C=O stays on the acetic acid side and the S bonds to it, giving a thioester: CH3C(=O)–S–CH2CH3. Acetyl-CoA, the fuel for the citric acid cycle, is a thioester of this type. Putting C=O on the ethyl side reverses the pieces.
x: This puts the C=O on the two-carbon ethyl side and a methyl on S, which reverses the pieces. The C=O stays with the acid's CH<sub>3</sub>.
This is an ordinary ester with an –O– link. The reactant here is a thiol, so its sulfur, not an oxygen, joins to the C=O carbon.
This has no C=O, so it is a sulfide. Condensation keeps the acid's carbonyl group.

q: Choline, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N<sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is needed to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. How is its nitrogen classified?
h: Count the carbon atoms bonded directly to nitrogen.
w: Nitrogen is bonded to four carbons (three CH3 and one CH2) and carries a + charge: quaternary ammonium ion. A tertiary amine has only three carbons on a neutral N.
x: A tertiary amine has three carbons on a neutral N. Count again: choline's N carries a CH<sub>2</sub> as well as three CH<sub>3</sub>, and it has a + charge.
A secondary amine has two carbons and one H on N. Choline's nitrogen has no H at all.
A primary amine has only one carbon on N. Count every carbon bonded to choline's nitrogen.

q: Acetaminophen is an amide, HO–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–NH–C(=O)–CH<sub>3</sub>. Which carboxylic acid and amine could form it by condensation?
h: The C=O side of an amide came from the carboxylic acid; the N side came from the amine.
w: The C(=O)CH3 piece is from acetic acid, and the HO–C6H4–NH– piece is from the amine 4-aminophenol: acetic acid and 4-aminophenol. 4-Hydroxybenzoic acid + methylamine would put the C=O on the ring side, a different compound.
x: Pairing 4-hydroxybenzoic acid with methylamine puts the C=O on the ring side and the CH<sub>3</sub> on N, a different compound. Check which side of the N the C=O is on.
Phenol has no nitrogen, so it cannot supply the N–H needed for an amide. The ring piece must come from an amine.
Formic acid supplies only an H–C=O piece. In acetaminophen the C=O carbon also carries a CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: What is the IUPAC name of HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH?
h: The carboxylic acid outranks the alcohol: it sets the suffix and its carbon is C1. Count all four carbons.
w: The –COOH carbon is C1 of a 4-carbon chain, and the –OH is on C4 as a hydroxy prefix: 4-hydroxybutanoic acid. 3-Hydroxypropanoic acid forgets that the COOH carbon is part of the chain.
x: The –COOH carbon is C1, and its OH is part of the acid group. The extra –OH is on the far end of the chain.
The -al ending is for an aldehyde, –CHO. This compound has a –COOH group, which takes the -oic acid ending.
This counts only 3 chain carbons. The –COOH carbon is part of the chain, so count it too.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH?
h: The ketone outranks the alcohol, so it gets the suffix and the lower number.
w: Number from the end nearest the C=O: ketone on C2, –OH on C4: 4-hydroxy-2-butanone. 1-Hydroxy-3-butanone gives the ketone the higher number, and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone is a different compound, CH3COCH(OH)CH3.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. The ketone outranks the alcohol, so number to give the C=O carbon the lowest number.
The -al ending is for an aldehyde, with C=O at the end of the chain. Here the C=O is in the middle, between two carbons.
3-Hydroxy would put the –OH on the carbon next to the C=O, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>. Here the –OH is on the end CH<sub>2</sub>.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: The longest chain may run into the group written in parentheses. Count every path from end to end.
w: Going from the propyl group through the CH to an ethyl group gives a 6-carbon chain with an ethyl branch on C3: 3-ethylhexane. 3-Propylpentane uses a shorter 5-carbon chain; 4-ethylhexane numbers from the wrong end. 3-Methylheptane is a different isomer of C8H18.
x: Pentane is not the longest chain. Follow a path that runs from the propyl group, through the CH, into one ethyl group.
This numbers from the wrong end. Number the chain so the branch gets the lowest possible number.
A 7-carbon chain is not possible here; the longest path is shorter. 3-Methylheptane is a different isomer of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>.

q: Ribulose, an intermediate in photosynthesis and the pentose phosphate pathway, has the open-chain structure CH<sub>2</sub>OH–CO–CHOH–CHOH–CH<sub>2</sub>OH. How is ribulose classified?
h: Count the carbons for the ending, then decide whether the C=O is at the end of the chain (aldehyde) or inside it (ketone).
w: Ribulose has 5 carbons (pentose) and its C=O is on carbon 2, inside the chain, so it is a ketone: ketopentose. An aldopentose (like ribose) has the C=O on carbon 1 as –CHO.
x: An aldopentose (like ribose) has a –CHO on carbon 1. Here carbon 1 is CH<sub>2</sub>OH and the C=O is on carbon 2.
Count the carbons in CH<sub>2</sub>OH–CO–CHOH–CHOH–CH<sub>2</sub>OH again: there are five, not six.
A tetrose has four carbons, and "aldo" means a –CHO at the end. This chain has five carbons and its C=O is inside the chain.

q: D-Glucose cyclizes to form β-D-glucopyranose, a six-membered ring. How many chiral carbons does β-D-glucopyranose have?
h: Open-chain glucose has chiral carbons C2–C5. What happens to the carbonyl carbon C1 when it becomes the hemiacetal carbon?
w: Open-chain glucose has 4 chiral carbons (C2–C5). On ring closure, C1 becomes a hemiacetal carbon bonded to –OH, –O– (ring), –H and C2: four different groups, so it is a new chiral center. Total: 5. C6 (–CH2OH) is never chiral.
x: 4 is the count for open-chain glucose (C2–C5). Ring closure turns C1 into a carbon with four different groups.
6 counts every carbon, but C6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH with two H atoms, so it is not chiral.
3 leaves out some of C2–C5, which are all chiral in glucose, and also misses the new center at C1.

q: In lactose (milk sugar), carbon 1 of β-D-galactose is bonded through an oxygen atom to carbon 4 of D-glucose. How is this glycosidic linkage labeled?
h: Name the linkage with the anomeric form of the first sugar, then the two carbon numbers that are joined.
w: The anomeric carbon (C1) of galactose is in the β form and is joined to C4 of glucose, so the linkage is β(1→4). Lactase must break this β bond; α(1→4) is the linkage in maltose and starch.
x: α would mean the galactose C1 bond is in the α form, as in maltose. The question tells you galactose is in the β form.
The β part is right, but the question says galactose bonds to carbon 4 of glucose, not carbon 6.
Check both parts: the galactose is in the β form, and it is bonded to carbon 4 of glucose.

q: Maltose is two glucose units joined by an α(1→4) linkage. Which statement correctly describes carbon 1 of each glucose unit in maltose?
c: The linked C1 is an acetal; the other C1 is a hemiacetal
Both C1 carbons are acetals, so maltose is not reducing
Both C1 carbons are hemiacetals, held by an ester bond
The linked C1 is a hemiacetal; the other C1 is an acetal
h: A hemiacetal carbon has one –OH and one –OR; an acetal carbon has two –OR groups. Which C1 is tied up in the glycosidic bond?
w: C1 of the first glucose bears the ring O and the glycosidic O (two –OR groups): an acetal. C1 of the second glucose still has a free –OH and the ring O: a hemiacetal, which can open to an aldehyde, so maltose is a reducing sugar.
x: Only one C1 is used in the α(1→4) bond. The second glucose's C1 keeps its –OH, so maltose is a reducing sugar.
A glycosidic bond is an ether-type C–O–C link, not an ester. Also, the C1 in the glycosidic bond carries two –OR groups, not one.
This has the two C1 carbons reversed. The C1 in the glycosidic bond carries two –OR groups; which C1 still has a free –OH?

q: How is the enantiomer of D-glucose drawn in a Fischer projection?
c: L-glucose: the –OH on all chiral carbons is moved to the opposite side
L-glucose: only the –OH on carbon 5 is moved to the opposite side
β-D-glucose: only the –OH on carbon 1 is moved to the opposite side
D-galactose: only the –OH on carbon 4 is moved to the opposite side
h: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. In a mirror image, which chiral centers are inverted?
w: An enantiomer is the mirror image, so all four chiral centers (C2–C5) are reversed, giving L-glucose. Flipping only C5 gives a different sugar (a diastereomer, not glucose); flipping only C4 gives galactose, an epimer.
x: Flipping only C5 changes the D/L label, but the result is not the mirror image of glucose; it is a different sugar (a diastereomer).
α and β anomers differ only at C1 of the ring form; they are not mirror images. An enantiomer is a full mirror image.
Flipping only C4 gives galactose, an epimer of glucose. A mirror image must reverse more than one chiral center.

q: α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose are called anomers because they differ only in
c: the position of the –OH on the hemiacetal carbon, C1
the position of the –OH on carbon 5, which sets D or L
the position of the –OH on carbon 4 of the ring
the size of the ring, five-membered versus six-membered
h: Anomers form when the ring closes. Which carbon becomes the new chiral center during cyclization?
w: Ring closure makes C1 (the anomeric carbon) a new chiral center, so the –OH there can be down (α) or up (β): anomers differ only at C1. Differing only at C4 makes epimers such as glucose and galactose.
x: Both α-D- and β-D-glucose are D sugars, so their C5 –OH is the same. Anomers differ at the carbon that becomes chiral when the ring closes.
Sugars that differ only at C4 are epimers, like glucose and galactose. Anomers differ at a different carbon.
α- and β-D-glucose here are both six-membered rings. Anomers have the same ring size and differ at one specific carbon.

q: Amylose, amylopectin, glycogen and cellulose are all hydrolyzed completely to which monosaccharide?
h: These four polysaccharides differ in their linkages and branching, not in their building block.
w: All four are polymers of glucose only; they differ in α versus β linkages and branching. Glucose + fructose make sucrose, and glucose + galactose make lactose.
x: Glucose + fructose is what sucrose gives on hydrolysis. None of these four polysaccharides contains fructose.
Glucose + galactose is what lactose gives on hydrolysis. These four polysaccharides contain no galactose.
These polymers contain no fructose. They differ in linkages and branching, not in their building block.

q: A dietitian notes that table sugar dissolves easily in water, but cooking oil does not. Which statement best explains why most simple carbohydrates are water soluble?
c: Their many –OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water
Their glycosidic bonds ionize to form charged ions in water
Their long hydrocarbon chains attract water molecules
Their ester groups are hydrolyzed by water as they dissolve
h: Look for groups that contain O–H. What intermolecular force can they form with water?
w: Sugars carry many polar –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water, so they dissolve. Lipids are mostly long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains with few H-bonding groups, so they are insoluble. Glycosidic bonds do not ionize.
x: Glycosidic bonds are covalent C–O–C bonds; they do not ionize in water. Look for polar groups that interact with water.
Long hydrocarbon chains are nonpolar and repel water; that describes oils, not sugars.
Simple sugars do not contain ester groups, and dissolving is a physical change, not a hydrolysis reaction.

q: Which biomolecule contains ester linkages as its key functional group?
h: An ester is –COO– joining an acid to an alcohol. Which molecule is made from glycerol plus fatty acids?
w: A triacylglycerol is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids (three ester bonds). Amylose has acetal (glycosidic) links, a tripeptide has amide (peptide) bonds, and cholesterol is a steroid alcohol with no ester.
x: Amylose's glucose units are joined by glycosidic (acetal) bonds, not esters.
A tripeptide's amino acids are joined by amide (peptide) bonds, not esters.
Cholesterol is a steroid alcohol: it has an –OH group but no ester group in its structure.

q: During β-oxidation, a fatty acyl chain is oxidized at its β carbon. Counting the carboxyl carbon as C1, which carbon is the β carbon?
c: C3, two carbons away from the carboxyl carbon
C2, the carbon right next to the carboxyl carbon
the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon at the far end of the chain
h: Greek letters start with the carbon attached to the carboxyl carbon: α first, then β.
w: The α carbon is C2 (attached to the carboxyl carbon) and the β carbon is C3. The CH3 carbon at the far end is the ω (omega) carbon, used to name omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.
x: C2, next to the carboxyl carbon, is the α carbon. β is the next letter after α.
The carboxyl carbon itself gets no Greek letter; lettering starts on the carbon attached to it.
The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon at the far end is the ω (omega) carbon, the last letter, not β.

q: An 18-carbon fatty acid has one double bond, between C9 and C10 (counting the carboxyl carbon as C1). How is it classified?
h: The omega number counts from the CH<sub>3</sub> end (the ω carbon is ω1) to the first carbon of the double bond.
w: The ω carbon is C18 (ω1), so C10 is 18 − 10 + 1 = ω9. The double bond starts 9 carbons from the methyl end: omega-9 (this is oleic acid in olive oil). Omega-10 comes from counting to C9 instead.
x: Omega-10 comes from counting to C9 instead of C10. Count from the CH<sub>3</sub> end (ω1 = C18) to the nearer carbon of the double bond.
Omega-3 would put the double bond near the CH<sub>3</sub> end, at C15–C16. This one is in the middle of the chain.
Omega-6 would put the double bond at C12–C13. Count again from C18 (ω1) down to C10.

q: Testosterone, estradiol, cortisol and aldosterone are hormones made in the body from which lipid?
h: These hormones all share the same four-fused-ring skeleton. Which lipid has that skeleton?
w: These are steroid hormones; their four fused rings come from cholesterol. Arachidonic acid is the starting material for eicosanoids (prostaglandins), not steroids.
x: Arachidonic acid is the starting material for eicosanoids such as prostaglandins, not steroid hormones.
Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids. It has no four-ring skeleton.
Lecithin is a glycerophospholipid used in membranes; it is not converted into hormones with four fused rings.

q: Which structural description fits a prostaglandin, an eicosanoid that causes inflammation?
c: a 20-carbon fatty acid with a five-membered carbon ring
four fused carbon rings with an –OH group on the first ring
glycerol joined to three long fatty acid chains by ester bonds
sphingosine bonded to a fatty acid, phosphate and choline
h: “Eicosa-” means 20. Eicosanoids are made from a 20-carbon fatty acid.
w: Prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid (20 C) and contain a five-membered ring within the 20-carbon fatty acid chain. Four fused rings describes a steroid; glycerol + 3 fatty acids is a triacylglycerol; sphingosine with a fatty acid, phosphate and choline is sphingomyelin.
x: Four fused rings with an –OH describes a steroid such as cholesterol, not an eicosanoid.
Glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds is a triacylglycerol, a storage fat.
Sphingosine bonded to a fatty acid, phosphate and choline is sphingomyelin, a membrane sphingolipid.

q: A triacylglycerol is heated with water and a strong acid catalyst (acid hydrolysis). What are the products?
c: glycerol and three fatty acid salts (soap)
three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid
one fatty acid and a diacylglycerol ester
h: Hydrolysis breaks each ester bond. Is a strong base present to turn the acids into carboxylate salts?
w: Acid hydrolysis breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three free fatty acids. Base hydrolysis (saponification with NaOH) gives glycerol and three fatty acid salts, which are soaps.
x: Fatty acid salts (soaps) form when a strong base such as NaOH is used. Here the catalyst is an acid.
Each triacylglycerol has just one glycerol backbone holding three fatty acid chains. This choice reverses those numbers.
That would be only one ester bond broken. With enough water and heat, hydrolysis breaks all three.

q: Which substance crosses a cell membrane mainly by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer?
h: The bilayer interior is nonpolar. Which molecules can slip through without a protein channel or carrier?
w: Small, nonpolar or uncharged molecules such as O2, CO2 and (to some extent) H2O diffuse directly through the bilayer. Glucose needs a carrier protein (facilitated transport), and charged ions need channels or pumps.
x: Glucose is large and polar, so it needs a carrier protein (facilitated transport) to cross the bilayer.
Na<sup>+</sup> is charged, so it cannot pass through the nonpolar interior of the bilayer; it needs channels or pumps.
K<sup>+</sup> is a charged ion, so it cannot slip through the nonpolar interior of the bilayer; it needs channels or pumps.

q: Nerve cells use the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump, which uses ATP to move 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out and 2 K<sup>+</sup> in, both from lower to higher concentration. This is an example of
h: Look at the direction (with or against the gradient) and whether ATP energy is spent.
w: Moving ions against their concentration gradients requires energy from ATP: active transport. Facilitated transport also uses a protein, but moves solutes from higher to lower concentration with no ATP.
x: Simple diffusion moves substances from higher to lower concentration with no protein or energy. Here ions move against their gradients using ATP.
Facilitated transport uses a protein but moves substances down their gradient with no ATP. Here ATP is spent to go against the gradient.
Osmosis is the movement of water across a membrane, not ions pumped by a protein.

q: Which biomolecule is correctly matched with the linkage that joins its building blocks?
h: Think of the condensation reaction that builds each polymer and the functional group it forms.
w: Amino acids are joined by amide (peptide) bonds. Fats use ester bonds, polysaccharides use glycosidic (acetal) bonds, and nucleic acids use phosphodiester bonds in their backbone.
x: Triacylglycerols are made from glycerol and fatty acids, which form ester bonds, not ether bonds.
Polysaccharides are linked by glycosidic bonds between sugar units. Ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol in fats.
DNA nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone, not amide bonds.

q: Alanine, H<sub>2</sub>N–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–COOH, has a pI of 6.0. Which form is present mainly in a strongly basic solution, at a pH far above its pI?
h: At a pH well above the pI, OH<sup>−</sup> removes H<sup>+</sup>. Which groups lose a proton?
w: Far above the pI both acidic groups are deprotonated: –COOH → –COO− and –NH+3 → –NH2, giving H2N–CH(CH3)–COO− (net −1). The zwitterion is the main form at the pI, not far above it.
x: This is the zwitterion, the main form at the pI. Far above the pI, OH<sup>−</sup> removes another H<sup>+</sup>.
This fully protonated form (net +1) is found in strongly acidic solution, far below the pI.
This uncharged form is almost never present in water. In strongly basic solution, ask which groups lose H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Aspartic acid has the side chain –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH. What is its net charge in blood at physiological pH (7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4, every –COOH is ionized and the α-amino group is still –NH+3. Add up the charges.
w: At pH 7.4: α-COO− (−1), side-chain COO− (−1), α-NH+3 (+1). Net = −1, which is why Asp is called an acidic amino acid. Answering 0 forgets the ionized side chain.
x: A net charge of 0 forgets that the side-chain –COOH is also ionized at pH 7.4. Count all three charged groups.
A +1 charge would require extra positive groups. At pH 7.4 the carboxyl groups are negative and only the α-amino group is positive.
−2 counts both –COO<sup>−</sup> groups but forgets the α-amino group, which is still –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.

q: A membrane protein has an α-helix that passes through the nonpolar interior of the lipid bilayer. Which side chains would most likely face the fatty acid tails?
h: “Like dissolves like”: which R groups are hydrocarbons with no charge or polar groups?
w: The lipid tails are nonpolar, so they contact nonpolar (hydrophobic) side chains such as Leu, Val and Ile. Basic, acidic and polar side chains prefer water and are found on surfaces exposed to the cytosol or the outside of the cell.
x: Lysine, arginine and histidine have basic side chains that can carry a positive charge. Charged groups avoid the nonpolar interior of the bilayer.
Aspartate and glutamate are negatively charged and serine is polar. These side chains prefer water, not fatty acid tails.
Serine, threonine and glutamine all have polar side chains (–OH or amide) that hydrogen bond with water, so they avoid the nonpolar lipid tails.

q: In a folded protein, which pair of side chains would most likely form a salt bridge?
h: A salt bridge is an ionic (electrostatic) attraction. Which pair carries opposite charges?
w: A salt bridge forms between a positively charged side chain (Lys) and a negatively charged one (Asp). Leu/Val form hydrophobic interactions, Ser/Thr form hydrogen bonds, and two Cys form a disulfide bond.
x: Leucine and valine have nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains with no charge. They attract each other by hydrophobic interactions.
Serine and threonine both have –OH groups, so they form hydrogen bonds. Neither is charged.
Two cysteine –SH groups form a covalent disulfide bond, not an ionic attraction.

q: Hemoglobin carries O<sub>2</sub> by binding it to the Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion in each heme group. Carbon monoxide poisoning is dangerous mainly because CO
c: binds the iron in hemoglobin more tightly than O<sub>2</sub> does
hydrolyzes the peptide bonds in hemoglobin's four chains
oxidizes the heme iron and converts hemoglobin into myoglobin
denatures plasma albumin so blood can no longer carry CO<sub>2</sub>
h: What happens if another molecule takes the O<sub>2</sub> spot on the iron and holds it tightly?
w: Hemoglobin in red blood cells transports O2 from the lungs to the tissues using Fe2+ in its heme groups. CO binds that iron far more tightly than O2, so less O2 is delivered. CO does not break peptide bonds.
x: CO does not break peptide bonds; that is hydrolysis. Think about what CO does at the iron where O<sub>2</sub> normally binds.
Hemoglobin cannot be converted into a different protein, myoglobin. Focus on how CO competes with O<sub>2</sub> at the heme iron.
CO's main danger involves hemoglobin and oxygen delivery, not albumin or CO<sub>2</sub>. Think about the Fe<sup>2+</sup> binding site.

q: Which amino acid side chain can form hydrogen bonds with water?
h: A hydrogen bond needs H bonded directly to F, O or N. Look for that in the side chain.
w: Serine has an O–H group in its side chain, so it can donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water (polar, hydrophilic). The other three side chains are only C and H, so they are nonpolar and hydrophobic.
x: Alanine's –CH<sub>3</sub> side chain has only C–H bonds, so it is nonpolar and cannot hydrogen bond with water.
Phenylalanine's side chain is a benzene ring plus CH<sub>2</sub>: only carbon and hydrogen, so it is nonpolar.
Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group made only of C and H, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.

q: An enzyme from the pancreas hydrolyzes the ester bonds of dietary triacylglycerols in the small intestine. What type of enzyme is it?
h: Enzyme names often come from the substrate plus “-ase.” What kind of biomolecule is a triacylglycerol?
w: A triacylglycerol is a lipid, so the enzyme is a lipase. Amylase digests starch, a protease digests proteins, and a nuclease digests nucleic acids.
x: Amylase hydrolyzes starch, a carbohydrate. A triacylglycerol is a different type of biomolecule.
A protease hydrolyzes the peptide bonds of proteins. Triacylglycerols contain ester bonds, not peptide bonds.
A nuclease hydrolyzes nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). Think about what class of biomolecule a triacylglycerol is.

q: In glycolysis, an enzyme converts glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate. Both have the formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>O<sub>9</sub>P<sup>2−</sup>. To which enzyme class does this enzyme belong?
h: The reactant and product have the same formula. What kind of change is that?
w: Only the arrangement of atoms changes (an aldose becomes a ketose), so the enzyme is an isomerase. No group moves to another molecule (transferase), and no water is added (hydrolase).
x: A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here one molecule just rearranges, keeping the same formula.
A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond, or breaks bonds without water. The formula here does not change at all.
A hydrolase adds water to split a molecule. The product has exactly the same formula as the reactant.

q: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (6 C) into two 3-carbon molecules by breaking a C–C bond, without adding water and without oxidation. To which enzyme class does aldolase belong?
h: Which class breaks (or forms) bonds without water and without a redox change?
w: A lyase cleaves C–C (or C–O, C–N) bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation, often forming double bonds or adding groups to them. A hydrolase would need water, and a ligase joins molecules using ATP.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. The question says no water is added.
An oxidoreductase catalyzes redox reactions. The question says there is no oxidation.
A ligase joins two molecules using energy from ATP. Aldolase splits one molecule into two.

q: Pyruvate carboxylase catalyzes the reaction below. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Two molecules are joined into one, and ATP energy is spent to do it.
w: Joining two molecules (pyruvate + CO2) with energy from ATP hydrolysis is the job of a ligase. A lyase can add groups to double bonds but does not use ATP; a transferase only moves a group from one molecule to another.

f.text: pyruvate + CO<sub>2</sub> + ATP → oxaloacetate + ADP + P<sub>i</sub>

x: A lyase can add groups to a double bond, but it does not use ATP. This reaction spends ATP to join two molecules.
A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here pyruvate and CO<sub>2</sub> are joined into one molecule with ATP energy.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Here two molecules are joined into one.

q: In a lab experiment, substrate is kept in large excess while the amount of enzyme is increased. How does a graph of reaction rate versus enzyme concentration look?
c: a straight line rising steadily as enzyme is added
a curve that rises and then levels off at a maximum
a bell-shaped curve with a peak at an optimum value
a line falling steadily as enzyme is added
h: With plenty of substrate, every new enzyme molecule finds substrate to work on. Is there anything to run out of?
w: When substrate is in excess, each added enzyme molecule works at full speed, so the rate is directly proportional to [E]: a straight, rising line. The leveling-off curve is the rate vs. [substrate] graph (active sites saturate); bell curves describe temperature and pH.
x: Leveling off is the rate vs. [substrate] graph, where active sites become saturated. Here substrate is always in excess.
Bell-shaped curves with an optimum describe temperature and pH. Changing the amount of enzyme does not have an optimum.
Adding more catalyst does not slow a reaction down. Each added enzyme molecule has plenty of substrate to work on.

q: An inhibitor slows an enzyme, but the inhibition disappears when a large excess of substrate is added. What type of inhibitor is it?
h: If substrate can “win,” the inhibitor and the substrate must be fighting over the same place.
w: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site, so a high [substrate] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the active site's shape, so adding substrate does not help.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site, so adding more substrate does not help.
An irreversible inhibitor bonds permanently, so extra substrate cannot reverse it.
An activator speeds an enzyme up. This molecule slows the enzyme.

q: Which fat-soluble vitamin is correctly matched with its main function?
c: vitamin K: needed for blood clotting
vitamin D: needed for night vision
vitamin A: needed for blood clotting
vitamin K: needed for calcium absorption
h: Recall which fat-soluble vitamin is needed for vision, which helps build bones, and which helps blood form clots.
w: Vitamin K is needed to make clotting factors (newborns get a vitamin K shot for this reason). Vitamin A forms retinal for vision, and vitamin D (made in skin exposed to sunlight) increases calcium absorption for bones.
x: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for bones. Night vision depends on a different vitamin.
Vitamin A is used to make retinal for vision. Clotting depends on a different vitamin.
Calcium absorption is the job of vitamin D. Recall what the "K" (Koagulation) stands for.

q: What is the structural difference between ribose and deoxyribose?
c: Deoxyribose has –H instead of –OH on carbon 2′
Deoxyribose has –H instead of –OH on carbon 3′
Deoxyribose has one fewer carbon atom than ribose
Deoxyribose is a six-membered ring; ribose has five atoms
h: “Deoxy” means “missing one oxygen.” Which ring carbon of the sugar carries –H instead of –OH in DNA?
w: Both are five-carbon sugars, but deoxyribose has –H in place of –OH at C2′. The 3′–OH is needed in both to form phosphodiester bonds, so it cannot be the missing one.
x: The 3′–OH is needed in both DNA and RNA to form phosphodiester bonds, so it is not the one that is missing.
Both ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon sugars. The difference is one oxygen atom, not a carbon.
Both sugars form the same five-membered ring (four carbons and one oxygen). The difference is one –OH group.

q: Which nitrogenous bases are purines, with a double (fused) ring structure?
h: Pyrimidines have a single six-membered ring. A mnemonic: “Pure As Gold.”
w: Adenine and guanine are purines (a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring). C, T and U are single-ring pyrimidines. Each base pair joins one purine with one pyrimidine.
x: Cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines, with a single six-membered ring.
Cytosine and uracil are pyrimidines, with one ring each.
Adenine is a purine, but thymine is a single-ring pyrimidine. Each base pair joins one purine with one pyrimidine.

q: In a human cell, where do DNA replication, transcription and translation occur?
c: replication and transcription in the nucleus; translation on ribosomes in the cytoplasm
replication in the nucleus; transcription and translation on ribosomes in the cytoplasm
all three occur on ribosomes attached to the endoplasmic reticulum
replication in the cytoplasm; transcription and translation in the nucleus
h: DNA stays in the nucleus. Which processes need DNA as a template, and where are the ribosomes?
w: Both replication and transcription use DNA as the template, so they happen in the nucleus. The mRNA then leaves through nuclear pores, and translation happens on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
x: Transcription uses DNA as its template, and DNA stays in the nucleus. Only one of these processes happens in the cytoplasm.
Replication and transcription need DNA, which is in the nucleus, not on ribosomes. Ribosomes carry out only one of the three processes.
This has the locations reversed. DNA is in the nucleus, so the processes that copy or read DNA happen there.

q: Which DNA replication enzyme is correctly matched with its job?
c: DNA ligase: seals the gaps between DNA fragments
helicase: adds nucleotides to the new strand
DNA polymerase: unwinds the parent double helix
h: Helicase unwinds, primase lays down a short RNA primer, polymerase builds DNA, and one enzyme “glues” pieces together.
w: DNA ligase forms the final phosphodiester bonds that join Okazaki fragments. Helicase breaks the H bonds to unwind the helix, primase makes the RNA primer, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides 5′→3′.
x: Helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases. Another enzyme adds nucleotides.
Primase makes the short RNA primer that starts a new strand. A different enzyme joins the fragments.
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the growing strand. Unwinding the helix is another enzyme's job.

q: During translation, the anticodon on a tRNA is held to the matching codon on the mRNA by
c: covalent peptide bonds between the bases
phosphodiester bonds between the two strands
ester bonds between the sugars of each RNA
h: Codon–anticodon pairing is temporary, like base pairing in the DNA double helix.
w: The codon and anticodon pair like DNA bases (A–U, G–C), held by hydrogen bonds, so the tRNA can leave after its amino acid is added. Peptide bonds form between amino acids, not between bases.
x: Peptide bonds join amino acids, not bases. Codon–anticodon pairing must also be temporary so the tRNA can leave.
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within one strand's backbone. They do not hold two separate RNAs together.
Ester bonds link parts within a single molecule's backbone. The pairing between tRNA and mRNA is a weaker, temporary attraction.

q: Before translation, each amino acid is attached to its tRNA. What bond joins them in the aminoacyl-tRNA?
c: an ester bond from the amino acid's –COOH to the 3′ end of the tRNA
a peptide bond from the amino acid's –NH<sub>2</sub> to the anticodon
hydrogen bonds between the amino acid's R group and the anticodon
a phosphodiester bond from the amino acid to the 5′ end of the tRNA
h: The 3′ end of every tRNA ends in a sugar with a free –OH. What forms when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol?
w: The amino acid's carboxyl group is joined to the –OH of the ribose at the 3′ end (…CCA) of the tRNA by an ester bond, using ATP. The anticodon is at the other end of the tRNA and pairs with mRNA, not with the amino acid.
x: The anticodon is at the opposite end of the tRNA from the amino acid, and it pairs with mRNA, not the amino acid.
Hydrogen bonds are too weak to carry the amino acid reliably, and the amino acid does not attach at the anticodon.
The amino acid attaches at the tRNA's 3′ end, not the 5′ end, and the link does not involve a phosphate.

q: Which statement about viruses is correct?
c: A virus has DNA or RNA in a protein coat and needs a host cell to reproduce
A virus has both DNA and RNA and its own ribosomes to make proteins
A retrovirus uses reverse transcriptase to make RNA from a DNA template
A virus can make its own proteins outside a cell if it is given amino acids
h: Viruses are not cells. What do they have, and what must they borrow from the cells they infect?
w: A virus is nucleic acid (DNA or RNA, not both) in a protein coat, and it must use the host cell's ribosomes, enzymes and ATP to reproduce. A retrovirus such as HIV makes DNA from its RNA, the reverse of the statement given.
x: A virus has DNA or RNA, not both, and it has no ribosomes. It uses the host cell's ribosomes.
This reverses the direction. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template.
A virus has no ribosomes or enzymes for protein synthesis, so it cannot make proteins outside a host cell.

q: In the citric acid cycle, malate is converted to oxaloacetate: a –CH(OH)– group becomes a C=O group. How is this step labeled?
c: oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
reduction; NADH is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
oxidation; FAD is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
hydration; H<sub>2</sub>O is added to the molecule
h: Count hydrogens: are 2 H removed or added? Then match the coenzyme to the group: alcohol → C=O or –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– → –CH=CH–.
w: Converting an alcohol (–CH(OH)–) to a ketone (C=O) removes 2 H: an oxidation. Alcohol → carbonyl oxidations use NAD+, which is reduced to NADH + H+. FAD is used when C–C becomes C=C.
x: Going from –CH(OH)– to C=O removes hydrogen, so the substrate loses H, not gains it. Check whether the coenzyme gains or loses H.
Removing 2 H makes this an oxidation, but FAD is used when a C–C becomes a C=C. Here an alcohol becomes a carbonyl.
No water is added; a C=O forms from an alcohol by removing two H atoms. Hydration adds water across a C=C.

q: In the citric acid cycle, fumarate (–CH=CH–) reacts to form malate (–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(OH)–). How is this step labeled?
c: hydration; H<sub>2</sub>O adds across the C=C
oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> accepts two H atoms
dehydration; H<sub>2</sub>O is removed from the C–C
h: Compare formulas: what was added across the double bond, an H on one carbon and an OH on the other?
w: An H adds to one carbon and an –OH to the other, so H2O has added across the double bond: hydration. No coenzyme is needed. Dehydration is the reverse (removing water to make a C=C).
x: No hydrogen is removed, and no coenzyme is involved. Compare formulas: something is added across the double bond.
Dehydration removes water to make a C=C. Here the C=C disappears and an –OH appears, so this is the reverse process.
No carbon is lost; fumarate and malate both have 4 carbons. Look at what adds across the C=C.

q: In the citric acid cycle, isocitrate (6 C) is converted to α-ketoglutarate (5 C) as an –OH group becomes C=O, a CO<sub>2</sub> is released, and NAD<sup>+</sup> becomes NADH. How is this step best described?
h: Two things happen: the carbon count drops by one, and an alcohol becomes a ketone using NAD<sup>+</sup>.
w: Losing CO2 (6 C → 5 C) is a decarboxylation, and alcohol → ketone with NAD+ → NADH is an oxidation: oxidative decarboxylation. “Carboxylation” would add CO2, not remove it.
x: Carboxylation adds CO<sub>2</sub> and reduction adds hydrogen. Here a CO<sub>2</sub> leaves and NAD<sup>+</sup> takes away hydrogen, so both words point the wrong way.
That fits citrate → isocitrate, the step before. This step loses a carbon and reduces NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Substrate-level phosphorylation makes GTP or ATP directly, as in succinyl CoA → succinate. No phosphate transfer happens here.

q: The last step of glycolysis is shown below. Which description fits this step?
c: a phosphate is transferred to ADP, forming ATP
PEP is oxidized as NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
a phosphate is added to pyruvate, using up an ATP
CO<sub>2</sub> is removed from PEP in a decarboxylation
h: Track the phosphate group: which molecule loses it and which gains it?
w: PEP loses its phosphate group and ADP is phosphorylated to ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation). This step makes ATP rather than using it, and no NAD+ or CO2 is involved.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> is not used in this step; no hydrogen is removed. Follow the phosphate group instead.
Pyruvate is the product, and it has no phosphate. This step makes ATP rather than spending it.
PEP and pyruvate both have 3 carbons, so no CO<sub>2</sub> is lost. Track where the phosphate group goes.

q: In the citric acid cycle, citrate is converted to isocitrate. Both have the formula C6H5O3−7; only the –OH group moves to the neighboring carbon. How is this step labeled?
h: Compare the formulas of the reactant and product. Did anything get added or removed overall?
w: Same formula, different arrangement: isomerization (it happens by removing and then re-adding water). There is no loss of H (oxidation), no water consumed overall (hydrolysis) and no CO2 lost.
x: Oxidation removes H atoms, but the formula is unchanged. Nothing has been lost overall.
Hydrolysis would split a bond using water and change the formula. Here reactant and product have the same formula.
Decarboxylation removes CO<sub>2</sub>, which would lower the carbon count. Both compounds have 6 carbons.

q: In the final step of each β-oxidation cycle, a 2-carbon acetyl unit is split off from the fatty acyl chain, and the shortened chain is attached to a new coenzyme. Which coenzyme is it?
h: The shortened fatty acid must stay “activated” as a thioester (acyl-CoA) to enter the next cycle.
w: Thiolysis uses HS–CoA to cleave the bond, releasing acetyl CoA and a fatty acyl CoA two carbons shorter. Acetyl CoA is the product that leaves, not the coenzyme that attaches; NAD+ and FAD are the oxidizing agents in earlier steps of the cycle.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> oxidizes the –OH to C=O in step 3. It does not attach to the shortened chain.
FAD forms the C=C in step 1 of each cycle. It does not become part of the shortened acyl chain.
Acetyl CoA is the 2-carbon product that leaves. The shortened chain needs a fresh coenzyme to stay activated as a thioester.

q: A granola bar contains the nutrients listed in the table. Using the energy values given, what is its energy content?
h: Multiply each mass by its energy value (4, 9, 4 kcal g⁻¹) and add.
w: (24.0 g × 4 kcal g⁻¹) + (9.0 g × 9 kcal g⁻¹) + (6.0 g × 4 kcal g⁻¹) = 96 + 81 + 24 = 201 kcal. Using 4 kcal g⁻¹ for everything gives 156 kcal; switching the fat and protein values gives 186 kcal; leaving out the protein gives 177 kcal.
x: 156 kcal uses 4 kcal g⁻¹ for every nutrient. Fat provides 9 kcal g⁻¹.
177 kcal leaves out the protein. Include all three nutrients from the table.
186 kcal switches the fat and protein values. Fat is the nutrient worth 9 kcal g⁻¹.

q: A serving of a snack food contains the nutrients listed in the table. Using the energy values given, what percent of its Calories (kcal) come from fat?
h: Find the kcal from each nutrient first, then divide fat kcal by the total kcal.
w: Fat: 12.0 × 9 = 108 kcal; carbohydrate: 30.0 × 4 = 120 kcal; protein: 8.0 × 4 = 32 kcal; total = 260 kcal. 108/260 × 100 = 42%. 47% leaves the protein out of the total (108/228); 58% is the percent that does not come from fat; 71% divides the fat kcal by the carbohydrate and protein kcal only (108/152).
x: 47% leaves the protein out of the total. Divide by the kcal from all three nutrients.
71% divides the fat kcal by only the carbohydrate and protein kcal. The total must include the fat kcal too.
58% is the share of Calories that does not come from fat. Find the fat portion instead.

q: Myristic acid is a saturated fatty acid with 14 carbons. How many β-oxidation cycles are needed to break it down completely, and how many acetyl CoA are produced?
h: Each cycle removes one 2-carbon unit, but the last cycle leaves two acetyl CoA at once.
w: Acetyl CoA = 14/2 = 7. Cycles = 14/2 − 1 = 6 cycles; 7 acetyl CoA. The final cycle splits a 4-carbon chain into two acetyl CoA, so one fewer cycle than acetyl CoA is needed.
x: 7 cycles counts one cycle per acetyl CoA. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA, so one fewer cycle is needed.
6 cycles is right, but the last cycle releases two acetyl CoA at once. Divide the carbons by 2 for the acetyl CoA count.
Each acetyl CoA carries 2 carbons, so 14 acetyl CoA would need 28 carbons. Also think about how the last cycle changes the number of cycles.
