q: Arachidic acid is a saturated fatty acid with 20 carbons. Using the ATP values in the table (subtract the activation cost), how many ATP form from its complete oxidation?
h: Cycles = C/2 − 1, acetyl CoA = C/2, and each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 10 acetyl CoA × 10 = 100; 9 cycles → 9 NADH × 2.5 = 22.5 and 9 FADH2 × 1.5 = 13.5. Total 136 − 2 (activation) = 134 ATP. 136 forgets the activation cost; 138 uses 10 cycles instead of 9.
x: 136 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
138 uses 10 β-oxidation cycles. The number of cycles is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
140 uses 10 cycles and also leaves out the 2-ATP activation cost.

q: In the electron transport chain, a mitochondrion oxidizes the reduced coenzymes listed in the table. How many ATP are produced?
h: Multiply each coenzyme by its own ATP value. NADH gives more ATP than FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 4 NADH × 2.5 = 10 ATP and 2 FADH2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP; total = 13 ATP. Using 2.5 for both coenzymes gives 15; the older values of 3 and 2 give 16; using 3 for all six coenzymes gives 18.
x: 18 counts all six coenzymes at 3 ATP each. Use the table: NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> have different values.
15 uses 2.5 ATP for every coenzyme. FADH<sub>2</sub> gives less ATP than NADH.
16 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 from the table.

q: A student eats a turkey sandwich. In her stomach and small intestine, the turkey's proteins are hydrolyzed into free amino acids. Which stage of catabolism is this?
h: Stage 1 breaks big food molecules into their building blocks; stage 2 turns those into pyruvate or acetyl CoA.
w: Hydrolyzing polymers (proteins, starch, fats) into monomers is stage 1, digestion. Stage 2 would degrade the amino acids further to smaller compounds such as acetyl CoA; stage 3 oxidizes acetyl CoA in the citric acid cycle and electron transport.
x: Stage 2 starts after the amino acids are absorbed, when they are degraded to smaller compounds such as acetyl CoA. Here the protein is just being cut into monomers.
Stage 3 is the citric acid cycle and electron transport inside mitochondria. Breaking food proteins in the gut happens much earlier.
Anabolism builds larger molecules. Hydrolyzing proteins into amino acids breaks molecules down.

q: Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation, which make most of a cell's ATP, are part of which stage of catabolism?
h: Glycolysis and β-oxidation stop at pyruvate or acetyl CoA. Which stage finishes the job and uses O<sub>2</sub>?
w: Acetyl CoA is oxidized in the citric acid cycle, and the NADH and FADH2 it makes feed electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation: stage 3, oxidation. Stage 2 (glycolysis, β-oxidation) only produces pyruvate and acetyl CoA; stage 1 is digestion.
x: Stage 2 includes glycolysis and β-oxidation, which stop at pyruvate or acetyl CoA. Electron transport comes after that.
Stage 1 is digestion of food polymers into monomers in the gut. It produces no NADH for electron transport.
Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation release energy from fuel, which is catabolism, not anabolism.

q: A patient has had most of his stomach surgically removed. The normal starting point for digesting which nutrient has been lost?
h: Think about which digestive enzyme works in an acidic environment and where each nutrient's digestion begins.
w: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where HCl and pepsin start hydrolyzing peptide bonds. Starch digestion begins in the mouth (salivary amylase), and fats and lactose are digested mainly in the small intestine, so those starting sites are untouched.
x: Starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase, which the surgery does not affect.
Triacylglycerols are digested mainly in the small intestine with bile salts and pancreatic lipase.
Lactose is digested in the small intestine by lactase. Think about which digestive enzyme works in an acidic environment.

q: In the liver, lactate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–COO<sup>−</sup>, is converted back to pyruvate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–COO<sup>−</sup>. Which coenzyme change accompanies this step?
h: Compare the carbon with the –OH before and after. Did it lose H atoms (oxidation) or gain them? Which coenzyme handles C–O bonds?
w: A C–OH becomes C=O: two H atoms are removed, so lactate is oxidized. Alcohol → carbonyl oxidations use NAD+, which is reduced: NAD+ → NADH + H+. FAD is used when a C=C forms; NADH + H+ → NAD+ would be the reverse reaction (pyruvate → lactate in muscle).
x: FAD is used when a C–C single bond becomes a C=C. Here an alcohol is oxidized to a C=O.
This is the coenzyme change for pyruvate → lactate in muscle, the reverse direction. Here lactate loses two H atoms.
No phosphate is transferred in this step. Compare the C–OH carbon before and after to see whether H is removed.

q: When ketone bodies form during fasting, acetoacetate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>, can be turned into β-hydroxybutyrate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>. Which statement about the coenzyme is TRUE?
c: NADH is the reducing agent and is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
NAD<sup>+</sup> is the oxidizing agent and is reduced to NADH.
NADH is the oxidizing agent and is reduced to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
FAD is the oxidizing agent and is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>.
h: C=O becoming CH–OH means the substrate gained H. Something had to donate it. A reducing agent itself gets oxidized.
w: The ketone C=O gains two H to become an alcohol: the substrate is reduced. The H comes from NADH + H+, so NADH is the reducing agent and is oxidized to NAD+. NAD+ → NADH would be the opposite direction (alcohol → ketone).
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH would accompany an oxidation, alcohol → ketone. Here the ketone C=O gains hydrogen to become an alcohol.
The direction is right, but NADH donates hydrogen, which makes it a reducing agent. An agent that is oxidized cannot be the oxidizing agent.
FAD is used for C–C → C=C oxidations. This step adds hydrogen to a C=O, so the substrate is reduced, not oxidized.

q: Succinate dehydrogenase, the citric acid cycle enzyme that converts succinate to fumarate, is part of Complex II in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Using the electron transport chain shown, to which electron carrier does its FADH<sub>2</sub> pass electrons?
h: FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons enter the chain after Complex I. Which mobile carrier collects electrons from both Complex I and Complex II?
w: Complex II hands electrons from FADH2 to coenzyme Q (CoQ → CoQH2), which carries them to Complex III. Because they skip Complex I, fewer protons are pumped, which is why FADH2 gives only about 1.5 ATP.
x: Cytochrome c carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV. FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons reach an earlier carrier first.
FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons skip Complex I entirely, which is why they pump fewer protons.
O<sub>2</sub> accepts electrons only at Complex IV, at the end of the chain. FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons still pass through several carriers first.

q: In the energy-investment half of glycolysis, how many ATP are used per glucose molecule?
h: Count the steps where a phosphate is added from ATP before fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split.
w: ATP is spent twice: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase) and fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. That is 2 ATP invested. 4 ATP are made later, which is why the net yield is 2.
x: Count again: ATP is spent at two separate phosphorylation steps before fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split.
4 ATP are made in the energy-payoff half, not spent in the investment half.
The first half is called the investment phase because it does spend ATP. Look for the steps where a phosphate is added from ATP.

q: In the glycolysis pathway shown, NADH is produced in only one step. Which conversion is it?
h: Find the step where NAD<sup>+</sup> goes in and NADH comes out. In that step an aldehyde carbon is oxidized.
w: In the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate step, the aldehyde (–CHO) is oxidized as Pi is attached, and NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The other three steps are phosphate transfers involving ATP and need no NAD+.
x: This step adds a phosphate from ATP. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD<sup>+</sup> is not involved.
This step transfers PEP's phosphate to ADP, making ATP. It is not an oxidation.
This first step adds a phosphate from ATP to glucose. Look for the step where an aldehyde carbon is oxidized.

q: In the citric acid cycle shown, which step forms GTP (or ATP) directly, without electron transport?
h: Find GTP on the wheel. It forms at the step where a high-energy thioester bond is broken.
w: Hydrolysis of the thioester in succinyl CoA → succinate is downhill enough overall (breaking the bond itself takes energy; more is released as the products form) to make GTP from GDP + Pi (substrate-level phosphorylation). The other three are oxidations that make NADH or FADH2, which give ATP only later through electron transport.
x: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate is an oxidative decarboxylation that makes NADH and CO<sub>2</sub>, not GTP.
Succinate → fumarate makes FADH<sub>2</sub>, which yields ATP only later through electron transport.
Malate → oxaloacetate makes NADH, which yields ATP only later through electron transport.

q: Use the citric acid cycle shown. Which list contains ONLY steps that reduce NAD<sup>+</sup> to NADH?
c: isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate; α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA; malate → oxaloacetate
citrate → isocitrate; succinate → fumarate; malate → oxaloacetate
isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate; succinate → fumarate; fumarate → malate
α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA; succinyl CoA → succinate; fumarate → malate
h: Find each NADH on the wheel and note the conversion it comes from.
w: The three NADH come from the two oxidative decarboxylations (isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate, α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA) and malate → oxaloacetate. Succinate → fumarate uses FAD; citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization and fumarate → malate a hydration; succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP.
x: Citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization, and succinate → fumarate reduces FAD, not NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Succinate → fumarate reduces FAD, and fumarate → malate is a hydration with no coenzyme.
Succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP, and fumarate → malate is a hydration. Neither reduces NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: Electrons from NADH travel through the electron transport chain. Which sequence shows the correct path?
c: Complex I → CoQ → Complex III → cyt c → Complex IV → O<sub>2</sub>
Complex I → cyt c → Complex III → CoQ → Complex IV → O<sub>2</sub>
Complex II → CoQ → Complex IV → cyt c → Complex III → O<sub>2</sub>
O<sub>2</sub> → Complex IV → cyt c → Complex III → CoQ → Complex I
h: The two mobile carriers alternate with the complexes: one small lipid-soluble carrier after Complex I, one small protein after Complex III.
w: NADH gives electrons to Complex I; CoQ carries them to Complex III; cytochrome c carries them to Complex IV, which reduces O2 to water: I → CoQ → III → cyt c → IV → O2. Electrons flow toward O2, not away from it.
x: The two mobile carriers are swapped. The small lipid-soluble carrier picks up electrons from Complex I; the small protein comes later.
NADH enters at Complex I, not Complex II, and Complex III comes before Complex IV.
This sequence runs backward. Electrons flow from NADH toward O<sub>2</sub>, not away from it.

q: Which component of the electron transport chain transfers electrons but does NOT pump H<sup>+</sup> into the intermembrane space?
h: Three complexes act as proton pumps. The one that does not is the entry point for FADH<sub>2</sub> from succinate.
w: Complexes I, III and IV pump H+, building the proton gradient. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) only passes electrons from FADH2 to CoQ, so FADH2 electrons drive fewer protons across the membrane.
x: Complex I, the NADH entry point, is a proton pump. Look for the complex where FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons enter.
Complex III pumps H<sup>+</sup> as it passes electrons from CoQ to cytochrome c.
Complex IV pumps H<sup>+</sup> as it passes electrons to O<sub>2</sub>.

q: Lignoceric acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>22</sub>COOH, is a saturated 24-carbon fatty acid. Using the ATP values in the table (subtract the activation cost), how many ATP are produced by its complete oxidation?
h: Acetyl CoA = carbons ÷ 2; β-oxidation cycles = acetyl CoA − 1; each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 24 C → 12 acetyl CoA × 10 = 120 ATP. Cycles = 11 → 11 NADH × 2.5 + 11 FADH2 × 1.5 = 44 ATP. Total = 120 + 44 − 2 = 162 ATP. 164 forgets the activation cost; 166 uses 12 cycles instead of 11; 197 uses the older values of 12 ATP per acetyl CoA, 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH2.
x: 164 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
166 uses 12 β-oxidation cycles. The number of cycles is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
197 uses the older values of 12 ATP per acetyl CoA, 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: Caprylic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>COOH, found in goat's milk, is completely broken down by β-oxidation. How many acetyl CoA, NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> are produced?
h: Count all carbons, including CH<sub>3</sub> and COOH. The last turn of the spiral releases two acetyl CoA at once.
w: CH3 + 6 CH2 + COOH = 8 C → 8/2 = 4 acetyl CoA. Cycles = 4 − 1 = 3, each giving 1 NADH and 1 FADH2: 4 acetyl CoA, 3 NADH, 3 FADH2. 4 NADH assumes one cycle per acetyl CoA.
x: 4 NADH and 4 FADH<sub>2</sub> assumes one cycle per acetyl CoA. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA.
3 acetyl CoA would be only 6 carbons. Count all the carbons, including the CH<sub>3</sub> and the COOH.
8 is the number of carbons, not acetyl CoA. Each acetyl CoA holds 2 carbons.

q: In one turn of β-oxidation: (1) a C=C forms between C2 and C3, (2) water adds across that C=C, (3) the new –OH is oxidized to C=O, and (4) HS–CoA cuts off acetyl CoA. Which coenzymes are reduced in reactions 1 and 3?
h: FAD handles –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– → –CH=CH–; NAD<sup>+</sup> handles C–OH → C=O.
w: Reaction 1 turns –CH2–CH2– into –CH=CH–, the kind of oxidation done by FAD; reaction 3 turns an alcohol into a ketone, done by NAD+. So each turn makes 1 FADH2, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl CoA.
x: The coenzymes are swapped. Forming a C=C from –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– uses one coenzyme, and oxidizing an alcohol to C=O uses the other.
Reaction 3 oxidizes an alcohol to a C=O. That type of oxidation does not use FAD.
Reaction 1 forms a C=C from a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group. That type of oxidation does not use NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: A child with an inherited carnitine deficiency becomes weak and has low blood glucose during fasting. Which process is directly impaired?
c: Moving fatty acyl groups into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation
Emulsifying dietary fats in the small intestine
Activating fatty acids by attaching them to CoA in the cytosol
h: Fatty acids are activated in the cytosol, but β-oxidation enzymes are inside the mitochondria. What carries them across?
w: Carnitine shuttles fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without it, fatty acyl groups cannot enter the matrix for β-oxidation, so fasting cells burn more glucose instead. Activation to fatty acyl CoA happens before carnitine is needed; bile salts and chylomicrons are digestion and transport steps.
x: Emulsifying dietary fat is done by bile salts in the intestine, not by carnitine.
Activation to fatty acyl CoA happens in the cytosol before carnitine is needed, so it still works. The problem comes in the next step.
Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the intestine. Carnitine works inside cells, at the mitochondrion.

q: Urea, H2N–CO–NH2, is made in the liver by the urea cycle shown. Carbamoyl phosphate is made from NH+4 and CO2. Where do the two nitrogen atoms of urea come from?
c: One from NH+4 (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from aspartate
Each from NH+4 released by transamination
Each from the amino group of glutamine in the kidney
One from CO<sub>2</sub> (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from ornithine
h: Look at the two nitrogen-containing compounds that enter the cycle. Which one is made from NH+4?
w: Carbamoyl phosphate (from NH+4 + CO2) supplies the first N, and aspartate supplies the second, leaving as fumarate. Transamination moves amino groups but does not release NH+4 (oxidative deamination does), and CO2 provides the carbon, not nitrogen.
x: Only one nitrogen comes from free NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, and transamination moves amino groups without releasing NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. Look for the second nitrogen-carrying compound that enters the cycle.
Urea is made in the liver, not the kidney, and the cycle uses two different nitrogen sources.
CO<sub>2</sub> contains no nitrogen; it provides urea's carbon. Ornithine is regenerated each turn rather than giving up its nitrogen.

q: Acetyl CoA cannot be converted into a net amount of glucose. The carbon skeleton of leucine is degraded only to acetyl CoA and acetoacetyl CoA. How is leucine classified?
c: Ketogenic: it cannot be used to make a net amount of glucose
Glucogenic: it can be converted to oxaloacetate
Essential and glucogenic: it can enter gluconeogenesis
Ketogenic: it is converted directly into urea
h: Gluconeogenesis needs pyruvate or a citric acid cycle intermediate. Acetyl CoA's two carbons are lost as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: Amino acids degraded to acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA can form ketone bodies or fatty acids but not a net amount of glucose, so leucine is ketogenic. Glucogenic amino acids give pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates. Urea comes from the amino group, not the carbon skeleton.
x: Leucine's skeleton gives only acetyl CoA and acetoacetyl CoA, not oxaloacetate. Glucogenic amino acids give pyruvate or cycle intermediates.
Leucine is essential, but its carbon skeleton cannot enter gluconeogenesis, because acetyl CoA's carbons leave as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Urea comes from the amino group, not the carbon skeleton. Classification depends on what the skeleton becomes.

q: The hydrolysis of ATP is shown below (energy released per mole of ATP). How much energy is released when 0.50 mol of ATP is hydrolyzed?
h: Energy released = moles × energy per mole.
w: 0.50 mol × 7.3 kcal mol⁻¹ = 3.7 kcal (2 significant figures). 15 kcal comes from multiplying by 2 instead of 0.50; 0.068 kcal comes from dividing 0.50 by 7.3.
x: 7.3 kcal is the energy for 1 mol of ATP. You have only 0.50 mol.
15 kcal multiplies by 2 instead of by 0.50. Half a mole releases less than one mole.
0.068 kcal divides 0.50 by 7.3. Multiply the moles by the energy per mole instead.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis) with β-oxidation?
c: Lipogenesis occurs in the cytosol and uses NADPH; β-oxidation occurs in mitochondria and uses FAD and NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Lipogenesis occurs in mitochondria and uses FAD; β-oxidation occurs in the cytosol and uses NADPH.
Each occurs in mitochondria and uses NAD<sup>+</sup> as the main coenzyme.
Lipogenesis removes 2-carbon units as acetyl CoA; β-oxidation adds 2-carbon units from malonyl CoA.
h: Building pathways need a reducing agent; breakdown pathways need oxidizing agents. They are kept in different compartments.
w: Lipogenesis is anabolic: in the cytosol, 2-carbon units from malonyl CoA are added on the acyl carrier protein and reduced by NADPH. β-Oxidation is catabolic: in the mitochondrial matrix, FAD and NAD+ remove H as 2-carbon units leave as acetyl CoA. The choice that has lipogenesis removing 2-carbon units reverses the two pathways.
x: The two pathways are switched: building fatty acids uses a reducing coenzyme, and breakdown uses oxidizing ones, in different compartments.
The two pathways are kept in different compartments and use different coenzymes; building needs a reducing agent, breakdown needs oxidizing agents.
This reverses the pathways. Lipogenesis builds chains, and β-oxidation cuts them down.

q: In DNA, which base has a single (pyrimidine) ring and pairs with adenine?
h: Pyrimidines have one ring. Adenine's partner differs between DNA and RNA.
w: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine, a pyrimidine, through two hydrogen bonds. Uracil also pairs with adenine but is found in RNA, not DNA; guanine is a purine and cytosine pairs with guanine.
x: Uracil pairs with adenine and is a pyrimidine, but it is found in RNA, not DNA.
Guanine is a purine, with a double (fused) ring. It pairs with cytosine.
Cytosine is a pyrimidine, but it pairs with guanine, not adenine.

q: In a nucleotide, to which carbons of the pentose sugar are the nitrogenous base and the phosphate group attached?
c: Base at C1′; phosphate at C5′
Base at C5′; phosphate at C1′
Base at C1′; phosphate at C2′
Base at C3′; phosphate at C5′
h: Primed numbers label sugar carbons. The base attaches at the anomeric carbon; the phosphate attaches at the CH<sub>2</sub>–OH carbon outside the ring.
w: The base forms an N-glycosidic bond to C1′, and the phosphate is esterified to the –CH2OH of C5′. The C3′ –OH is used to link to the next nucleotide's phosphate, and C2′ is where ribose and deoxyribose differ.
x: This swaps the two positions. C5′ is the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon outside the ring, and C1′ is the anomeric carbon next to the ring oxygen.
C2′ is where ribose and deoxyribose differ (–OH or –H). The phosphate is not attached there.
C3′ carries an –OH that links to the next nucleotide's phosphate. The base attaches at a different carbon, next to the ring oxygen.

q: A eukaryotic pre-mRNA contains three exons separated by two introns, with the lengths shown in the table (5′ to 3′). After splicing, how many nucleotides from these regions remain in the mature mRNA?
h: Splicing removes the intervening (noncoding) sequences and joins the expressed sequences together.
w: Introns are cut out and exons are joined: 120 + 85 + 210 = 415 nucleotides. 450 is the total intron length that is removed, and 865 is the unspliced length.
x: 865 is the unspliced length: all five regions added together. Splicing removes some of them.
450 is the total length of the two introns, the part that is cut out, not the part that remains.
535 is the two introns plus exon 2. Splicing keeps the expressed sequences, not the intervening ones.

q: Which event occurs during the processing of eukaryotic pre-mRNA in the nucleus?
c: Introns are removed and exons are joined together.
Exons are removed and introns are joined together.
Thymine bases are replaced by uracil bases.
Codons are paired with tRNA anticodons.
h: Processing prepares the transcript before it leaves the nucleus. Which segments carry the code for the protein?
w: Exons are the expressed (coding) regions, so introns are cut out and the exons are spliced together. RNA is made with uracil from the start, and codon–anticodon pairing happens later, during translation on the ribosome.
x: This is backwards. Exons are the expressed (coding) regions that stay; think about which segments are cut out.
RNA is made with uracil from the start. There is no step that swaps thymine for uracil.
Codon–anticodon pairing happens during translation on the ribosome, after the mRNA leaves the nucleus.

q: A gene's coding (non-template) DNA strand reads 5′-ATGCCTAG-3′. Which mRNA does RNA polymerase produce from this gene?
h: The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, so it matches the coding strand except for one base.
w: The template strand is 3′-TACGGATC-5′; its complement is the mRNA, which has the same sequence as the coding strand with U in place of T: 5′-AUGCCUAG-3′. Taking the complement of the coding strand gives the template-like sequence 5′-UACGGAUC-3′, the most common mistake.
x: These letters are the complement of the coding strand, but the 5′ and 3′ ends are not reversed. The mRNA has the same sequence and direction as the coding strand, with U in place of T.
This is the template strand's sequence with U written for T. The mRNA is complementary to the template, so it matches the coding strand instead.
This is the coding strand itself, with T. RNA uses U in place of T.

q: Use this partial genetic code: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, CCG = Pro, AAA = Lys, UAA = stop. What peptide is made from the mRNA 5′-AUGUUUGGCUAA-3′?
h: Read the mRNA in groups of three from the 5′ end; a stop codon adds no amino acid.
w: Codons: AUG | UUU | GGC | UAA → Met, Phe, Gly, stop. The peptide is Met–Phe–Gly, written from the N-terminus. Reading 3′ → 5′ gives the reversed order, and UAA codes for no amino acid.
x: This swaps Phe and Gly. Read the codons in order from the 5′ end: the second codon is UUU.
This reverses the order. Peptides are written from the N-terminus, which comes from the first codon at the 5′ end.
UAA is a stop codon, so no amino acid is added there. Lys would need the AAA codon.

q: Transcription of the template triplet 3′-TAC-5′ gives an mRNA codon. What anticodon must a tRNA carry to recognize that codon?
h: Go two steps: DNA template → mRNA codon (complementary, U for T), then codon → anticodon (complementary and antiparallel).
w: Template 3′-TAC-5′ gives the codon 5′-AUG-3′. The antiparallel anticodon is 3′-UAC-5′ (= 5′-CAU-3′): it has the template's sequence, but with U for T. 5′-UAC-3′ has the right letters with the wrong orientation.
x: 3′-AUG-5′ is the codon's letters but written with the ends reversed. An anticodon must be complementary to the codon, not a copy of it.
This contains T, but tRNA is RNA and uses U instead of T.
These letters are right, but the ends are flipped. The anticodon must be antiparallel to the codon, which runs 5′→3′.

q: Compare the two DNA strands. Original: 5′-GATTACCA-3′. Mutated: 5′-GATACCA-3′. What type of mutation occurred?
h: Count the bases in each strand first.
w: The original has 8 bases and the mutant has 7: one T is missing, so this is a deletion. A substitution would keep the same length with one base changed. A single-base deletion also shifts the reading frame.
x: An insertion makes the strand longer. Count the bases: the mutated strand is shorter.
A substitution swaps one base for another, so the length stays the same. Count the bases in each strand.
A silent substitution changes one base without changing the length. Here the number of bases is different.

q: Which change in the coding region of a gene would NOT cause a frameshift?
h: The mRNA is read three bases at a time. Which change keeps the downstream codons in groups of three?
w: Removing three consecutive nucleotides removes one whole codon (one amino acid), and the reading frame downstream stays the same. Adding or removing 1 or 2 nucleotides shifts every codon after the mutation.
x: Deleting one nucleotide shifts every codon after it, so this does cause a frameshift.
Inserting two nucleotides leaves the downstream bases out of their groups of three, so the frame shifts.
One extra nucleotide moves every downstream codon over by one base, a classic frameshift.

q: During DNA replication, in which direction does DNA polymerase build the new (daughter) strand?
c: 3′ → 5′, adding nucleotides to the 5′ phosphate end
5′ → 3′ on the leading strand but 3′ → 5′ on the lagging strand
Toward and away from each fork at random
h: A new nucleotide's phosphate bonds to a free sugar –OH on the growing chain. Which end has that free –OH?
w: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the free 3′ –OH, so every new strand grows 5′ → 3′. The lagging strand also grows 5′ → 3′; it is made in short Okazaki fragments because it runs away from the fork.
x: DNA polymerase cannot add to a 5′ phosphate end. New nucleotides are joined to the free –OH on the growing strand.
The lagging strand grows in the same chemical direction as the leading strand. It is made in pieces for a different reason.
DNA polymerase always works in one fixed direction; it is not random. Think about which end of the strand has a free –OH.

q: Two double-stranded DNA samples have the same length. Sample X is 60% G + C and sample Y is 35% G + C. Which sample needs a higher temperature to separate its two strands, and why?
c: X, because G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds
X, because G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds
Y, because A–T pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds
Y, because more A–T pairs make a longer helix
h: Count hydrogen bonds per base pair for A–T and for G–C.
w: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs only two, so the G–C-rich sample X has more hydrogen bonds to break. Base pairs between strands are hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
x: Base pairs between strands are held by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds. Compare how many hydrogen bonds each type of pair has.
A–T pairs have two hydrogen bonds, not three. Recount the hydrogen bonds in each type of pair.
Both samples have the same length, and A–T pairs are not longer. Compare how many hydrogen bonds each pair has.

q: During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand. Which base is placed in the RNA opposite each adenine (A) in the template?
h: A pairs with the same partner in RNA as in DNA, but RNA does not contain one of the DNA bases.
w: Adenine pairs with a T/U-type base. RNA has no thymine, so uracil is placed opposite each A. Thymine would be used in DNA replication, not transcription.
x: Thymine pairs with adenine in DNA, but RNA does not contain thymine.
Adenine does not pair with another adenine. A purine pairs with a pyrimidine.
Guanine pairs with cytosine, not adenine.

q: Isocitrate dehydrogenase removes hydrogen from isocitrate and transfers it to NAD<sup>+</sup>. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: The name ends in “dehydrogenase.” What kind of reaction is removal of hydrogen?
w: Dehydrogenases catalyze oxidation–reduction reactions (substrate oxidized, NAD+ reduced), so they are oxidoreductases. Transferases move groups such as –NH2 or phosphate between molecules, which is a different reaction.
x: A transferase moves a group such as –NH<sub>2</sub> or phosphate between molecules. Removing hydrogen and giving it to NAD<sup>+</sup> is a different kind of reaction.
A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. No water is involved here.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Here hydrogen is removed and given to NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), measured in liver-function blood tests, moves an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate. To which enzyme class does ALT belong?
h: An amino group is moved from one molecule to another, with no water, no redox and no ATP.
w: Moving a functional group (here –NH2) from one substrate to another is the job of a transferase. Oxidative deamination, which releases NH+4 using NAD+, would be an oxidoreductase reaction.
x: A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond, or breaks bonds without water. Here a group is moved between two molecules.
A ligase joins two molecules using ATP energy. No ATP is used here.
An oxidoreductase moves electrons, usually with NAD<sup>+</sup> or FAD. No redox coenzyme is used in this reaction.

q: Which line lists a digestive enzyme with the nutrient it hydrolyzes and the organ where it mainly works?
h: Match each enzyme name to its substrate (amyl- = starch, lip- = fat), then check where that enzyme works.
w: Pepsin hydrolyzes proteins in the acidic stomach. Salivary amylase acts on starch, not fats; pancreatic lipase acts on fats, not starch; trypsin works in the small intestine, not the mouth.
x: Salivary amylase does work in the mouth, but it digests starch, not triacylglycerols (fats).
Pancreatic lipase does work in the small intestine, but it digests fats, not starch.
Trypsin does digest proteins, but it works in the small intestine, not the mouth.

q: Stomach acid (HCl, pH about 2) helps protein digestion. Which statement best describes how?
c: It denatures proteins, unfolding them so pepsin can reach the peptide bonds.
It hydrolyzes every peptide bond on its own, releasing free amino acids.
It breaks the primary structure by oxidizing the side chains of each amino acid.
It converts proteins to glucose so they can be absorbed into the blood.
h: Low pH disrupts salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Which levels of structure does that affect, and which bonds does pepsin hydrolyze?
w: HCl denatures proteins, disrupting secondary and tertiary structure so the chain unfolds and pepsin can hydrolyze the exposed peptide bonds. Acid alone does not break the primary structure into free amino acids; the enzymes do that.
x: Acid alone does not hydrolyze every peptide bond in the stomach. Breaking the chain into free amino acids is the job of digestive enzymes.
Stomach acid does not oxidize side chains, and the primary structure is held by covalent peptide bonds. Think about which weaker interactions low pH disrupts.
Proteins are digested to amino acids, not glucose. Think about what low pH does to a protein's folded shape.

q: The body makes nonessential amino acids by transferring an –NH<sub>2</sub> from glutamate to an α-keto acid. Why can't essential amino acids be made this way?
c: The body cannot make the α-keto acid carbon skeletons of essential amino acids.
There is not enough glutamate in cells to donate amino groups to every α-keto acid.
Essential amino acids contain no amino group, so they cannot accept one.
Transamination works only in the stomach, not inside the cells that need them.
h: Transamination needs two partners: an amino group donor and an α-keto acid acceptor. Which one is missing?
w: Transamination puts an –NH2 onto an α-keto acid. The body can make the keto acids (such as pyruvate → alanine) for nonessential amino acids but cannot synthesize the carbon skeletons of essential ones, so they must come from the diet. Amino groups (from glutamate) are not the limiting part.
x: Glutamate is not the limiting partner; amino groups are readily available. Ask which other partner in transamination the body cannot supply.
Every amino acid, essential or not, has an α-amino group. The issue is the rest of the molecule.
Transamination happens inside cells, mainly in the liver. The problem is a missing partner, not the location.

q: After fat digestion, triacylglycerols are re-formed inside intestinal cells. How are they transported away from the intestine?
c: Packaged into chylomicrons that enter the lymph
Dissolved directly in the blood plasma
Bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells
Converted to glucose before entering the blood
h: Triacylglycerols are nonpolar and do not dissolve in water. They need a coat of protein and phospholipid.
w: Triacylglycerols are coated with proteins and phospholipids to form chylomicrons, lipoproteins that enter the lymph and then the bloodstream. Fats are too nonpolar to dissolve in plasma, and hemoglobin carries O2, not lipids.
x: Triacylglycerols are nonpolar and do not dissolve in watery plasma. They need a coat of protein and phospholipid to travel.
Hemoglobin carries O<sub>2</sub>, not lipids. Fats are moved in lipoprotein particles.
The body cannot turn fatty acids into glucose. The re-formed triacylglycerols are shipped out intact.

q: Gram for gram, fat stores provide more than twice as much energy as glycogen. Which is the best explanation?
c: Fatty acid carbons are more reduced, so oxidizing them yields more NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>.
Fatty acids have more oxygen atoms per carbon, so they release more energy when oxidized.
Fats skip the citric acid cycle and electron transport, so less energy is lost as heat.
Fats are stored with extra water, and that water adds to the energy they release.
h: Compare a –CH<sub>2</sub>– group in a fatty acid with an H–C–OH group in glucose. Which one can still be oxidized more?
w: The –CH2– carbons of fatty acids are highly reduced, so oxidizing them yields more reduced coenzymes and more ATP per gram (about 9 vs 4 kcal g⁻¹). Glucose carbons already carry O. Fat is also stored nearly water-free, while glycogen holds water, which adds mass but no energy.
x: It is the reverse: fatty acids have fewer oxygen atoms per carbon. Carbons that already carry O have less left to oxidize.
Fatty acids do go through the citric acid cycle and electron transport: β-oxidation makes acetyl CoA, NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> that feed into them.
Water provides no energy when oxidized. In fact fat is stored nearly water-free, while glycogen holds extra water.

q: Sucrase, an enzyme on the lining of the small intestine, hydrolyzes table sugar. Which monosaccharides are absorbed as a result?
h: Name the two monosaccharides that make up sucrose.
w: Sucrose is glucose bonded to fructose, so its hydrolysis gives glucose and fructose. Glucose + galactose come from lactose (lactase), and two glucose units come from maltose (maltase).
x: Glucose and galactose come from lactose (milk sugar), digested by lactase. Table sugar has a different partner for glucose.
Two glucose units come from maltose, digested by maltase. Sucrose contains only one glucose unit.
Galactose is not part of sucrose; it comes from milk sugar. Recall the two sugars that make up table sugar.

q: Three of these alkenes give 2-methylbutane when H<sub>2</sub> adds over a Pt catalyst. Which alkene gives a different alkane?
h: Hydrogenation adds H to each C=C carbon but never changes the carbon skeleton. Which choice does not have a branched four-carbon chain?
w: H2 only saturates the C=C; the skeleton stays the same. The three branched alkenes all have a CH3 on carbon 2 of a four-carbon chain, so each gives 2-methylbutane. CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3 (1-pentene) is unbranched and gives pentane instead.
x: CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a CH<sub>3</sub> branch on carbon 2 of a four-carbon chain, so H<sub>2</sub> turns it into 2-methylbutane. Look for a skeleton without a branch.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub> is branched; saturating its C=C gives 2-methylbutane. Look for a skeleton without a branch.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH=CH<sub>2</sub> is branched; saturating its C=C gives 2-methylbutane. Look for a skeleton without a branch.

q: Bromine is red-brown. When Br<sub>2</sub> is added to 1-butene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, the color disappears. Which compound forms?
h: Halogenation of an alkene is an addition: open the double bond and put one Br on each of its two carbons.
w: Br–Br adds across the C=C, one Br on each double-bond carbon: CH2BrCHBrCH2CH3 (1,2-dibromobutane). CH3CHBrCH2CH3 would come from HBr, not Br2.
x: This has only one Br, on C2: that is the HBr product. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
This has only one Br. Br<sub>2</sub> supplies two Br atoms, one for each carbon of the C=C.
This puts a Br on C3, which was not part of the double bond. Both Br atoms go on the two carbons of the C=C.

q: Predict the alcohol formed in greatest amount when H<sub>2</sub>O (acid catalyst) adds to (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, 2-methyl-2-butene.
h: Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C. Markovnikov: the H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: The C=C carbons are C2 (no H) and C3 (one H). H adds to C3 and OH adds to C2, giving (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3 (2-methyl-2-butanol). Putting OH on C3 is the anti-Markovnikov mistake.
x: This puts the OH on C3, the double-bond carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. The OH goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
The OH here is on C4, a carbon that was not part of the C=C. Hydration only adds to the two double-bond carbons.
This alkane has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: 1-Butene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with HI to give 2-iodobutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHICH<sub>3</sub>. Which type of reaction is this?
h: Look at what added across the double bond: H<sub>2</sub>, X<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O or H–X?
w: An H and an I (from H–I) added across the C=C, so this is hydrohalogenation, an addition reaction. Halogenation would add two halogen atoms (X2); dehydrohalogenation is the reverse, removing H–X to make an alkene.
x: Halogenation adds X<sub>2</sub>, putting a halogen on both carbons. Here an H and only one I were added.
That name describes removing H and a halogen to make an alkene. Here something was added to the alkene, not removed.
Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub>, giving an alkane with no I. Look at what actually added across the double bond.

q: An alkyne has the condensed formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C≡CCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Which name is correct?
h: Give the triple bond the lowest number first. If that is a tie, number so the branch gets the lower number.
w: The chain has 6 carbons and the C≡C starts at C3 from either end, so the tie is broken by the branch: numbering from the isopropyl end puts the CH3 on C2: 2-methyl-3-hexyne. 5-Methyl gives the branch a higher number, and "-ene" would mean a C=C.
x: 5-Methyl numbers from the wrong end. The triple bond gets C3 either way, so the tie goes to the numbering that gives the branch the lower number.
-Ene means a C=C double bond. This molecule has a C≡C triple bond, which uses the -yne ending.
4-Hexyne gives the triple bond a higher number than needed. Number from the end that gives the C≡C the lowest number.

q: A branched alkane has the condensed formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Which name follows IUPAC rules?
h: Find the longest chain, number from the end nearest the first branch, and list substituents alphabetically.
w: The longest chain has 6 carbons. Numbering from the left puts branches at C2 (methyl) and C4 (ethyl); from the right they would be 3 and 5. Alphabetical order (ethyl before methyl) gives 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane.
x: The numbers are right, but substituents must be listed in alphabetical order. Compare the first letters of ethyl and methyl.
3 and 5 come from numbering from the end farther from the first branch. Number from the end that reaches a branch first.
An ethyl group on C2 means the chain was not the longest one: that ethyl would extend the main chain. Also check which end is nearer the first branch.

q: Light shines on a mixture of cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, and Br<sub>2</sub>. Which set of products forms?
h: An alkane has no double bond to open, so in light a halogen can only swap places with one H.
w: Alkanes undergo substitution: one H is replaced by Br, and that H leaves with the other Br as HBr: C6H11Br + HBr. Adding Br2 across a bond only happens with alkenes.
x: Br<sub>2</sub> cannot add to an alkane: there is no double bond to open. In light, a Br replaces an H instead.
The H removed from carbon pairs with the other Br atom, not with another H. Also, one Br<sub>2</sub> replaces only one H.
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Br is right, but the H that leaves does not form H<sub>2</sub>. It combines with the second Br atom of Br<sub>2</sub>.

q: Octane is a major component of gasoline. When the equation below for its complete combustion is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of O<sub>2</sub>?
h: Balance C, then H, then O. If O<sub>2</sub> needs a half, double every coefficient.
w: C8H18 → 8 CO2 + 9 H2O needs 8(2) + 9 = 25 O atoms = 12.5 O2. Doubling everything gives 2 C8H18 + 25 O2 → 16 CO2 + 18 H2O. Answering 12.5 stops before doubling, which is not a whole number; 16 copies the CO2 coefficient; 17 adds 8 + 9.
x: 12.5 balances the atoms, but it is not a whole number. Double every coefficient so all of them are whole numbers.
17 adds the CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O coefficients (8 + 9). Count O atoms instead: 2 per CO<sub>2</sub> and 1 per H<sub>2</sub>O, then divide by 2.
16 copies the CO<sub>2</sub> coefficient after doubling. The O<sub>2</sub> coefficient comes from counting every O atom in the products.

q: Name this alkene, in which the CH<sub>3</sub> group and the propyl group lie on opposite sides of the C=C: CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
h: Same side = cis, opposite sides = trans. Then number the chain so the C=C gets the lowest number.
w: The six-carbon chain is numbered from the end nearer the C=C, so the double bond starts at C2, and groups on opposite sides are trans: trans-2-hexene. Numbering from the other end (4-hexene) gives a higher number, and "hexyne" would mean a triple bond, which cannot be cis or trans.
x: Cis means the two carbon groups are on the same side of the C=C. In this molecule they are on opposite sides.
4-Hexene numbers from the end farther from the double bond. Number so the C=C gets the lowest number.
Hexyne means a C≡C triple bond. This compound has a C=C double bond; a triple bond cannot have cis or trans forms.

q: 2-Methyl-1-butene reacts with HCl as shown below. Predict the major organic product.
h: Hydrogen wants to make the most friends: H goes to the C=C carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: C1 (=CH2) has two H and C2 has none, so H adds to C1 and Cl adds to C2: CH3CCl(CH3)CH2CH3, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. 1-Chloro-2-methylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product; a dichloride would need Cl2.
x: Cl on C1 is the anti-Markovnikov product. C1 already has two H, so it gets the new H; Cl goes to the other double-bond carbon.
This puts the Cl next to the branch, on a carbon that was not part of the C=C. HCl adds only to the two double-bond carbons.
Two Cl atoms would need Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.

q: To which class of alcohol does isobutyl alcohol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH, belong?
h: Go to the carbon holding the –OH and count how many carbons are bonded to it.
w: The –OH carbon is a –CH2– bonded to only one other carbon, so this is a primary (1°) alcohol. The branch is on the next carbon over, so it does not change the classification.
x: A secondary alcohol has two carbons bonded to the C–OH carbon. Here the –CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon has only one carbon neighbor; the branch is one carbon over.
A tertiary alcohol has three carbons on the C–OH carbon. The branched carbon here does not hold the –OH.
A phenol has –OH directly on a benzene ring. This molecule has no ring.

q: Potassium dichromate oxidizes 3-pentanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Which compound forms?
h: Classify the alcohol first: 1° → aldehyde → acid, 2° → ketone, 3° → no reaction.
w: 3-Pentanol is a 2° alcohol (the –OH carbon has two carbons attached and one H), so oxidation turns C–OH into C=O on the same carbon: CH3CH2COCH2CH3 (3-pentanone).
x: An aldehyde comes from oxidizing a primary alcohol, with the –OH on an end carbon. Here the –OH is on the middle carbon, and oxidation does not move it.
This alkene would come from dehydration (loss of water), not oxidation with K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.
Only tertiary alcohols resist oxidation. The C–OH carbon in 3-pentanol still has an H to lose.

q: With an excess of K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, 1-butanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is oxidized as far as it can go. Which compound is the final product?
h: A 1° alcohol is oxidized in two steps. With excess oxidizing agent, does it stop after the first step?
w: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. With excess oxidant the aldehyde (butanal) is oxidized again to CH3CH2CH2COOH, butanoic acid. A ketone can only come from a 2° alcohol.
x: Butanal is the product of the first oxidation step. With excess K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> it does not stop there.
This is a ketone, which comes only from a secondary alcohol. 1-Butanol's –OH is on an end carbon, and oxidation does not move it.
This alkene comes from dehydration, not oxidation. K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> adds C–O bonds.

q: An alcohol with the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives no reaction when treated with K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. Which alcohol is it?
h: To be oxidized, the carbon holding the –OH must still have an H atom to lose.
w: Only a 3° alcohol has no H on the –OH carbon. In (CH3)3COH (tert-butyl alcohol) that carbon carries three CH3 groups, so it is not oxidized. The 2° alcohol would give a ketone and the 1° alcohols an aldehyde/acid.
x: This is a secondary alcohol; its C–OH carbon has one H, so it would be oxidized to a ketone.
This is a primary alcohol (the branch is not on the C–OH carbon), so it would be oxidized.
This is a primary alcohol with two H atoms on the C–OH carbon, so it would be oxidized.

q: Cyclohexanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, producing cyclohexene and water. This reaction is classified as
h: Compare reactant and product: what small molecule was removed, and was something added or taken away?
w: An –OH and an H from the neighboring carbon leave together as H2O and a C=C forms: an elimination called dehydration. Hydration is the reverse (adding water to an alkene).
x: Hydration adds water, usually to an alkene. Here water is a product, not a reactant.
Dehydrogenation removes only H<sub>2</sub>. Here an –OH and an H leave together.
Oxidation would form a C=O, giving cyclohexanone. Here a C=C forms and the oxygen leaves the molecule.

q: Which alkene forms in the greatest amount when 2-methyl-2-pentanol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, loses water in hot H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Remove the OH and an H from a neighboring carbon. When there is a choice, take the H from the neighbor that has fewer H atoms.
w: The –OH carbon (C2) has neighbors CH3 (3 H) and CH2 (2 H). Removing H from the CH2 (fewer H) gives the more substituted alkene, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH3 (2-methyl-2-pentene). CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH2CH3 forms too, but only as the minor product.
x: This alkene does form, but it is minor: the H came from a CH<sub>3</sub>, which has more H atoms. Zaitsev's rule favors the other neighbor.
Here the C=C is not on the carbon that held the –OH. Dehydration forms the double bond between the C–OH carbon and a neighbor.
This is an alkane, with no C=C. Losing water from an alcohol forms a double bond.

q: Skunk spray contains the thiol (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>SH. What is its IUPAC name?
h: An –SH group is a thiol: number the longest chain from the end nearer the –SH, then add the suffix -thiol.
w: The longest chain holding the –SH has 4 carbons; numbering from the –SH end puts SH on C1 and the CH3 on C3: 3-methyl-1-butanethiol. Numbering from the other end (2-methyl-4-...) gives the –SH a higher number, "-butanol" would need –OH, and "pentane" counts the branch into the chain.
x: Numbering from this end gives the –SH a higher number. Number from the end nearer the –SH group.
The -ol ending means an alcohol (–OH). This compound has –SH, so it is a thiol.
3-Methyl-1-pentanethiol has six carbons in all, but this molecule has only five. Count the longest chain holding the –SH, then count the branch separately.

q: Ethers are named by listing the two groups on the oxygen. How is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> named?
h: Name the two alkyl groups on the oxygen (watch for a Y-shaped branch), list them alphabetically, then add "ether".
w: One side is –CH2CH3 (ethyl); the other is –CH(CH3)2, a three-carbon Y-shaped group attached through its middle carbon (isopropyl): ethyl isopropyl ether. A propyl group would be the straight –CH2CH2CH3.
x: Propyl is a straight chain attached at its end, –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. The –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> group is attached through its middle carbon.
Methyl is one carbon. The left group on the O, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–, has two.
sec-Butyl has four carbons. Count the carbons in –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: there are three.

q: Number the parent chain so the –OH gets the lowest locant. Which IUPAC name fits CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Number the longest chain from the end that gives the carbon bearing –OH the lowest number.
w: The chain has 5 carbons. Numbering from the right puts –OH on C2 and the methyl on C4: 4-methyl-2-pentanol. Numbering from the left (2-methyl-4-pentanol) gives the –OH a higher number, which is not allowed.
x: Numbering from this end gives the –OH a higher number. The –OH carbon should get the lowest locant possible.
Hexanol would need six carbons in the main chain. The CH<sub>3</sub> branch is a substituent, not part of the longest chain.
2-Methyl-2-pentanol would have the CH<sub>3</sub> and the –OH on the same carbon. Here they are on different carbons.

q: The aldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CHO contributes to the aroma of cheese and chocolate. Which IUPAC name is correct?
h: The –CHO carbon is always C1 of an aldehyde chain. Count from there to the branch.
w: Start numbering at the –CHO carbon (C1); the chain has 4 carbons and the CH3 branch is on C3: 3-methylbutanal. Numbering from the other end (2-methyl) ignores the rule that the aldehyde carbon is C1.
x: 2-methyl comes from numbering from the branched end. In an aldehyde the –CHO carbon is always C1.
The -one ending is for ketones. A –CHO at the end of the chain is an aldehyde.
The -ol ending is for alcohols. This compound has a –CHO group, not an –OH.

q: A nerve-damaging workplace solvent, methyl butyl ketone, has the structure CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Under IUPAC rules it is called
h: CO in the middle of a condensed formula is a ketone C=O. Number so the carbonyl carbon gets the lowest number.
w: The C=O is on the second carbon of a six-carbon chain, so it is a ketone: 2-hexanone. Counting from the other end (5-hexanone) gives a higher number; hexanal would need a –CHO at the end.
x: Hexanal is an aldehyde with –CHO at the end of the chain. Here the C=O carbon has a CH<sub>3</sub> on one side.
5 comes from numbering from the wrong end. Number so the C=O carbon gets the lowest possible number.
2-Hexanol is an alcohol with –OH. This formula has a C=O, so it is not an alcohol.

q: Reduction ([H]) of pentanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, gives which compound?
h: Reduction is the reverse of oxidation: [H] adds H atoms across the C=O on the same carbon.
w: H adds to the C and O of the –CHO, so the end carbon becomes –CH2OH: CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH (1-pentanol), a 1° alcohol. The carboxylic acid would be an oxidation product.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> has the OH on carbon 2. Reduction puts the OH on the carbon that held the C=O, the end carbon.
The carboxylic acid is an oxidation product. [H] is a reduction.
An alkene has no oxygen. [H] adds H atoms across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.

q: When 3-methyl-2-butanone, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCOCH<sub>3</sub>, is reduced with [H] (a reducing agent), which product and alcohol class result?
h: A ketone's C=O carbon already has two carbon neighbors. What kind of alcohol does it become when C=O becomes CH–OH?
w: The C=O becomes CH–OH on the same carbon: (CH3)2CHCH(OH)CH3. That carbon has two carbons attached, so the product is 3-methyl-2-butanol, a 2° alcohol. Ketones always reduce to 2° alcohols; the skeleton and OH position do not move.
x: The name is right, but check the class. The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons and one H.
A carboxylic acid would be an oxidation product, and a ketone cannot form one. Adding [H] is reduction.
This moves the OH to a different carbon. Reduction keeps the oxygen on the same carbon that held the C=O.

q: Hemiacetals form when an aldehyde adds one alcohol molecule. Which structure is a hemiacetal?
h: Find a carbon with two oxygens on it. A hemiacetal carbon has one –OH, one –OR and no C=O.
w: In CH3CH(OH)OCH2CH3 one carbon holds –OH, –OCH2CH3 and an H (it came from an aldehyde plus one ethanol), so it is a hemiacetal. Two –OR groups = acetal; CH3COOCH2CH3 has C=O and –OR on one carbon, so it is an ester; the remaining structure has –OH and –OR on different carbons.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OCH<sub>3</sub>)OCH<sub>3</sub> has two –OR groups and no –OH, so two alcohol molecules have added: a full acetal.
CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a C=O and an –OR on the same carbon: that is an ester.
Here the –OH and the –OR are on different carbons, so it is an alcohol and an ether. A hemiacetal has both on one carbon.

q: Which reactants form the ketal (an acetal made from a ketone) CH<sub>3</sub>C(OCH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (with H<sup>+</sup> catalyst)?
h: Remove the two –OR groups and put back a C=O on that carbon. Is it at the end of the chain or in the middle?
w: The carbon with the two –OCH3 groups also has two carbon groups (CH3 and CH2CH3), so it came from a ketone, butanone, CH3COCH2CH3. Each –OCH3 came from methanol: butanone and two CH3OH.
x: Butanal has its C=O at the end of the chain, so it would give an acetal with an H on that carbon. The –OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon here has two carbon groups.
Ethanol would put –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the carbon. This ketal has –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups.
Alcohols and ethers do not combine to make a ketal. A ketal forms when alcohol molecules add to a C=O.

q: Propanal and butane have the same molar mass but very different boiling points (see table). What best explains the difference?
c: The polar C=O gives propanal dipole–dipole attractions.
Propanal molecules hydrogen bond to one another.
Propanal has much stronger London dispersion forces.
Propanal molecules form ionic bonds to each other.
h: Does propanal have an H on O, N or F? If not, what attraction does a polar bond give?
w: The C=O bond is polar, so propanal has dipole–dipole attractions that butane lacks. Propanal cannot H-bond to itself because it has no O–H; with equal molar masses, the London forces are similar.
x: Propanal has no H on O, N or F, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself.
London forces depend mostly on molar mass and size. These two have the same molar mass, so their London forces are similar.
Propanal is a neutral covalent molecule; it does not form ions or ionic bonds.

q: In uncontrolled diabetes, a patient's breath can smell like acetone, one of the ketone bodies. Which compound is a ketone?
h: Start at the C=O carbon: a ketone has a carbon on BOTH sides of it.
w: In CH3COCH2CH3 the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone (butanone). –CHO is an aldehyde, –COO– is an ester and C–O–C is an ether.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO ends in –CHO, so its C=O carbon has an H: that is an aldehyde.
CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a C=O and an –O– on the same carbon: that is an ester.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has no C=O at all; C–O–C is an ether.

q: Butanal reacts with ethanol under acid catalysis, as shown below. This reaction is an example of
h: Look at the product carbon: how many –OR groups and how many –OH groups does it have?
w: One alcohol added across the C=O of an aldehyde, giving a carbon with one –OH and one –OCH2CH3: hemiacetal formation. Acetal formation needs a second alcohol and gives two –OR groups with no –OH.
x: Acetal formation needs a second alcohol and gives two –OR groups with no –OH. Check how many –OH groups the product carbon has.
Esterification uses a carboxylic acid and gives a product with a C=O. Butanal is an aldehyde, and its C=O is used up.
Hydration adds water, giving two –OH groups. Here the reactant adding is ethanol, which brings an –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: This ester has a fruity smell: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Choose its correct name.
h: Split the ester at the single C–O next to C=O. The O–alkyl side is named first (-yl); the C=O side ends in -oate.
w: The C=O side, CH3CH2CO–, has 3 carbons (propanoate); the alkyl on the O, –CH2CH2CH3, is propyl: propyl propanoate. "Ethyl butanoate" comes from splitting on the wrong side of the C=O carbon.
x: That comes from splitting the ester on the wrong side of the C=O carbon. Count the C=O side as CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO–, carbonyl carbon included.
Ethanoate means two carbons on the C=O side. Here CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO– has three, counting the carbonyl carbon.
Butyl means four carbons on the O. The group on the single-bonded O, –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, has three.

q: Butanoic acid reacts with ethanol (H<sup>+</sup>, heat) to make ethyl butanoate, which smells like pineapple. Which is the ester?
h: The double-bond O side comes from the acid (4 carbons); the O–alkyl side comes from the alcohol (2 carbons).
w: Esterification removes –OH from the acid and H from the alcohol (lost as H2O): CH3CH2CH2CO– + –OCH2CH3 = CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3. CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3 is an isomer (propyl propanoate) with the carbons split the wrong way.
x: This is propyl propanoate: three carbons on each side. The C=O side must keep all four carbons of butanoic acid, and the O side has ethanol's two.
This has no –O– between the C=O and the ethyl group, so it is a ketone. An ester needs a C(=O)–O–C link.
This has no C=O at all, so it is an ether. Esterification keeps the acid's carbonyl group.

q: Isopentyl acetate, CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, gives bananas their smell. Which acid and alcohol are used to make it?
h: The C=O side came from the carboxylic acid; the group on the single-bonded O came from the alcohol.
w: CH3CO– is the acetate (acetic acid) part. The O–alkyl group –CH2CH2CH(CH3)2 came from HOCH2CH2CH(CH3)2, 3-methyl-1-butanol: acetic acid and 3-methyl-1-butanol.
x: This swaps the two sides. The C=O side, CH<sub>3</sub>CO–, has only two carbons, so it came from a two-carbon acid.
In 2-methyl-1-butanol the branch is on C2, right next to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon. In this ester two CH<sub>2</sub> groups sit between the O and the branch.
The C=O side has only two carbons, so it is not a five-carbon acid. The branched group is on the single-bonded O.

q: Isobutyl formate, HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, adds a raspberry-like note to flavorings. If this ester undergoes acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, which products form?
h: Acid hydrolysis cuts the single C–O bond next to the C=O; the C=O side becomes a carboxylic acid.
w: Breaking the C–O bond gives HCOOH (the C=O side) and HOCH2CH(CH3)2 (the O–alkyl side): methanoic acid and 2-methyl-1-propanol. Swapping the sides gives 2-methylpropanoic acid and methanol; a carboxylate salt only forms in base (NaOH), not in acid.
x: This swaps the sides of the ester. The C=O side, HCO–, has just one carbon; the branched group is on the single-bonded O.
A carboxylate salt forms only in base (NaOH). In acid hydrolysis the C=O side comes out as the neutral acid.
Methanal is an aldehyde. Hydrolysis adds water across the ester bond and turns the C=O side into a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde.

q: Saponification of ethyl propanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, with NaOH yields which two products?
h: In base hydrolysis (saponification), the acid part comes out as a salt. Which side of the ester is the acid part?
w: Saponification splits the ester at the C–O next to the C=O. The C=O side becomes the carboxylate salt CH3CH2COO−Na+ and the O–alkyl side becomes CH3CH2OH: sodium propanoate and ethanol. Propanoic acid itself would be the acid-hydrolysis product.
x: Propanoic acid forms in acid hydrolysis. In NaOH, the acid is neutralized as soon as it forms.
This swaps the sides. The C=O side, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CO–, has three carbons; the group on the single-bonded O has two.
An acid and sodium ethoxide cannot exist together in water; the base would take the acid's H<sup>+</sup>. Which fragment carries the Na<sup>+</sup>?

q: Isocaproic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, has an unpleasant cheesy odor. Which IUPAC name is correct for this acid?
h: The –COOH carbon is C1. Count along the longest chain from it to the branch.
w: The carboxyl carbon is C1; the chain has 5 carbons and the CH3 is on C4: 4-methylpentanoic acid. Counting the branch carbon into the chain (hexanoic) or numbering from the other end (2-methyl) are the usual slips; "-al" would mean an aldehyde.
x: Number from the –COOH carbon, which is always C1. Counting from it, the CH<sub>3</sub> branch is far from C2.
Hexanoic means a six-carbon chain. The branch CH<sub>3</sub> is a substituent, not part of the main chain; count only to the end of the longest chain.
The -al ending is for aldehydes (–CHO). This compound has a –COOH group.

q: Butanoic acid, which gives rancid butter its odor, reacts with sodium hydroxide as shown below. Which term best describes this reaction?
h: Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid and NaOH is a base. What happens when an acid meets a base?
w: The base removes the acidic H from –COOH to make a carboxylate salt (sodium butanoate) and water: neutralization. Saponification also uses NaOH, but its reactant is an ester, not an acid.
x: Saponification is the reaction of an ester with a base. Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid, not an ester.
Esterification needs an alcohol to react with the acid. Here the acid reacts with a base, NaOH.
Hydrolysis uses water to split a molecule such as an ester. Here an acid simply gives its H<sup>+</sup> to a base.

q: After it is swallowed, aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is hydrolyzed at its ester group by enzymes in the body. Which two products form?
h: Find aspirin's ester group. Its C=O side is an acetyl group (2 carbons); its O side is attached to the ring.
w: Aspirin's ester is Ar–O–CO–CH3. Hydrolysis breaks that C–O bond: the C=O side becomes acetic acid and the O side becomes the phenol –OH of salicylic acid: salicylic acid and acetic acid. Methanol would come from methyl salicylate, a different ester.
x: Ethanol would come from an ethyl ester. In aspirin the O of the ester is attached directly to the ring, so that part becomes a phenol.
Benzoic acid has no –OH on the ring. The ester oxygen stays on the ring after hydrolysis and becomes an –OH.
Methanol would come from a methyl ester such as methyl salicylate. In aspirin the C=O side of the ester is a two-carbon acetyl group.

q: An ester is written as CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of it produces which pair?
h: Do not just read left to right. Find the C=O carbon: that side becomes the acid.
w: The C=O carbon is bonded to –CH2CH3, so the acid part is CH3CH2COOH (3 C); the –OCH3 becomes methanol. This is methyl propanoate, so the products are propanoic acid and methanol. Acetic acid and ethanol would come from its isomer ethyl ethanoate.
x: Those come from ethyl ethanoate, an isomer. Here the C=O carbon is bonded to –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and the O carries a –CH<sub>3</sub>.
That swaps the sides. The –CH<sub>3</sub> is on the single-bonded O, so it leaves as an alcohol; the C=O side has three carbons.
A sodium salt forms only in base (saponification). Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis gives the neutral carboxylic acid.

q: How is tetramethylammonium chloride, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>N<sup>+</sup> Cl<sup>−</sup>, classified?
h: Count the carbon groups bonded to nitrogen. What happens when there are four?
w: Nitrogen has four C–N bonds, no N–H and a + charge, so this is a quaternary ammonium salt. A tertiary amine has three carbon groups and a neutral N; its salt, R3NH+, still has an N–H.
x: A tertiary ammonium salt is a protonated 3° amine, R<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>+</sup>, which still has an N–H. This nitrogen has no H.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on a neutral N. This N has more carbon groups and carries a + charge.
A primary amine salt is RNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, with just one carbon on N. Count the CH<sub>3</sub> groups on this nitrogen.

q: Methamphetamine is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)NHCH<sub>3</sub>. Its amine group is classified as
h: For amines, count carbons bonded directly to the N, not to the carbon next to it.
w: The N is bonded to two carbons (the CH and the CH3) and one H: secondary (2°). A 1° answer misses one of the two carbons on N; 3° or quaternary would need three or four carbons on N.
x: A primary amine has only one carbon on N, as in an –NH₂ group. Here the N is bonded to two carbons, the CH and the CH₃, and keeps one H.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on N and no N–H. Methamphetamine's N still has one H.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons on a positively charged N. This N is neutral and bears an H.

q: How would you name CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, a secondary amine, using common (alkyl + amine) naming?
h: Name each alkyl group attached to N, in alphabetical order, then add "amine".
w: The N carries one ethyl and one methyl group: ethylmethylamine, a 2° amine. Propylamine has all three carbons in one chain, and an "-amide" would need a C=O on the N.
x: Propylamine has all three carbons in one chain on N. Here the N sits between a CH<sub>3</sub> and a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, two separate groups.
Diethylamine has two ethyl groups on N, four carbons in all. This compound has only three carbons.
An amide name needs a C=O carbon bonded to N. CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has no carbonyl group.

q: Dimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, and acetic acid are heated together and water is driven off. Which amide forms?
h: Remove –OH from the acid and the H from the N. The amine keeps both of its other groups.
w: The acid's –OH and the N–H combine as H2O and the new C–N bond joins CH3CO– to –N(CH3)2: CH3CON(CH3)2, N,N-dimethylethanamide. CH3CONHCH3 loses one of the amine's methyl groups.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> has only one methyl on N. Dimethylamine loses only its H in amidation, so both methyl groups stay.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an amine, not an amide. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl group.
HCON(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has an H on the C=O carbon, so it comes from formic acid. Acetic acid supplies CH<sub>3</sub>CO–.

q: When ethylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is mixed with hydrochloric acid, which substance is formed?
h: Amines are organic bases. What does a base do with the H<sup>+</sup> from an acid?
w: The lone pair on N accepts H+ from HCl, giving the salt CH3CH2NH+3 Cl− (ethylammonium chloride). Nothing is substituted; it is a simple acid–base (neutralization) reaction.
x: No bond to carbon is broken; the C–N bond stays intact. An amine is a base, so think about what the N does with H<sup>+</sup>.
HCl does not attach Cl to nitrogen or release H<sub>2</sub>. This is a simple acid–base reaction.
An amine is a base, so its N gains H<sup>+</sup> rather than losing it. Forming H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> would make the amine act as an acid.

q: Hot aqueous HCl hydrolyzes propanamide, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>. Which products result?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond. In acid, what happens to the nitrogen piece that is released?
w: Water splits the C–N bond: the C=O side becomes CH3CH2COOH and the N side is NH3, which picks up H+ in acid: propanoic acid and NH4Cl. A sodium salt plus NH3 is what forms in NaOH instead.
x: Sodium propanoate and NH<sub>3</sub> form in NaOH (basic hydrolysis). Here the solution is acidic HCl.
Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond but leaves the C=O in place. An alcohol would need the carbonyl to be reduced.
Propanamine has no C=O, and hydrolysis adds water rather than producing it. The amide C–N bond is what breaks.

q: Name the amide CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> using IUPAC rules.
h: The chain that includes the C=O carbon is the parent. Groups on the nitrogen get the prefix N-.
w: The C=O chain, CH3CH2CH2CH2CO–, has 5 carbons (pentanamide) and the CH3 on N is named N-methyl: N-methylpentanamide. Counting the N–CH3 into the chain gives the wrong "hexanamide"; "-amine" ignores the C=O.
x: Hexanamide counts the N–CH<sub>3</sub> carbon as part of the chain. The parent chain includes only the carbons on the C=O side.
That name puts a five-carbon group on N and a one-carbon C=O piece. Here the C=O is at the end of the five-carbon chain, with CH<sub>3</sub> on N.
The -amine ending ignores the C=O bonded to the nitrogen. An N attached to a carbonyl carbon makes this an amide.

q: Which compound will NOT form an amide when heated with acetic acid?
h: Amidation needs to remove an H from the nitrogen to make water. Which nitrogen has no H?
w: Forming the amide removes –OH from the acid and an H from N. (CH3)3N, a 3° amine, has no N–H, so it can only form a salt with the acid, not an amide. NH3, 1° and 2° amines all have N–H.
x: Dimethylamine still has one N–H, which can leave with the acid's –OH as water. It can form an amide.
Methylamine has two N–H bonds, so it can lose one H as water and form an amide.
NH<sub>3</sub> has three N–H bonds and forms a simple amide with acetic acid on heating.

q: Fish smells "fishy" partly because of volatile amines such as trimethylamine. Squeezing lemon juice on fish reduces the odor mainly because
c: the acid converts the amines into nonvolatile ammonium salts
the acid converts the amines into amides that have no smell
the acid oxidizes the amines to carboxylic acids that do not evaporate
the acid converts the amines into esters, which smell fruity
h: Amines are organic bases; lemon juice contains citric acid. What forms when an acid and a base react?
w: Citric acid donates H+ to the amine N, forming an ammonium salt. The ionic salt is water-soluble and not volatile, so it does not reach your nose. Amides would require heating, and a 3° amine cannot form one.
x: Making an amide requires heating with water driven off, not a squeeze of lemon. Trimethylamine also has no N–H, so it cannot form one.
Citric acid is not an oxidizing agent, and amines do not oxidize to carboxylic acids. Think acid plus base.
Esters form from carboxylic acids and alcohols. Amines are bases, so what does an acid do to them?

q: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O can be an aldehyde or a ketone. Including branched skeletons, how many such carbonyl compounds exist?
h: Draw every four-carbon skeleton and place a C=O: at the end of a chain (aldehyde) or in the middle (ketone).
w: Aldehydes: CH3CH2CH2CHO and (CH3)2CHCHO; ketone: CH3COCH2CH3. Total = 3. C=O on C2 from the other end is the same butanone, not a new compound.
x: One is missing. The branched 4-carbon skeleton can also carry a C=O at the end of a chain.
One of these is a repeat. A C=O on the second carbon from either end is the same butanone.
This counts repeats or impossible structures. A ketone C=O needs two carbons attached, and the central carbon of the branched skeleton already has three.

q: Butanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, and butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, are best described as
h: Count the atoms in each. Same molecular formula? Then decide whether the atoms are connected the same way.
w: Both are C4H8O, but the C=O is at the end in one and in the middle in the other, so they are constitutional isomers (different functional groups, even). Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or ring with the same connections.
x: In one the C=O is at the end of the chain and in the other it is in the middle. Different connections cannot be the same compound.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring with identical connections. Here the C=O is in different places.
Enantiomers are mirror images with identical connections. Here the atoms are connected differently.

q: A student writes 2-butanol two ways: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. How are these two formulas related?
h: Name each one. Writing a condensed formula from the other end does not make a new molecule.
w: Both are a four-carbon chain with –OH on the second carbon: 2-butanol written from opposite ends. They are the same compound. Isomers would need a different connection, such as 1-butanol.
x: Both have the –OH on the second carbon of a 4-carbon chain. Writing the chain from the other end does not change the connections.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. 2-Butanol has neither.
Count the atoms: both formulas are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O. Writing a chain backward does not change the formula.

q: Cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, is a saturated ring. Which compound below is its constitutional isomer?
h: Isomers must have exactly the same molecular formula. Count C and H in each choice.
w: A ring and a C=C each remove 2 H from the alkane formula, so an open-chain alkene with one C=C has the same formula as a cycloalkane. 1-Hexene is C6H12; hexane is C6H14, and 1,5-hexadiene (two C=C) and 1-hexyne (one C≡C) are both C6H10.
x: Hexane is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>, two H more than cyclohexane. Isomers must have exactly the same formula.
This diene has two C=C bonds, so it is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, two H fewer than cyclohexane. Each C=C or ring removes 2 H.
A C≡C triple bond removes 4 H, so 1-hexyne is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, two H fewer than cyclohexane. Isomers need exactly the same formula.

q: Replacing one H of a C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkane with Br gives C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Br. Counting all carbon skeletons, how many structurally different bromides are possible?
h: Draw the three C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> skeletons, then put Br on each different kind of carbon in each skeleton.
w: Pentane: Br on C1, C2 or C3 (3). 2-Methylbutane: four different carbon positions (4). 2,2-Dimethylpropane: all CH3 are equal (1). Total = 3 + 4 + 1 = 8. Answering 3 counts only the straight chain.
x: This counts only the straight-chain pentane skeleton. C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> has two branched skeletons as well.
This puts Br on each of the five pentane carbons, but C1 and C5 (and C2 and C4) are equivalent. It also leaves out the branched skeletons.
Some positions are missing. 2-Methylbutane has four different kinds of carbon, and 2,2-dimethylpropane adds one more.

q: Which of these alkene names is invalid, because the molecule cannot have cis and trans forms?
h: Cis–trans isomerism needs each C=C carbon to carry two different groups.
w: In 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, C2 carries two identical CH3 groups, so swapping sides gives the same molecule. cis-2-Methyl-2-butene is therefore not a valid name. In the other three, each C=C carbon has two different groups (e.g. 2-pentene: H/CH3 on C2, H/CH2CH3 on C3).
x: 2-Pentene has H and CH<sub>3</sub> on one C=C carbon and H and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the other, so it does have cis and trans forms.
4-Methyl-2-pentene has two different groups on each C=C carbon, so a trans form exists. Check each name for a C=C carbon with two identical groups.
2-Butene has H and CH<sub>3</sub> on each C=C carbon, so it does have cis and trans forms.

q: A chiral carbon is bonded to four different groups. Which compound has a chiral carbon?
h: For each carbon bearing Br, list its four groups. Watch for two identical alkyl groups.
w: In CH3CHBrCH2CH3 the C–Br carbon holds H, Br, CH3 and CH2CH3, all different, so 2-bromobutane is chiral. 3-Bromopentane has two identical ethyl groups, and the other carbons have two or three H atoms or CH3 groups.
x: This is 3-bromopentane. The C–Br carbon carries two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral.
Every carbon here is a CH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>, with at least two identical H atoms, so none has four different groups.
The C–Br carbon holds three identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups and no H, so it does not have four different groups.
