q: Threonine, an essential amino acid, is CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Check each carbon: CH<sub>3</sub> and –COOH carbons cannot be chiral. Look at the two CH carbons.
w: The CH(OH) carbon holds H, OH, CH3 and CH(NH2)COOH; the CH(NH2) carbon holds H, NH2, COOH and CH(OH)CH3. Both have four different groups: 2 chiral carbons.
x: Too few. Check both CH carbons in threonine: the one with –OH and the one with –NH<sub>2</sub>. List the four groups on each.
Too many. The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has three identical H atoms, and the –COOH carbon has a C=O double bond, so neither is chiral.
Threonine has only four carbons, and the CH<sub>3</sub> and –COOH carbons cannot be chiral. Count only carbons with four different groups.

q: D-Glucose and D-galactose have the same formula and differ only in the arrangement at carbon 4 (one of their several chiral carbons). They are
h: Enantiomers are opposite at EVERY chiral carbon. What do you call stereoisomers that differ at only some of them?
w: Same connections, different 3-D arrangement at only one of several chiral carbons, and not mirror images: diastereomers. Enantiomers (like D- and L-glucose) are opposite at every chiral carbon.
x: Enantiomers are opposite at every chiral carbon. Glucose and galactose differ at only one of their several chiral carbons.
Constitutional isomers have atoms bonded in a different order. Glucose and galactose have the same bonding; only the 3-D arrangement at C4 differs.
They are different sugars: the different arrangement at carbon 4 means the two cannot be superimposed.

q: Ribose, the sugar in RNA, has 3 chiral carbons in its open-chain form. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers possible?
h: Each chiral carbon has two possible arrangements. Multiply the possibilities.
w: Maximum stereoisomers = 2n = 23 = 8. Those 8 are four pairs of enantiomers, so 4 counts the pairs instead of the compounds; 6 comes from 2 × 3 and 3 from counting the chiral carbons themselves.
x: 6 comes from multiplying 2 × 3. Each chiral carbon doubles the number of possibilities, so use 2 raised to the power of the number of chiral carbons.
3 is the number of chiral carbons, not the number of stereoisomers. Each chiral carbon has two possible arrangements.
4 is the number of enantiomer pairs. The question asks for individual stereoisomers, and each pair contains two compounds.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the pain reliever ibuprofen, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH (the ring is a para-disubstituted benzene)?
h: Benzene ring carbons, CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub> and COOH carbons are not chiral. Check the two CH carbons.
w: The CH in (CH3)2CH– has two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral. The CH(CH3)COOH carbon holds H, CH3, COOH and the ring: chiral. Total = 1.
x: Look at the carbon bonded to –CH<sub>3</sub>, –COOH, H and the ring. Are all four of its groups different?
That count includes the CH in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–, which has two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not chiral.
Ring, CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub> and –COOH carbons cannot be chiral. Only the two CH carbons are worth checking, and one has two identical groups.

q: A chiral molecule has exactly two chiral carbons. In a wedge-and-dash drawing, you swap two groups on BOTH chiral carbons. The new structure is
c: a constitutional isomer of the original
h: Swapping two groups on one chiral carbon inverts that center. What is the relationship when every center is inverted?
w: Each swap inverts one chiral carbon. Inverting both (all) chiral carbons gives the mirror image, and because the molecule is chiral, that mirror image is the enantiomer. Inverting only one of the two would give a diastereomer; connectivity never changes, so it is not a constitutional isomer.
x: A diastereomer would result from inverting only some of the chiral carbons. Here every chiral carbon is inverted.
Each swap inverts that chiral carbon, so the structure has changed at both centers. Since the molecule is chiral, its mirror image is a different compound, not the original.
Swapping groups on a chiral carbon changes only 3-D arrangement; every atom keeps the same bonding partners, so this is not a constitutional isomer.

q: Vanillin, the flavor of vanilla, is a benzene ring bearing –OH, –OCH<sub>3</sub> and –CHO groups. Which functional groups does it contain?
h: –OH on a benzene ring has a special name. An O between two carbons with no C=O is ... ? –CHO is ... ?
w: –OH bonded directly to a benzene ring = phenol; Ar–O–CH3 (no C=O next to the O) = ether; –CHO = aldehyde: phenol, ether, aldehyde. An ester needs –COO–.
x: –OH on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol. An ester needs a C=O next to the O, and –CHO (C=O with H) is not a ketone.
An ester needs –COO–, a C=O next to the oxygen. The –OCH<sub>3</sub> here has no C=O beside it.
–OH directly on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol. And –CHO has no –OH, so it is not a carboxylic acid.

q: A skeletal (line-angle) formula is a zigzag of four line segments with a double line for the first segment and no other atoms shown. What is its molecular formula?
h: Four segments have five ends/corners, each a carbon. Fill in H so each carbon has four bonds.
w: Four segments connect 5 carbons: CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3. Adding H to give each C four bonds: 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10 H, so C5H10. Counting segments instead of carbons gives C4; ignoring the double line gives C5H12.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> ignores the double line. A C=C double bond means two fewer H than an alkane.
This counts segments instead of carbons. Each end and each corner is a carbon, and four segments have five of these.
C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> would need two double bonds or a triple bond. There is only one double line here.

q: Count the atoms in (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>. Which molecular formula is correct?
h: Count each group: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> counts twice. The COO has no H.
w: C: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6. H: 6 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 12. O: 2. Formula = C6H12O2. C6H14O2 is what you get by assuming every compound has 2n + 2 H; the ester C=O removes two.
x: That is the alkane formula, 2n + 2 H. The C=O in the ester group removes two H.
This is one carbon short. Remember (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> means two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and the –OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon counts too.
This is one H short. Recount: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives 6 H, then CH, CH<sub>2</sub> and OCH<sub>3</sub>.

q: In propyne, CH<sub>3</sub>C≡CH, what angle is formed by the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon and the two triple-bonded carbons?
h: Count the electron groups around a triple-bonded carbon. Two groups → which geometry?
w: Each triple-bonded carbon has only two electron groups (the triple bond counts as one), so it is linear: 180°. 109.5° applies to the CH3 carbon, and 120° to C=C carbons.
x: 120° goes with a carbon that has three electron groups, like a C=C carbon. A triple-bonded carbon has fewer groups.
109.5° is the angle around the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon, which has four single bonds. The question asks about the angle at a triple-bonded carbon.
90° angles are not found around carbon in this course. Count the electron groups on the middle carbon; the triple bond counts as one.

q: Lidocaine, a local anesthetic used in dentistry, is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>3</sub>–NH–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–N(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Which two nitrogen-containing groups does it have?
h: Is each N bonded to a C=O carbon? If not, count the carbons on that N.
w: The –NH– is bonded to a C=O carbon, so it is an amide (not a 2° amine). The other N carries three carbons (CH2 and two ethyls) with no C=O: a 3° amine. There is no –COO–, so no ester.
x: The –NH– is bonded to a C=O carbon, which makes it an amide, not an amine. Then count carbons on the other N.
An ester needs –COO–, a C=O next to an oxygen. The C=O here is bonded to nitrogen.
There is no –NH<sub>2</sub>, so no 1° amine. The C=O carbon is bonded to N, so it is not a ketone either.

q: Rank the compounds in the table, which have similar molar masses, from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: Same size, so compare the strongest attraction: H-bonding (and how many), dipole–dipole, or only London forces.
w: Carboxylic acids form two H-bonds per pair (dimers) → highest. Alcohols H-bond once. Propanal has dipole–dipole only, and butane only London forces: acetic acid > 1-propanol > propanal > butane. Putting the alcohol first underrates the acid's stronger H-bonding.
x: This puts the alcohol above the acid. A carboxylic acid has both an O–H and a C=O, so its molecules pair up through two hydrogen bonds.
This puts propanal above 1-propanol. Propanal has no O–H, so dipole–dipole is its strongest force; the alcohol can hydrogen bond.
This puts propanal first and the acid last among the polar compounds, reversing the order of IMF strength.

q: Lidocaine, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>22</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O, is a dental anesthetic. What is its molar mass?
h: Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript and add: C 12.01, H 1.008, N 14.01, O 16.00.
x: 220.33 counts only one N. The formula has N<sub>2</sub>, so multiply 14.01 by 2.
218.34 leaves out the oxygen. Include 16.00 for the one O atom.
250.34 counts two O atoms. The formula has just one O.

q: A base that is 100% dissociated in aqueous solution is called strong. Pick the strong base.
h: Strong bases ionize completely in water. Decide which choices accept H⁺ from water only partly.
w: KOH dissociates completely into K+ and OH−, so it is a strong base. Ammonia, amines and carboxylate ions accept H+ only partially: they are weak bases.
x: NH<sub>3</sub> accepts H<sup>+</sup> from water only partly, so it is a weak base.
CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is an amine. Like ammonia, it accepts H<sup>+</sup> from water only partly: a weak base.
Acetate, CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, is the conjugate base of a weak acid. It accepts H<sup>+</sup> only partly, so it is a weak base.

q: Which compound's molecules attract each other ONLY through London dispersion forces?
h: Molecules with O or N are generally polar. Check each choice for polar bonds and for an H on N or O.
w: Pentane has only C–H and C–C bonds, so it is nonpolar and has only London forces. The ether and aldehyde are polar (dipole–dipole), and the amine has N–H for hydrogen bonding.
x: This is an ether: its bent C–O–C makes it polar, so it has dipole–dipole forces as well as dispersion.
This is an aldehyde: the polar C=O gives dipole–dipole attractions as well as dispersion.
This is an amine with N–H bonds, so its molecules also hydrogen bond with each other.

q: 1,4-Dichlorobenzene is used in some toilet-bowl deodorizers. Which name describes the same compound?
h: Ortho = neighbors (1,2), meta = one carbon in between (1,3), para = opposite (1,4).
w: Substituents on carbons 1 and 4 are directly across the ring from each other: para-dichlorobenzene. Cyclohexane is a saturated ring, not benzene.
x: Ortho is 1,2, neighboring carbons. Carbons 1 and 4 are directly across the ring from each other.
Meta is 1,3, with one carbon between the groups. Carbons 1 and 4 have two carbons between them on each side.
Cyclohexane is a saturated ring with no double bonds, so 1,4-dichlorocyclohexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>) is a different compound. The question names a benzene ring.

q: A benzene ring carries an –OH group and an –NO<sub>2</sub> group directly across the ring from each other. What is its name?
h: With –OH on the ring, the parent name is phenol. Then decide ortho, meta or para.
w: –OH on benzene makes the parent phenol; groups opposite each other (1,4) are para: p-nitrophenol. Toluene would need a –CH3 instead of –OH.
x: Meta (1,3) has one ring carbon between the two groups. Groups directly across the ring are 1,4.
Ortho (1,2) means the groups are on neighboring carbons, not across the ring.
Toluene is the parent name for a ring with a –CH<sub>3</sub> group. This ring has an –OH group, which sets a different parent name.

q: Nitration of benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, uses HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> as a catalyst. Which products form?
h: Benzene's ring is very stable, so it keeps all three double bonds. Does it add or substitute?
w: Benzene undergoes substitution, not addition: one ring H is replaced by –NO2, and that H joins the OH from HNO3 as water: C6H5NO2 + H2O (nitrobenzene). Adding HNO3 across a double bond (C6H7NO3) would destroy the aromatic ring.
x: Count oxygens: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> has three O atoms, but C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> has only two. The H removed from the ring pairs up with the OH left over from HNO<sub>3</sub>.
That formula is benzene plus all of HNO<sub>3</sub>, which is what addition across a C=C would give. Benzene's ring resists addition because it would lose its aromatic stability.
That would put an –OH on the ring. HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> attaches the nitrogen to the ring, not an –OH.

q: An aldohexose is drawn as a Fischer projection. Reading from C2 down to C5, its –OH groups point right, left, left, right. Which sugar is it?
h: Start from D-glucose (right, left, right, right). Find which carbon is different, then use the last chiral carbon (C5) for D or L.
w: D-glucose is right, left, right, right. This sugar differs only at C4, which makes it galactose, and the –OH on C5 points right, so it is D-galactose. L-galactose would have every –OH reversed, not just one.
x: In L-galactose every –OH is reversed. Here the bottom chiral carbon (C5) has its –OH on the right, which means D.
D-mannose differs from D-glucose at C2 (left, left, right, right). Here C2 points right, just as in glucose.
D-glucose is right, left, right, right. Compare carbon by carbon: one position here is different.

q: In the Fischer projection of D-mannose, the –OH groups on C2, C3, C4 and C5 point left, left, right, right. How are these –OH groups drawn in L-mannose?
h: L-mannose is the enantiomer (mirror image) of D-mannose. What happens to every chiral carbon in a mirror image?
w: Enantiomers are mirror images, so every chiral –OH switches sides: left, left, right, right → right, right, left, left. Flipping only C5 (left, left, right, left) gives a different sugar (a diastereomer), not the enantiomer.
x: This flips only C5. That changes the D/L label but gives a different sugar, not the mirror image of D-mannose.
This flips C2, C3 and C4 but leaves C5 on the right. A mirror image reverses every chiral carbon, including C5.
This is the same pattern as D-mannose itself, so nothing has been mirrored. An enantiomer has every –OH on the opposite side.

q: D-Ribose is an aldopentose. How many chiral carbons does its open-chain form have, and how many stereoisomers (2<sup>n</sup>) are possible for an aldopentose?
h: The aldehyde carbon (C1) and the end CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon are not chiral. Count only carbons with H and OH on the sides.
w: C1 (–CHO) and C5 (–CH2OH) are not chiral, so C2, C3 and C4 are: n = 3, and 23 = 8 stereoisomers (3 chiral carbons). Counting all 5 carbons as chiral is the common mistake.
x: 4 chiral carbons and 16 stereoisomers fit an aldohexose. Ribose has only five carbons, and its ends are not chiral.
The chiral count is right, but the number of stereoisomers is 2 raised to the power n, not 2 × n.
This counts all five carbons as chiral. C1 (–CHO) and C5 (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH) do not have four different groups.

q: Dihydroxyacetone, HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is the active ingredient in sunless tanning lotions. How is it classified?
h: Count the carbons for the size, then decide whether the C=O is an aldehyde (end carbon) or a ketone (middle carbon).
w: It has 3 carbons (triose), and the C=O is on the middle carbon, so it is a ketone: a ketotriose. Its isomer glyceraldehyde, with –CHO at C1, is the aldotriose.
x: An aldotriose (glyceraldehyde) has –CHO on an end carbon. In HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH the C=O is on the middle carbon.
Count the carbons in HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH: there are three, not four.
Count the carbons in HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>OH again: there are three, not five.

q: Compare open-chain D-glucose with D-mannose: same formula, but the C2 –OH points left in mannose and right in glucose, with C3–C5 identical. What is the relationship?
h: Compare the chiral carbons. How many are different, and are the sugars mirror images?
w: Stereoisomers that differ at only one chiral carbon are epimers. Enantiomers differ at every chiral carbon; anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon of a ring (C1), not at C2 of the open chain.
x: Enantiomers are mirror images that differ at every chiral carbon. Here C3–C5 are identical, so they are not mirror images.
Anomers differ at the anomeric carbon (C1) of a ring form. These are open-chain sugars that differ at C2.
Structural isomers have atoms connected in a different order. Here the connections are identical; only the 3-D arrangement at one carbon differs.

q: A Haworth projection of a D-hexopyranose shows the –OH on C1 pointing up, the –OH on C2 pointing down, the –OH on C3 pointing up and the –OH on C4 pointing up. Which sugar is it?
h: Anomeric –OH up = β, down = α (for D-sugars). D-glucose in a Haworth ring has C2 down, C3 up, C4 down. Which carbon is different?
w: The C1 –OH is up, so it is β. Glucose has its C4 –OH down; here C4 is up, so it is galactose (the C4 epimer): β-D-galactose. Calling it glucose misses the C4 difference.
x: For a D-sugar, an anomeric –OH pointing down is α. Here the C1 –OH points up.
In β-D-glucose the C4 –OH points down. Here the C4 –OH points up, so this is not glucose.
Check two things: the C1 –OH points up here (not the α position), and the C4 –OH points up, which does not match glucose.

q: A food-science student heats four sugar solutions with Benedict's reagent (blue Cu<sup>2+</sup>). Which solution forms an orange-red precipitate?
h: Benedict's reagent is reduced only by sugars with a free aldehyde or a hemiacetal that can open to one.
w: Lactose keeps a free hemiacetal on its glucose unit, so it reduces Cu2+ to Cu2O. Sucrose has both anomeric carbons tied up; sorbitol has no carbonyl; gluconic acid is already oxidized.
x: In sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so no ring can open to an aldehyde. It gives no precipitate.
Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol with no aldehyde or hemiacetal, so it cannot reduce Cu<sup>2+</sup>.
Gluconic acid's C1 is already oxidized to –COOH, so there is no aldehyde left to reduce Cu<sup>2+</sup>.

q: When D-galactose reacts with a mild oxidizing agent, its –CHO group is oxidized. What is the product?
h: Oxidizing an aldehyde gives a carboxylic acid; the sugar name changes to an '-onic acid'.
w: The –CHO on C1 becomes –COOH, giving D-galactonic acid. D-galactitol (an '-itol' sugar alcohol) is the product of reduction, not oxidation.
x: An "-itol" name is a sugar alcohol, which forms by reduction of the –CHO, not oxidation.
Gluconic acid comes from oxidizing glucose. Oxidation changes C1 only, so the product keeps the parent sugar's name.
Lactic acid is a three-carbon product of anaerobic glucose breakdown. Mild oxidation changes only the –CHO of the six-carbon sugar.

q: Isomaltose, a product of starch digestion at the branch points, joins two glucose units: the α anomeric carbon of one unit links via –O– to C6 of the other. Which label describes this bond?
h: The label gives the anomer (α or β) of the sugar using its anomeric carbon, then the two carbon numbers joined.
w: The first glucose uses its α anomeric carbon (C1), and it joins C6 of the next unit: α(1→6), the same link found at the branch points of amylopectin and glycogen.
x: The question says the linking anomeric carbon is in the α form, so a β label does not fit.
α(1→4) joins C1 to C4, as in maltose and the straight parts of starch. Here the bond goes to C6 of the other unit.
β(1→4) is the cellulose and lactose linkage. Here the anomeric carbon is α and it links to C6.

q: In sucrose, C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose are both used in the glycosidic bond. Which functional groups are present at these two anomeric carbons?
c: an acetal at glucose C1 and a ketal at fructose C2
a hemiacetal at glucose C1 and a hemiketal at fructose C2
a hemiacetal at glucose C1 and a ketal at fructose C2
a ketal at glucose C1 and an acetal at fructose C2
h: An anomeric carbon with –OR and –O– (ring) is a full acetal/ketal; one with –OH and –O– is a hemi-. Glucose came from an aldehyde, fructose from a ketone.
w: Both anomeric carbons carry two –O–R groups and no free –OH, so neither is 'hemi'. Glucose C1 (from an aldehyde) is an acetal, fructose C2 (from a ketone) is a ketal. With no hemiacetal left, sucrose is not a reducing sugar.
x: A "hemi-" carbon still has a free –OH. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are used in the glycosidic bond, so neither has an –OH left.
Glucose C1 is part of the glycosidic bond, so it has no free –OH. A hemiacetal there would make sucrose a reducing sugar.
The labels are swapped. Acetal goes with a carbon that came from an aldehyde, and ketal with one that came from a ketone.

q: Salivary amylase begins hydrolyzing the amylose in a cracker while it is being chewed. Which disaccharide is a major product?
h: Amylose is a chain of glucose units with α(1→4) bonds. Which disaccharide is two glucose units with that same linkage?
w: Breaking amylose's α(1→4) chain into two-glucose pieces gives maltose (glucose–α(1→4)–glucose). Lactose and sucrose contain galactose or fructose; cellobiose has a β(1→4) bond, like cellulose.
x: Lactose contains galactose, which is not part of amylose. Amylose is built only from glucose.
Sucrose contains fructose, which is not part of amylose. Amylose is built only from glucose.
Cellobiose is two glucose units joined β(1→4), the repeat unit of cellulose. Amylose has α(1→4) bonds.

q: Sucrose is completely hydrolyzed by the enzyme sucrase. How many grams of glucose are produced from 34.2 g of sucrose?
h: Write the hydrolysis: sucrose + H<sub>2</sub>O → ? Find moles of sucrose, then use the mole ratio to glucose.
w: Sucrose + H2O → glucose + fructose, a 1 : 1 ratio. 34.2 g ÷ 342.3 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0999 mol sucrose → 0.0999 mol glucose × 180.16 g mol⁻¹ = 18.0 g. 36.0 g assumes two glucose per sucrose, which is true for maltose, not sucrose.
x: 36.0 g assumes two glucose per sucrose. That is true for maltose; sucrose gives one glucose and one fructose.
34.2 g is the mass of sucrose you started with. Convert to moles and use the mole ratio to glucose.
9.00 g assumes only half a glucose forms per sucrose. Check the 1 : 1 ratio in the hydrolysis equation.

q: Palmitoleic acid, found in macadamia nut oil, is CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>CH=CH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>7</sub>COOH. Counting from the methyl (omega) end, which type of fatty acid is it?
h: Make the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon number 1 and count toward the C=C. The omega number is the first carbon of the double bond.
w: CH3 is ω1, the five CH2 groups are ω2–ω6, so the double bond starts at ω7: an omega-7 fatty acid. Counting from the –COOH end puts the double bond at C9, which is the tempting omega-9 mistake.
x: Omega-9 is what you get by counting from the –COOH end (the C=C starts at C9). Omega numbering starts at the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
Omega-6 is a miscount. Make CH<sub>3</sub> carbon 1, then count each of the five CH<sub>2</sub> groups before reaching the C=C.
Omega-3 would need only one CH<sub>2</sub> between the CH<sub>3</sub> and the C=C. Here there are five, (CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>5</sub>.

q: Rank by chain length: lauric, myristic, palmitic and stearic acids are saturated and occur in animal fats. Which one stays solid to the highest temperature?
h: For saturated fatty acids, how does chain length affect the dispersion forces between chains?
w: Longer saturated chains have more surface contact and stronger dispersion forces, so they melt at higher temperatures. The 18-carbon stearic acid melts highest.
x: Palmitic acid (16 C) melts high, but one acid here has a longer chain with more surface contact and stronger dispersion forces.
Myristic acid (14 C) is shorter than two of the other choices, so its dispersion forces are weaker.
Lauric acid (12 C) has the shortest chain here, so it has the weakest dispersion forces and melts lowest.

q: Elaidic acid is the trans isomer of oleic acid (an 18-carbon acid with one cis double bond). Elaidic acid melts at a much higher temperature than oleic acid. Why?
c: The trans chains are nearly straight and pack closely.
The trans double bond adds hydrogen bonds between chains.
Elaidic acid has fewer carbon atoms than oleic acid has.
The trans double bond puts a sharper kink in each chain.
h: Picture the chain shape around a cis double bond and around a trans double bond. Which shape stacks better?
w: A cis double bond puts a kink in the chain that keeps chains apart. A trans double bond leaves the chain nearly straight, so the chains pack closely, raising the melting point, which is why trans fats behave like saturated fats.
x: Fatty acid chains are hydrocarbon and cannot hydrogen bond to each other; a C=C has no O–H or N–H.
Elaidic acid is the trans isomer of oleic acid, so it has the same 18 carbons. Only the shape at the double bond differs.
That describes a cis double bond. A trans double bond keeps the chain fairly straight.

q: A soap maker heats glyceryl tripalmitate (a triacylglycerol made from three palmitic acids) with aqueous KOH. What are the products?
c: three glycerol and one potassium palmitate
h: This is saponification (base hydrolysis). Each ester bond breaks, and in base the fatty acids end up as their salts.
w: Base breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three potassium palmitate (soap). Free palmitic acid forms only in acid hydrolysis; in KOH the acid is deprotonated to its K+ salt.
x: Free palmitic acid forms in acid hydrolysis. In KOH, the acid is deprotonated to its potassium salt.
One triacylglycerol has only one glycerol backbone, holding three palmitic acids. This choice reverses those numbers.
KOH breaks all three ester bonds, so three fatty acid salts form, not one.

q: A soap maker converts 0.250 mol of olive-oil triacylglycerol into soap. What mass of sodium hydroxide (40.00 g mol⁻¹) does the reaction consume?
h: A triacylglycerol has three ester bonds. How many NaOH does each molecule need?
w: Each triacylglycerol needs 3 NaOH: 0.250 mol × 3 = 0.750 mol NaOH × 40.00 g mol⁻¹ = 30.0 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 10.0 g.
x: 10.0 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio of NaOH to triacylglycerol. Each triacylglycerol has three ester bonds.
3.33 g divides by 3 instead of multiplying. Each triacylglycerol needs three NaOH, so you need more moles of NaOH than of fat.
20.0 g assumes 2 NaOH per triacylglycerol. Count the ester bonds again.

q: A lipid from brain tissue is hydrolyzed. The products are sphingosine, one fatty acid and galactose; no phosphate or glycerol is found. What type of lipid is it?
h: Look at the backbone (sphingosine or glycerol) and whether the head group is a phosphate or a sugar.
w: A sphingosine backbone with a monosaccharide head group and no phosphate is a glycolipid (cerebroside). Sphingomyelin also has sphingosine but carries a phosphate–choline head group.
x: Sphingomyelin has a phosphate–choline head group. The products here include no phosphate, but they do include a sugar.
Glycerophospholipids have a glycerol backbone and phosphate, and neither was found here.
A wax is one ester of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol. It has no sphingosine or sugar.

q: Which lipoprotein carries cholesterol from the liver to the body's tissues, and is linked to plaque buildup in arteries when its level is high?
h: One lipoprotein delivers cholesterol out to cells; another brings excess cholesterol back to the liver.
w: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) delivers cholesterol to cells; when it is high, cholesterol deposits in artery walls. HDL does the opposite, returning cholesterol to the liver.
x: HDL does the opposite: it carries excess cholesterol from the tissues back to the liver.
Chylomicrons carry dietary triacylglycerols from the intestine through the lymph, not cholesterol from the liver to tissues.
VLDL leaves the liver carrying mostly triacylglycerols. The particle that mainly delivers cholesterol to tissues is a different one.

q: A nutrition label separates fats into saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated. Which of these fatty acids belongs in the polyunsaturated group?
c: linoleic acid, with two C=C bonds
oleic acid, with one C=C bond
stearic acid, with no C=C bonds
palmitic acid, with no C=C bonds
h: 'Poly' means more than one. Count the carbon–carbon double bonds.
w: A polyunsaturated fatty acid has two or more C=C bonds, so linoleic acid fits. Oleic acid, with one C=C, is monounsaturated; stearic and palmitic acids are saturated.
x: One C=C makes oleic acid monounsaturated. "Poly" means more than one.
Stearic acid has no C=C, so it is saturated.
Palmitic acid has no C=C, so it is saturated.

q: Triolein, a liquid oil, contains three oleic acids (18 carbons, one cis C=C each). It is completely hydrogenated with H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst. What is the product?
h: Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> across each C=C without changing the number of carbons. Which saturated 18-carbon acid results?
w: Adding H2 to each C=C turns every 18-carbon oleic acid into stearic acid, so the product is tristearin, a solid fat. Hydrogenation does not break the ester bonds (that would be hydrolysis) or shorten the chains.
x: Hydrogenation does not change the chain length: oleic acid has 18 carbons, and palmitic acid has 16. A saturated fat is also not a liquid oil.
Breaking the ester bonds to give glycerol is hydrolysis, which needs water. Hydrogenation only adds H<sub>2</sub> to the C=C bonds.
Trilinolein has more C=C bonds. Hydrogenation removes double bonds; it does not add them.

q: Cholesterol makes up about 25% of the lipid in some animal cell membranes. What is its main role there?
c: It fits between phospholipid tails and regulates membrane fluidity.
It forms channels that carry ions and small polar molecules across the membrane.
It provides the polar head groups that face the water.
It is broken down in the membrane to supply energy for the cell.
h: Cholesterol is a rigid, mostly nonpolar steroid. Where in the bilayer would it sit, and what would it change?
w: Rigid cholesterol molecules slip between the fatty acid tails, keeping the membrane from becoming too fluid or too rigid. Ion channels are membrane proteins, and cholesterol is not used as a fuel.
x: Ion channels are membrane proteins. Cholesterol is a small, mostly nonpolar molecule and does not form channels.
Phospholipids provide the polar heads. Cholesterol has only one small –OH and is mostly a rigid, nonpolar ring system.
Cholesterol is not used as a fuel in the membrane; its ring system is not broken down for energy.

q: When glycerol reacts with three fatty acids to make one triacylglycerol, how many ester bonds form and how many water molecules are released?
h: Esterification is a condensation: each –OH of glycerol joins one –COOH. What small molecule leaves each time?
w: Each of glycerol's three –OH groups condenses with one –COOH, forming one ester bond and losing one water each time: 3 ester bonds and 3 H2O.
x: Each ester bond forms in its own condensation step, and each step releases one H<sub>2</sub>O. Three bonds means more than one water.
Three fatty acids attach to glycerol's three –OH groups, so more than one ester bond forms.
Each ester bond releases only one H<sub>2</sub>O, so the number of waters matches the number of ester bonds.

q: A free lysine molecule, side chain –(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub>, is dissolved in blood plasma (pH 7.4). Adding up all its ionized groups gives what overall charge?
h: At pH 7.4, the α-carboxyl is –COO− and the α-amino is –NH+3. What happens to a basic side-chain amine?
w: –COO− (−1) + –NH+3 (+1) + side-chain –NH+3 (+1) = +1. Answering 0 forgets that the basic side chain is also protonated at physiological pH.
x: 0 forgets the side-chain amine. At pH 7.4 that basic –NH<sub>2</sub> picks up H<sup>+</sup> too, adding another positive charge.
A negative net charge would need more –COO<sup>−</sup> groups than –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> groups. Lysine has only one carboxyl group.
+2 counts both amino groups but forgets the α-carboxyl group, which is ionized as –COO<sup>−</sup> at pH 7.4.

q: Of these four amino acids, only one is classified as basic, with a side chain that is protonated (+) in body fluids. Which one?
h: Basic side chains contain an extra amine-type nitrogen that can accept H<sup>+</sup>. An amide nitrogen is not basic.
w: Arginine's side chain (a guanidino group) is protonated and positive at pH 7.4. Glutamine contains N, but in an amide, which is neutral; aspartic acid is acidic and negative.
x: Glutamine's side chain nitrogen is part of an amide, which is not basic. Its side chain stays neutral at pH 7.4.
Serine's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The –OH is polar but does not accept H<sup>+</sup>, so it is neutral.
Aspartic acid's side chain has a –COOH that loses H<sup>+</sup> to become –COO<sup>−</sup>, so it is acidic and negative, not basic.

q: In the tertiary structure of an enzyme, the side chain of leucine lies next to the side chain of isoleucine in the protein's interior. Which interaction holds them together?
h: Classify both side chains: are they polar, charged, sulfur-containing or nonpolar hydrocarbons?
w: Leucine and isoleucine both have nonpolar hydrocarbon side chains, so they cluster together away from water by hydrophobic interactions. Salt bridges need opposite charges, and disulfide bonds need two cysteines.
x: Salt bridges need opposite charges. Leucine and isoleucine side chains are uncharged hydrocarbons.
Disulfide bridges form only between two cysteine –SH groups. Leucine and isoleucine contain no sulfur.
Hydrogen bonds need H on O or N. Leucine and isoleucine side chains contain only C and H.

q: In the tetrapeptide Met–Lys–Trp–Glu, which amino acid is at the C-terminal end, with a free –COO<sup>−</sup> group?
h: Peptides are written from the N-terminus (free –NH+3) on the left to the C-terminus on the right.
w: By convention, the N-terminal amino acid is written first (Met) and the C-terminal amino acid last, so Glu has the free carboxylate group.
x: Met is written first, so it is the N-terminal residue with the free –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group.
Lys is in the middle of the chain, so both its backbone ends are tied up in peptide bonds.
Trp is an interior residue: its backbone amino and carboxyl groups are both used in peptide bonds.

q: A student links leucine, histidine and tyrosine into a three-residue chain, using each just once but in any order (for example, Leu–His–Tyr or Tyr–Leu–His). How many distinct sequences are possible?
h: Leu–His–Tyr and Tyr–His–Leu are different peptides because the N- and C-terminal ends differ. Count the possible orders.
w: There are 3 choices for the first position, 2 for the second and 1 for the last: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. 27 (33) would allow repeats, which the problem does not.
x: 3 counts each amino acid once as a starting point but forgets the different ways to order the other two.
9 multiplies 3 × 3, as if two positions each had three choices. Once a residue is used it cannot be used again.
27 is 3 × 3 × 3, which allows the same amino acid to repeat. Here each one is used only once.

q: Mercury and lead poisoning damage many enzymes. Heavy-metal ions such as Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Pb<sup>2+</sup> denature proteins mainly by
c: binding to cysteine –SH groups and breaking disulfide bonds
hydrolyzing the peptide bonds that join the amino acids
adding water across the C=O groups of the peptide backbone
forming new hydrogen bonds that tighten the α helix
h: Denaturation changes shape (secondary and higher), not the amino acid sequence. Which side chain is especially attracted to heavy metals?
w: Heavy-metal ions bind strongly to sulfur in –SH groups and to carboxylates, breaking disulfide bonds and salt bridges so the protein unfolds. Denaturation leaves the peptide bonds (primary structure) intact.
x: Denaturation does not break peptide bonds; that is hydrolysis. Heavy metals change shape by binding to certain side chains.
Adding water across backbone groups would be a hydrolysis-type reaction, which heavy metals do not do. Think about which side chain atom metals attract.
Heavy metals unfold proteins rather than tightening them. Think about which side chain groups Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Pb<sup>2+</sup> bind.

q: Red blood cells carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin. How does one hemoglobin molecule bind O<sub>2</sub>?
c: Each of its four heme groups holds an Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion that binds one O<sub>2</sub>.
Its single polypeptide chain binds one O<sub>2</sub> at a time.
It stores O<sub>2</sub> in muscle tissue rather than carrying it in blood.
Its iron must be Fe<sup>3+</sup> to bind O<sub>2</sub>.
h: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with one heme. What metal ion and charge are in the heme?
w: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with a heme whose Fe2+ binds one O2, so one hemoglobin carries up to four O2. Storing O2 in muscle is the job of myoglobin; Fe3+ (methemoglobin) cannot bind O2.
x: Hemoglobin is not a single chain: it has four subunits (two α and two β), each able to bind O<sub>2</sub>.
Storing O<sub>2</sub> in muscle is myoglobin's job. Hemoglobin carries O<sub>2</sub> in red blood cells.
Iron in the Fe<sup>3+</sup> state (methemoglobin) cannot bind O<sub>2</sub>. The heme iron must be in the other oxidation state.

q: A biochemist treats a protein with a reducing agent that breaks all its disulfide bonds but no other bonds. Which level of structure is NOT changed?
c: the cross-links between cysteine side chains
h: For each level of structure, ask what holds it together. Which level would still be the same if every –S–S– link were cut?
w: Disulfide bridges link side chains and help hold the tertiary (and sometimes quaternary) structure. The sequence of amino acids, held by peptide bonds, is untouched: the primary structure stays the same.
x: Disulfide bonds help hold tertiary structure, so breaking them does change it. Look for the level held only by peptide bonds.
The folded 3-D shape depends partly on disulfide bonds, so breaking them changes it.
The cross-links between cysteine side chains are the disulfide bonds themselves, so the reducing agent removes them.

q: Corn protein is low in lysine, and bean protein is low in methionine. A vegetarian eats tortillas and beans at the same meal. Why is this a good choice?
c: Together they are complementary proteins supplying all essential amino acids.
Beans cause the body to synthesize the missing lysine from extra glucose.
Corn supplies nonessential amino acids, which then become essential ones.
Eating them together prevents the proteins from being hydrolyzed in digestion.
h: Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body. What happens when two foods are low in different essential amino acids?
w: Each food supplies the essential amino acid the other lacks, so together they are complementary proteins that provide all the essential amino acids. The body cannot make lysine (an essential amino acid) from glucose.
x: The body cannot make lysine from glucose; lysine is essential and must come from food.
Nonessential amino acids cannot be turned into essential ones. The body cannot make the carbon skeletons of essential amino acids.
Proteins are still hydrolyzed in digestion no matter how they are combined. The benefit is in which amino acids each food supplies.

q: Using the molar masses in the table, what is the molar mass of the tripeptide Gly–Gly–Gly?
h: Each peptide bond forms by condensation, releasing one H<sub>2</sub>O. How many peptide bonds are in a tripeptide?
w: A tripeptide has 2 peptide bonds, so 2 H2O are lost: 3(75.07) − 2(18.02) = 225.21 − 36.04 = 189.17 g mol⁻¹. 225.21 forgets the water lost; 207.19 removes only one water; 243.23 adds a water instead of removing them.
x: 225.21 is just 3 × 75.07. It forgets that a water molecule is lost each time a peptide bond forms.
207.19 removes only one water. A tripeptide has more than one peptide bond.
243.23 adds a water instead of subtracting. Forming peptide bonds is condensation, which releases water.

q: Which amino acid contains sulfur AND can form a disulfide bridge with another molecule of the same amino acid?
h: A disulfide bridge, –S–S–, forms when two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized.
w: Cysteine has a –CH2SH side chain, and two –SH groups oxidize to –S–S–. Methionine also contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH3) with no –SH, so it cannot form disulfides.
x: Methionine contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no –SH group, so it cannot form a disulfide.
Serine's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. It has oxygen, not sulfur.
Threonine's side chain has an –OH group and no sulfur.

q: Fumarase adds a water molecule across the C=C double bond of fumarate to form malate. To which enzyme class does fumarase belong?
h: Hydrolases use water to split a bond into two molecules. Which class adds groups (like H<sub>2</sub>O) to a double bond, or removes them to form one?
w: Adding H2O to a C=C without splitting the molecule is the job of a lyase. A hydrolase would use water to cut one molecule into two pieces, which does not happen here.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split one molecule into two. Here water is added across a double bond and the molecule stays in one piece.
An oxidoreductase catalyzes redox reactions with a coenzyme such as NAD<sup>+</sup>. Adding H<sub>2</sub>O across a C=C is not a redox step here.
An isomerase rearranges atoms without changing the formula. Malate has one more H<sub>2</sub>O than fumarate.

q: Glutamine synthetase joins glutamate and NH+4 to form glutamine, using the energy of ATP hydrolysis. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Which class joins two molecules into one and needs energy from ATP to do it?
w: Joining two molecules with energy from ATP is the definition of a ligase (a synthetase). A transferase only moves a group from one molecule to another.
x: A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here two molecules are joined into one, and ATP is spent to do it.
A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond and does not use ATP. This reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis.
A hydrolase uses water to split a molecule apart. This reaction builds a bigger molecule instead.

q: Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose-1-phosphate into glucose-6-phosphate by moving the phosphate group to a different carbon of the same molecule. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Compare the formulas of the substrate and the product. Is a group moved to a different molecule or within one molecule?
w: The reactant and product have the same formula; only the phosphate's position changes, so the enzyme rearranges a molecule into its isomer: an isomerase (a mutase). A transferase moves a group from one molecule to a different molecule.
x: A transferase moves a group to a different molecule. Here the phosphate moves to another carbon of the same molecule.
A ligase joins two molecules using ATP. Only one molecule is involved here, and its formula does not change.
A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond, or breaks bonds without water. Compare the formulas of the reactant and product.

q: Which type of digestive enzyme hydrolyzes the phosphodiester bonds in DNA and RNA?
h: Enzyme names often tell the substrate: prote-, lip-, amyl- … Which matches nucleic acids?
w: A nuclease hydrolyzes the phosphodiester links in nucleic acids. Proteases break peptide bonds, lipases break the ester bonds of fats, and amylases break the glycosidic bonds of starch.
x: Proteases hydrolyze the peptide bonds in proteins. DNA and RNA are a different type of biomolecule.
Lipases hydrolyze the ester bonds in fats. Phosphodiester bonds are found in a different type of biomolecule.
Amylases hydrolyze the glycosidic bonds in starch. Think about which enzyme name matches nucleic acids.

q: An enzyme from a bacterium that lives in hot springs has its maximum activity at 75 °C. How does its activity at 37 °C compare?
c: Lower, because molecules collide less often and with less energy at 37 °C
Lower, because the enzyme is denatured at 37 °C
Higher, because 37 °C is the optimum for all enzymes
The same, because temperature does not affect enzymes below their optimum
h: On a rate-versus-temperature graph, what happens to the rate on the low-temperature side of the peak?
w: Below the optimum, the rate rises with temperature because more substrate collisions occur with enough energy. At 37 °C this enzyme is slower but not denatured; denaturation happens on the high-temperature side of the peak.
x: Denaturation happens when an enzyme is heated above its optimum. 37 °C is well below this enzyme's optimum of 75 °C.
37 °C is the optimum for most human enzymes, not all enzymes. This bacterial enzyme has its peak at 75 °C.
Below the optimum, temperature still matters: the rate rises as temperature rises toward the peak.

q: A noncompetitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. On a graph of rate versus substrate concentration, how does the curve change?
c: The maximum rate is lower, even at very high substrate concentration.
The curve reaches the same maximum rate, but only at higher substrate concentration.
The maximum rate becomes higher than without the inhibitor.
The curve is unchanged because the inhibitor binds away from the active site.
h: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds outside the active site and changes the enzyme's shape. Can adding more substrate push it out?
w: The inhibitor changes the enzyme's shape, so some enzyme is inactive no matter how much substrate is added: the curve levels off at a lower maximum rate. Reaching the same maximum at higher substrate describes a competitive inhibitor.
x: Reaching the same maximum rate only at higher substrate is what a competitive inhibitor does, since substrate can push it out.
An inhibitor slows an enzyme; it never makes the maximum rate higher.
Binding away from the active site still changes the enzyme's shape, so the curve does change.

q: Sulfanilamide, an early antibiotic, has a structure very similar to PABA, a substrate bacteria use to make the vitamin folic acid. Sulfanilamide binds in the PABA site of the enzyme. What type of inhibitor is it?
h: Ask whether the inhibitor resembles the substrate and where on the enzyme it binds.
w: A molecule that looks like the substrate and competes for the active site is a competitive inhibitor; raising the PABA concentration can reduce its effect. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. Sulfanilamide looks like PABA and binds in the PABA site.
An irreversible inhibitor forms a permanent covalent bond. Nothing here says sulfanilamide bonds covalently.
An activator speeds an enzyme up. Sulfanilamide slows the bacterial enzyme down.

q: Carbonic anhydrase is active only when a Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion is bound in its active site. Without the Zn<sup>2+</sup>, the inactive protein part is called the
h: A metal ion helper is a cofactor. What is the name for the protein alone, without its helper?
w: The protein portion alone is the apoenzyme; adding the cofactor (here the metal ion Zn2+) makes the active holoenzyme. A coenzyme is an organic cofactor, often made from a vitamin.
x: A coenzyme is an organic helper molecule, often made from a vitamin. The question asks for the name of the protein part alone.
The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on, not part of the enzyme.
Isoenzymes are different forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction. That is not the protein without its metal ion.

q: The coenzyme FAD, which accepts hydrogen when a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group is oxidized to –CH=CH–, is made from which vitamin?
h: Think of the name: FAD = flavin adenine dinucleotide.
w: The 'flavin' in FAD comes from riboflavin (vitamin B2). Niacin forms NAD+, and pantothenic acid forms coenzyme A.
x: Niacin (B<sub>3</sub>) is used to make NAD<sup>+</sup>, a different coenzyme. Think about the "flavin" in FAD.
Pantothenic acid (B<sub>5</sub>) is part of coenzyme A, not FAD.
Thiamine (B<sub>1</sub>) is used to make TPP, which helps remove CO<sub>2</sub>. It is not part of FAD.

q: Why must the B vitamins be eaten regularly, while vitamin A can be stored for months?
c: B vitamins are water-soluble and excreted in urine; vitamin A is fat-soluble and stored.
B vitamins are destroyed by stomach acid, while vitamin A passes through the stomach unchanged.
B vitamins are fat-soluble and burned for energy; vitamin A is water-soluble and recycled.
B vitamins act as enzymes that are used up in each reaction; vitamin A is never used up.
h: Group the vitamins by solubility. Which group dissolves in body fat, and which leaves the body easily?
w: B vitamins are water-soluble, so extra amounts are excreted in urine and must be replaced, while fat-soluble vitamin A is stored in fatty tissue and the liver. B vitamins act as coenzymes and are not consumed in each reaction.
x: The difference is not stomach acid. Sort the vitamins by solubility: which group can be stored in body fat?
This has the solubilities backward. Recall which vitamins dissolve in fat (A, D, E, K) and which in water.
B vitamins act as coenzymes, and coenzymes are not used up in each reaction. The real reason is how the body stores or excretes them.

q: A forensic lab analyzes a double-stranded DNA sample and finds that 28% of its bases are cytosine. What percentage of the bases are thymine?
h: Base pairing: C pairs with G and A pairs with T, so %C = %G and %A = %T. All four must add to 100%.
w: %G = %C = 28%, so G + C = 56%. A + T = 100% − 56% = 44%, and T is half: 22%. 44% is A and T together, not T alone.
x: 28% is the cytosine value. Thymine pairs with adenine, not with cytosine, so it shares what is left after G and C.
44% is A and T together. Since A = T, split that amount between them.
72% is everything except cytosine. Remember guanine equals cytosine, so G also takes 28%.

q: A 10-base-pair segment of double-stranded DNA contains 4 G–C pairs and 6 A–T pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands of this segment together?
h: G–C pairs are held by 3 hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs by 2.
w: 4 G–C × 3 = 12 and 6 A–T × 2 = 12, total 24 hydrogen bonds. Swapping the numbers (G–C = 2, A–T = 3) gives 26; using 3 for every pair gives 30; 48 counts each hydrogen bond twice, once from each strand.
x: 48 counts each hydrogen bond twice, once from each strand. Each bond joins one base on each strand.
26 swaps the numbers, giving G–C two hydrogen bonds and A–T three. Check which pair has three.
30 uses 3 hydrogen bonds for every pair. Only one type of pair has three.

q: Hydrolysis of a DNA building block gives guanine, deoxyribose and a single phosphate. What was the building block called?
h: Base + sugar = nucleoside; add phosphates to get a nucleotide. A 'd' marks deoxyribose.
w: Guanine + deoxyribose is the nucleoside deoxyguanosine; one phosphate makes it the nucleotide deoxyguanosine monophosphate (dGMP), a DNA building block. GMP would contain ribose.
x: GMP contains ribose, the RNA sugar. This building block contained deoxyribose.
A nucleoside is just base + sugar. Hydrolysis also released a phosphate, so the building block had one.
A triphosphate would release three phosphates on hydrolysis. Only a single phosphate was found.

q: An mRNA vaccine delivers mRNA for a viral protein into human muscle cells. Which statement describes what happens to that mRNA?
c: It is translated by cytoplasmic ribosomes; the cell's DNA is not changed.
It is copied into DNA by DNA polymerase inside the cell's nucleus.
It is transcribed into a new viral protein inside the cell's nucleus.
It replaces one of the cell's own genes during DNA replication.
h: Transcription (DNA → RNA) happens in the nucleus. Where does translation (mRNA → protein) happen, and which enzyme would be needed to turn RNA into DNA?
w: mRNA is translated by ribosomes in the cytoplasm into protein. The mRNA stays in the cytoplasm and is broken down after use; it does not enter the nucleus, and DNA polymerase cannot use an RNA template, so the cell's DNA is unchanged.
x: DNA polymerase cannot use an RNA template, and the vaccine mRNA is not copied into DNA.
Transcription turns DNA into RNA, and proteins are not made in the nucleus. Think about where mRNA is used to build protein.
The vaccine mRNA stays in the cytoplasm and never enters the nucleus, so it cannot replace a gene. It is translated and then broken down.

q: An mRNA has the sequence 5′-AUGGCA-3′. What is the sequence of the DNA template strand from which it was transcribed, written 5′ to 3′?
h: The template strand is complementary and antiparallel to the mRNA, with T instead of U. Write it 3′→5′ under the mRNA, then reverse it.
w: Under 5′-AUGGCA-3′ the template reads 3′-TACCGT-5′; written 5′ to 3′ that is 5′-TGCCAT-3′. 5′-TACCGT-3′ has the right bases in the wrong direction, and 5′-ATGGCA-3′ is the coding strand.
x: These are the right bases in the wrong direction: this is the template read 3′→5′ but labeled 5′→3′. Reverse it.
This is the coding strand, which matches the mRNA. The template strand is complementary to the mRNA.
This contains U, but DNA uses T. It is also not correctly reversed to read 5′ to 3′.

q: Which type of RNA is the most abundant in a cell and combines with proteins to form the ribosome?
h: The name of this RNA comes from the organelle it builds.
w: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) makes up most of the cell's RNA and forms the ribosome together with proteins. mRNA carries the code, and tRNA brings amino acids.
x: mRNA carries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome. It is not a structural part of the ribosome.
tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome. It is not part of the ribosome's structure.
snRNA helps remove introns in the nucleus. It is a small, minor fraction of cellular RNA.

q: Capric acid, a saturated 10-carbon fatty acid found in goat's milk, is completely oxidized. Using the ATP values in the table (subtract the activation cost), how many ATP are produced?
h: Find acetyl CoA (carbons ÷ 2) and β-oxidation cycles (acetyl CoA − 1). Each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 5 acetyl CoA × 10 = 50; 4 cycles give 4 NADH × 2.5 = 10 and 4 FADH2 × 1.5 = 6. 50 + 10 + 6 − 2 = 64 ATP. 66 forgets the activation cost; 68 uses 5 cycles instead of 4; 114 uses 10 acetyl CoA (one per carbon instead of one per two carbons).
x: 66 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
68 uses 5 β-oxidation cycles. The number of cycles is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
114 uses 10 acetyl CoA, one per carbon. Each acetyl CoA carries 2 carbons.

q: A bottle of sports drink provides 120 kcal, all from carbohydrate. Using 4 kcal g⁻¹ for carbohydrate, how many grams of carbohydrate does it contain?
h: Divide the energy by the energy value per gram for that type of food.
w: 120 kcal ÷ 4 kcal g⁻¹ = 30 g of carbohydrate. 13 g uses 9 kcal g⁻¹, which is the value for fat, and 480 g multiplies instead of dividing.
x: 13 g uses 9 kcal g⁻¹, the value for fat. This drink's energy comes from carbohydrate.
480 g multiplies the kcal by 4 instead of dividing. A larger mass would give far more energy.
120 is the number of kcal, not grams. Convert using the energy value per gram.

q: One glucose is completely oxidized to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O by glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle and electron transport. Using the ATP values in the table (count the NADH from glycolysis at the same value), what is the total ATP yield?
h: Tally the ATP, NADH, FADH₂ and GTP from each stage for one glucose. Remember that one glucose gives two pyruvate and two turns of the citric acid cycle.
w: NADH: 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 × 2.5 = 25; FADH2: 2 × 1.5 = 3; ATP + GTP made directly: 2 + 2 = 4. Total = 32 ATP. 34 counts the 4 ATP made in glycolysis without subtracting the 2 invested; 38 comes from the older 3 ATP/NADH and 2 ATP/FADH2 values, and 36 uses those values but counts each glycolysis NADH as only 2 ATP.
x: 34 counts the 4 ATP made in glycolysis without subtracting the 2 ATP invested at the start.
36 is an older total that uses 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub> but counts each glycolysis NADH as only 2 ATP. Use 2.5 and 1.5 from the table for every carrier.
38 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: A pathway chart labels four processes: (1) building glycogen from glucose, (2) splitting glucose into two pyruvate, (3) making new glucose from lactate, (4) cutting a fatty acid into acetyl CoA. Which ones break molecules down?
h: Catabolic pathways break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy. Anabolic pathways build molecules and use energy. In these names, genesis means making and lysis means splitting.
w: Glycolysis splits glucose and β-oxidation breaks down fatty acids, so 2 and 4 are catabolic. Glycogenesis (making glycogen) and gluconeogenesis (making new glucose) are anabolic.
x: Processes 1 and 3 both build molecules (genesis = making), so they are anabolic.
Process 1 builds glycogen from glucose, which is anabolic. Only one of these two breaks molecules down.
Process 3 makes new glucose from lactate, which is anabolic. Only one of these two breaks molecules down.

q: In glycolysis, fructose-6-phosphate is converted to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Which coenzyme change accompanies this step?
h: A second phosphate group is added. Where does a phosphate come from in metabolism?
w: Adding a phosphate group (phosphorylation) uses one ATP, which becomes ADP: ATP → ADP. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD+ and FAD are not involved; ADP → ATP happens in steps that release a phosphate.
x: ATP is made later in glycolysis, when a phosphate is released. In this step a phosphate is added to the sugar.
No hydrogen is removed here, so NAD<sup>+</sup> is not involved. A phosphate group is being added.
FAD is used when a C=C forms. This step adds a second phosphate group to the sugar.

q: In each pair below, a coenzyme changes from the first form to the second. In which pair does the coenzyme gain hydrogen and get reduced?
h: In biochemistry, reduction usually means gaining hydrogen atoms (with their electrons).
w: FAD gains two hydrogen atoms (2 H+ + 2 e−) to become FADH2, a reduction. NADH → NAD+ and FADH2 → FAD lose hydrogen (oxidation), and ATP hydrolysis is not a redox change.
x: NADH loses hydrogen to become NAD<sup>+</sup>, so it is oxidized, not reduced.
FADH<sub>2</sub> loses hydrogen to become FAD, which is an oxidation. Look for the form that gains H.
ATP hydrolysis transfers a phosphate group; it is not a redox change and involves no gain of hydrogen.

q: Transamination removes alanine's amino group and leaves pyruvate behind. On that basis, which label fits alanine?
c: glucogenic, because pyruvate can be used to make glucose
ketogenic, because pyruvate forms ketone bodies only
essential, because pyruvate cannot be made in the body
h: Amino acids whose skeletons become pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates can feed gluconeogenesis.
w: Pyruvate can be turned into glucose by gluconeogenesis, so alanine is glucogenic. Ketogenic amino acids are degraded only to acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA, which cannot give a net gain of glucose.
x: Pyruvate does not form only ketone bodies; it can be made into glucose by gluconeogenesis.
Pyruvate is made in the body all the time from glucose. Being essential means the amino acid must come from the diet.
Pyruvate does not enter β-oxidation, which breaks down fatty acids. Think about what the liver can build from pyruvate.

q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin. Which process does insulin stimulate in the liver and muscle?
h: Insulin signals that fuel is plentiful. Will the body store glucose or release more of it?
w: Insulin promotes storage, so liver and muscle make glycogen from glucose: glycogenesis. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis raise blood glucose and are stimulated by glucagon between meals.
x: Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen down to raise blood glucose. It is stimulated by glucagon between meals.
Gluconeogenesis makes new glucose, which would raise blood glucose further. It is stimulated by glucagon, not insulin.
Ketogenesis happens when insulin is low, such as during fasting or uncontrolled diabetes.

q: After a glass of wine, alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) into acetaldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO). Which coenzyme takes part?
c: NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
FAD, which is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
NADH, which is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP
h: An alcohol losing two H atoms to become a C=O is an oxidation. Which coenzyme handles C–O oxidations, and which handles C–C?
w: Oxidizing an alcohol to a carbonyl removes 2 H, which are accepted by NAD+ → NADH. FAD is used when a C–C single bond becomes a C=C double bond.
x: FAD is used when a C–C single bond becomes a C=C. Here an alcohol becomes a C=O.
NADH → NAD<sup>+</sup> accompanies a reduction. Ethanol → acetaldehyde removes two H atoms, so it is an oxidation.
No phosphate is transferred in this step. The alcohol loses two H atoms to a coenzyme.

q: When a sprinter's leg muscles contract, the energy released by ATP hydrolysis is converted mainly into which form of energy?
h: Muscle contraction makes the body move. What type of energy is associated with motion?
w: Muscle proteins use the chemical energy of ATP hydrolysis to slide past each other, producing movement: chemical energy becomes mechanical energy (with some lost as heat).
x: Nuclear energy comes from changes in atomic nuclei, as in a power plant. Muscle contraction involves no nuclear reactions.
Some organisms such as fireflies turn ATP energy into light, but muscles do not. Think about what muscles do.
Making glucose would store energy, not use it. A contracting muscle is doing work.

q: One glucose gives two acetyl CoA, and each one goes around the citric acid cycle shown. In total, how many NADH, FADH<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> and GTP do these two turns produce?
h: Count what one turn of the wheel releases, then remember one glucose sends two acetyl CoA around the cycle.
w: One turn releases 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 2 CO2 and 1 GTP. Two turns per glucose double each: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 4 CO2, 2 GTP. "8 NADH, 6 CO2" also counts the pyruvate → acetyl CoA step, which is not part of the cycle.
x: These are the products of just one turn. One glucose sends two acetyl CoA around the cycle.
8 NADH and 6 CO<sub>2</sub> also count the pyruvate → acetyl CoA step, which happens before the cycle.
Count again how many FADH₂ and GTP the wheel releases in a single turn before doubling for two turns.

q: In the citric acid cycle shown, which conversion is an oxidative decarboxylation?
h: An oxidative decarboxylation does two things at once: a coenzyme is reduced and a carbon leaves as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate releases both NADH and CO2: the substrate is oxidized (NAD+ → NADH) and loses a carbon as CO2. Succinate → fumarate is an oxidation (FAD) with no CO2; citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization; succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP but neither oxidizes nor decarboxylates.
x: Succinate → fumarate is an oxidation by FAD, but no carbon is lost as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization; the formula does not change and no coenzyme is reduced.
Succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP. It is neither an oxidation nor a loss of CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Acetyl CoA enters the cycle shown as indicated by the blue arrow. Which 4-carbon compound does the 2-carbon acetyl group combine with to form citrate (6 C)?
h: Find the compound that comes right before citrate in the wheel; it is regenerated at the end of every turn.
w: Citrate (6 C) = acetyl group (2 C) + oxaloacetate (4 C). Oxaloacetate is the last compound of the wheel, so it is regenerated each turn, which is why the pathway is a cycle. Succinyl CoA, succinate and fumarate are also 4-carbon compounds, but they come earlier in the cycle and do not react with acetyl CoA.
x: Succinate is a 4-carbon compound in the middle of the cycle. It does not react with acetyl CoA.
Succinyl CoA forms after a CO<sub>2</sub> is lost, partway around the cycle. It does not react with acetyl CoA.
Fumarate is a 4-carbon compound late in the cycle, but it is hydrated to malate rather than joined to acetyl CoA.

q: In the citric acid cycle shown, the reduced coenzyme labeled X is formed when succinate is converted to fumarate. What is X, and why is this coenzyme used here?
c: FADH<sub>2</sub>; a C–C single bond is oxidized to a C=C double bond
NADH; a C–OH group is oxidized to a C=O group
FADH<sub>2</sub>; a C–OH group is oxidized to a C=O group
NADH; a C–C single bond is oxidized to a C=C double bond
h: Compare the structures: succinate is a saturated chain; fumarate has a C=C. Which coenzyme handles alkane → alkene oxidations?
w: Succinate → fumarate removes 2 H from neighboring carbons and makes a C=C, the type of oxidation done by FAD, so X = FADH2. NAD+ is used when C–OH is oxidized to C=O, as in malate → oxaloacetate.
x: Succinate has no C–OH group, and NAD<sup>+</sup> is not the coenzyme here. Compare the two structures: what new bond forms?
Succinate has no C–OH group. Compare the structures to see what new bond forms.
NAD⁺ is used when a C–OH group becomes a C=O, as in malate → oxaloacetate. Check whether that is the kind of change from succinate to fumarate.

q: Four acetyl CoA from the breakdown of a fatty acid go through the citric acid cycle shown. How many NADH and how many CO<sub>2</sub> are produced?
h: Read the NADH and CO<sub>2</sub> released in one trip around the wheel; each acetyl CoA makes one trip.
w: One turn: 3 NADH and 2 CO2. Four turns: 4 × 3 = 12 NADH and 4 × 2 = 8 CO2, so 12 NADH and 8 CO2. Each turn releases both carbons of the acetyl group as CO2; 16 NADH wrongly adds a pyruvate dehydrogenase NADH, which fatty acid acetyl CoA never passes through.
x: Each turn makes 3 NADH, not 1. Count the NADH released in one trip around the wheel.
Each turn releases 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, both carbons of the acetyl group, not just 1.
16 NADH adds a pyruvate → acetyl CoA NADH for each acetyl CoA. Acetyl CoA from a fatty acid never goes through that step.

q: Glycolysis is shown. For one glucose, what are the net yields of ATP and NADH?
h: Add up the ATP made, then subtract the ATP invested in the early steps.
w: ATP made: 2 + 2 = 4; ATP invested: 1 + 1 = 2; net = 2 ATP. NADH: 2 (one from each glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate). "4 ATP" forgets the 2 ATP spent in the energy-investment steps.
x: 4 ATP is the gross amount made. Subtract the 2 ATP spent in the energy-investment steps.
Glucose splits into two 3-carbon pieces, and each one is oxidized once, so the NADH count is not 1.
4 ATP forgets the ATP invested, and only one step per 3-carbon piece makes NADH.

q: In the glycolysis pathway shown, two labels are hidden. What are Y and Z?
h: Y goes in and ADP comes out at the same step. Z forms when NAD<sup>+</sup> goes in.
w: Steps 1 and 3 are the energy-investment steps: a phosphate group is transferred from ATP, leaving ADP. When glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is oxidized, 2 NAD+ are reduced to 2 NADH. Glycolysis makes no FADH2 and releases no CO2.
x: ADP comes out of these steps, so it cannot also be what goes in. The phosphate donor must be the higher-energy form.
Glycolysis makes no FADH<sub>2</sub>. The oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate uses a different coenzyme.
Glycolysis releases no CO<sub>2</sub>; all six carbons end up in the two pyruvates. Z forms when a coenzyme is reduced.

q: A muscle cell breaks down 3 glucose molecules by the pathway shown. How many pyruvate and how many net ATP form?
h: Find the yield per glucose from the pathway, then multiply by the number of glucose molecules.
w: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate and a net 2 ATP. For 3 glucose: 3 × 2 = 6 pyruvate and 3 × 2 = 6 ATP. 12 ATP is the gross yield, before subtracting the 6 ATP invested.
x: Each glucose splits into 2 pyruvate, so 3 glucose give more than 3 pyruvate.
12 ATP is the gross yield. Subtract the 6 ATP invested in the early steps for 3 glucose.
3 ATP uses a net of only 1 ATP per glucose. Recount the ATP made and spent in the pathway for one glucose, then multiply by 3.

q: During a sprint, muscle cells run low on O<sub>2</sub> and carry out the pathway shown. What is the main purpose of the last step, pyruvate → lactate?
c: to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> so that glycolysis can continue
to make 2 more ATP for each glucose
to convert pyruvate into acetyl CoA for the citric acid cycle
to release CO<sub>2</sub> so that the muscle cells stay neutral
h: Follow the NADH made in glycolysis. What happens to it in the last step, and why would glycolysis need that?
w: Glycolysis needs NAD+ to oxidize glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. Without O2, NADH cannot be reoxidized by electron transport, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate and NAD+ is regenerated. The step makes no ATP and releases no CO2; acetyl CoA forms only under aerobic conditions.
x: Pyruvate → lactate makes no ATP. Follow what happens to the NADH made earlier in glycolysis.
Acetyl CoA forms only when oxygen is plentiful. Here O<sub>2</sub> is low and pyruvate becomes lactate.
Pyruvate → lactate releases no CO<sub>2</sub>; both have 3 carbons. Think about which coenzyme is changed.

q: For one glucose, both pyruvate molecules go through the step shown. How many CO<sub>2</sub> and NADH are produced in this step?
h: Each pyruvate makes the trip once. One glucose gives how many pyruvate?
w: One glucose → 2 pyruvate. Each pyruvate → acetyl CoA releases 1 CO2 and 1 NADH, so the total is 2 CO2 and 2 NADH. "1 and 1" is per pyruvate, not per glucose; 6 CO2 is the total for complete oxidation of glucose.
x: 1 CO<sub>2</sub> and 1 NADH is the yield for one pyruvate. One glucose gives two pyruvate.
Each pyruvate gives one CO<sub>2</sub> and one NADH, so the two counts must be equal.
6 CO<sub>2</sub> is the total for complete oxidation of glucose. This single step releases only some of them.

q: Using the pathway and the ATP value in the table, how many ATP in total come from converting one glucose into two acetyl CoA (count the ATP made directly plus the ATP made when all the NADH shown is oxidized)?
h: Add the NADH from both steps, multiply by its ATP value, then add the ATP made directly in glycolysis.
w: NADH: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (pyruvate oxidation) = 4; 4 × 2.5 = 10 ATP. Add the 2 net ATP from glycolysis: 12 ATP. 7 counts only the glycolysis NADH (5 + 2); 10 forgets the 2 ATP made directly; 2 counts only the ATP made directly and ignores the NADH.
x: 7 counts the glycolysis NADH and the 2 ATP made directly, but leaves out the 2 NADH from pyruvate oxidation shown in the second step.
10 counts all the NADH but forgets the 2 net ATP made directly in glycolysis.
2 counts only the ATP made directly in glycolysis. The NADH must also be converted to ATP.

q: Stearic acid (18 C) is activated to stearoyl CoA and broken down completely by the β-oxidation spiral shown. How many times does the spiral turn, and how many acetyl CoA are produced?
h: Each turn cuts off 2 carbons. The last turn splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA.
w: 18 C ÷ 2 = 9 acetyl CoA. The final turn produces two acetyl CoA at once, so the number of turns is one less: 8 turns. "9 turns" forgets that the last 4-carbon piece gives two acetyl CoA in one turn.
x: 9 turns forgets that the last turn splits a 4-carbon piece into two acetyl CoA at once.
8 turns is right, but the last turn releases two acetyl CoA. Divide the carbons by 2 for the acetyl CoA count.
18 acetyl CoA counts one per carbon; each acetyl CoA has 2 carbons. The turn count is also one too many.

q: Myristic acid (14 C), found in coconut oil and nutmeg, is broken down completely by the β-oxidation spiral shown. How many NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> does β-oxidation itself produce (not counting the citric acid cycle)?
h: Each turn of the spiral gives one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>. How many turns does a 14-carbon acid need?
w: 14 C → 7 acetyl CoA, made in 7 − 1 = 6 turns. Each turn gives 1 FADH2 and 1 NADH: 6 NADH and 6 FADH2. "7 and 7" uses the number of acetyl CoA instead of the number of turns.
x: 7 and 7 uses the number of acetyl CoA instead of the number of turns. The last turn gives two acetyl CoA.
13 is far more turns than a 14-carbon chain needs. Each turn removes 2 carbons, not 1.
Every turn makes one FADH<sub>2</sub> in its first step, when a C=C forms. FADH<sub>2</sub> cannot be zero.

q: Lauric acid (12 C), the main fatty acid in coconut oil, is oxidized by the spiral shown and the citric acid cycle. Using the ATP values in the table, what is the net ATP yield?
h: Find the acetyl CoA (C ÷ 2) and the turns (one fewer). Each turn gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>; subtract the activation cost.
w: 6 acetyl CoA × 10 = 60; 5 turns → 5 NADH × 2.5 = 12.5 and 5 FADH2 × 1.5 = 7.5. Total 60 + 12.5 + 7.5 − 2 = 78 ATP. 80 forgets the 2-ATP activation cost; 82 uses 6 turns instead of 5; 95 uses the older values throughout (3 ATP per NADH, 2 per FADH2 and 12 per acetyl CoA).
x: 80 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
82 uses 6 turns. The number of turns is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
95 uses the older values throughout: 3 ATP per NADH, 2 per FADH₂ and 12 per acetyl CoA. Use the values in the table.

q: Arachidic acid, a saturated 20-carbon fatty acid in peanut oil, is oxidized by the spiral shown and every acetyl CoA then goes through the citric acid cycle (3 NADH per acetyl CoA). How many NADH form in total?
h: Add two sources: the NADH from the turns of the spiral and the NADH from the acetyl CoA in the citric acid cycle.
w: 20 C → 10 acetyl CoA in 9 turns. β-Oxidation: 9 NADH. Citric acid cycle: 10 × 3 = 30 NADH. Total = 39 NADH. 36 sends only 9 acetyl CoA through the cycle (confusing turns with acetyl CoA); 9 and 30 each count only one of the two sources.
x: 9 counts only the NADH from the β-oxidation turns. The acetyl CoA also make NADH in the citric acid cycle.
30 counts only the NADH from the citric acid cycle. Add the NADH made in the β-oxidation turns.
36 sends only 9 acetyl CoA through the cycle, confusing turns with acetyl CoA. A 20-carbon acid gives 10 acetyl CoA.

q: A 14-carbon fatty acyl CoA has gone around the β-oxidation spiral shown three times. How many carbons are left in the shortened fatty acyl CoA, and how many acetyl CoA have been released so far?
h: Look at the last step: each turn removes a 2-carbon unit as one acetyl CoA.
w: Each turn releases one acetyl CoA (2 C). After 3 turns: 14 − 3 × 2 = 8 C remain, with 3 acetyl CoA released. "11 C" removes only 1 carbon per turn; "6 acetyl CoA" counts 2 per turn.
x: Each turn cuts off a 2-carbon acetyl unit, not 1 carbon. Subtract 2 carbons for every turn.
Each turn releases just one acetyl CoA (one 2-carbon piece). Six acetyl CoA would mean two per turn.
This counts one turn too many. Three turns remove three 2-carbon units; check the carbon count and acetyl CoA count again.

q: Electrons flow through the electron transport chain shown. What is the final electron acceptor at the position marked "?"
c: O<sub>2</sub>, which is reduced to H<sub>2</sub>O
NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
H<sub>2</sub>O, which is oxidized to O<sub>2</sub>
CO<sub>2</sub>, which is reduced to glucose
h: Why do we need to breathe? The last carrier hands its electrons to something we inhale.
w: Complex IV passes the electrons to O2, which picks up H+ and is reduced to H2O. This is why aerobic metabolism needs O2. NAD+ is reduced at the start of the process (in the citric acid cycle), not at the end of the chain.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced earlier, in pathways like the citric acid cycle. At the end of the chain, electrons go to a gas we breathe in.
This runs backward: water splitting into O<sub>2</sub> happens in photosynthesis. In our cells the last carrier hands electrons to something that becomes water.
Reducing CO<sub>2</sub> to glucose is photosynthesis in plants. Human cells release CO<sub>2</sub>; they do not use it to accept electrons.

q: In the electron transport chain shown, electrons from FADH<sub>2</sub> enter through complex II and go directly to coenzyme Q. Why does each FADH<sub>2</sub> give fewer ATP (1.5) than each NADH (2.5)?
c: Its electrons bypass complex I, so fewer H<sup>+</sup> are pumped
Its electrons go to O<sub>2</sub> without passing complex IV
FADH<sub>2</sub> carries only one electron instead of two
FADH<sub>2</sub> makes ATP only by substrate-level phosphorylation
h: Count the H<sup>+</sup> pumping steps each type of electron passes through on the way to O<sub>2</sub>.
w: NADH electrons pass all three pumping sites (complexes I, III and IV). FADH2 electrons enter at coenzyme Q, skipping complex I, so fewer H+ are pumped and ATP synthase makes less ATP. Both carriers deliver 2 electrons, and both still pass through complex IV to O2.
x: Electrons from FADH<sub>2</sub> still pass through complex IV on their way to O<sub>2</sub>. Look at where they enter the chain instead.
FADH<sub>2</sub> and NADH each deliver 2 electrons. The difference is in how many H<sup>+</sup> pumping complexes those electrons pass through.
FADH<sub>2</sub> feeds the electron transport chain, so its ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation. Substrate-level phosphorylation does not use FADH<sub>2</sub>.

q: In the electron transport chain shown, carrier X accepts electrons from both complex I (from NADH) and complex II (from FADH2) and passes them to complex III. What is X?
h: X is a small mobile carrier that sits between complexes I/II and complex III.
w: Both NADH (via complex I) and FADH2 (via complex II) hand their electrons to coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), which carries them to complex III. Cytochrome c is the carrier between complexes III and IV; ATP synthase makes ATP but does not carry electrons.
x: Cytochrome c shuttles electrons later in the chain, between complexes III and IV. X sits before complex III.
ATP synthase uses the H<sup>+</sup> gradient to make ATP; it does not carry electrons between complexes.
NAD<sup>+</sup> is the oxidized form left after NADH gives up its electrons at complex I. It does not carry electrons on to complex III.

q: In the urea cycle shown (in the liver), which compound is released at the step marked "?" and carried by the blood to the kidneys for excretion?
h: This is the step that splits arginine and regenerates ornithine, so the cycle can start again.
w: Arginine is hydrolyzed to urea, which is excreted in urine, and ornithine, which starts the next turn. Fumarate leaves at the earlier step, NH+4 is the toxic waste the cycle removes, and aspartate enters the cycle.
x: Fumarate leaves at an earlier step, when argininosuccinate is split. It goes to the citric acid cycle, not to the kidneys.
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is the toxic waste the cycle is designed to get rid of. The cycle converts it into a safer compound before it leaves the liver.
Aspartate enters the cycle, bringing in a nitrogen. It is not released at the step that regenerates ornithine.
