q: Each turn of the urea cycle shown makes one urea, H<sub>2</sub>N–CO–NH<sub>2</sub>. If a patient's liver puts 12 nitrogen atoms into urea, how many turns of the cycle occur, and how many aspartate molecules enter?
h: Count the N atoms in one urea. One N comes from carbamoyl phosphate and one from aspartate in each turn.
w: Each urea carries 2 N, so 12 N ÷ 2 = 6 turns (one urea per turn). One aspartate enters per turn, supplying one of the two N, so 6 aspartate are used. "12 turns" forgets that each urea removes two N atoms at once.
x: This assumes one N per urea. Look at H<sub>2</sub>N–CO–NH<sub>2</sub>: each urea carries two N atoms, so fewer turns are needed.
The turns are right, but only one aspartate enters per turn. The other N comes from carbamoyl phosphate.
This assumes one N per urea for the turns. Each urea carries two N, and one aspartate enters per turn, so the two numbers should match.

q: In the urea cycle shown, one product leaves the cycle and can enter the citric acid cycle, linking the two pathways. Which compound is it?
h: Which product of the urea cycle is also an intermediate in the citric acid cycle?
w: Argininosuccinate is split into arginine and fumarate. Fumarate is also an intermediate of the citric acid cycle (fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate), so it links the two cycles. Urea is excreted, and citrulline and carbamoyl phosphate stay within the urea cycle.
x: Urea is the waste product carried to the kidneys and excreted. It is not a citric acid cycle intermediate.
Citrulline stays within the urea cycle; it reacts with aspartate in the next step. It is not part of the citric acid cycle.
Carbamoyl phosphate is the entry compound that brings NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> into the urea cycle. It does not leave to join the citric acid cycle.

q: The alkene shown reacts with H<sub>2</sub> over a platinum catalyst. What is the product?
h: Hydrogenation adds one H to each carbon of the C=C. Nothing else in the molecule changes.
w: H2 adds across the C=C, giving methylcyclohexane: the ring and the methyl group stay in place. The aromatic ring (toluene) would need H2 to be removed; the alcohol would need water (hydration); the open chain would need the ring to break.
x: This is toluene, an aromatic ring with fewer H atoms than the reactant. Making it would require removing H<sub>2</sub>, not adding it.
This is an alcohol with an OH group, which would come from adding water. H<sub>2</sub> supplies only hydrogen atoms.
This is an open seven-carbon chain. Hydrogenation does not break the ring; it only adds H across the C=C.

q: Sorbic acid, a food preservative, is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub> and a nickel catalyst. What is the product?
h: Excess H<sub>2</sub> saturates every C=C. Under these conditions the C=O of a carboxylic acid is not reduced.
w: Both C=C double bonds take up H2 (2 H2 total), giving hexanoic acid. Keeping one C=C means only one H2 was added. The carboxyl group (COOH) is not reduced by H2/Ni, so the aldehyde and the alcohol are wrong.
x: This structure still has one C=C, so only one H<sub>2</sub> was added. Excess H<sub>2</sub> saturates every C=C.
This is an alcohol: the COOH group has been reduced to CH<sub>2</sub>OH. H<sub>2</sub>/Ni does not reduce a carboxylic acid group.
This is an aldehyde: the COOH group has lost an O. H<sub>2</sub>/Ni does not change the carboxylic acid group.

q: Cyclopentene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> as shown. What is the product?
h: In halogenation, one halogen atom adds to each carbon of the double bond.
w: The Cl–Cl adds across the C=C: one Cl on each of the two former double-bond carbons, giving 1,2-dichlorocyclopentane. A single Cl would come from HCl, not Cl2. Putting both Cl on one carbon, or on carbons that were not part of the C=C, is not addition across the double bond.
x: This has only one Cl, which is what HCl would give. Cl<sub>2</sub> adds two Cl atoms.
Here the two Cl atoms are on carbons with a CH<sub>2</sub> between them. Only neighboring carbons were joined by the C=C.
Both Cl atoms are on the same carbon. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Cl.

q: 3-Methyl-1-butene, shown, reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>. What is the product?
h: Br<sub>2</sub> adds one Br to each carbon that was in the C=C. Find those two carbons first.
w: The C=C is between C1 and C2, so Br adds to both: 1,2-dibromo-3-methylbutane. The structures with only one Br come from HBr, not Br2. Placing a Br on C3 puts it on a carbon that was not part of the double bond.
x: This has only one Br, on C2: that is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
This puts a Br on C3, the carbon carrying the methyl. C3 was not part of the C=C.
This has only one Br, on the end carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> supplies a Br for each of the two double-bond carbons.

q: 2-Methyl-2-butene, shown, reacts with HBr. What is the major product?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: The C=C carbons are C2 (no H) and C3 (one H). H adds to C3 and Br adds to the more substituted C2: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. Br on C3 is the anti-Markovnikov product. Two Br atoms would need Br2, and an OH would need water.
x: This puts Br on the double-bond carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. Br goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
This has two Br atoms, which would require Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HBr adds an H and a Br.

q: 2-Methylpropene, shown, reacts with HCl. What is the major product?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H adds to the C=C carbon with more H atoms; Cl ends up on the other carbon.
w: H adds to the CH2 end and Cl to the carbon bearing the two methyl groups, giving tert-butyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylpropane). Cl on the CH2 end (isobutyl chloride) is the anti-Markovnikov product; two Cl atoms would need Cl2.
x: This puts Cl on the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has more H, so it receives the H.
This has two Cl atoms, which would require Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HCl adds an H and a Cl.

q: 1-Butene, shown, reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst (H+). What is the major product?
h: Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C and follows Markovnikov's rule.
w: H adds to C1 (the CH2 end, more H) and OH adds to C2, giving 2-butanol. 1-Butanol is the anti-Markovnikov product; the diol adds OH to both carbons; butane comes from adding H2, not water.
x: This puts the OH on C1, the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. C1 has more H, so it receives the H.
This diol has two OH groups. Water adds one H and one OH across the C=C.
Butane has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: 1-Methylcyclopentene, shown, is heated with H2O and H2SO4 (acid catalyst). What is the major product?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the OH goes to the double-bond carbon that has fewer H atoms.
w: The ring carbon bearing the methyl group has no H; the other C=C carbon has one H. H adds to the CH carbon and OH to the methyl-bearing carbon: 1-methylcyclopentanol, a tertiary alcohol. 2-Methylcyclopentanol is the anti-Markovnikov product.
x: This puts the OH on the ring carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. The OH goes to the double-bond carbon with fewer H atoms.
This diol has two OH groups. Water adds one H and one OH across the C=C.
This has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanol, shown, is heated with concentrated H2SO4. What is the major organic product?
h: Dehydration removes H<sub>2</sub>O. Zaitsev's rule: the major alkene has the most carbon groups on the C=C.
w: H2O is lost from the C–OH carbon and a neighboring C–H. Removing the H from the carbon bearing the methyl group gives the more substituted alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene (Zaitsev product). 3-Methylcyclohexene is the minor product; the ketone would require oxidation, not dehydration.
x: This is 3-methylcyclohexene, the minor product. Its C=C carbons carry fewer carbon groups than the alternative.
Here the C=C is outside the ring, on a carbon that never held the –OH. Dehydration forms the double bond at the C–OH carbon and a neighbor.
This is a ketone, which would come from oxidation. Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with heat removes water to make a C=C.

q: 2-Pentanol, shown, is heated with H2SO4. Which is the major alkene formed?
h: The H is removed from the neighboring carbon that has fewer H atoms (Zaitsev's rule), giving the more substituted alkene.
w: The OH carbon (C2) has two neighbors: C1 (CH3) and C3 (CH2). Removing H from C3 puts the C=C between C2 and C3: 2-pentene, the more substituted (major) product. Losing H from C1 gives 1-pentene, the minor product. 2-Pentanone is an oxidation product, and pentane would need H2 added.
x: This is 1-pentene, formed when the H comes from the CH<sub>3</sub> end. It forms, but as the minor product: Zaitsev's rule favors the neighbor with fewer H atoms.
This is a ketone, 2-pentanone, which comes from oxidation. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with heat removes water to make a C=C.
This is pentane, with no C=C. It would need H<sub>2</sub> added; dehydration forms a double bond instead.

q: Isoamyl alcohol (3-methyl-1-butanol), shown, is oxidized with a mild oxidizing agent [O] so that the reaction stops at the first stage. What is the product?
h: A primary alcohol is oxidized first to an aldehyde. Only the carbon bearing the OH changes.
w: The CH2OH carbon loses two H and becomes CHO: 3-methylbutanal. Further oxidation to the carboxylic acid is over-oxidation, which the mild conditions prevent. The ketone oxidizes the wrong carbon, and the alkene is a dehydration product.
x: This is the carboxylic acid, the second oxidation stage. Mild conditions stop the reaction one step earlier.
This puts a C=O on an inner carbon, making a ketone. Oxidation changes only the carbon that holds the –OH, which here is an end CH<sub>2</sub>.
This is an alkene, which comes from dehydration (loss of water). Oxidation forms a C=O, not a C=C.

q: 1-Butanol, shown, is treated with excess potassium dichromate, K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (a strong oxidizing agent). What is the final organic product?
h: With excess strong oxidizer, a primary alcohol does not stop at the first stage.
w: A 1° alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde, and with excess [O] the aldehyde is oxidized again to butanoic acid. Butanal is only the intermediate. 2-Butanone would require the OH on C2, and 1-butene is a dehydration product.
x: Butanal is the first oxidation product. With excess strong oxidizing agent the reaction does not stop there.
This is a ketone with the C=O on C2. 1-Butanol has its –OH on C1, and oxidation does not move the oxygen.
This is 1-butene, a dehydration product. K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> oxidizes the alcohol rather than removing water.

q: 3-Methyl-2-butanol, shown, is oxidized with [O]. What is the product?
h: Classify the alcohol first. Oxidation turns the C–OH into C=O on the same carbon.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons, so this is a 2° alcohol; it is oxidized to a ketone, 3-methyl-2-butanone. The aldehyde puts the C=O on an end carbon that never had the OH. The alkene comes from dehydration, and the other alcohol just moves the OH.
x: This aldehyde has its C=O on an end carbon that never held the –OH. Oxidation works on the C–OH carbon itself.
This alkene comes from dehydration (loss of water), not oxidation. [O] forms a C=O.
This is just another alcohol with the –OH moved to a different carbon. Oxidation turns C–OH into C=O.

q: 2-Methyl-2-butanol, shown, is mixed with the oxidizing agent K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> [O]. What happens?
h: Check how many H atoms are on the carbon that holds the OH. Oxidation must remove one of them.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to three carbons, so this is a 3° alcohol. It has no H on that carbon, so it cannot form a C=O: no reaction occurs. The aldehyde, ketone and acid shown would each require moving the oxygen to a different carbon.
x: This aldehyde puts the oxygen on a different carbon. Oxidation can only change the carbon that already holds the –OH; check how many H atoms it has.
This ketone has the oxygen on a different carbon from the one in the starting alcohol. Oxidation cannot move the oxygen.
This carboxylic acid puts the oxygen on an end carbon that never held the –OH. Check the C–OH carbon: does it have an H to lose?

q: 1-Propanethiol, shown, gives freshly cut onions part of their odor. When two molecules of it are mildly oxidized [O], what product forms?
h: Oxidation of thiols removes the H from each –SH group and joins the two sulfur atoms.
w: Each –SH loses its H and the two S atoms bond: R–SH + HS–R → R–S–S–R, dipropyl disulfide (the same reaction links cysteines in proteins). The sulfide has lost a sulfur atom, and the peroxide replaces S with O.
x: This sulfide has only one S, so a sulfur atom was lost. Oxidation removes just the H from each –SH.
This has O–O in place of S–S. The sulfur atoms stay in the product; no oxygen is added to the chain.
This has a C=S on one molecule, which would come from removing H from carbon. Two thiol molecules are joined by oxidation here.

q: Benzaldehyde (almond flavor), shown, is reduced with [H] (a reducing agent); the benzene ring is not affected. What is the product?
h: Reduction adds H atoms across the C=O. What kind of alcohol does an aldehyde give?
w: [H] adds H atoms across the C=O, turning the aldehyde CHO into CH2OH: benzyl alcohol, a 1° alcohol. Benzoic acid is the oxidation product (the opposite reaction). Toluene would require removing the oxygen entirely, and the benzene ring is unchanged under these conditions.
x: This drawing is benzoic acid, the oxidation product. [H] is a reducing agent.
This drawing is toluene: the oxygen is gone completely. [H] adds H atoms across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.
This drawing has a cyclohexane ring instead of benzene. The question says the ring is not affected.

q: 3-Pentanone, shown, is reduced with [H] (a reducing agent). What is the product?
h: Reduction converts C=O into CH–OH on the same carbon.
w: H adds to the carbonyl C and O, so C3 becomes CH–OH: 3-pentanol, a 2° alcohol (ketones reduce to 2° alcohols). 2-Pentanol puts the OH on the wrong carbon; pentane removes the oxygen; pentanoic acid is an oxidation product.
x: This drawing is 2-pentanol, with OH on carbon 2. Reduction puts the OH on the carbon that held the C=O, carbon 3.
This drawing is pentane: the oxygen is gone. [H] adds H atoms across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.
This drawing is pentanoic acid, an oxidation product. [H] is a reducing agent, and a ketone cannot give an acid.

q: Propanal reacts with one molecule of methanol in the presence of acid, as shown. What is the product?
h: An aldehyde plus one alcohol gives a hemiacetal: the carbonyl carbon ends up with both –OH and –OR.
w: The CH3O– group of methanol bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiacetal (one OH and one OCH3 on the same carbon). Two OCH3 groups (acetal) need a second methanol. Methyl propanoate is an ester, which forms from a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde.
x: This drawing has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups, which needs two methanol molecules. Only one methanol reacts here.
This drawing is methyl propanoate, an ester with a C=O. Esters form from carboxylic acids; the aldehyde's C=O is used up here.
This drawing is an ether with only one oxygen; the original carbonyl oxygen has disappeared. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen.

q: Acetaldehyde (ethanal), shown, reacts with two molecules of ethanol in acid, with loss of water. What is the final product?
h: The first ethanol makes a hemiacetal; the second replaces the –OH with another –OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: Ethanal + 2 ethanol → acetal (two –OCH2CH3 groups on the former carbonyl carbon) + H2O. The structure with one OH and one OEt is only the hemiacetal intermediate. Ethyl acetate is an ester, and placing the two OEt groups on different carbons is wrong: both bond to the former carbonyl carbon.
x: This drawing has one –OH and one ethoxy group: the intermediate after one ethanol. The second ethanol replaces the –OH.
This drawing is ethyl acetate, an ester with a C=O. Esters come from carboxylic acids, not aldehydes.
This drawing puts the two ethoxy groups on different carbons. Both alcohols add to the same former carbonyl carbon.

q: Acetone reacts with one molecule of ethanol under acid catalysis. What is the product?
h: A ketone + one alcohol → hemiketal. The former carbonyl carbon ends up with an –OH and an –OR.
w: The ethoxy group adds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiketal (C bonded to OH, OCH2CH3 and two CH3). Two ethoxy groups (ketal) need a second ethanol; the ether has lost an oxygen; the remaining structure puts the groups on two different carbons.
x: This drawing has two ethoxy groups, which needs two ethanol molecules. Only one ethanol reacts here.
This drawing is an ether with only one oxygen: the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen as –OH.
This drawing puts the –OH and the ethoxy group on different carbons. Both end up on the former carbonyl carbon.

q: Acetic acid and isoamyl alcohol react with an acid catalyst (H<sup>+</sup>) to make isoamyl acetate, which smells like bananas. Which structure is the ester formed?
h: The C=O side of the ester comes from the acid; the alcohol supplies the –O–R part. Water is lost.
w: The –OH from the acid and the H from the alcohol leave as H2O, joining CH3C(=O)– to –O–CH2CH2CH(CH3)2: isoamyl acetate. The first wrong ester puts the C=O on the alcohol side (ethyl 3-methylbutanoate); the ether has lost the C=O; the last one attaches the O to the wrong carbon of the alcohol.
x: This ester has the C=O on the branched side and an ethyl on the O (ethyl 3-methylbutanoate). Acetic acid's two carbons should stay with the C=O.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an ether. Esterification keeps the acid's carbonyl group.
Here the ester O is on a branched carbon in the middle of the chain. Isoamyl alcohol's –OH is on the end CH<sub>2</sub>, and that carbon keeps the O.

q: Salicylic acid reacts with methanol in acid to make methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen, used in muscle rubs). Which structure is the product?
h: Esterification joins a carboxylic acid (–COOH) and an alcohol. Which group of salicylic acid is the acid?
w: Methanol reacts with the –COOH group, giving the methyl ester –COOCH3; the phenol –OH is unchanged. Methylating the phenol O gives an ether, not the ester. The structure with an acetyl group is aspirin, made with acetic acid, not methanol.
x: Here methanol has bonded to the phenol O, making an ether, and the –COOH is unchanged. Esterification happens at the carboxylic acid group.
This structure has an acetyl ester on the phenol O. That is aspirin, which is made with acetic acid (or its anhydride), not methanol.
Both oxygens are methylated here, so the phenol –OH became an ether too. Only one group of salicylic acid reacts with methanol in esterification.

q: Ethyl butanoate (pineapple flavor), shown, is heated with water and an acid catalyst. What are the products?
h: Acid hydrolysis splits the ester at the C–O single bond next to the C=O and adds H and OH.
w: The ester bond between the carbonyl carbon and the –O– breaks; OH goes to the acyl group and H to the oxygen: butanoic acid + ethanol. Butanol + acetic acid splits the molecule at the wrong place; the sodium salt forms only in base (NaOH); two alcohols would require reduction.
x: This is 1-butanol plus acetic acid, which splits the ester on the wrong side of the C=O. The four-carbon C=O side should keep its carbonyl.
A carboxylate sodium salt forms only in base (NaOH). This reaction uses acid and water.
Two alcohols would mean the C=O was reduced, not hydrolyzed. Hydrolysis keeps the C=O and gives it an –OH.

q: Ethyl propanoate, shown, is heated with aqueous NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
h: In base, the carboxylic acid that forms is immediately neutralized. Which fragment carries the C=O?
w: NaOH breaks the C–O bond next to the C=O; the acyl part becomes the carboxylate salt and the –OCH2CH3 part becomes ethanol: sodium propanoate + ethanol. Propanoic acid + ethanol are the acid-hydrolysis products; the other choices put the Na+ or the C=O on the wrong fragment.
x: A carboxylic acid plus ethanol is what acid hydrolysis gives. In NaOH the acid is neutralized as it forms.
This drawing gives the Na<sup>+</sup> to the alcohol (sodium ethoxide) and leaves the acid un-neutralized. The base reacts with the acidic –COOH.
This drawing puts the C=O on the two-carbon fragment (acetate) and makes 1-propanol. In the ester, the C=O is bonded to the three-carbon side.

q: Methyl benzoate, shown, is saponified with NaOH. One product, sodium benzoate, is used as a food preservative. What are the products?
h: Saponification gives the alcohol and the salt of the carboxylic acid. The C=O stays with the acid part.
w: The ester splits at the C–O bond next to the C=O: the benzoyl part becomes sodium benzoate and the –OCH3 part becomes methanol. Benzoic acid + methanol form in acid, not base; the remaining choice puts the C=O on the wrong side of the ester oxygen (acetate + phenol).
x: Benzoic acid plus methanol is the product of acid hydrolysis. In NaOH, the acid is neutralized as it forms.
This drawing gives the Na<sup>+</sup> to methanol (sodium methoxide) and leaves benzoic acid as –COOH. Which fragment is acidic and reacts with the base?
This drawing shows sodium acetate and phenol, as if the C=O were on the methyl side. In methyl benzoate the C=O is attached to the ring.

q: Propanoic acid and methylamine, shown, are heated together so that water is removed. What is the organic product?
h: Amidation: –OH from the acid and H from the amine leave as water; the C=O stays with the acid part.
w: The acid carbonyl carbon bonds to the N of methylamine, giving N-methylpropanamide. N-Ethylacetamide has the C=O on the wrong side; the amine has lost the C=O; the methyl ester would come from methanol, not methylamine.
x: This drawing is N-ethylacetamide: the C=O is on a two-carbon piece and an ethyl is on N. The acid's C=O must stay with its three-carbon chain.
This drawing is an amine (N-methylpropylamine) with no C=O. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl oxygen.
This drawing is an ester, methyl propanoate, with an O between the C=O and the CH<sub>3</sub>. An ester would need methanol; methylamine gives a C–N bond.

q: N-Ethylacetamide, shown, is heated with water and HCl (acid hydrolysis). What are the products?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond of the amide. In acid, what happens to the amine that forms?
w: Water breaks the amide C–N bond, giving acetic acid and ethylamine; in HCl the amine is protonated, so the products are acetic acid + ethylammonium chloride. "Ethylamine" ignores that the solution is acidic; acetamide + ethanol breaks the wrong bond (N–Cethyl).
x: This shows neutral ethylamine, but the reaction runs in HCl. An amine in acid picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
This drawing breaks the N–ethyl bond, giving acetamide and ethanol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.
This shows acetate ion, which cannot survive in HCl; it would be protonated. There is also no chloride ion to balance the ammonium charge.

q: Trimethylamine gives spoiled fish its odor. It reacts with HCl as shown. What is the product?
h: Amines are bases: the lone pair on N picks up H<sup>+</sup> from the acid.
w: The N lone pair accepts H+, giving the ammonium ion (CH3)3NH+ with Cl−: trimethylammonium chloride, an odorless, water-soluble salt (why lemon juice helps with fish odor). No new C–Cl or N–Cl bond forms, and no methyl group is added (that would be a quaternary ammonium salt).
x: This drawing has four CH<sub>3</sub> groups on N, a quaternary ammonium salt. HCl adds only H<sup>+</sup> to the nitrogen, not a methyl group.
This drawing puts Cl on a carbon (CH<sub>2</sub>Cl). HCl does not make C–Cl bonds with an amine; it is an acid–base reaction.
This drawing bonds Cl directly to N. The nitrogen lone pair picks up H<sup>+</sup>, and chloride stays a separate ion.

q: Benzene, shown, is heated with HNO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. What is the organic product?
h: Benzene undergoes substitution, not addition: a group replaces one H and the ring stays aromatic.
w: Nitration replaces one ring H with an –NO2 group, giving nitrobenzene + H2O. The ring keeps its three alternating double bonds. Nitrocyclohexane would mean the ring lost its aromaticity; aniline (–NH2) and phenol (–OH) are not formed by nitration.
x: That is aniline, with an –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Nitration attaches an N bonded to two O atoms; turning it into –NH<sub>2</sub> would take a separate reduction step.
That ring has no double bonds left (nitrocyclohexane), so it is no longer aromatic. Nitration of benzene keeps the aromatic ring.
That is phenol, with an –OH group. HNO<sub>3</sub> puts a nitrogen-containing group on the ring, not –OH.

q: Benzene, shown, reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> in the presence of an FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst. What is the organic product?
h: Unlike an alkene, benzene keeps its stable ring: Br replaces one H and HBr is the by-product.
w: Aromatic substitution: one H is replaced by Br, giving bromobenzene + HBr. Adding Br2 across a double bond (the dibromo-cyclohexadiene) is what alkenes do, not benzene. Two Br would require a second substitution, and bromocyclohexane has lost all the double bonds.
x: Here Br<sub>2</sub> added across one ring double bond, leaving only two. That is alkene behavior; the benzene ring keeps all three double bonds.
This has two Br atoms on the ring. One Br<sub>2</sub> puts only one Br on the ring; the other Br leaves as HBr with the displaced H.
This ring has no double bonds left (bromocyclohexane), so it is not aromatic. Reaction with Br<sub>2</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> keeps the benzene ring intact.

q: Eugenol, shown, is the main component of clove oil and is used in dentistry in temporary fillings and as a mild pain reliever. Which functional groups does eugenol contain?
h: Look at each oxygen: is it bonded to H, or between two carbons, and is there any C=O? Then look at the side chain.
w: The –OH on the benzene ring is a phenol; the –O– between the ring and CH3 is an ether (no C=O, so not an ester); the side chain has a C=C, an alkene. There is no C=O anywhere, so ketone and ester are wrong, and there is no triple bond.
x: An ester needs a C=O next to the oxygen. Eugenol has no C=O; the –O– between the ring and CH<sub>3</sub> has only single bonds.
–OH on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol, and the side chain has a C=C double bond, not a triple bond.
A ketone needs a C=O. Look again: none of eugenol's oxygens is double-bonded to carbon.

q: Lidocaine, shown, is a local anesthetic that dentists inject before filling a tooth. Which functional groups does it contain (besides the benzene ring)?
c: an amide and a tertiary (3°) amine
an ester and a tertiary (3°) amine
an amide and a primary (1°) amine
a ketone and a secondary (2°) amine
h: A C=O bonded directly to N is one group. For the other N, count the carbons attached to it.
w: The C=O is bonded to N–H, so that part is an amide (not a ketone, and not an ester since there is no –O–). The other N is bonded to three carbons (two ethyl groups and a CH2), so it is a tertiary amine. (Older anesthetics like procaine are esters.)
x: An ester needs a C=O next to an oxygen (–COO–). In lidocaine the C=O is bonded to a nitrogen, and there is no –O– at all.
A primary amine has –NH<sub>2</sub>, with only one carbon on N. Count the carbons on the N that is not next to the C=O.
A ketone needs a C=O between two carbons, but here the C=O is bonded to N. And an N–H next to a C=O is not an amine.

q: Which of the alcohols shown is a tertiary (3°) alcohol?
h: Go to the carbon that holds the OH and count how many carbons are bonded to it.
w: In II the C–OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (the methyl and two ring carbons), so II is 3°. I is 1° (the OH carbon has one carbon neighbor, even though the chain is branched), and III and IV are 2°. Branching elsewhere in the molecule does not matter; only the C–OH carbon counts.
x: In I the C–OH carbon is a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to only one carbon, so it is primary. The branch is one carbon away.
In III the C–OH carbon is bonded to two ring carbons and still has an H, so it is secondary. The methyl is on the neighboring carbon.
In IV the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons (a CH<sub>3</sub> and a CH<sub>2</sub>), so it is secondary.

q: Menthol, shown, gives mint toothpaste and cough drops their cooling feel. How many chiral carbons does menthol have?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups. In a ring, compare the two paths around the ring from that carbon.
w: The ring carbons bearing the OH, the methyl group and the isopropyl group each have four different groups (H, the substituent and two ring paths that are not the same), so menthol has 3 chiral carbons. CH2 ring carbons and the isopropyl CH (two identical CH3 groups) are not chiral.
x: Too few. Check each ring carbon that carries a substituent: compare the two paths around the ring from that carbon.
Too few. Each of the ring carbons bearing a group (–OH, –CH<sub>3</sub>, isopropyl) has two ring paths that are not the same. Check all of them.
That count likely includes the isopropyl CH, which has two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Ring CH<sub>2</sub> carbons are not chiral either.

q: Ibuprofen, shown, is a common pain reliever. How many chiral carbons does it contain?
h: Check each carbon with four single bonds that has one H: does it have four different groups? Carbons in the benzene ring and CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>2</sub> groups never qualify.
w: Only the carbon next to the COOH group has four different groups: H, CH3, COOH and the ring, so there is 1 chiral carbon. The CH in the isobutyl group carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral; ring carbons have only three groups.
x: Look at the carbon bonded to –CH<sub>3</sub>, –COOH, H and the ring. Are all four of its groups different?
That count includes the CH in the isobutyl group, which has two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not chiral.
Ring carbons have a double bond, and CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub> and –COOH carbons cannot be chiral. Only one CH carbon has four different groups.

q: Pseudoephedrine, shown, is a nasal decongestant. How are its alcohol group and its amine group classified?
h: For the alcohol, count carbons on the C–OH carbon. For the amine, count carbons bonded directly to N.
w: The C–OH carbon is bonded to the ring carbon and to the CH(CH3) carbon: a 2° alcohol. The N is bonded to two carbons (CH3 and the chain CH) and one H: a 2° amine. For amines, count the carbons on the N itself, not on a neighboring carbon.
x: The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons: the ring carbon and the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) carbon. Count them again for the alcohol.
The N is bonded to two carbons (a CH<sub>3</sub> and the chain CH) plus one H. Count carbons on the nitrogen itself.
The C–OH carbon still has an H, and the N still has an H. Neither group has three carbons attached.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkane shown?
h: Find the longest continuous chain first (it may bend), then number from the end nearer the first branch. List substituents alphabetically.
w: The longest chain has 6 carbons (hexane). Numbering from the end nearer the branches gives a methyl on C2 and an ethyl on C4: 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane (ethyl before methyl alphabetically). "Heptane" miscounts the chain; the other names put the branches on the wrong carbons.
x: Recount the longest chain carefully. Following the bends gives 6 carbons, not 7, whichever path you take.
An ethyl group on C2 means the chain is not the longest: the ethyl would extend it. Find the longest chain first, then number.
3-Ethyl-2-methyl puts the branches on neighboring carbons. In this structure a CH<sub>2</sub> sits between the two branch points.

q: The ester shown is a solvent with a fruity odor used in some nail-polish removers. What is its name?
h: Name the alkyl group on the –O– first, then the acid part (the side with the C=O) as "-oate".
w: The –O– carries an isopropyl group (attached at its middle carbon), and the C=O side has 2 carbons (ethanoate, from ethanoic/acetic acid): isopropyl ethanoate (isopropyl acetate). Propyl has the O on an end carbon; ethyl 2-methylpropanoate swaps the two sides; propanoate has 3 carbons on the C=O side.
x: Propyl has the O attached at an end carbon. In this ester the O is attached to the middle carbon of the three-carbon group.
This swaps the sides of the ester. The C=O side here has only two carbons; the branched group is on the single-bonded O.
Propanoate would need three carbons on the C=O side. Here the C=O side is CH<sub>3</sub>C(=O)–.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Number the main chain from the OH end. Which carbon carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch?
w: The chain is HO–C1–C2–C3–C4 with the CH3 branch on C2 (the CH right next to the CH2OH): 2-methyl-1-butanol, C5H12O. The most tempting wrong drawing moves the branch one carbon away from the OH (3-methyl-1-butanol); another puts the OH on the branched carbon; the 4-carbon one has dropped a CH2.
x: This drawing has only four carbons (2-methyl-1-propanol). The condensed formula has five carbons; one CH<sub>2</sub> is missing.
Here the branch is two carbons away from the C–OH carbon (3-methyl-1-butanol). In the formula, the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) sits right next to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
Here the –OH is on the branched carbon, which also holds two CH<sub>3</sub> groups (2-methyl-2-butanol). In the formula the –OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub> at the end.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Count the carbons (every line end and corner is a C), then find which two carbons share the double bond.
w: Five carbons with the C=C between C2 and C3: 2-pentene. Putting the double bond at the end of the chain gives 1-pentene, a common slip when a drawing starts the zig-zag at the double bond. 2-Butene is one carbon short, and 2-methyl-2-butene has a branch the formula does not show.
x: Here the double bond is at the end of the chain (1-pentene). The formula starts with CH<sub>3</sub>, so the C=C begins at the second carbon.
This drawing has only four carbons (2-butene). Count the carbons in the formula again.
This drawing has a CH<sub>3</sub> branch on a double-bond carbon (2-methyl-2-butene). The formula is an unbranched chain.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH– means a carbon holding two methyl groups. Count the longest chain and locate the branch.
w: The longest chain is five carbons with one CH3 on C2: 2-methylpentane. The drawing with the branch on the middle carbon is 3-methylpentane (branch moved), the 2-methylbutane drawing is one CH2 short, and the one with two methyls on C2 has an extra carbon.
x: Here the branch is on the middle carbon of a five-carbon chain (3-methylpentane). (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH– puts the branch one carbon from the end.
This drawing has only five carbons in all (2-methylbutane). The formula has six; one CH<sub>2</sub> is missing.
Here one carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> branches, for seven carbons. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH– means a CH holding two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, one of which is part of the main chain.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: A C=O in the middle of a chain written as "CO" is a ketone. Which carbon holds the oxygen?
w: CO sits with two CH2CH3 groups on either side, so the C=O is on C3 of a five-carbon chain: 3-pentanone. 2-Pentanone moves the C=O one carbon over; butanone is one carbon short; pentanal puts the C=O at the end (an aldehyde, written CHO).
x: Here the C=O is on the second carbon (2-pentanone). In the formula, CO has a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on each side.
This drawing has only four carbons (butanone). Count the carbons on both sides of the CO again.
Here the C=O is at the end of the chain, an aldehyde (pentanal). In the formula the CO is in the middle, between two carbons.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Write the main chain left to right: C1 has the OH-bearing neighbor; the last CH holds two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
w: C1 = CH3, C2 = CH(OH), C3 = CH2, C4 = CH with a CH3 branch, and C5 is the other CH3: 4-methyl-2-pentanol. The tempting near-miss puts the methyl branch on C3, right beside the OH carbon (3-methyl-2-pentanol). Another moves the OH to the end of the chain, and 3-methyl-2-butanol is one CH2 short.
x: Here the –OH is on the end carbon of the chain (4-methyl-1-pentanol). In the formula the OH is on the CH next to the first CH<sub>3</sub>.
Here the CH<sub>3</sub> branch is right beside the C–OH carbon (3-methyl-2-pentanol). In the formula a CH<sub>2</sub> separates them.
This drawing has only five carbons (3-methyl-2-butanol). The CH<sub>2</sub> between the C–OH carbon and the branched CH is missing.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: An O written between two carbon groups is an ether oxygen. Count the carbons on each side of it.
w: Two carbons on one side of the O and three on the other: ethyl propyl ether. Moving the O so it has one carbon on one side gives methyl butyl ether (same formula, wrong structure); diethyl ether has only four carbons; 1-pentanol has an OH at the end, not an O between carbons.
x: Here the O has one carbon on one side and four on the other (methyl butyl ether). The formula has two carbons on one side and three on the other.
This drawing has only four carbons, two on each side of the O. Count the carbons on each side in the formula again.
This has an –OH at the end of a chain, an alcohol. In the formula the O sits between two carbon groups and has no H.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: In COOCH<sub>3</sub>, the C=O carbon is attached to the chain on its left; the CH<sub>3</sub> is on the single-bonded O.
w: Three carbons + the C=O carbon make a four-carbon acid part, and CH3 sits on the –O–: methyl butanoate. Ethyl propanoate has the same formula but the carbons are split 3 + 2 around the ester O; methyl propanoate is one carbon short; propyl acetate reverses which side carries the C=O.
x: Here the carbons are split 3 on the C=O side and 2 on the O side (ethyl propanoate). The formula has CH<sub>3</sub> alone on the single-bonded O.
This drawing has only four carbons (methyl propanoate). Count the carbons before the COO again: three plus the C=O carbon.
Here the C=O is on the short side and the long chain is on the –O– (propyl acetate). In the formula the long chain is attached to the C=O carbon.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: Start at the CH<sub>2</sub>= end: the double bond is C1=C2. Which carbon carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch?
w: C1=C2 double bond, then C3 holds the CH3 branch, then an ethyl end: 3-methyl-1-pentene. The drawing with the double bond inside the chain (3-methyl-2-pentene) moved the C=C; the 4-methyl one moved the branch; 3-methyl-1-butene is one carbon short.
x: Here the double bond is inside the chain (3-methyl-2-pentene). CH<sub>2</sub>= at the start of the formula puts the C=C at the very end.
Here the branch is two carbons from the C=C (4-methyl-1-pentene). In the formula the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) comes right after CH<sub>2</sub>=CH.
This drawing has only five carbons (3-methyl-1-butene). The formula ends with a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, not just a CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: HC≡C– puts the triple bond at the very end of the chain. Then count to the carbon with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
w: C1≡C2, a CH2, then a CH bearing two CH3 groups: 4-methyl-1-pentyne. Moving the triple bond inside the chain gives 4-methyl-2-pentyne (no CH2 left between); 3-methyl-1-butyne lacks the CH2; 3-methyl-1-pentyne moves the branch next to the triple bond.
x: Here the triple bond is inside the chain (4-methyl-2-pentyne). HC≡C– at the start of the formula puts it at the very end.
This drawing has no CH<sub>2</sub> between the triple bond and the branched CH (3-methyl-1-butyne). The formula has one.
Here the branch is right next to the triple bond, followed by an ethyl end (3-methyl-1-pentyne). In the formula a CH<sub>2</sub> comes first, then a CH with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.

q: Which line (skeletal) structure represents the compound whose condensed formula is shown?
h: The NH<sub>2</sub> in parentheses is attached to the CH written just before it.
w: The NH2 is on the second carbon from the right end of a five-carbon chain: 2-pentanamine. 3-Pentanamine moves the NH2 to the middle carbon; 1-pentanamine puts it at the end; 2-butanamine is one CH2 short.
x: Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is on the end carbon (1-pentanamine). In the formula the NH<sub>2</sub> is on a CH, not a CH<sub>2</sub>.
Here the –NH<sub>2</sub> is on the middle carbon (3-pentanamine). In the formula the CH(NH<sub>2</sub>) has a CH<sub>3</sub> on one side.
This drawing has only four carbons (2-butanamine). Count the CH<sub>2</sub> groups in the formula again.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: Find the carbon bonded to the O. Is it at the end of the chain or inside it?
w: The O–H hangs from the second carbon of a four-carbon chain, so that carbon is written CH(OH): CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (2-butanol). Writing CH2OH at the end would move the OH to C1; an O between two carbons would be an ether.
x: This puts the –OH on the end carbon (1-butanol). In the drawing the O is attached to a carbon inside the chain that has only one H.
This has an O between two carbons, an ether. In the drawing the O is bonded to H, so it is an –OH group.
This is a branched chain with the OH on a CH<sub>2</sub>. The drawing is an unbranched four-carbon chain.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: The end carbon has a C=O and one H. How is that group written in condensed form?
w: An end carbon with =O and one H is an aldehyde group, written CHO: CH3CH2CHO (propanal). CH3COCH3 would put the C=O in the middle (a ketone). Reading CHO as "C–O–H" leads students to the alcohol, but the drawing has no O–H bond.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> has its C=O in the middle of the chain, a ketone. In the drawing the C=O carbon is at the end and carries an H.
This is an alcohol with an O–H. The drawing has no O–H bond; the end carbon has a double bond to O and one H.
This has a C=C and an –OH. The drawing has no C=C and no O–H; the double bond is between C and O.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: A C=O carbon also bonded to an –O–C is an ester. Which side of the ester O does each carbon sit on?
w: CH3 on the C=O carbon, then –O–CH3: CH3COOCH3 (methyl acetate). Propanoic acid and ethyl formate have the same formula (C3H6O2) but different connections; the drawing has no O–H, so it is not an acid.
x: This is a carboxylic acid, with an O–H. The drawing has no O–H; the second O is bonded to a CH<sub>3</sub>.
Here the C=O carbon carries an H and the O carries an ethyl group. In the drawing the C=O carbon carries a CH<sub>3</sub>, and the O carries a CH<sub>3</sub>.
This has a C=O between two carbons plus an –OH. In the drawing the C=O carbon is bonded to an O–CH<sub>3</sub>, and there is no O–H.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: Count the carbons and note which one has three carbon neighbors.
w: The middle carbon is bonded to three CH3 groups and one H: CH3CH(CH3)CH3 (2-methylpropane, isobutane). The branch drawn downward is still a CH3 attached to the middle carbon, so the straight-chain butane formula is wrong; the other two have five carbons.
x: This is the straight chain, butane. In the drawing the middle carbon has three carbon neighbors, so there is a branch.
This has five carbons, a central C with four CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Count the carbons in the drawing again.
This has five carbons. The drawing has four carbons in all.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: The N sits inside the chain and carries one H. How many carbons are on each side of it?
w: One carbon on the left of N, two on the right, and one H on N: CH3NHCH2CH3 (ethylmethylamine, a 2° amine). Propylamine and trimethylamine have the same formula, C3H9N, but N–H counts of two and zero; diethylamine has four carbons.
x: This is propylamine, with N at the end bearing two H. In the drawing the N sits between two carbon groups and has one H.
Trimethylamine has three CH<sub>3</sub> groups on N and no N–H. The drawing has an N–H and an ethyl group.
This has two ethyl groups on N, four carbons in all. The drawing has a CH<sub>3</sub> on one side of N.

q: Which condensed formula represents the structure drawn?
h: Locate the C=C first, then the carbon with the CH<sub>3</sub> branch. Start writing from the CH<sub>2</sub>= end.
w: The C=C is at the end (CH2=CH–), and the next carbon is a CH bearing two CH3 groups: CH2=CHCH(CH3)2 (3-methyl-1-butene). CH3CH=C(CH3)2 moves the double bond to the branched carbon; the other two choices move the branch or remove it.
x: This moves the double bond to the branched carbon. In the drawing the C=C is at the end, as CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–.
This puts the CH<sub>3</sub> branch on a double-bond carbon. In the drawing the branched carbon has only single bonds.
This is an unbranched chain. In the drawing one carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: The O in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> is written between two carbon groups. Is it bonded to an H?
w: The O is bonded to a CH2 on one side and a CH3 on the other, with no H on O: an ether, ethyl methyl ether. 1-Propanol and 2-propanol have the same formula (C3H8O) but contain O–H; the remaining drawing has an extra CH2.
x: This drawing has an O–H on the end carbon, an alcohol (1-propanol). In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> the O has carbons on both sides and no H.
This drawing has an O–H on the middle carbon, an alcohol (2-propanol). In the formula the O sits between two carbon groups.
This drawing has a propyl group on the O, four carbons in all. The formula has an ethyl group on one side of O and a CH<sub>3</sub> on the other.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: CHO at the end of a formula is not C–O–H. Which group has a C=O plus an H on the same carbon?
w: CHO is the aldehyde group: the end carbon has a double bond to O and one H, giving acetaldehyde (ethanal). Reading CHO as C–O–H gives an alcohol, but ethanol has two more H atoms (C2H6O). The acid has an extra O, and dimethyl ether has no C=O.
x: This drawing is ethanol, with C–O–H. CHO means a C=O with an H on the same carbon, and there is no O–H.
This drawing has both a C=O and an O–H on the end carbon, a carboxylic acid. CHO has only one O.
This drawing has an O between two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, an ether. CHO means the O is double-bonded to the end carbon.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: In CONH<sub>2</sub>, the C has a double bond to O and a single bond to the NH<sub>2</sub>.
w: CH3–C(=O)–NH2: the carbonyl carbon is bonded to both O and N, which makes acetamide, an amide. N-Methylformamide (CH3NHCHO) and aminoacetaldehyde have the same formula but the C=O is not where the condensed formula puts it; ethylamine has no O.
x: Here the CH<sub>3</sub> is on the N, and the C=O carbon carries an H. In CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> the CH<sub>3</sub> is on the C=O carbon.
This drawing has no oxygen at all (ethylamine). The CO in the formula is a C=O.
Here the NH<sub>2</sub> is on a CH<sub>2</sub> and the C=O is at the other end with an H. In the formula the NH<sub>2</sub> is on the C=O carbon.

q: Which expanded structural formula matches the condensed formula shown?
h: COOH at the end of a formula is a carboxyl group: one C with =O and –OH.
w: The last carbon has =O and –OH, so the drawing is propanoic acid. Methyl acetate and ethyl formate are esters with the same formula, C3H6O2: they have an O between two carbons and no O–H. The hydroxy ketone moves the C=O into the chain.
x: This drawing has an O between the C=O carbon and a CH<sub>3</sub>, and no O–H. COOH needs an –OH on the C=O carbon.
This drawing has an H on the C=O carbon and an ethyl group on the other O, with no O–H. COOH needs an –OH on the C=O carbon.
Here the C=O is inside the chain and the –OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub>. In COOH both oxygens are on the same end carbon.

q: In this line structure of 1-butene, every corner is drawn at 120°. What is the actual C–C–C bond angle at carbon a, approximately?
h: Count the groups around carbon a, including the hydrogens the line drawing does not show. Does it have a double bond?
w: Carbon a has four single bonds (two C and two hidden H), so its groups point to the corners of a tetrahedron: about 109.5°. The zig-zag drawing makes every corner look like 120°, but only the two C=C carbons are really 120°.
x: 120° is the drawn angle, and it is real only at the two C=C carbons. Carbon a has only single bonds.
180° goes with two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Count the groups around carbon a, including hidden H.
90° is not the angle for any carbon in this molecule. Count the groups around carbon a, including the two hidden H.

q: Butanone (methyl ethyl ketone) is a common solvent. What is the approximate C–C–C bond angle at carbon a?
h: Count the groups of electrons around carbon a. A double bond counts as one group.
w: Carbon a has three groups (two C and the C=O), which spread out in a flat triangle: about 120°. 109.5° applies to a carbon with four single bonds; the C=O counts as only one group.
x: 109.5° goes with a carbon that has four single bonds. Carbon a has a C=O, which counts as one group.
180° goes with two electron groups, like a triple-bonded carbon. Count the groups around carbon a.
90° is not the angle for any carbon in this molecule. Count the groups around carbon a; a double bond counts once.

q: What is the approximate C–C–C bond angle at carbon a in 2-pentyne?
h: A triple bond counts as one group. How many groups surround carbon a?
w: Carbon a has only two groups (the triple bond and one single bond), so they point in opposite directions: 180°, which is why the four carbons around the C≡C are drawn in a straight line. 120° is the angle at a double-bonded carbon.
x: 120° goes with three groups, like a C=C carbon. Carbon a is part of a triple bond, which counts as one group.
109.5° goes with four single bonds. Carbon a has a triple bond and only one other bond.
90° is not the angle for any carbon here. Count the groups around carbon a; the triple bond counts once.

q: Diethyl ether was one of the first surgical anesthetics. What is the approximate C–O–C bond angle at oxygen a?
h: Oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs. Count all four groups, not just the bonds.
w: Oxygen a has two bonds and two lone pairs, four groups arranged roughly tetrahedrally, so the C–O–C angle is about 109.5° (bent; the real value is a bit larger). Choosing 180° counts only the two bonds and ignores the lone pairs.
x: 120° goes with three electron groups. Oxygen a has two bonds plus two lone pairs, so count those too.
180° counts only the two bonds and ignores the two lone pairs on oxygen. Lone pairs push the bonds closer together.
90° is not a normal angle around oxygen. Count all of oxygen's electron groups, bonds and lone pairs.

q: Butanal, a sharp-smelling aldehyde, is drawn below. What are the approximate bond angles around carbons a and b?
h: Carbon a has only single bonds (two to hidden H atoms). Carbon b has a C=O and a hidden H. Count groups on each.
w: Carbon a has four single bonds (two C and two hidden H): 109.5°. Carbon b has three groups (C, =O and a hidden H): 120°. "Both 120°" trusts the 120° corners of the drawing instead of counting groups around each carbon.
x: Carbon a is drawn at a 120° corner, but it has four single bonds (two to hidden H). Count groups instead of trusting the drawing.
Carbon b has a C=O, so it has only three electron groups (C, =O and a hidden H). Four single bonds would be needed for 109.5°.
Carbon a has four single bonds, and carbon b has a double bond, not a triple bond. Count the groups on each.

q: Methamphetamine is shown. What is the approximate C–N–C bond angle at nitrogen a?
h: This nitrogen has two bonds to carbon, one hidden H and one lone pair. How many groups is that?
w: N a has three bonds (two C and one H) plus one lone pair: four groups, pointing toward the corners of a tetrahedron, so the angle is about 109.5° and the shape around N is pyramidal. 120° trusts the zig-zag drawing and ignores the hidden H and the lone pair.
x: Trigonal planar trusts the zig-zag drawing. This N also has a hidden H and a lone pair; count every group.
180° would need only two electron groups. N a has two C, one hidden H and a lone pair.
Electron groups spread out in 3-D, not in a flat square. Count the four groups on N, including the lone pair.

q: Toluene is drawn below. What is the approximate C–C–C bond angle at ring carbon a?
h: Count the groups around carbon a. Remember the hidden H, and that a double bond counts once.
w: Each benzene-ring carbon has three groups (two ring carbons and one H, with one double bond), so the ring is flat and every angle is 120°, a perfect hexagon. 109.5° would need four single bonds on the carbon.
x: 109.5° would need four single bonds. Ring carbon a has two ring carbons, one hidden H and one double bond: three groups.
180° goes with two electron groups. A benzene ring carbon has more groups than that.
90° would make a square, but a benzene ring is a flat hexagon. Count the three groups around carbon a.

q: In 4-methyl-2-pentyne, which statement about the bond angles at carbons a and b is correct?
c: a is about 109.5° and b is 180°
a is about 120° and b is 180°
a is about 109.5° and b is 120°
h: Carbon a has only single bonds; carbon b is part of the triple bond. Count groups on each.
w: Carbon a has four single bonds (three C plus one hidden H): 109.5°. Carbon b has two groups (the triple bond and one single bond): 180°. Choosing 120° for a trusts how the branch is drawn; it is not a double-bond carbon.
x: Carbon a is drawn with branches at 120°, but it has four single bonds (three C and a hidden H). Count groups, not drawn angles.
Carbon a is not part of the triple bond. It has four single bonds, so it is not linear.
Carbon b is part of the triple bond, so it has only two groups. 120° would need three groups, as at a C=C carbon.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Write the molecular formula of each. Same formula with different connections means one thing; identical connections means another.
w: Both are C5H12, but I is an unbranched chain (pentane) and II has four carbons bonded to one central carbon (2,2-dimethylpropane). Same formula, different connections: constitutional isomers. They are not the same compound, because no bonds can be rotated to turn one into the other.
x: I is an unbranched chain and II has four carbons bonded to one central carbon. No rotation turns one into the other.
Count the atoms: both are C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, so they are isomers of some kind.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. Both of these are open-chain alkanes.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Find the longest continuous carbon chain in each drawing, even if it turns a corner at a branch.
w: In II the longest chain runs through the "ethyl" branch: it is six carbons with a CH3 on C3, exactly like I. Both are 3-methylhexane, so they are the same compound drawn two ways. Students who only compare how the drawings look call them constitutional isomers.
x: Find the longest chain in II: it turns the corner through the ethyl branch. Then compare the names.
Count the carbons: both are C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. Ask whether the connections really differ.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. These are open-chain alkanes.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Count C, H and O in each. Then look at what the O is bonded to.
w: Both are C3H8O. In I the O carries an H (an alcohol, 1-propanol); in II the O is between two carbons (an ether, ethyl methyl ether). Same formula, different connections: constitutional isomers.
x: In I the O carries an H (alcohol); in II the O is between two carbons (ether). Different connections cannot be the same compound.
Count the atoms: both are C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O. Same formula means they are isomers of some kind.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. Neither compound has one.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: A ring and a double bond each remove two H atoms from the alkane formula. Compare the molecular formulas.
w: Cyclohexane (I) and 1-hexene (II) are both C6H12, but one has a ring and the other a C=C: constitutional isomers. Students who think a ring compound can only be an isomer of another ring miss this.
x: I is a ring and II is an open chain with a C=C. Different connections cannot be the same compound.
Count the H: a ring and a C=C each remove two H from the alkane formula, so both are C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>.
Cis–trans isomers need the same connections. A ring and an open chain are connected differently. Also, a C=C at the end of a chain has no cis or trans form.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Count the hydrogens: every corner of the ring is a CH<sub>2</sub>. What about the open chain?
w: Cyclohexane (I) is C6H12; hexane (II) is C6H14. Different molecular formulas, so they are different compounds, not isomers. Having the same number of carbons is not enough.
x: Isomers must have the same formula. Count the H: the ring has no chain ends, but the open chain has two CH<sub>3</sub> ends.
A ring and an open chain cannot be the same compound. Count the hydrogens in each.
Cis–trans isomers need the same formula and connections. Count the hydrogens in each.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Number each chain from the end nearest the OH. Which carbon holds it in each drawing?
w: Both are five-carbon chains with the OH on C2 (2-pentanol); II is simply drawn from the other end. They are the same compound drawn two ways. Flipping a drawing left-to-right never makes an isomer.
x: Number each chain from the end nearest the OH. Constitutional isomers would need the OH on a different carbon.
Count the atoms: both are C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O. Flipping a drawing does not change the formula.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. These are open-chain alcohols.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Both have a C=O. Write each molecular formula, then ask where the C=O sits.
w: Butanal (I, an aldehyde: C=O at the end) and butanone (II, a ketone: C=O inside the chain) are both C4H8O: constitutional isomers. Students who see two different functional groups sometimes say "not isomers", but only the formula matters.
x: In I the C=O is at the end of the chain; in II it is inside the chain. Different connections cannot be the same compound.
Different functional groups do not rule out isomers. Count the atoms: both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.
Cis–trans isomers need a C=C or a ring. These have a C=O, which does not give cis and trans forms.

q: 2-Methylpentane is shown. Which structure is a constitutional isomer of it?
h: An isomer needs the same molecular formula but a different structure. Watch for a drawing of the same molecule turned around.
w: 2-Methylpentane is C6H14. Moving the branch to C3 gives 3-methylpentane, also C6H14: an isomer. The drawing with the branch on the second carbon from the left end is 2-methylpentane again (same compound, not an isomer); 2-methylbutane is C5H12, and the alkene is C6H12.
x: Turn this drawing around: the branch is on the second carbon from the left end, so it is 2-methylpentane again, the same compound.
This drawing has only five carbons (2-methylbutane, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>). Isomers must have the same formula, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>.
This drawing contains a C=C, so it is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, two H fewer than 2-methylpentane.

q: Ethyl acetate, shown, is the solvent in many nail-polish removers. Which compound is a constitutional isomer of it?
h: Write the molecular formula of ethyl acetate first. Then find the choice with exactly the same C, H and O counts.
w: Ethyl acetate is C4H8O2, and so is butanoic acid (esters and carboxylic acids with the same carbons are isomers). Butanal (C4H8O) has one O too few, ethyl propanoate has an extra CH2, and 1-butanol is C4H10O.
x: This drawing is butanal, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O: it has one O fewer than ethyl acetate.
This drawing is ethyl propanoate, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>: it has one more CH<sub>2</sub> than ethyl acetate.
This drawing is 1-butanol, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O: it has one O fewer and two H more than ethyl acetate.

q: Cyclopentane, shown, is a constitutional isomer of which compound?
h: A ring removes two H atoms from the alkane formula, just like one double bond does.
w: Cyclopentane is C5H10; 1-pentene is also C5H10, so they are isomers. Cyclopentene (C5H8) has a ring and a C=C; pentane (C5H12) has neither; methylcyclopentane has six carbons.
x: This drawing is cyclopentene. It has a ring and a C=C, so it is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, two H fewer than cyclopentane.
This drawing is pentane, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. With no ring and no C=C it has two more H than cyclopentane.
This drawing is methylcyclopentane, which has six carbons. Isomers need the same number of each atom.

q: Which structure is cis-2-pentene?
h: In a cis alkene, the two carbon chains attached to the C=C carbons are on the same side of the double bond.
w: In cis-2-pentene the CH3 (C1) and the CH2CH3 (C4–C5) are on the same side of the C2=C3 bond, giving a U-shaped drawing. The zig-zag with the groups on opposite sides is trans-2-pentene; 1-pentene and 2-methyl-2-butene cannot be cis or trans at all.
x: This drawing is the zig-zag with the CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on opposite sides of the C=C, which is the trans form.
This drawing is 1-pentene. Its end carbon holds two H, so it cannot be cis or trans.
This drawing is 2-methyl-2-butene. One C=C carbon holds two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it cannot be cis or trans.

q: Which structure is trans-4-methyl-2-pentene?
h: Find the C2=C3 double bond. In the trans isomer, the chain carbons on each end point to opposite sides.
w: In trans-4-methyl-2-pentene the CH3 on C2 and the isopropyl group on C3 lie on opposite sides of the C=C. The drawing with them on the same side is the cis isomer. Moving the double bond to C1 or to the branched carbon gives alkenes with no cis/trans form.
x: In this drawing the CH<sub>3</sub> on C2 and the isopropyl group on C3 are on the same side of the C=C. That is the cis form.
This drawing has the C=C at the end of the chain (4-methyl-1-pentene). Its end carbon holds two H, so it has no trans form.
This drawing has the C=C at the branched carbon, which holds two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. That alkene has no cis or trans form.

q: What is the name of the alkene drawn?
h: Number the chain so the double bond gets the lowest number, then check whether the chain continues on the same or opposite sides.
w: Numbering from the end nearer the C=C puts it at C2 (never "3-pentene"). The CH3 and the CH2CH3 are on opposite sides, so it is trans-2-pentene. Choosing cis comes from looking at the H atoms (not drawn) instead of the carbon chain.
x: Cis means the carbon chain continues on the same side of the C=C. Follow the CH<sub>3</sub> and the CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: which sides are they on?
3-Pentene numbers from the wrong end. Number from the end nearer the C=C.
This numbers from the wrong end; a C=C in pentene is never at 3. Also check which sides the two carbon groups are on.

q: cis-3-Hexen-1-ol gives freshly cut grass its smell. The hydrocarbon part is drawn below without the OH. What is its name?
h: Count the carbons, number from the end nearer the C=C, and see whether the two ethyl groups are on the same side.
w: Six carbons, C=C between C3 and C4 (the same from either end), and both CH2CH3 groups on the same side: cis-3-hexene. Trans would put them on opposite sides (a straight zig-zag); 2-hexene would need the C=C one carbon closer to an end.
x: Trans would put the two ethyl groups on opposite sides of the C=C. Look at the drawing: which side is each ethyl on?
2-Hexene would have a CH<sub>3</sub> directly on one double-bond carbon. Here each double-bond carbon carries an ethyl group.
Count the carbons: there are six, so the parent is hexene, not heptene.

q: Which alkene cannot exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Look at each carbon of the C=C. If one of them holds two identical groups, swapping sides gives the same molecule.
w: In 2-methyl-2-butene, one C=C carbon carries two CH3 groups, so there is no "same side" vs. "opposite side" difference. The other three each have two different groups on both C=C carbons, so they can be cis or trans (as drawn, two are trans and one is cis).
x: This drawing is 2-pentene. Each C=C carbon holds an H and a different carbon group, so cis and trans forms exist.
This drawing is 3-hexene. Each C=C carbon holds an H and an ethyl group, so cis and trans forms exist.
This drawing is 2-butene. Each C=C carbon holds an H and a CH<sub>3</sub>, so cis and trans forms exist.

q: Which of these alkenes has no cis and trans forms?
h: A double bond at the very end of a chain has a CH<sub>2</sub>= carbon. What are its two groups?
w: In 1-butene, C1 holds two H atoms, so flipping groups across the C=C gives the same molecule. 2-Butene, 2-hexene and 3-methyl-2-pentene each have two different groups on both carbons of the C=C, so they show cis–trans isomerism. A branch alone does not prevent it.
x: This drawing is 2-butene. Each C=C carbon holds an H and a CH<sub>3</sub>, so it does have cis and trans forms.
This drawing is 2-hexene. Each C=C carbon holds two different groups, so it does have cis and trans forms.
This drawing is 3-methyl-2-pentene. The branch does not prevent cis–trans isomerism: each C=C carbon still holds two different groups.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Same formula and same connections? Then look at which side of the C=C each CH<sub>3</sub> is on.
w: Both are 2-butene, C4H8, with identical connections. In I the CH3 groups are on the same side (cis); in II they are on opposite sides (trans). The C=C cannot rotate, so these are cis–trans isomers, not the same compound and not constitutional isomers.
x: Constitutional isomers have different connections. Here both are 2-butene with every atom bonded to the same neighbors.
Look at which side of the C=C each CH<sub>3</sub> is on. The C=C cannot rotate, so these two cannot turn into each other.
Both are C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> with the same connections, so they are isomers of some kind.

q: How are compounds I and II related?
c: the same compound drawn two ways
h: Turn one drawing over in your mind. Are the carbon groups on the same side or opposite sides of the C=C in each?
w: Both drawings have the CH3 and CH2CH3 on opposite sides of C2=C3: both are trans-2-pentene, just flipped. They are the same compound drawn two ways. Calling them cis–trans isomers comes from comparing which way the drawings point instead of the sides of the C=C.
x: Both drawings are 2-pentene with the C=C in the same place. Turning a drawing around does not change its connections.
Count the atoms: both are C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.
Compare the sides of the C=C, not the direction each drawing points. Check whether the CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> are on the same or opposite sides in each.

q: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is shown. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?
h: Every corner and line end is a carbon. Fill in enough hidden H atoms to give each carbon four bonds, then add the masses.
w: Counting every carbon and every hidden H gives C9H8O4: 9(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 4(16.00) = 180.15 g mol⁻¹. 173.10 g mol⁻¹ counts only the H atoms written on O or N and forgets the H atoms hidden on the carbons (the most common mistake); 168.14 g mol⁻¹ misses one carbon (count every corner and line end); 94 g mol⁻¹ adds atomic numbers instead of atomic masses.
x: That total uses only the H atoms written on O or N. Add the hidden H atoms on the carbons too, enough to give each carbon four bonds.
That total is one carbon short. Every corner and line end is a carbon, including ring corners and the ends of short branches.
That is what you get by adding atomic numbers. Use the atomic masses from the table, multiplied by the number of each atom.

That total is one carbon short. Every corner and line end is a carbon, including ring corners and the ends of short branches.

q: Dopamine, a neurotransmitter, is shown. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?

q: Lactic acid, which builds up in muscles during intense exercise, is shown. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?

w: Counting every carbon and every hidden H gives C3H6O3: 3(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 90.08 g mol⁻¹. 86.05 g mol⁻¹ counts only the H atoms written on O or N and forgets the H atoms hidden on the carbons (the most common mistake); 78.07 g mol⁻¹ misses one carbon (count every corner and line end); 48 g mol⁻¹ adds atomic numbers instead of atomic masses.

q: Caffeine has the molecular formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?
h: Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript in the formula, then add.

That total uses 7 carbons instead of 8. Check the C subscript in the formula.
That is what you get by adding atomic numbers. Use the atomic masses from the table, multiplied by each subscript.

q: Lidocaine, a local anesthetic used by dentists, is shown. Using the atomic masses in the table, what is its molar mass?
h: Every corner and line end is a carbon. Fill in enough hidden H atoms to give each carbon four bonds, then add the masses.
w: Counting every carbon and every hidden H gives C14H22N2O: 14(12.01) + 22(1.008) + 2(14.01) + 1(16.00) = 234.34 g mol⁻¹. 213.17 g mol⁻¹ counts only the H atoms written on O or N and forgets the H atoms hidden on the carbons (the most common mistake); 222.33 g mol⁻¹ misses one carbon (count every corner and line end); 128 g mol⁻¹ adds atomic numbers instead of atomic masses.

q: Amphetamine, a stimulant used to treat ADHD, is shown. How is the nitrogen labeled a classified?
h: For amines, count the carbon atoms bonded directly to the nitrogen, not to the carbon that holds it.
w: The N is bonded to only one carbon (plus two H), so amphetamine is a primary (1°) amine. Calling it 2° uses the alcohol rule (the carbon holding the group is bonded to two carbons); amines are classified by the N itself.
x: That uses the alcohol rule: the carbon holding the N has two carbon neighbors. For amines, count carbons bonded directly to N.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on N and no N–H. Nitrogen a is –NH<sub>2</sub>.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons on a positive N. Nitrogen a is neutral and carries two H.

q: Diphenhydramine, the antihistamine in Benadryl, is shown. How is the nitrogen labeled a classified?
h: Count the carbons bonded directly to N. In a line drawing, each line from N that ends without a letter is a CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The N has three bonds to carbon (two CH3 line ends and the CH2 of the chain) and no H: a tertiary (3°) amine. Students who count only the chain carbon miss the two methyl line ends; a quaternary ion would need four carbons and a + charge.
x: A secondary amine has an N–H. Nitrogen a has no H; remember each line ending at N without a label is a CH<sub>3</sub>.
A primary amine has an –NH<sub>2</sub> with one carbon. Count the CH<sub>3</sub> line ends on nitrogen a as well as the chain carbon.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons and a + charge on N. Nitrogen a is neutral.

q: Lidocaine, a local anesthetic, has two nitrogen atoms, a and b. Which statement is correct?
c: a is a 3° amine; b is part of an amide
a is a 3° amine; b is a 2° amine
a is a 2° amine; b is part of an amide
a is part of an amide; b is a 1° amine
h: An N bonded to a C=O carbon belongs to an amide, not an amine. For the other N, count the attached carbons.
w: N a is bonded to three carbons (two ethyls and a CH2): a 3° amine. N b is bonded to the C=O carbon, so it is part of an amide. Calling b a 2° amine counts its two carbons but misses the C=O, which makes it an amide (much less basic).
x: N b is bonded to a C=O carbon. An N attached to a carbonyl carbon belongs to an amide, not an amine.
N a has two ethyl groups and a CH<sub>2</sub>: count every carbon on it, including both ethyls.
N a is not bonded to the C=O carbon; a CH<sub>2</sub> sits between them. N b is bonded to the C=O and to the ring, so it is not an –NH<sub>2</sub>.

q: Nicotine is shown. How is the nitrogen labeled a, in the five-membered ring, classified?
h: Ring carbons count too. Count every carbon bonded directly to nitrogen a, including the CH<sub>3</sub> line end.
w: N a is bonded to two ring carbons and the CH3, with no H: a tertiary (3°) amine. Choosing 2° counts only the two ring bonds and forgets the methyl line end.
x: That counts only the two ring bonds. The line from nitrogen a ending with no label is a CH<sub>3</sub>, a third carbon.
A primary amine has an –NH<sub>2</sub>. Nitrogen a has no H; it is bonded to ring carbons and a CH<sub>3</sub>.
A quaternary ammonium ion needs four carbons and a + charge on N. Nitrogen a is neutral.

q: Which of these drugs or neurotransmitters is a secondary (2°) amine?
h: A 2° amine N is bonded to two carbons and one H, and neither carbon is a C=O carbon.
w: Methamphetamine has an N–H with a CH3 and a chain carbon on N: 2°. Acetaminophen also has an N bonded to two carbons and one H, but one of those carbons is a C=O, so it is an amide, not an amine. Dopamine is 1°, and nicotine (both N have no H) is not 2°.
x: This is dopamine: its N is an –NH<sub>2</sub> on the end of a chain, bonded to only one carbon.
This is acetaminophen: its N–H nitrogen is bonded to a C=O carbon, which makes it part of an amide, not an amine.
This is nicotine: neither nitrogen has an H. The ring N with the CH<sub>3</sub> is bonded to three carbons.

q: Which structure contains a quaternary ammonium ion?
h: Quaternary means four carbons on the nitrogen. A + charge alone is not enough.
w: Acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter at nerve–muscle junctions, has N+ bonded to four carbons (three CH3 and a CH2). Protonated methamphetamine (the form in its hydrochloride salt) is also positive, but its N+ has only two carbons and two H: it is just a protonated 2° amine. Dopamine and lidocaine are neutral amines.
x: This N is positive, but it carries two H and only two carbons: it is just a protonated 2° amine. Quaternary needs four carbons on N.
This is dopamine, with a neutral –NH<sub>2</sub>. It has only one carbon on N and no charge.
This is lidocaine: its amine N has three carbons and no charge, and the other N is part of an amide.

q: Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between methanol and water?
h: A hydrogen bond needs an H that is bonded to O, N or F, pointing at a lone pair on another O, N or F.
w: Only the picture where the H of methanol's O–H points at the O of water is a hydrogen bond: a δ+ H on oxygen attracted to a lone pair on oxygen. The most tempting wrong picture uses an H from the CH3 group, but a C–H bond is almost nonpolar, so that H has no real δ+ charge. H···H and H···C lines have no lone pair to accept the H.
x: Here the dotted line comes from an H on the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon. A C–H bond is almost nonpolar, so that H is not δ+ enough to hydrogen bond.
Here the dotted line joins two H atoms. Both are δ+, so they repel; a hydrogen bond needs a lone pair on O, N or F at the other end.
Here water's H points at methanol's carbon. Carbon has no lone pair to accept the H.

q: Acetone dissolves in water. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between acetone and water?
h: Acetone has no O–H, so which molecule must supply the H? What on acetone can accept it?
w: Water supplies the H (bonded to O), and the lone pair on acetone's C=O oxygen accepts it. The tempting wrong pictures use an H from acetone's CH3 group, but H on carbon is not δ+ enough to hydrogen bond. A dotted line to the carbonyl carbon is wrong because carbon has no lone pair.
x: This uses an H from acetone's CH<sub>3</sub> group. H on carbon is not δ+ enough to hydrogen bond.
Here water's H points at the carbonyl carbon. That carbon is δ+ and has no lone pair to accept a hydrogen bond.
This joins two acetone molecules through a C–H. Acetone has no O–H, so it has no H to donate.

q: Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line)?
h: Check both ends of the dotted line: the H must be on N, O or F, and the other end must be an N, O or F atom.
w: The N–H of methylamine pointing at the oxygen of water is a hydrogen bond. The tempting N–H···CH3 picture has a good donor but a bad acceptor: a carbon has no lone pair and is not very electronegative. C–H···N fails at the donor end, and H···H has two δ+ atoms facing each other.
x: The N–H donor is fine, but the line points at a CH<sub>3</sub> carbon. Carbon has no lone pair and is not very electronegative.
The line here starts from an H on carbon. A C–H bond is nearly nonpolar, so that H cannot donate a hydrogen bond.
This line joins two H atoms. Both are δ+, so they repel each other rather than forming a hydrogen bond.

q: Trimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N, is mixed with water. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line)?
h: Trimethylamine has no N–H, but its N still has a lone pair. A hydrogen bond always has an H in the middle.
w: Water's O–H points at the lone pair on the nitrogen, so that is a hydrogen bond. A 3° amine cannot donate, but it can accept. The N···O picture has no H between the atoms, so it is not a hydrogen bond at all, and the CH3 pictures use H on carbon or a carbon acceptor.
x: This uses an H from a CH<sub>3</sub> group on the amine. H on carbon is not δ+ enough to hydrogen bond.
This line goes directly from N to O with no H in between. A hydrogen bond always has an H in the middle.
Here water's H points at a CH<sub>3</sub> carbon. Carbon has no lone pair to accept the H.

q: Diethyl ether (ethoxyethane) is slightly soluble in water. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line)?
h: Which molecule here has an H on oxygen? The ether can only take part through its oxygen's lone pairs.
