w: Only water has an O–H, so water must be the donor: water's H pointing at the ether oxygen. The most tempting wrong picture shows two ether molecules joined C–H···O, but ethers have no O–H or N–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other. A dotted line to a carbon of the ether is wrong because carbon has no lone pair.
x: This joins two ether molecules through a C–H. Ethers have no O–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
Here water's H points at a carbon of the ether. Carbon has no lone pair to accept a hydrogen bond.
This uses an H on the ether's carbon. A C–H hydrogen is not δ+ enough to donate a hydrogen bond, even to water.

q: Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between two molecules of the same compound?
h: For a compound to hydrogen bond to itself, each molecule needs an O–H or N–H, and the H must point at an O or N.
w: Ethanol O–H···O ethanol is correct: ethanol has an O–H (donor) and an O with lone pairs (acceptor). The tempting dimethyl ether picture uses an H on carbon, and ethers cannot hydrogen bond to themselves. O–H···H–O puts two δ+ H atoms together, and O–H···C points at a carbon with no lone pair.
x: This is dimethyl ether using an H on carbon. Ethers have no O–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to themselves.
This line joins two O–H hydrogens. Both are δ+, so they repel; the H must point at a lone pair.
The O–H donor is fine, but the line points at a carbon. Carbon has no lone pair to accept the H.

q: In proteins, amide groups hold helices and sheets in shape by hydrogen bonding. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between two acetamide molecules?
h: Amides have an N–H (donor) and a C=O (acceptor). Which atom of the C=O group has the lone pairs?
w: The N–H of one amide points at the C=O oxygen of the other, the same N–H···O=C link that holds protein helices and sheets together. The tempting wrong picture points the N–H at the carbonyl carbon, but the lone pairs are on the oxygen. C–H···O and N–H···H–N are not hydrogen bonds.
x: The N–H donor is fine, but the line points at the carbonyl carbon. The lone pairs of the C=O group are on another atom.
This line starts from an H on the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon. A C–H bond is nearly nonpolar, so that H cannot donate.
This line joins two N–H hydrogens. Both are δ+, so they repel instead of forming a hydrogen bond.

q: Methane and water are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: No. The H is bonded to carbon, and a C–H bond is not polar enough.
Yes. The H is pointing at a lone pair on the oxygen of water.
Yes. Any H atom near an O, N or F atom forms a hydrogen bond.
No. The oxygen of water cannot accept a hydrogen bond.
h: Look at what the H on the left is bonded to. Is that bond polar?
w: The acceptor (water's O) is fine, but the donor is not: C and H have nearly the same electronegativity, so the H has almost no δ+ charge. Not a hydrogen bond. The tempting "yes" answer only checks the acceptor end; both ends must be right. Water's O certainly can accept hydrogen bonds.
x: Water's O does have lone pairs, but a hydrogen bond also needs a δ+ H. Check what the H at the other end is bonded to.
Being near O, N or F is not enough. The H itself must be bonded to O, N or F to carry a real δ+ charge.
Water's oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds; it has two lone pairs. The problem is at the other end of the dotted line.

q: Water and acetaldehyde (ethanal) are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: Yes. An H on oxygen points at a lone pair on the C=O oxygen.
No. Acetaldehyde has no O–H, so it cannot take part in hydrogen bonding.
No. A hydrogen bond needs an O–H group on both molecules.
Yes. The H of water is attracted to the C=O carbon.
h: A hydrogen bond needs a donor (H on N, O or F) and an acceptor (a lone pair on N, O or F). Must both molecules be able to donate?
w: Water donates its O–H hydrogen, and the lone pair on the aldehyde oxygen accepts it, so this is a hydrogen bond. The tempting "no" confuses the two jobs: aldehydes cannot hydrogen bond to each other (no O–H), but they can accept from water. That is why small aldehydes dissolve in water.
x: Acetaldehyde cannot donate, but its C=O oxygen has lone pairs that can accept an H from water. Only one partner needs an O–H.
Only one partner needs to supply the H. The other just needs a lone pair on O, N or F.
The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and has no lone pair, so it cannot accept a hydrogen bond. Look again at which atom the dotted line reaches.

q: Dimethylamine and ethane are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: No. The H points at a carbon, which has no lone pair.
Yes. The H is bonded to N, so it is a hydrogen-bond donor.
No. Only H atoms bonded to oxygen can form hydrogen bonds.
Yes. The N–H hydrogen is δ+ and the carbon is δ−.
h: Check both ends of the dotted line, not just the H end.
w: The donor end is fine (H on N), but the other end is a CH3 carbon: no lone pair and not electronegative, so no hydrogen bond. The tempting "yes" only checks the donor. N–H hydrogens do hydrogen bond (to N, O or F), so "only O–H" is wrong.
x: The donor end is fine, but both ends matter. Check the atom the H points at: does it have a lone pair?
N–H hydrogens can hydrogen bond too, as can F–H. The real problem is at the other end of the line.
Carbon in a CH<sub>3</sub> group is not meaningfully δ−, and it has no lone pair to accept a hydrogen bond.

q: Two ethanol molecules are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: No. Both ends are δ+ H atoms; the H must point at a lone pair on O, N or F.
Yes. Both H atoms are bonded to oxygen, so they attract each other.
No. Ethanol molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
Yes. Opposite partial charges on the two H atoms attract each other.
h: What partial charge does an H on oxygen carry? Would two of them attract?
w: Both H atoms are δ+, so they repel; a hydrogen bond joins a δ+ H to a lone pair on an electronegative atom. Not a hydrogen bond. Ethanol can hydrogen bond to itself, but the line would have to run from the O–H hydrogen of one molecule to the O of the other.
x: Both H atoms are bonded to O, so both are δ+. Two δ+ atoms repel, so they cannot attract each other.
Ethanol can hydrogen bond to itself through its O–H. The problem is how this particular dotted line is drawn.
Both H atoms are bonded to O, so both carry δ+ charges. They are not opposite, so they repel.

q: Water and N,N-dimethylethylamine (a 3° amine) are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: Yes. The H on oxygen points at the lone pair on the nitrogen.
No. A 3° amine has no N–H, so it cannot take part in hydrogen bonding.
No. Hydrogen bonds can form only between two oxygen atoms.
Yes. The N is bonded to three carbons, which makes it δ+.
h: A 3° amine cannot donate an H. Can it still accept one?
w: Water supplies the δ+ H, and the amine nitrogen still has a lone pair to accept it, so this is a hydrogen bond. The tempting "no" mixes up donating and accepting: a 3° amine cannot hydrogen bond to itself, but it does hydrogen bond with water, which is why small 3° amines are water-soluble.
x: A 3° amine cannot donate, but its N still has a lone pair that can accept an H from water.
Hydrogen bonds can involve N and F as well as O, as donors or as acceptors.
Nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon, so it is δ−, not δ+. It is the N lone pair that matters here.

q: Which compound can hydrogen bond to other molecules of itself in the pure liquid?
h: To hydrogen bond to itself, a molecule needs an H bonded directly to O or N.
w: 1-Propanol has an O–H, so one molecule's O–H hydrogen can point at another molecule's oxygen. Methoxyethane (an ether), propanal and propanone all have O atoms that could accept, but no O–H to donate, so between their own molecules the strongest attractions are dipole–dipole attractions. The most common mistake is counting any oxygen as enough.
x: This is an ether: it has an O but no O–H. Its H atoms are all on carbon, so it cannot donate to itself.
This is an aldehyde: its C=O oxygen can accept, but it has no O–H to donate. Its molecules attract by dipole–dipole forces.
This is a ketone: its C=O oxygen can accept, but it has no O–H or N–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself.

q: Which compound can accept hydrogen bonds from water but cannot hydrogen bond to other molecules of itself?
h: Look for a molecule with an O or N lone pair but no H bonded to O or N.
w: Ethyl acetate (an ester) has oxygen lone pairs that accept H from water, but no O–H or N–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself. Butanoic acid and butylamine have O–H or N–H, so they do hydrogen bond to themselves. Hexane has neither, so it cannot hydrogen bond even with water.
x: This carboxylic acid has an O–H, so its molecules do hydrogen bond to each other.
This amine has N–H bonds, so its molecules do hydrogen bond to each other.
This hydrocarbon has no O or N, so it cannot even accept a hydrogen bond from water.

q: Which compound cannot form hydrogen bonds with water at all?
h: Water can donate its H to any O or N lone pair. Which molecule has no O or N?
w: Cyclohexane is only C and H, so it has no lone pair to accept water's H and no polar H to donate. The tempting wrong answers (cyclohexanone, diethyl ether, triethylamine) cannot hydrogen bond to themselves, but each has an O or N lone pair that accepts an H from water.
x: Cyclohexanone cannot hydrogen bond to itself, but its C=O oxygen has lone pairs that accept an H from water.
Diethyl ether cannot hydrogen bond to itself, but its oxygen lone pairs accept an H from water.
Triethylamine has no N–H, but its N lone pair can accept an H from water.

q: The four amines shown are isomers, C4H11N. Which one cannot hydrogen bond to other molecules of itself?
h: Classify each amine: 1°, 2° or 3°. Which kind has no H on the nitrogen?
w: The 3° amine (N,N-dimethylethylamine) has three carbons on N and no N–H, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond to another molecule of itself. The 1° amine (two N–H) and the 2° amines (one N–H) can. A 3° amine still accepts hydrogen bonds from water through its N lone pair.
x: This is butylamine, a 1° amine with two N–H bonds, so its molecules can hydrogen bond to each other.
This is a 2° amine (N-methylpropylamine). Its one N–H lets molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
This is diethylamine, a 2° amine with one N–H, so it can hydrogen bond to itself.

q: Pure samples of compounds I–IV are shown. In how many of them do the molecules hydrogen bond to each other?
h: For each one, ask: is there an H bonded directly to O or N?
w: 2: 1-butanol (I) has an O–H and butanamide (IV) has N–H bonds. Butanal (II) and diethyl ether (III) have oxygen lone pairs but no O–H or N–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to themselves. Answering 1 usually means the amide N–H was missed; answering 3 or 4 means any oxygen was counted.
x: Recheck each structure for an H bonded to O or N. The –NH<sub>2</sub> in compound IV counts too, not just the –OH.
3 counts at least one compound that has an O but no O–H or N–H. A C=O or C–O–C oxygen can accept but cannot donate.
4 counts every compound with an O. Butanal and diethyl ether have no H on O or N, so they cannot donate to each other.

q: How many of the compounds I–IV can form hydrogen bonds with water?
h: Water can be the donor. Any O or N lone pair in the other molecule can accept water's H.
w: 3: diethyl ether (II), cyclohexanone (III) and 1-pentanol (IV) all have oxygen lone pairs that accept an H from water (the alcohol can also donate). Only pentane (I), with just C and H, cannot. Answering 1 is the common mistake of counting only molecules with an O–H.
x: 1 counts only the compound with an O–H. Water can donate its H to any oxygen lone pair, including a C=O or an ether O.
Recheck each compound for an oxygen lone pair. Water donates its H to ether and ketone oxygens as well as to alcohols.
4 includes pentane, which has only C and H. It has no lone pair to accept water's H and no polar H to donate.

q: Acetone (propanone), shown, mixes with water in all proportions. What is the main attraction between acetone and water molecules?
c: Water's O–H hydrogen bonds to the oxygen of acetone's C=O.
Acetone's C–H hydrogens hydrogen bond to water's oxygen.
Acetone molecules hydrogen bond to each other through their C=O.
The carbon of acetone's C=O accepts a hydrogen bond from water.
h: Acetone has no O–H. Which molecule donates the H, and which atom has lone pairs?
w: Water donates its δ+ H to a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen. Acetone's H atoms are all on carbon, so they cannot donate, and acetone cannot hydrogen bond to itself. The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and has no lone pair, so it cannot accept a hydrogen bond.
x: Acetone's H atoms are all on carbon. C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar, so they cannot donate hydrogen bonds.
Acetone has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself. And the question asks about attraction to water.
The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and has no lone pair, so it cannot accept a hydrogen bond.

q: Ethanol (I) and dimethyl ether (II) have the same formula, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O. Ethanol boils at 78 °C, but dimethyl ether boils at −24 °C. Why?
c: Ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other; dimethyl ether has no O–H.
Ethanol has a larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are stronger.
Boiling dimethyl ether breaks its weak C–O covalent bonds.
Dimethyl ether is nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act.
h: Same formula means same molar mass. What does ethanol have that the ether lacks?
w: Ethanol's O–H lets its molecules hydrogen bond to each other, which takes much more energy to overcome. The two have identical molar masses (46.07 g mol⁻¹), so dispersion cannot explain it. Dimethyl ether is actually polar (bent C–O–C), so it has dipole–dipole attractions, just no hydrogen bonds. Boiling never breaks covalent bonds.
x: Both have the same formula, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O, so their molar masses are identical. Dispersion forces cannot explain the difference.
Boiling separates whole molecules from each other; no covalent bonds break. Compare the forces between molecules.
Dimethyl ether is polar: its C–O–C is bent, so it has dipole–dipole attractions. Look for a stronger force that only ethanol has.

q: Phenol (I) boils at about 182 °C, but anisole (methoxybenzene, II) boils at about 154 °C. Which statement best explains this?
c: Phenol has an O–H, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other; anisole cannot.
Phenol has the larger molar mass, so its London dispersion forces are stronger.
Anisole is nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act between its molecules.
Only phenol has an aromatic ring, which raises the boiling point.
h: Anisole is phenol with the H on oxygen replaced by CH<sub>3</sub>. What does that remove?
w: Replacing the O–H hydrogen with CH3 removes the hydrogen-bond donor, so anisole molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other and anisole boils lower. Molar mass points the other way (anisole 108.14 g mol⁻¹ vs phenol 94.11 g mol⁻¹). Anisole is still polar (dipole–dipole), and both compounds have a benzene ring.
x: Anisole is actually heavier (108 vs 94 g mol⁻¹), so molar mass would predict the opposite. Look at what the CH<sub>3</sub> replaced.
Anisole is polar: its C–O–C is bent, so it has dipole–dipole forces. The difference lies in another type of force.
Both compounds have a benzene ring. Compare the groups on the oxygen instead.

q: Which hydrocarbon has the strongest London dispersion forces between its molecules?
h: Dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons, so compare the size of the molecules.
w: Nonane (C9H20) is the largest molecule, with the most electrons and the most surface contact, so it has the strongest dispersion forces (bp 151 °C). Hexane, cyclopentane and 2-methylbutane are smaller. Being a ring or a branched chain does not make up for having fewer carbons.
x: Hexane has only six carbons. A larger molecule here has more electrons and stronger dispersion forces.
Cyclopentane has only five carbons. Being a ring does not make up for a small size.
2-Methylbutane has only five carbons and is branched, which makes its dispersion forces weaker still.

q: All four alkanes shown are isomers of C8H18. Which has the highest boiling point?
h: Same formula means the same number of electrons. Which shape gives the most contact between neighboring molecules?
w: Unbranched octane (bp 126 °C) is long and can lie alongside its neighbors, giving the most surface contact and the strongest London dispersion forces. Branching makes molecules more compact, so 2,3,4-trimethylpentane (114 °C), 2,5-dimethylhexane (109 °C) and 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (99 °C) boil lower. Same molar mass does not mean same boiling point.
x: This is 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, a very compact, highly branched isomer. Branching reduces contact between molecules and lowers the boiling point.
This is 2,5-dimethylhexane. Its two branches make it more compact than an unbranched isomer, so it boils lower.
This is 2,3,4-trimethylpentane. Its three branches make it compact, which weakens dispersion forces.

q: All four alkanes shown are isomers of C6H14. Which has the lowest boiling point?
h: More branching makes a molecule more compact (closer to a ball). How does that affect contact between molecules?
w: 2,2-Dimethylbutane is the most branched and most compact, so it has the least surface contact and the weakest London dispersion forces (bp 50 °C). Hexane is the highest (69 °C). The tempting choice, hexane, is the opposite trend: long unbranched chains boil highest.
x: Hexane is unbranched, so it has the most surface contact and boils highest of these isomers, not lowest.
3-Methylpentane has only one branch. A more branched, rounder isomer has less contact and boils lower.
2-Methylpentane has only one branch. A more branched, rounder isomer has less contact and boils lower.

q: Rank alkanes I–IV from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: First compare size (number of carbons). For the isomers with the same size, less branching means a higher boiling point.
w: Hexane (II, six carbons) is largest: 69 °C. The other three are C5H12 isomers: unbranched pentane (IV, 36 °C) > 2-methylbutane (I, 28 °C) > the very compact 2,2-dimethylpropane (III, 9.5 °C). So II > IV > I > III. Putting III high reverses the branching rule.
x: This puts III, the most compact C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> isomer, second and unbranched IV last. More branching lowers the boiling point.
This order is reversed. The largest molecule, hexane (II), has the strongest dispersion forces, not the weakest.
This puts the branched isomer I above unbranched pentane (IV). Among isomers, less branching means a higher boiling point.

q: Pentane (I) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (II) are both C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. Which statement is correct?
c: Pentane boils higher: its long shape gives more contact and stronger dispersion forces.
2,2-Dimethylpropane boils higher: its compact shape packs its electrons closer together.
They boil at the same temperature because they have the same molar mass.
Pentane boils higher because its molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
h: Both are nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act. Which shape lets molecules touch over more area?
w: Rod-shaped pentane molecules lie alongside each other and touch over a large area, so pentane has stronger dispersion forces and boils higher (36 °C vs 9.5 °C). Same molar mass does not guarantee the same boiling point; shape matters. Neither compound has an O–H or N–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding.
x: A compact shape gives less surface contact between molecules, so dispersion forces get weaker, not stronger.
Same molar mass does not guarantee the same boiling point. Shape changes how much neighboring molecules touch.
Neither compound has an O–H or N–H, so neither can hydrogen bond. Both are nonpolar.

q: Which hydrocarbon has the highest boiling point?
h: All four are nonpolar. Which has the most carbons (the most electrons for London dispersion forces)?
w: 2-Hexene has six carbons, the most electrons and the largest surface, so it has the strongest London dispersion forces (bp about 68 °C). 1-Pentyne (40 °C), 1,3-butadiene (−4 °C) and propene (−48 °C) are smaller. The number or type of double and triple bonds matters much less than the size of the molecule.
x: 1-Pentyne has only five carbons. A triple bond barely changes the boiling point; molecular size matters much more.
1,3-Butadiene has only four carbons. Having two double bonds does not make up for its small size.
Propene has only three carbons, so its dispersion forces are very weak; it is a gas at room temperature.

q: Which compound is the most soluble in water?
h: Water dissolves small molecules that can hydrogen bond (–OH, –COOH, –NH<sub>2</sub>, C=O). Which group hydrogen bonds most strongly?
w: Butanoic acid mixes with water in all proportions: its –COOH group has both a C=O and an O–H, so it accepts and donates hydrogen bonds to water. 1-Butanol (about 77 g L⁻¹) and butanal (about 71 g L⁻¹) are only partly soluble. Butane has no O or N and is nearly insoluble.
x: 1-Butanol has one –OH, which helps, but it is only partly soluble. Look for a group that both donates and accepts more hydrogen bonds.
Butanal can accept hydrogen bonds at its C=O but has no O–H to donate, so it is only partly soluble.
Butane has no O or N, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water and is nearly insoluble.

q: Which compound is the least soluble in water?
h: Which molecule has nothing that can hydrogen bond with water?
w: Hexane has only C and H; it is nonpolar and cannot hydrogen bond with water, so it is essentially insoluble. 1-Hexanol, hexanoic acid and hexylamine each have a polar group that hydrogen bonds with water (all three are slightly soluble, about 6–12 g L⁻¹), even though their six-carbon chains limit how much dissolves.
x: 1-Hexanol has an –OH that hydrogen bonds with water, so it dissolves slightly. Look for a compound with no polar group at all.
Hexanoic acid has a –COOH that hydrogen bonds with water, so it dissolves slightly.
Hexylamine has an –NH<sub>2</sub> that hydrogen bonds with water, so it dissolves slightly.

q: Rank alcohols I–IV from most to least soluble in water.
h: All have one –OH. What happens to solubility as the nonpolar carbon chain gets longer?
w: Each has one –OH that hydrogen bonds with water, but the nonpolar chain gets longer from methanol (II, miscible) to 1-butanol (IV, about 77 g L⁻¹) to 1-hexanol (I, about 6 g L⁻¹) to 1-octanol (III, about 0.5 g L⁻¹). So II > IV > I > III. The reverse order comes from thinking bigger molecules have "more" to attract water; only the –OH does.
x: This order is reversed. Each has one –OH, so the longer the nonpolar chain, the less it dissolves.
This puts 1-hexanol (I) above 1-butanol (IV). A longer nonpolar chain lowers solubility.
This puts 1-butanol (IV) above methanol (II). Methanol has the smallest nonpolar part, so it dissolves best.

q: All four compounds have five carbons. Which is the most soluble in water?
h: With the same chain length, more groups that hydrogen bond with water means higher solubility.
w: 1,5-Pentanediol has two –OH groups, one at each end, so it hydrogen bonds with water strongly enough to mix in all proportions. 1-Pentanol, with one –OH, dissolves only about 22 g L⁻¹; pentanal (one C=O, no O–H) about 12 g L⁻¹; pentane is insoluble. More polar groups on the same chain beat one polar group.
x: 1-Pentanol has only one –OH on five carbons, so it is only partly soluble. Look for more polar groups on the same chain.
Pentanal can only accept hydrogen bonds at its C=O; it has no O–H to donate, so it is only partly soluble.
Pentane has no O or N, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water and is insoluble.

q: Rank compounds I–IV from most to least soluble in water.
h: First: which compounds can hydrogen bond with water at all? Then compare chain lengths among those that can.
w: The three alcohols hydrogen bond with water, and the shorter the chain the better: ethanol (III, miscible) > 1-butanol (IV, about 77 g L⁻¹) > 1-hexanol (I, about 6 g L⁻¹). Hexane (II) cannot hydrogen bond and is nearly insoluble: III > IV > I > II. Ranking IV above III assumes a bigger alcohol dissolves better; the extra CH2 groups are nonpolar.
x: This puts 1-butanol (IV) above ethanol (III). The extra CH<sub>2</sub> groups are nonpolar and lower solubility.
This puts 1-hexanol (I) above 1-butanol (IV). A longer nonpolar chain means lower solubility.
This puts hexane (II) above 1-hexanol (I). Hexane cannot hydrogen bond with water at all, while the alcohol's –OH can.

q: 1-Octanol, shown, has an –OH group but is almost insoluble in water (about 0.5 g L⁻¹). Why?
c: Its long nonpolar carbon chain outweighs the one polar –OH group.
Its –OH group cannot hydrogen bond with water because it is at the end of the chain.
Alcohols with more than five carbons lose their –OH group in water.
Its molar mass is too large for any molecule to dissolve in water.
h: Think of the molecule as two parts: a polar "head" and a nonpolar "tail." Which part is bigger here?
w: The –OH does hydrogen bond with water, but the 8-carbon chain is nonpolar and must push water molecules apart without forming hydrogen bonds. The large nonpolar part dominates, so 1-octanol barely dissolves. The –OH works fine at the end of a chain (methanol and ethanol mix completely), and size alone is not the issue: glucose (180 g mol⁻¹) dissolves easily.
x: An –OH at the end of a chain hydrogen bonds with water just fine; methanol and ethanol mix completely with water.
Alcohols do not lose their –OH group in water. The –OH stays attached; the issue is the rest of the molecule.
Size alone does not stop a molecule from dissolving: glucose (180 g mol⁻¹) dissolves easily. What matters is how much of the molecule is nonpolar.

q: Which compound is the most soluble in water?
h: Which molecule has an H on N or O and a lone pair to share with water? Thiols (–SH) and alkyl halides hydrogen bond very weakly.
w: Propylamine mixes with water in all proportions: its –NH2 both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds. 1-Chloropropane (about 2.7 g L⁻¹) and 1-propanethiol (about 1.9 g L⁻¹) are only slightly soluble because S and Cl do not form useful hydrogen bonds; the –SH looks like –OH but sulfur is not electronegative enough. Butane is nearly insoluble.
x: 1-Chloropropane has no H on N or O, and Cl does not form useful hydrogen bonds, so it is only slightly soluble.
–SH looks like –OH, but sulfur is not electronegative enough for strong hydrogen bonds, so this thiol is only slightly soluble.
Butane has no O, N or other polar group, so it is nearly insoluble.

q: Benzoic acid is used to preserve liquid medicines and sodas. Which form shown is the most soluble in water?
h: An ionic compound dissolves by ion–dipole attractions, which are stronger than hydrogen bonds to one –COOH group.
w: Sodium benzoate is an ionic salt: the Na+ and the –COO− group are each surrounded by water molecules, so it dissolves very well (over 500 g L⁻¹). That is why preservatives are added as the salt. Benzoic acid itself dissolves only about 3 g L⁻¹ because its benzene ring is nonpolar; chlorobenzene and toluene (about 0.5 g L⁻¹ each) cannot hydrogen bond with water at all.
x: Benzoic acid can hydrogen bond with water through its –COOH, but its large nonpolar ring keeps it only slightly soluble. Look for a form that is ionic.
Chlorobenzene has no O–H or ions, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water and is nearly insoluble.
Toluene is a hydrocarbon; it is nonpolar and has no way to hydrogen bond with water.

q: Cholesterol, shown, is found in every cell membrane. How is cholesterol best described?
c: Mostly nonpolar: one –OH on a big hydrocarbon frame, so it is fat-soluble.
Mostly polar: its –OH group makes the whole molecule dissolve easily in water.
Mostly polar: its four rings and C=C bond carry partial charges.
Ionic: the –OH group gives the molecule a negative charge in blood.
h: Compare the size of the polar part with the size of the C–H part.
w: Cholesterol (C27H46O) has one –OH on 27 carbons, so it is mostly nonpolar and fat-soluble; that is why it travels in blood inside lipoproteins. The one –OH makes only one end slightly polar, so cholesterol sits in membranes with its OH facing the water. One polar group cannot carry a molecule this large into water.
x: One –OH cannot carry a 27-carbon molecule into water. Most of cholesterol is hydrocarbon.
Rings and C=C bonds contain only C and H, so they are nonpolar. They do not carry partial charges.
An alcohol –OH does not lose H<sup>+</sup> in blood, so cholesterol is a neutral molecule, not an ion.

q: Vitamin C (I) is water-soluble, but vitamin A (retinol, II) is fat-soluble. Which statement best explains the difference?
c: Vitamin C has four –OH groups on six carbons; vitamin A has one –OH on 20.
Vitamin A has no oxygen atoms, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water at all.
Vitamin C has the larger molar mass, so it attracts more water molecules.
Vitamin A's C=C double bonds are polar, so they repel water.
h: Count the –OH groups in each and compare them with the number of carbons.
w: Vitamin C (C6H8O6) has four –OH groups and two more O atoms on only six carbons, so it hydrogen bonds extensively with water. Retinol (C20H30O) has a single –OH at the end of a 20-carbon hydrocarbon, so the nonpolar part wins. Retinol does have an O, and it is actually heavier (286 vs 176 g mol⁻¹); C=C bonds are nonpolar.
x: Vitamin A does have an oxygen: an –OH at the end of its chain. The difference is how much hydrocarbon surrounds it.
Vitamin C is actually the lighter molecule (176 vs 286 g mol⁻¹). Molar mass is not what controls solubility here.
C=C bonds contain only carbon, so they are nonpolar. Compare the number of –OH groups to the number of carbons.

q: Vitamins I–IV are shown (II is a form of vitamin K). Which one is water-soluble?
h: Water-soluble vitamins have several groups that hydrogen bond with water on a small carbon frame.
w: III is vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): three –OH groups and a ring N on only eight carbons, so it hydrogen bonds well with water. I (vitamin A, retinol), II (menadione, vitamin K) and IV (vitamin D3) are mostly hydrocarbon, with at most one –OH or two C=O groups on a large nonpolar frame, so they are fat-soluble. The tempting choice I has an –OH, but one –OH is not enough for a 20-carbon molecule.
x: I is vitamin A (retinol): one –OH on a 20-carbon hydrocarbon frame, so it is fat-soluble.
II has two C=O groups but no O–H, on a mostly hydrocarbon ring system, so it is fat-soluble.
IV is a large ring-and-chain hydrocarbon with only one –OH, so it is fat-soluble.

q: Estradiol, shown, is the main estrogen hormone. Which labeled carbon is bonded to a polar group that can hydrogen bond with water?
h: Polar regions contain O or N bonded to H. A carbon bonded only to C and H atoms is in a nonpolar region.
w: Carbon c carries the phenol –OH, whose O–H can donate and whose O can accept hydrogen bonds. Carbons a, b and d are bonded only to C and H (ring-fusion carbon, methyl group, ring C–H), so they are in nonpolar regions; the tempting d is in the same ring as the –OH but bonded only to C and H. Estradiol has only two –OH groups on 18 carbons, so it is mostly nonpolar and passes easily through cell membranes.
x: Carbon a is a ring-fusion carbon bonded only to other carbons. It is in a nonpolar region.
Carbon d is in the aromatic ring but is bonded only to C and H. Look for a carbon bonded to O.
Carbon b is the methyl group, bonded only to C and H, so it is nonpolar.

q: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), shown, is only slightly soluble in water. Which part of the molecule can hydrogen bond with water?
c: the CH<sub>3</sub> next to the –COOH group
h: Hydrogen bonding with water needs O or N atoms. Where are the O atoms?
w: Only the –COOH group has O atoms: its O–H donates and both oxygens accept hydrogen bonds. The benzene ring, the isobutyl group and the CH3 are all hydrocarbon and nonpolar. Because 12 of its 13 carbons are in nonpolar parts and only one group is polar, ibuprofen dissolves poorly in water (about 0.02 g L⁻¹).
x: The benzene ring contains only C and H, so it is nonpolar and cannot hydrogen bond with water.
The isobutyl group is a hydrocarbon chain, so it is nonpolar and cannot hydrogen bond with water.
A CH<sub>3</sub> has only C–H bonds, which are nearly nonpolar. Hydrogen bonding needs O or N.

q: Acetaminophen (Tylenol), shown, has the formula C8H9NO2. How many of its hydrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond donors?
h: A donor H must be bonded directly to N, O or F. Find every O–H and N–H.
w: Acetaminophen has one O–H (the phenol) and one N–H (the amide), so 2 donor H atoms. The other seven H atoms are on carbon. Answering 1 misses the amide N–H; answering 9 counts every H in the formula. The C=O oxygen is an acceptor, not a donor.
x: 1 finds only one of the donor H atoms. Look for every H on O and every H on N.
3 counts one H too many. Only H bonded directly to N or O counts; the CH<sub>3</sub> and ring H atoms are on carbon.
9 counts every H in the formula. Most of them are on carbon, and C–H hydrogens cannot donate hydrogen bonds.

q: Albuterol, shown, is the drug in rescue inhalers for asthma. How many of its hydrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond donors?
h: Count every H bonded to O or N. Look at each O and the N carefully, including the one between carbons.
w: Albuterol has three –OH groups (a phenol, a CH2OH and a secondary alcohol) and one N–H (a 2° amine): 4 donor H atoms. Answering 3 misses the N–H, which is easy to overlook because the N sits in the middle of the chain. The tert-butyl group has only C–H bonds.
x: 3 misses one donor. Check the N in the middle of the chain: does it carry an H?
2 misses two donors. Count each –OH (there is more than one) and check the N for an H.
5 counts one H too many. Each –OH has one donor H and the N has one; the tert-butyl H atoms are on carbon.

q: Propofol, shown, is an IV anesthetic. It is so insoluble in water that it is given as a milky oil-in-water emulsion. What feature of its structure explains this?
c: Its one –OH is surrounded by a benzene ring and two isopropyl groups.
It has no O or N atoms, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water at all.
Its –OH group makes it ionic, and ionic compounds do not dissolve in water.
Its molar mass is over 1000 g mol⁻¹, too large to dissolve in water.
h: Find the one polar group and compare it with the size of the hydrocarbon part around it.
w: Propofol (C12H18O) has a single –OH on a 12-carbon hydrocarbon, and the two bulky isopropyl groups crowd around it, so the molecule is mostly nonpolar. It does have an oxygen that can hydrogen bond, so "no O or N" is wrong. It is a neutral molecule (not ionic), and its molar mass is only 178.3 g mol⁻¹.
x: Propofol does have an oxygen, in its –OH group, and that O–H can hydrogen bond. The problem is the size of the hydrocarbon part.
An –OH group does not make a molecule ionic. Propofol is a neutral molecule.
Propofol is small: C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O is about 178 g mol⁻¹. Its insolubility comes from its mostly nonpolar structure.

q: Acetaminophen (I) dissolves in water at about 14 g L⁻¹, while ibuprofen (II) dissolves at only about 0.02 g L⁻¹. Which explanation fits their structures?
c: I has two polar groups on 8 carbons; II has one polar group on 13 carbons.
II is less soluble because only I contains a benzene ring.
II's –COOH is less polar than any group in I, so II cannot hydrogen bond with water.
I is more soluble because it is the larger molecule, with more atoms to attract water.
h: Count the polar groups in each, then count carbons. Which has more polar groups per carbon?
w: Acetaminophen has two polar groups (phenol O–H and amide N–H/C=O) on 8 carbons; ibuprofen has one –COOH on 13 carbons, so its nonpolar part dominates. Both molecules have a benzene ring, and ibuprofen's –COOH does hydrogen bond with water; it just cannot outweigh the large hydrocarbon part. Acetaminophen is the smaller molecule.
x: Both molecules contain a benzene ring, so the ring cannot explain the difference.
A –COOH group is very polar and does hydrogen bond with water. The issue is how much nonpolar structure surrounds it.
Acetaminophen is actually the smaller molecule (8 carbons vs 13). Bigger size does not raise water solubility.

q: What is the name of the compound shown?
h: Count the ring positions between the two Cl atoms: next to each other (1,2), one apart (1,3), or across the ring (1,4)?
w: The two Cl atoms are on adjacent ring carbons (1,2), which is ortho. Meta is 1,3 and para is 1,4 (directly across). The ring is a benzene ring (alternating double bonds), not cyclohexane, so "dichlorocyclohexane" is wrong.
x: Meta (1,3) would have one ring carbon between the two Cl atoms. Look at the drawing: is there a carbon between them?
Para (1,4) would put the Cl atoms directly across the ring from each other. In the drawing they are not opposite each other.
The ring in the drawing has alternating double bonds, so it is a benzene ring. A cyclohexane ring would have only single bonds.

q: m-Cresol is the preservative that keeps multi-dose insulin vials sterile. It is a phenol with a methyl group on the ring. Which structure is m-cresol?
h: m = meta = 1,3: one ring carbon between the two groups.
w: In m-cresol the –OH and –CH3 are 1,3 on the ring, with one carbon between them. The 1,2 isomer is o-cresol and the 1,4 isomer is p-cresol. Methoxybenzene (anisole) has the same formula, C7H8O, but it is an ether with no –OH, so it is not a phenol at all.
x: Here the –OH and –CH3 are on neighboring carbons (1,2). That is o-cresol; meta needs one ring carbon between them.
Here the –OH and –CH3 are directly across the ring (1,4). That is p-cresol; meta needs one ring carbon between them.
This has an O–CH<sub>3</sub> group (methoxybenzene, an ether) and no –OH. Cresols are phenols, so they need an –OH on the ring.

q: Hydroquinone, shown, is used as a photographic developer and in some prescription creams that fade dark patches of skin (melasma). How are its two –OH groups arranged on the ring?
h: Are the two groups next to each other, one carbon apart, or directly across the ring?
w: The two –OH groups are directly across the ring, 1,4: para. Hydroquinone is p-dihydroxybenzene (benzene-1,4-diol). Trans is a word for alkenes and rings with tetrahedral carbons; benzene rings are flat, so positions on them are named ortho, meta and para instead.
x: Meta (1,3) would leave one ring carbon between the two –OH groups. Look again at where they sit in the drawing.
Ortho (1,2) would put the two –OH groups on neighboring carbons. In the drawing they are farther apart than that.
Cis and trans describe groups on a C=C or on a ring of tetrahedral carbons. Positions on a flat benzene ring are described as ortho, meta or para.

q: Each C–Cl bond is polar. Which compound shown is nonpolar overall?
h: Draw an arrow along each C–Cl bond toward Cl. In which molecule do the arrows point in exactly opposite directions?
w: In para-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles point in exactly opposite directions across the flat ring and cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar (dipole moment 0). In the ortho and meta isomers the dipoles are at an angle and only partly cancel. Chlorobenzene has one C–Cl dipole with nothing to cancel it.
x: In this ortho isomer the two C–Cl dipoles are only 60° apart, so they add together instead of cancelling. It is the most polar of the three dichlorobenzenes.
In this meta isomer the two C–Cl dipoles are 120° apart. They partly cancel, but a net dipole remains.
Chlorobenzene has only one C–Cl dipole, with nothing to cancel it, so the molecule is polar.

q: Which compound shown is the most polar (largest dipole moment)?
h: Bond dipoles add like arrows. Two arrows pointing in nearly the same direction give the biggest total.
w: In ortho-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles are only 60° apart, so they add up to the largest total (about 2.5 D). In the meta isomer they are 120° apart and partly cancel (about 1.7 D), and in para they cancel completely (0 D). Two polar bonds are not automatically more polar than one: chlorobenzene (1.7 D) beats the para isomer.
x: In this meta isomer the C–Cl dipoles are 120° apart and partly cancel (about 1.7 D). Is there an isomer whose dipoles point more nearly the same way?
In this para isomer the two C–Cl dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel completely: 0 D, nonpolar.
Chlorobenzene's single C–Cl dipole gives about 1.7 D. Two dipoles that point nearly the same way can add up to more than one.

q: The three difluorobenzene isomers I–III are shown. Rank them from most polar to least polar.
h: Identify each as ortho, meta or para. The closer the two C–F dipoles point in the same direction, the larger the total.
w: III is ortho (C–F dipoles 60° apart, add strongly, about 2.5 D), I is meta (120°, partly cancel, about 1.6 D), II is para (180°, cancel to 0 D): III > I > II. Ranking para first assumes groups far apart give a bigger dipole, but opposite arrows cancel.
x: This order is upside down: it puts para first. In para the two C–F dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel to 0 D.
Para is correctly last, but ortho and meta are swapped. Dipoles 60° apart (ortho) add up more than dipoles 120° apart (meta).
Para cannot rank above meta: para dipoles cancel completely (0 D), while meta dipoles only partly cancel.

q: para-Dichlorobenzene, shown, is used in mothballs. Its C–Cl bonds are polar, yet the molecule is nonpolar. Why?
c: The two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
Carbon and chlorine have the same electronegativity.
The benzene ring is nonpolar, so it cancels any polar bond attached to it.
Chlorine atoms bonded to a ring have no lone pairs.
h: Polarity of a molecule depends on bond polarity AND shape. Where are the two Cl atoms relative to each other?
w: The flat ring holds the two Cl atoms directly across from each other (1,4), so the two equal C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, like CCl4 or CO2. Cl is more electronegative than C, so each bond is polar. The ring does not "cancel" polarity on its own: ortho-dichlorobenzene has the same ring and is polar.
x: Cl (3.0) is more electronegative than C (2.5), so each C–Cl bond is polar, as the question says. The reason must come from how the two bond dipoles are arranged.
A ring cannot cancel a polar bond. ortho-Dichlorobenzene has the same ring and the same two C–Cl bonds, yet it is polar.
A Cl atom bonded to carbon still has three lone pairs. Lone pairs are not what makes this molecule nonpolar.

q: Ibuprofen is shown with four carbons labeled. Which labeled carbon is a chiral carbon?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups. Carbons with a double bond, or with two identical groups, cannot be chiral.
w: Carbon b carries H, CH3, –COOH and the benzene ring: four different groups, so it is chiral. Carbon d is the tempting wrong answer, but it carries two identical CH3 groups. Carbon a (in the ring) and carbon c (the C=O carbon) have a double bond, so they have only three groups.
x: Carbon d is the CH of the isobutyl group. It carries two identical CH3 groups, so it is not chiral.
Carbon a is a benzene ring carbon. It has a double bond, so it has only three groups attached.
Carbon c is the C=O carbon of the –COOH group. With a double bond it has only three groups, so it cannot be chiral.

q: Carvone, shown, gives spearmint its smell; its mirror image smells like caraway. Which labeled carbon is the chiral carbon?
h: In a ring, compare the two paths around the ring from each carbon. Are they the same?
w: Carbon c has H, the isopropenyl group and two different ring paths (one toward the C=O, one toward the C=C), so it is chiral. Carbon d is a CH2 (two identical H atoms). Carbon a (ring C=C) and carbon b (the C=C of the side chain) each have a double bond, so neither has four groups.
x: Carbon a is part of the ring C=C double bond, so it has only three groups attached.
Carbon b is part of the side-chain C=C double bond, so it has only three groups attached.
Carbon d is a ring CH2. Its two identical H atoms mean it cannot have four different groups.

q: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed), shown, is a nasal decongestant. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Check every carbon with one H and no double bond. Does each have four different groups?
w: The carbon bearing the –OH (H, OH, ring, rest of chain) and the carbon bearing the N (H, CH3, NHCH3, rest of chain) each have four different groups: 2 chiral carbons. Ring carbons have a double bond, and the CH3 carbons have three identical H atoms. Answering 1 usually means the C–N carbon was missed.
x: Too few. Check both carbons in the chain that have one H: the one bearing –OH and the one bearing the N. Does each have four different groups?
Too many. Ring carbons have a double bond, and each CH<sub>3</sub> carbon has three identical H atoms. Only carbons with one H in the chain can qualify.
Look at the chain carbons bearing –OH and –NH–. List the four groups on each and compare them.

q: The open-chain form of fructose (fruit sugar) is shown. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: End carbons (CH<sub>2</sub>OH) have two identical H atoms, and the C=O carbon has a double bond. Check the rest.
w: Fructose has six carbons. The two CH2OH carbons have two H atoms each, and the ketone carbon (C=O) has only three groups, so they are not chiral. The 3 CH(OH) carbons in between each have four different groups. Answering 4 is the count for glucose, an aldose with four CH(OH) carbons; 6 counts every carbon.
x: 4 is the count for glucose, an aldose. Fructose is a ketose: its C=O carbon is inside the chain and has only three groups.
That count includes carbons that cannot be chiral. The C=O carbon has a double bond, and each CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon has two identical H atoms.
That counts every carbon. The two CH<sub>2</sub>OH end carbons have two H atoms each, and the C=O carbon has only three groups.

q: Which molecule shown is chiral?
h: Look for a carbon with four different groups: H, and three different non-H groups.
w: Lactic acid has a carbon bonded to H, CH3, OH and COOH: four different groups, so the molecule is chiral. Glycerol is the tempting wrong answer: its middle carbon has H and OH but two identical –CH2OH groups. Glycine's CH2 has two H atoms, and 2-propanol has two identical CH3 groups.
x: This is glycine. Its only carbon without a double bond is a CH<sub>2</sub> with two identical H atoms, so it is not chiral.
This is 2-propanol. Its C–OH carbon carries two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not chiral.
This is glycerol. Its middle carbon has H and OH but two identical –CH<sub>2</sub>OH groups, so it is not chiral.

q: Which molecule shown is achiral (has no chiral carbon)?
h: For the carbon bearing the OH, NH<sub>2</sub> or Cl, are the two carbon groups attached to it the same or different?
w: In 3-pentanol the C–OH carbon has H, OH and two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral. In 2-pentanol the two carbon groups differ (CH3 vs propyl), so it is chiral; alanine and 2-chlorobutane each also have one chiral carbon. Having an OH on a middle carbon does not by itself make a carbon chiral.
x: This is alanine. Its middle carbon carries H, CH<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>2</sub> and COOH: four different groups, so it is chiral.
This is 2-pentanol. The C–OH carbon carries a CH<sub>3</sub> on one side and a propyl group on the other, so it is chiral.
This is 2-chlorobutane. The C–Cl carbon carries H, Cl, CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: four different groups, so it is chiral.

q: Thalidomide, shown, was given to pregnant women in the late 1950s; one mirror-image form eased morning sickness, while the other caused severe birth defects. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Ignore carbons with double bonds (C=O, ring C=C) and CH<sub>2</sub> groups. What is left?
w: Only the ring carbon bonded to H, the N of the other ring system, a C=O carbon and a CH2 has four different groups: 1 chiral carbon. All the C=O and benzene carbons have double bonds, and the two CH2 carbons have two H atoms each. Even one chiral carbon is enough to give two mirror-image forms.
x: Look again at the ring carbon bonded to H, the nitrogen of the other ring system, a C=O carbon and a CH<sub>2</sub>. Are those four groups all different?
Too many. The C=O and benzene ring carbons have double bonds, and each CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has two identical H atoms.
Too many. Ignore every carbon with a double bond and every CH<sub>2</sub>; only one carbon is left with four different groups.

q: Alanine, shown, has one chiral carbon, so it exists in two forms that are nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other. What are these two forms called?
h: Think of left and right hands: mirror images that cannot be stacked on top of each other.
w: Two nonsuperimposable mirror images are enantiomers (like L- and D-alanine). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; for chiral-carbon compounds that takes at least two chiral carbons. Structural isomers have different connections between atoms, and cis–trans isomers come from a C=C or a ring, not from a chiral carbon.
x: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images. Alanine has only one chiral carbon, so its two forms are mirror images of each other.
Structural (constitutional) isomers have atoms connected in a different order. Both forms of alanine have identical bonding; only the 3-D arrangement differs.
Cis–trans isomers come from a C=C double bond or a ring. Alanine's two forms come from a chiral carbon instead.

q: Epinephrine (adrenaline), shown, is the drug in an EpiPen. How many chiral carbons does it have?
h: Check each carbon in the side chain. A CH<sub>2</sub> has two identical H atoms; ring carbons have a double bond.
w: Only the carbon bonded to the –OH has four different groups (H, OH, the ring and CH2NHCH3): 1 chiral carbon. The tempting answer 2 counts the CH2 next to N, but it has two H atoms. Ring carbons and the N-methyl carbon are not chiral, and N atoms are not counted as chiral carbons.
x: That count includes the CH<sub>2</sub> next to the N, but it has two identical H atoms, so it is not chiral.
Look at the carbon bonded to –OH, H, the ring and CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub>. Are those four groups all different?
Too many. Ring carbons have a double bond, CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub> carbons have identical H atoms, and N is not a carbon.

q: Cyclohexene quickly decolorizes a red-brown solution of Br<sub>2</sub>. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: Halogenation of an alkene is an addition: the Br–Br bond breaks and one Br adds to each carbon of the C=C.
w: One Br adds to each carbon of the C=C, giving 1,2-dibromocyclohexane (the color disappears because Br2 is used up). Bromocyclohexane has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. The 1,1-isomer puts both Br on one carbon, and in the 1,3-isomer a Br sits on a carbon that was never part of the double bond.
x: This has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
Both Br atoms are on the same carbon. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Br.
Here the two Br atoms have a CH<sub>2</sub> between them, so one sits on a carbon that was never part of the C=C.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 1-methylcyclohexene shown?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H adds to the C=C carbon that already has more H atoms; Br goes to the other carbon.
w: The ring carbon holding the CH3 has no H; the other C=C carbon has one H. H adds to the CH carbon and Br to the carbon with the methyl group: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane. 1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane is the anti-Markovnikov product. Two Br atoms would need Br2, and an OH would need water.
x: This puts Br on the ring carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. Br goes to the double-bond carbon with fewer H atoms.
This has two Br atoms, which would require Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HBr adds an H and a Br.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 4-methyl-2-pentyne shown?
h: Two H<sub>2</sub> add across a C≡C, two H atoms on each carbon. Hydrogenation never moves a branch.
w: Two H2 saturate the triple bond, and the carbon skeleton is unchanged: 2-methylpentane. The alkene (4-methyl-2-pentene) is what one H2 gives. Hexane and 2,3-dimethylbutane have the same formula, C6H14, but their carbon skeletons differ from the reactant, and H2 cannot rearrange carbons.
x: This alkene still has a C=C, so only one H<sub>2</sub> was added. Two H<sub>2</sub> fully saturate the triple bond.
Hexane is unbranched, so the branch has been lost. Hydrogenation never changes the carbon skeleton.
2,3-Dimethylbutane has a different carbon skeleton from the reactant. H<sub>2</sub> cannot move carbon atoms around.

q: Limonene gives oranges their scent. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: Count the C=C bonds. Excess H<sub>2</sub> adds to every one of them.
w: Limonene has two C=C bonds and excess H2 adds to both (2 H2), giving 1-isopropyl-4-methylcyclohexane. The two structures that still have one C=C show only one H2 added. The benzene ring structure has fewer H atoms than limonene, so it would need H2 removed, not added.
x: The ring C=C is still there; only the side-chain C=C was saturated. Excess H<sub>2</sub> adds to every C=C.
The side-chain C=C is still there; only the ring was saturated. Excess H<sub>2</sub> adds to every C=C.
This benzene ring has fewer H atoms than limonene. Adding H<sub>2</sub> increases the H count, so it cannot form an aromatic ring.

q: Which alkene gives 1-chloro-1-ethylcyclohexane, shown, as the major product when it reacts with HCl?
h: Work backward: the Cl sits on a carbon that was part of the C=C, and by Markovnikov's rule it was the C=C carbon with fewer H atoms.
w: In 1-ethylcyclohexene the ring carbon holding the ethyl group has no H, so H adds to its neighbor and Cl adds to the ethyl-bearing carbon, giving the product shown. In 3- and 4-ethylcyclohexene the C=C carbons have no ethyl group, so the Cl cannot end up on the ethyl-bearing carbon. Vinylcyclohexane puts Cl on the side chain: 1-chloro-1-cyclohexylethane.
x: In 3-ethylcyclohexene the C=C carbons do not carry the ethyl group. HCl adds only to the C=C carbons, so the Cl could not land on the ethyl-bearing carbon.
Here the C=C is in the side chain, not the ring. HCl would put the Cl on the side-chain carbon next to the ring, not on a ring carbon.
In 4-ethylcyclohexene the C=C is on the far side of the ring from the ethyl group, so Cl would end up on a different ring carbon.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 2-methyl-2-pentene shown?
h: Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C. The OH goes on the C=C carbon with fewer H atoms.
w: C2 (bonded to two CH3 groups) has no H and C3 has one H, so H adds to C3 and OH to C2: 2-methyl-2-pentanol, a 3° alcohol. 2-Methyl-3-pentanol is the anti-Markovnikov product. 2-Methylpentane comes from H2, not water, and the diol adds two OH groups.
x: This puts the OH on C3, the double-bond carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. The OH goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
This alkane has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.
This diol has two OH groups. Water adds one H and one OH across the C=C.

q: Styrene is used to make polystyrene. What is the major product of the reaction shown?
h: Only the C=C outside the ring reacts. Apply Markovnikov's rule to its two carbons.
w: The CH2 end of the C=C has more H, so it gets the H and Br goes to the carbon attached to the ring: 1-bromo-1-phenylethane. Br on the CH2 end is the anti-Markovnikov product. The benzene ring does not add HBr, and putting Br on the ring would need Br2 with FeBr3. Two Br atoms would need Br2.
x: This puts Br on the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has more H, so it receives the H.
Here the C=C is untouched and a Br has replaced a ring H. HBr adds across the alkene C=C; the aromatic ring does not react.
This has two Br atoms, which would require Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene shown?
h: H<sub>2</sub> adds one H to each carbon of the C=C. The methyl groups stay where they are.
w: H2 adds across the C=C, giving 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane; both methyl groups stay on neighboring carbons. 1,1-Dimethylcyclohexane moves a methyl group. The aromatic ring (1,2-dimethylbenzene) has fewer H atoms, and the alcohol would come from hydration, not H2.
x: This is an aromatic ring with fewer H atoms than the reactant. H<sub>2</sub> adds hydrogen, so the product has more H, not fewer.
Here both methyl groups are on the same carbon, so a methyl has moved. Hydrogenation does not move groups.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. H<sub>2</sub> supplies only hydrogen atoms.

q: What is the product of the reaction of trans-2-pentene shown?
h: Find the two carbons of the C=C. In halogenation, one Cl adds to each of them.
w: The C=C is between C2 and C3, so Cl adds to both: 2,3-dichloropentane. 2-Chloropentane has only one Cl, which HCl would give. 3,3-Dichloropentane puts both Cl on one carbon, and 1,2-dichloropentane uses C1, which was not part of the double bond.
x: This has only one Cl, which is what HCl would give. Cl<sub>2</sub> adds two Cl atoms.
Both Cl atoms are on the same carbon. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Cl.
This puts a Cl on C1, the CH<sub>3</sub> end. C1 was not part of the C=C.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 1-hexene shown?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H adds to the C=C carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: C1 (CH2) has more H than C2 (CH), so H adds to C1 and Cl to C2: 2-chlorohexane. 1-Chlorohexane is the anti-Markovnikov product. 1,2-Dichlorohexane would need Cl2, and 3-chlorohexane puts Cl on a carbon that was not in the C=C.
x: This puts Cl on C1, the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. C1 has more H, so it receives the H.
This has two Cl atoms, which would require Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.
This puts Cl on C3, which was not part of the C=C. HCl adds only to the two double-bond carbons.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene shown?
h: Br<sub>2</sub> adds one Br to each carbon of the C=C, even when those carbons are crowded with methyl groups.
w: Each C=C carbon gets one Br: 2,3-dibromo-2,3-dimethylbutane. The single-Br product comes from HBr. Putting a Br on a CH3 group uses a carbon outside the double bond, and 2,3-dimethylbutane is the H2 product.
x: This has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
One Br here is on a CH<sub>3</sub> group, a carbon outside the double bond. Each Br goes on a carbon of the C=C.
This alkane has no Br; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of methylenecyclohexane shown?
h: One C=C carbon is CH<sub>2</sub> and the other is in the ring with no H. Which one gets the OH?
w: The CH2 end has more H, so it takes the H and becomes a CH3; the OH goes to the ring carbon: 1-methylcyclohexanol. Cyclohexylmethanol is the anti-Markovnikov product. 2-Methylcyclohexanol puts the OH on a ring carbon that was not part of the C=C, and methylcyclohexane would come from H2.
x: This puts the OH on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon outside the ring: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> end has more H, so it receives the H.
Here the OH is on a ring carbon next to the one that was in the C=C. Hydration only adds to the two double-bond carbons.
This has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 2-ethyl-1-butene shown?
h: Markovnikov's rule: Cl ends up on the C=C carbon with fewer H atoms.
w: C1 (=CH2) gets the H and becomes CH3; Cl goes to C2, which holds the two ethyl groups: 3-chloro-3-methylpentane. 1-Chloro-2-ethylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product. The alcohol needs water, and the dichloride needs Cl2.
x: This puts Cl on the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has more H, so it receives the H.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HCl adds an H and a Cl.
This has two Cl atoms, which would require Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown?
h: The product has one Cl and the C=C is gone. Which reagent adds H to one carbon and Cl to the other?
w: Hydrohalogenation with HCl adds H to one C=C carbon and Cl to the other, giving chlorocyclohexane. Cl2 (with or without FeCl3) adds a Cl to both carbons, giving 1,2-dichlorocyclohexane. Aqueous NaCl only supplies Cl− ions, which do not add to an alkene.
x: Cl<sub>2</sub> adds a Cl to both carbons of the C=C, giving a dichloride. The product here has only one Cl, and an H was added too.
FeCl<sub>3</sub> is the catalyst for substituting Cl onto a benzene ring. With an alkene, Cl<sub>2</sub> still puts a Cl on both C=C carbons.
Aqueous NaCl provides only Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions; it has no H to add and does not react with an alkene.

q: What is the product of the reaction of cyclohexanol shown?
h: Classify the alcohol first. Oxidation turns C–OH into C=O on the same carbon.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to two ring carbons, so cyclohexanol is a 2° alcohol and oxidizes to the ketone cyclohexanone. Cyclohexene comes from dehydration (H2SO4, heat), not [O]. The aldehyde has an extra carbon, and hexanal would mean the ring broke open.
x: Cyclohexene comes from dehydration (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, heat), not oxidation. [O] forms a C=O.
This aldehyde has a CHO carbon outside the ring, one carbon more than cyclohexanol. Oxidation does not add carbons.
This is hexanal, an open chain. Oxidation does not break the ring; it changes only the C–OH carbon.

q: 2-Phenylethanol gives roses their scent. What is the final organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Is the alcohol 1°, 2° or 3°? Excess oxidizing agent keeps going past the first product.
w: The –CH2OH group is a 1° alcohol. Excess [O] oxidizes it to the aldehyde and then on to the carboxylic acid: phenylacetic acid. The aldehyde is only the first product. The ketone puts C=O on the carbon next to the ring, which never held the OH, and styrene is a dehydration product.
x: This aldehyde is the first oxidation product. With excess K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> the reaction does not stop there.
This ketone has the C=O on the carbon next to the ring, which never held the –OH. Oxidation does not move the oxygen.
This is styrene, an alkene from dehydration. K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> oxidizes the alcohol instead of removing water.

q: 1-Hexanol is treated with a mild oxidizing agent, so the reaction stops at the first oxidation product. What is formed in the reaction shown?
h: A 1° alcohol (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH) becomes an aldehyde (–CHO). Keep the same number of carbons.
w: The end carbon loses two H (one from O, one from C) and forms C=O: hexanal. Hexanoic acid is over-oxidation, which needs excess [O]. 2-Hexanone puts the C=O on the wrong carbon, and 1-hexene is a dehydration product.
x: This is the carboxylic acid, which needs excess or strong oxidizing agent. Mild [O] stops one step earlier.
This ketone has its C=O on C2. 1-Hexanol's –OH is on C1, and oxidation does not move the oxygen.
This is 1-hexene, a dehydration product. Oxidation forms a C=O, not a C=C.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 4-methyl-2-pentanol shown?
h: The OH is on C2. How many carbons is that carbon bonded to?
w: C2 is bonded to two carbons, so this is a 2° alcohol and gives a ketone at the same carbon: 4-methyl-2-pentanone (methyl isobutyl ketone, a solvent). The aldehyde and the carboxylic acid put C=O on an end carbon, as if the alcohol were 1°. The alkene comes from dehydration, not oxidation.
x: This aldehyde has its C=O on an end carbon, as if the alcohol were primary. The –OH here is on C2, and oxidation does not move it.
A carboxylic acid would need the –OH on an end carbon (a primary alcohol). Check how many carbons are bonded to the C–OH carbon.
This alkene comes from dehydration (loss of water), not oxidation. [O] forms a C=O.

q: Which compound gives cyclopentanone, shown, when it is oxidized with [O]?
h: A ketone comes from a 2° alcohol oxidized at the same carbon.
w: Cyclopentanol is a 2° alcohol whose OH is on a ring carbon, so [O] turns that C–OH into the ring C=O. Cyclopentylmethanol is a 1° alcohol and gives an aldehyde. 1-Methylcyclopentanol is 3° and does not react. The ring ether has the same formula (C5H10O) as cyclopentanol, but ethers have no O–H and are not oxidized.
x: Here the –OH is on a CH<sub>2</sub> outside the ring, so this is a primary alcohol. Oxidizing it would give an aldehyde, not a ring ketone.
Here the C–OH carbon also carries a CH<sub>3</sub>, so it is bonded to three carbons and has no H. A tertiary alcohol is not oxidized.
This is a ring ether: the O is part of the ring and has no H. Ethers are not oxidized to ketones.

q: 1-Methylcyclohexanol is mixed with an oxidizing agent, as shown. What happens?
h: Count the H atoms on the carbon that holds the OH. Oxidation must remove one of them.
w: The OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and the CH3), so this is a 3° alcohol. With no H on that carbon it cannot form C=O: no reaction. 2-Methylcyclohexanone moves the oxygen to another carbon, 1-methylcyclohexene is a dehydration product (H2SO4, heat), and cyclohexanone would require breaking off the methyl group.
x: This ketone has the C=O on a neighboring ring carbon. Oxidation can only change the carbon that holds the –OH, never move the oxygen.
1-Methylcyclohexene comes from dehydration (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, heat), not an oxidizing agent.
This would require breaking off the CH<sub>3</sub> group. Oxidation does not remove carbon groups; check the H atoms on the C–OH carbon.

q: All four alcohols shown are isomers of C6H14O. Which one does not react with the oxidizing agent K2Cr2O7?
h: Look at the carbon bonded to the OH. Oxidation needs an H on that carbon.
w: In 3-methyl-3-pentanol the OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (3° alcohol) and carries no H, so it cannot be oxidized. The other choices are 2° alcohols (OH carbon bonded to two carbons, giving ketones) or a 1° alcohol (–CH2OH, giving an aldehyde and then an acid).
x: Here the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons and still has one H, so this secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone.
This is a primary alcohol (–CH<sub>2</sub>OH), even though the chain is branched. It is readily oxidized.
Here the C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons and has one H, so this secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone.

q: What is the organic product of the reaction of 3-pentanol shown?
h: Dehydration removes the OH and an H from a neighboring carbon. The C=C forms between those two carbons.
w: The OH is on C3 and both neighbors (C2 and C4) are CH2 groups, so either way the C=C forms between C2 and C3: 2-pentene + H2O. 1-Pentene would need an H removed from C1, which is not next to the OH carbon. 3-Pentanone is an oxidation product, and pentane would need H2.
x: 1-Pentene has its C=C at C1, which is not next to the carbon that held the –OH. Dehydration forms the C=C at the C–OH carbon.
This is a ketone, 3-pentanone, which comes from oxidation. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with heat removes water instead.
This is pentane, with no C=C. It would need H<sub>2</sub> added; dehydration forms a double bond.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 2,3-dimethyl-2-butanol shown?
h: The C=C forms toward the neighboring carbon with fewer H atoms (Zaitsev), giving the most substituted alkene.
w: The OH carbon has two kinds of neighbors: CH3 groups (3 H) and a CH (1 H). Removing the H from the CH gives the C=C with four carbon groups: 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene, the major product. 2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene (H taken from a CH3) is the minor, less substituted alkene. 3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene has a different carbon skeleton, and the alkane would need H2.
x: This alkene forms when the H comes from a CH<sub>3</sub>. It is the minor product: only two carbon groups sit on its C=C.
This is an alkane with no C=C. It would need H<sub>2</sub> added; dehydration forms a double bond.
This alkene has a different carbon skeleton, with three methyls on one carbon. Dehydration does not rearrange the carbons here.

q: Which alkene is the major product of the reaction of 2-methyl-3-pentanol shown?
h: Compare the two carbons next to the OH carbon. The H is removed from the one with fewer H atoms.
w: The OH is on C3. Its neighbors are C2 (CH, 1 H) and C4 (CH2, 2 H). Removing the H from C2 gives the more substituted alkene, 2-methyl-2-pentene (three carbon groups on the C=C). 4-Methyl-2-pentene, from C4, is the minor product. 2-Methyl-1-pentene puts the C=C away from the OH carbon, and the ketone is an oxidation product.
x: This alkene forms when the H comes from the CH<sub>2</sub> side. It is the minor product: Zaitsev's rule favors the neighbor with fewer H atoms.
This is a ketone, which comes from oxidation. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with heat removes water to make a C=C.
Here the C=C does not include the carbon that held the –OH. Dehydration forms the double bond between the C–OH carbon and a neighbor.

q: Two molecules of 2-propanethiol are oxidized as shown. What is the organic product?
h: Oxidation of thiols removes the H from each –SH and joins the two sulfur atoms.
w: Each –SH loses its H and the two S atoms bond: 2 R–SH + [O] → R–S–S–R + H2O, here diisopropyl disulfide (the same S–S link joins cysteines in proteins). The sulfide has lost a sulfur atom, the peroxide has O in place of S, and dipropyl disulfide attaches S to the end carbon instead of the middle one.
x: This sulfide has only one S, so a sulfur atom was lost. Oxidation removes just the H from each –SH.
This has O–O in place of S–S. The sulfur atoms stay in the product.
This disulfide has S on the end carbon of straight propyl chains. In 2-propanethiol the S is on the middle carbon, and that does not change.

q: Diallyl disulfide, shown, contributes to the odor of garlic. Which thiol forms it when two molecules are oxidized [O]?
h: Split the S–S bond and give each sulfur back its H.
w: Breaking the S–S bond and adding an H to each S gives two molecules of 2-propene-1-thiol (allyl thiol, CH2=CHCH2SH). The alcohol has O instead of S and cannot form an S–S bond. 1-Propanethiol has no C=C, so it gives dipropyl disulfide. Diallyl sulfide has no S–H to oxidize.
x: This is an alcohol, with O instead of S. Only thiols oxidize to form an S–S bond.
This thiol has no C=C. The disulfide has a C=C in each half, so the thiol must have one too.
This sulfide has no S–H, so it cannot be oxidized to a disulfide. It also has only one S atom.

q: 2-Heptanone is found in blue cheese. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: Reduction is the reverse of oxidation: [H] adds H atoms across the C=O, which becomes C–OH on the same carbon.
w: H atoms add to the C=O at C2, so a ketone gives a 2° alcohol: 2-heptanol. 1-Heptanol puts the OH on the end carbon, which never held the oxygen. Heptane has lost the oxygen completely, and heptanoic acid is an oxidation product (and would need the C=O at the end).
x: This drawing has the OH on the end carbon, which never held the oxygen. Reduction puts the OH on the former C=O carbon.
This drawing is heptane: the oxygen is gone. [H] adds H atoms across the C=O; it does not remove the oxygen.
This drawing is heptanoic acid, an oxidation product. [H] is a reducing agent.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 2-methylpropanal shown?
h: An aldehyde is reduced at the CHO carbon. What class of alcohol does that give?
w: [H] adds H atoms across the C=O, so –CHO becomes –CH2OH: 2-methyl-1-propanol (isobutyl alcohol), a 1° alcohol. tert-Butyl alcohol puts the OH on the branch carbon, which was never the carbonyl carbon. 2-Methylpropanoic acid is the oxidation product, and 2-methylpropane has lost the oxygen.
x: This drawing puts the OH on the branch carbon, which was never the carbonyl carbon. Reduction keeps the oxygen where the C=O was.
This drawing is 2-methylpropanoic acid, the oxidation product. [H] is a reducing agent.
This drawing is 2-methylpropane: the oxygen is gone. [H] adds H atoms across the C=O; it does not remove oxygen.

q: Which compound gives 1-phenylethanol, shown, when it is treated with [H] (a reducing agent)? The benzene ring does not react.
h: The OH carbon in the product was the C=O carbon before reduction. Which carbon carries the OH?
w: The OH is on the carbon bonded to the ring, a 2° alcohol carbon, so it came from the ketone acetophenone (C=O on that same carbon). Phenylacetaldehyde gives 2-phenylethanol (OH on the end carbon). 4-Methylbenzaldehyde has the same formula as acetophenone but gives a 1° alcohol. Styrene has no oxygen, so reducing it cannot create an –OH.
x: This drawing is phenylacetaldehyde, with the C=O on the end carbon. Reducing it gives a 1° alcohol with OH on the end carbon.
This drawing is 4-methylbenzaldehyde: its CHO reduces to a 1° alcohol, CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The product has a 2° alcohol carbon.
This drawing is styrene, which has no oxygen. Reducing it could not create an –OH.

q: The product of the reaction of 3-methylbutanal shown is partly responsible for foot odor. What is it?
h: Aldehydes oxidize easily: the –CHO carbon gains an O and becomes –COOH. Keep every carbon and branch.
w: The H on the CHO carbon is replaced by OH, giving 3-methylbutanoic acid. 3-Methyl-1-butanol is the reduction product ([H]), the opposite reaction. The ketone, 3-methyl-2-butanone, moves the C=O to a different carbon, and 2-methylpropanoic acid has lost a carbon.
x: This drawing is 3-methyl-1-butanol, the reduction product. [O] means oxidation.
This drawing is a ketone with the C=O moved to a different carbon. Oxidation keeps the oxygen on the original –CHO carbon.
This drawing has only four carbons; one carbon is missing. Oxidation keeps every carbon and branch.

q: 2-Hexanone is mixed with a mild oxidizing agent that readily oxidizes aldehydes, as shown. What happens?
h: An aldehyde is oxidized by losing the H on its C=O carbon. Does a ketone have that H?
w: In a ketone the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons and has no H to lose, so a mild oxidizing agent gives no reaction (this is how Tollens' and Benedict's tests tell aldehydes from ketones). Hexanoic acid is what the aldehyde hexanal would give. 2-Hexanol is a reduction product, and hexanal is an isomer, not a product.
x: This drawing is hexanoic acid, which would come from the aldehyde hexanal. Does 2-hexanone's C=O carbon have an H to lose?
This drawing is 2-hexanol, a reduction product. A mild oxidizing agent cannot add H to the C=O.
This drawing is hexanal, an isomer. An oxidizing agent cannot move the C=O to the end of the chain.

q: Pentanal reacts with one molecule of methanol, as shown. What is the product?
h: One alcohol adds across the C=O: the carbonyl carbon ends up with both an –OH and an –OR.
w: The O of methanol bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiacetal, 1-methoxy-1-pentanol. Two –OCH3 groups (an acetal) need a second methanol. Methyl pentanoate is an ester, which forms from a carboxylic acid, and the ether has lost the OH.
x: This drawing has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups, which needs two methanol molecules. Only one methanol reacts here.
This drawing is methyl pentanoate, an ester with a C=O. Esters form from carboxylic acids, not aldehydes.
This drawing is an ether with only one oxygen: the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen as –OH.

q: Butanal reacts with two molecules of methanol, and water is released. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: The first methanol gives a hemiacetal; the second replaces its –OH with another –OCH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The carbonyl O leaves in H2O and the former C=O carbon ends up with two –OCH3 groups: the acetal 1,1-dimethoxybutane. The structure with one OH and one OCH3 is the hemiacetal that forms first. Methyl butanoate is an ester, and the remaining structure puts the two –OCH3 groups on different carbons.
x: This drawing has an –OH and one –OCH<sub>3</sub>: the intermediate after one methanol. The second methanol replaces the –OH.
This drawing is methyl butanoate, an ester with a C=O. Esters form from carboxylic acids, not aldehydes.
This drawing puts the two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups on different carbons. Both alcohols add to the same former carbonyl carbon.

q: Cyclohexanone reacts with one molecule of methanol, as shown. What is the product?
h: A ketone plus one alcohol gives a hemiketal: an –OH and an –OR on the former C=O carbon.
w: The methoxy group adds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH: a hemiketal, 1-methoxycyclohexanol. Two –OCH3 groups (a ketal) need a second methanol. The ether has lost the OH, and 2-methoxycyclohexanol splits the two groups between neighboring carbons.
x: This drawing has two –OCH<sub>3</sub> groups, which needs two methanol molecules. Only one methanol reacts here.
This drawing is an ether with no –OH: the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding an alcohol keeps that oxygen as –OH.
This drawing puts the –OH and the –OCH<sub>3</sub> on neighboring carbons. Both groups end up on the former carbonyl carbon.

q: Cyclopentanone reacts with two molecules of ethanol, and water is released. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: In a ketal, both –OR groups are on the carbon that was the C=O carbon.
w: Two ethanol molecules bond to the carbonyl carbon and the carbonyl O leaves as H2O: the ketal 1,1-diethoxycyclopentane. The structure with an OH and one ethoxy group is only the hemiketal. Putting the ethoxy groups on two different carbons, or keeping only one with no OH, does not match ketal formation.
x: This drawing has an –OH and one ethoxy group: the intermediate after one ethanol. The second ethanol replaces the –OH.
This drawing puts the two ethoxy groups on neighboring ring carbons. Both alcohols add to the same former carbonyl carbon.
This drawing has only one ethoxy group and no –OH; an oxygen has been lost. Two ethanol molecules should add.

q: 5-Hydroxypentanal, shown, has an –OH and a –CHO in the same molecule. In solution it forms a six-membered ring, the same way glucose does. Which structure is the ring form?
h: The –OH oxygen adds to the C=O carbon, forming a cyclic hemiacetal. That carbon keeps an –OH.
w: The O of the –OH bonds to the aldehyde carbon and the C=O becomes C–OH, closing a ring of five C and one O: a cyclic hemiacetal with the OH on the carbon next to the ring O. The C=O version is a cyclic ester (an oxidation product), the ring without an OH has lost an oxygen, and putting the OH on a carbon away from the ring O does not match hemiacetal formation.
x: This drawing keeps a C=O in the ring: a cyclic ester, which is an oxidation product. When the –OH adds, the C=O becomes C–OH.
This ring has no –OH at all, so the carbonyl oxygen has been lost. Adding the –OH to the C=O keeps that oxygen.
This drawing puts the –OH on a carbon that is not next to the ring oxygen. The former C=O carbon bonds to the ring O and keeps the –OH.

q: The five-membered cyclic hemiacetal shown resembles the ring of ribose. Which compound forms it in solution?
