h: A cyclic hemiacetal forms when an –OH in the same molecule adds to an aldehyde C=O. Count the ring atoms.
w: The ring has four C and one O. In 4-hydroxybutanal the –OH on C4 can reach the C1 aldehyde carbon, forming exactly that five-membered ring with an OH on the former C=O carbon. 5-Hydroxypentanal gives a six-membered ring. 3-Hydroxybutanal would give a strained four-membered ring with a methyl group. Butanoic acid has no aldehyde.
x: 5-Hydroxypentanal would close a six-membered ring (five C and one O). The ring shown has five atoms.
Here the –OH is on C3, so ring closure gives a four-membered ring with a CH<sub>3</sub> branch. The ring shown has five atoms and no branch.
Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid with no aldehyde and no separate –OH group. A cyclic hemiacetal needs both in one molecule.

q: 3-Phenylpropanal is reduced under conditions that do not affect the benzene ring. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: [H] adds one H to the C and one H to the O of the C=O.
w: The aldehyde –CHO becomes –CH2OH, a 1° alcohol: 3-phenyl-1-propanol. 3-Phenylpropanoic acid is the oxidation product, the opposite reaction. 1-Phenyl-2-propanol has the OH on the wrong carbon, and propylbenzene has lost the oxygen.
x: This drawing is 3-phenylpropanoic acid, the oxidation product. [H] is a reducing agent.
This drawing puts the OH on the middle carbon of the chain. Reduction keeps the oxygen on the carbon that held the C=O, the end carbon.
This drawing is propylbenzene: the oxygen is gone. [H] adds H atoms across the C=O; it does not remove oxygen.

q: Which carbonyl compound and alcohol react (H<sup>+</sup>) to form the hemiacetal shown?
h: Find the carbon holding both –OH and –OR. It was the C=O carbon; the –OR came from the alcohol.
w: The carbon bonded to both –OH and –OCH2CH3 also carries H and an isopropyl group, so it was the CHO carbon of 2-methylpropanal, and the –OCH2CH3 came from ethanol. The other pairs give isomers (same formula, C6H14O2) in which different groups sit on the oxygen and on the hemiacetal carbon; acetone + 1-propanol gives a hemiketal.
x: Propanal + 2-propanol would put an ethyl on the hemiacetal carbon and an isopropyl on the oxygen. The drawing has these the other way around.
Ethanal + 2-methyl-1-propanol would put a CH<sub>3</sub> on the hemiacetal carbon and a four-carbon group on the oxygen. Check what is on each side.
Acetone is a ketone, so it gives a hemiketal with two carbon groups and no H on that carbon. The drawn carbon has an H.

q: What is the organic product of the reaction of benzoic acid and ethanol shown?
h: Esterification: the acid loses –OH, the alcohol loses H, and the acid C=O carbon bonds to the alcohol O.
w: The C=O carbon of benzoic acid bonds to the O of ethanol, and H2O is lost: ethyl benzoate. Benzyl acetate has the same formula but puts the C=O on the ethanol side. The ether has lost the C=O oxygen, and the ketone joins carbon to carbon instead of through oxygen.
x: This is benzyl acetate: the C=O is on the two-carbon side and the ring is on the O side. Benzoic acid's C=O carbon is attached directly to the ring and should stay that way.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an ether. Esterification keeps the acid's carbonyl group.
This is a ketone: the ethyl group is bonded straight to the C=O carbon with no O between. An ester needs a C(=O)–O–C link.

q: Which ester forms in the reaction of 2-methylpropanoic acid and methanol shown?
h: The acid keeps all its branches and its C=O. Swap its –OH for –O–CH<sub>3</sub> from methanol.
w: The branched acid becomes the "-oate" part and methanol supplies –OCH3: methyl 2-methylpropanoate + H2O. Isopropyl acetate is an isomer with the C=O on the wrong side of the ester oxygen. The ether has no C=O, and the ketone joins the CH3 directly to carbon.
x: This is isopropyl acetate, an isomer with the C=O on the wrong side. The branched C=O side of the acid should keep its carbonyl, and the methyl goes on the O.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an ether. Esterification keeps the acid's carbonyl group.
This is a ketone: a CH<sub>3</sub> is bonded straight to the C=O carbon. An ester needs an O between the C=O carbon and the methanol carbon.

q: Benzyl acetate, shown, gives jasmine its scent. Which carboxylic acid and alcohol react (H<sup>+</sup>, heat) to make it?
h: Split the ester at the single C–O bond next to the C=O. The C=O side was the acid; the other side was the alcohol.
w: The C=O side is CH3C(=O)– (from acetic acid) and the –O–CH2–C6H5 side is from benzyl alcohol. Benzoic acid + ethanol puts the C=O on the ring side (ethyl benzoate), and phenylacetic acid + methanol gives methyl phenylacetate; both are isomers. Acetic acid + phenol gives phenyl acetate, which is missing the CH2.
x: Benzoic acid + ethanol gives ethyl benzoate, with the C=O attached to the ring. In benzyl acetate the C=O is on the two-carbon side.
Phenylacetic acid + methanol gives methyl phenylacetate, an isomer. In benzyl acetate the CH<sub>2</sub>–ring group is on the single-bonded O, not the C=O side.
Phenol has its –OH right on the ring, so it would give phenyl acetate. Benzyl acetate has a CH<sub>2</sub> between the ester O and the ring.

q: Butyl acetate is a solvent with a pear-like odor. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Break the single C–O bond next to the C=O. Add OH to the carbonyl carbon and H to the other O.
w: Water splits the ester into the acid part and the alcohol part: acetic acid + 1-butanol. Butanoic acid + ethanol breaks the molecule on the wrong side of the oxygen. Sodium acetate only forms in base (saponification), and two alcohols would require reduction.
x: Butanoic acid + ethanol splits the ester on the wrong side. The C=O carbon here carries only a CH<sub>3</sub>, and the four-carbon chain is on the O.
A sodium salt forms only in base (NaOH, saponification). These conditions use water and acid.
Two alcohols would mean the C=O was reduced. Hydrolysis keeps the C=O and adds an –OH to it.

q: What are the products of the saponification of ethyl 2-methylpropanoate shown?
h: Same split as acid hydrolysis, but in base the acid part comes out as its sodium salt (–COO<sup>−</sup> Na<sup>+</sup>).
w: NaOH breaks the C–O bond next to the C=O: the acid part becomes sodium 2-methylpropanoate and the –OCH2CH3 part becomes ethanol. The neutral acid + ethanol are the products in acid, not base. Putting Na+ on the ethanol O, or the C=O on the two-carbon piece, splits the ester wrongly.
x: The neutral acid plus ethanol is what acid hydrolysis gives. In NaOH the acid is neutralized as it forms.
This drawing puts the Na<sup>+</sup> on ethanol's O and leaves the acid as –COOH. The base reacts with the acidic –COOH group.
This drawing moves the C=O onto the two-carbon fragment and makes a branched alcohol. In the ester the C=O is on the branched side.

q: Lactic acid builds up in hard-working muscle. What is the organic product of the neutralization shown?
h: Only the acidic H of –COOH reacts with a base. Everything else stays the same.
w: OH− removes the H from the –COOH group, giving sodium lactate (used in lactated Ringer's IV solution) + H2O. The alcohol –OH is far less acidic and is not deprotonated by NaOH. Sodium pyruvate would require oxidation of the alcohol, and the C=C product would require dehydration.
x: This drawing removes the H from the alcohol –OH and leaves –COOH intact. NaOH reacts with the far more acidic H on the –COOH group.
Here the alcohol carbon became a C=O (pyruvate). That is oxidation, which NaOH does not do.
Here the –OH is gone and a C=C formed, which is dehydration. A neutralization changes only the acidic H.

q: Hexanoic acid gives goats their strong odor. In the reaction shown, bubbles of CO<sub>2</sub> form. What is the organic product?
h: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to react with bicarbonate. Where do the CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O come from?
w: HCO−3 removes the acidic H, giving sodium hexanoate, and the H2CO3 formed breaks down to CO2 + H2O. The CO2 comes from the bicarbonate, not from the acid, so pentane is wrong. Hexanol would need reduction, and "no reaction" ignores that the bubbling shows a reaction.
x: Pentane would mean the acid lost its whole –COOH carbon. The CO<sub>2</sub> bubbles come from the bicarbonate, not from the acid.
1-Hexanol would require reducing the –COOH group. Bicarbonate is a base, not a reducing agent.
The CO<sub>2</sub> bubbles show something happened. Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to react with bicarbonate.

q: An ester is heated with NaOH. The products are sodium butanoate and 2-propanol, shown. Which ester was used?
h: Rejoin the pieces: the carboxylate C=O carbon bonds to the O of the alcohol.
w: Joining the butanoyl group to the O of 2-propanol gives isopropyl butanoate. Propyl butanoate would give 1-propanol (O on the end carbon). Propyl 2-methylpropanoate puts the isopropyl group on the C=O side. The ether has no C=O and is not saponified.
x: Propyl butanoate has the O on an end carbon of the propyl group, so it would give 1-propanol. 2-Propanol has its –OH on the middle carbon.
This puts a branched group on the C=O side and a straight propyl on the O. Sodium butanoate tells you the C=O side was a straight four-carbon chain.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an ether. Ethers are not saponified, and no carboxylate salt could form from it.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown (heating is used)?
h: The product side shows a carboxylate salt with Na<sup>+</sup>. Which reaction makes a salt instead of a carboxylic acid?
w: Saponification with NaOH splits the ester into sodium pentanoate and methanol. H2O/H+ also splits the ester but gives neutral pentanoic acid, not the sodium salt. H2/Ni does not reduce an ester C=O, and K2Cr2O7 oxidizes alcohols, not esters.
x: H<sub>2</sub>O with H<sup>+</sup> also splits the ester, but it gives the neutral carboxylic acid. Look at the Na<sup>+</sup> in the product.
H<sub>2</sub> with Ni is used for hydrogenation, such as adding H<sub>2</sub> across C=C. It does not split an ester into a salt and an alcohol.
K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is an oxidizing agent for alcohols and aldehydes. It cannot make a sodium salt from an ester.

q: Formic acid and ethanol react as shown to make an ester with a rum-like odor. Which structure is the ester?
h: Formic acid supplies H–C(=O)–; ethanol supplies –O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The formyl carbon bonds to the ethanol oxygen and water is lost: ethyl formate (ethyl methanoate), H–C(=O)–O–CH2CH3. Methyl acetate and propanoic acid have the same formula, C3H6O2, but the carbons are arranged differently. Ethyl methyl ether has no C=O.
x: This is methyl acetate: two carbons on the C=O side and one on the O. Formic acid has only one carbon, so the C=O side should be just H–C(=O)–.
This is propanoic acid, a carboxylic acid with an –OH still on the C=O. Esterification replaces that –OH with the alcohol's –O–R.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an ether. Esterification keeps the acid's carbonyl group.

q: Methyl salicylate is the active ingredient in wintergreen muscle rubs. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Find the ester group (C=O bonded to O–CH<sub>3</sub>). Only that bond is hydrolyzed; the ring –OH stays.
w: Water splits the –C(=O)–O–CH3 bond, giving salicylic acid + methanol. The sodium salt only forms with NaOH. Turning the C=O into CH2OH would be reduction. Salicylic acid + acetic acid are the hydrolysis products of aspirin, a different ester.
x: A carboxylate sodium salt forms only in base (NaOH). These conditions are water and acid.
Here the C=O has become a CH<sub>2</sub>OH, which would be a reduction. Hydrolysis keeps the C=O and adds an –OH to it.
Acetic acid would come from an acetyl ester like aspirin. In methyl salicylate the group on the ester O is a single CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Butanoic acid and ethylamine are heated together and water is driven off. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Amidation: the acid loses –OH and the amine loses an H from N; the new C–N bond makes an amide.
w: The acid C=O carbon bonds to the N of ethylamine: N-ethylbutanamide + H2O. N-Butylacetamide is an isomer with the C=O on the wrong side of the N. The ammonium carboxylate salt forms when the two are just mixed (acid–base), but heating drives off water to make the amide. The amine has lost the C=O oxygen.
x: This drawing is N-butylacetamide: the C=O is on a two-carbon piece with a butyl on N. The acid's C=O must stay with its four-carbon chain.
This ammonium carboxylate salt forms when the two are simply mixed. Heating with water driven off gives a different product.
This drawing is an amine with no C=O. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl oxygen.

q: Nicotinic acid (niacin, vitamin B<sub>3</sub>) is heated with NH<sub>3</sub> and water is removed, as shown. The product is another form of vitamin B<sub>3</sub>. What is it?
h: Heating with water removed is a condensation, not a simple proton transfer. Which new bond forms, and what stays the same?
w: The –COOH loses –OH, NH3 loses an H, and a C–N bond forms: nicotinamide (–CONH2). Ammonium nicotinate is only the acid–base salt, which loses water on heating to form the amide. The other two have lost the C=O oxygen or the whole carbonyl carbon.
x: This is ammonium nicotinate, the acid–base salt. Heating removes water and forms a new bond instead.
This drawing has lost the whole carbonyl carbon: the N is bonded straight to the ring. Amidation keeps the C=O carbon.
This drawing has a CH<sub>2</sub> where the C=O should be; the carbonyl oxygen is gone. Amidation keeps the C=O.

q: Acetanilide was one of the first fever reducers. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O. In acid, what happens to the amine that forms?
w: Water breaks the amide C–N bond, giving acetic acid and aniline; in HCl the amine picks up H+, so the products are acetic acid + anilinium chloride. Neutral aniline ignores the acid present. Acetamide + phenol breaks the N–ring bond instead of the amide bond, and sodium acetate forms only in NaOH.
x: This shows neutral aniline, but the reaction runs in HCl. An amine in acid picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
This drawing breaks the N–ring bond, giving acetamide and phenol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.
Sodium acetate forms only in NaOH. With HCl as the reagent, no sodium is present.

q: DEET is the active ingredient in many insect repellents. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Base hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O. Think about which acid and base forms can last in NaOH.
w: OH− breaks the amide C–N bond: the carbonyl side becomes sodium 3-methylbenzoate and the N side becomes diethylamine. In base the carboxylic acid cannot stay neutral, and the amine cannot be protonated (no Na+ appears in the ammonium salt choice). Breaking an N–ethyl bond (giving ethanol) does not hydrolyze the amide group.
x: An ammonium ion like this cannot exist in strong base; OH<sup>−</sup> removes its H<sup>+</sup>. There is also no Na<sup>+</sup> to pair with the carboxylate.
This shows a neutral carboxylic acid, which cannot survive in NaOH. In base the acid is converted to its salt.
This drawing breaks an N–ethyl bond, giving an N-ethyl amide and ethanol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.

q: What are the products of the reaction of N-ethylbenzamide shown?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O. Look at the reagent: what does HCl do to each piece?
w: Water breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O: benzoic acid + ethylammonium chloride (the ethylamine is protonated by HCl). Neutral ethylamine ignores the acid. Benzamide + ethanol breaks the N–ethyl bond instead, and sodium benzoate + ethylamine are the products in NaOH.
x: This shows neutral ethylamine, but the reaction runs in HCl. An amine in acid picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
This drawing breaks the N–ethyl bond, giving benzamide and ethanol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.
Sodium benzoate forms only in NaOH. With HCl as the reagent, no sodium is present.

q: Amphetamine, a prescription stimulant, is sold as a salt made by the reaction shown. What is the product?
h: Amines are bases. What does the lone pair on N do with the H⁺ from HCl?
w: The lone pair on N accepts H+ from HCl, giving the ammonium ion with Cl−: amphetamine hydrochloride, a water-soluble salt. No C–Cl or N–Cl bond forms: Cl replacing –NH2, Cl on the ring, or Cl on N are all wrong.
x: This drawing has Cl replacing the –NH<sub>2</sub>. HCl does not swap out the nitrogen; it is an acid–base reaction.
This drawing puts Cl on the benzene ring and leaves the –NH<sub>2</sub> unchanged. HCl reacts with the basic N, not the ring.
This drawing has an N–Cl bond. The nitrogen lone pair picks up H<sup>+</sup>, and chloride stays a separate ion.

q: What is the product of the reaction of ethylenediamine (1,2-ethanediamine) shown?
h: Each amine group is a base. With excess acid, how many N atoms are protonated?
w: Both –NH2 groups accept H+, so with excess HCl the product is ethylenediammonium chloride, with two –NH+3 groups and two Cl− ions. Protonating only one N would be the product with just one HCl. HCl does not make N–Cl or C–Cl bonds.
x: This protonates only one –NH<sub>2</sub>, which is what one equivalent of HCl would do. With excess acid, check the other nitrogen too.
This drawing bonds Cl to each N. HCl gives H<sup>+</sup> to the nitrogen; chloride stays a separate ion.
This drawing replaces an –NH<sub>2</sub> with Cl and releases NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. HCl does not break C–N bonds; it is an acid–base reaction.

q: Which carboxylic acid and amine, heated together, form the amide shown?
h: Break the C–N bond next to the C=O. The C=O side is the acid; the N side is the amine.
w: The C=O side, CH3CH2C(=O)–, comes from propanoic acid, and the N bonded to the middle carbon of a three-carbon group comes from isopropylamine. 2-Methylpropanoic acid + ethylamine gives an isomer with the C=O on the other side. 2-Propanol gives an ester, not an amide, and propylamine attaches N to an end carbon.
x: 2-Methylpropanoic acid + ethylamine makes an isomer with the branch on the C=O side and ethyl on N. In the target, the C=O side is an unbranched ethyl.
2-Propanol is an alcohol, so heating it with an acid gives an ester, not an amide. An amide needs an amine.
Propylamine would put the N on an end carbon. In the drawing the N is bonded to the middle carbon of a branched three-carbon group.

q: Phenylacetic acid and dimethylamine are heated together and water is removed. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Replace the –OH of the acid with the N of the amine, keeping both methyl groups on N.
w: The acid C=O carbon bonds to the N of dimethylamine and H2O is lost: N,N-dimethyl-2-phenylacetamide. The dimethylammonium salt is the acid–base product before heating removes water. The amine has lost the C=O oxygen, and N,N-dimethylbenzamide is missing the CH2 between the ring and the C=O.
x: This dimethylammonium carboxylate salt is the acid–base product of simply mixing. Heating drives off water and forms a new bond.
This drawing has a CH<sub>2</sub> where the C=O should be, so it is an amine. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl oxygen.
This drawing has the C=O bonded directly to the ring, missing the CH<sub>2</sub> of phenylacetic acid. That would come from benzoic acid.

q: What are the products of the reaction of benzamide shown?
h: Base hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O. Can a neutral acid or an NH₄⁺ ion last in strong base?
w: OH− breaks the C–N bond: sodium benzoate + NH3. Benzoic acid + NH4Cl are the products in HCl, not NaOH. In base the acid cannot stay neutral, and NH+4 cannot exist in strong base (it gives up H+ to OH−).
x: Benzoic acid and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl are the products of acid hydrolysis with HCl. Here the reagent is NaOH.
This shows a neutral carboxylic acid, which cannot survive in NaOH; the base converts it to its salt.
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> cannot exist in strong base: it gives its H<sup>+</sup> to OH<sup>−</sup>. Also, no Na<sup>+</sup> is shown to balance the charge.

q: 1,4-Dimethylbenzene (p-xylene) has four equivalent ring H atoms. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: An aromatic ring undergoes substitution, not addition: one ring H is replaced and HBr is the by-product.
w: FeBr3 helps Br replace one ring H, giving 2-bromo-1,4-dimethylbenzene + HBr, and the ring stays aromatic. Adding Br2 across a ring C=C is what alkenes do, not benzene rings. Br on a CH3 group happens with Br2 and light, not FeBr3. Two Br atoms would need a second substitution.
x: Here Br<sub>2</sub> added across a ring double bond, leaving only two. That is alkene behavior; the aromatic ring does substitution instead.
Here Br replaced an H on a CH<sub>3</sub> group. That happens with Br<sub>2</sub> and light, as with alkanes, not with an FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
This has two Br atoms on the ring. One Br<sub>2</sub> replaces only one ring H; a second Br would need a second substitution.

q: 1,3,5-Trimethylbenzene has three equivalent ring H atoms. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Nitration replaces one ring H with an –NO<sub>2</sub> group. The methyl groups are not touched.
w: One ring H is replaced by –NO2, giving 1,3,5-trimethyl-2-nitrobenzene + H2O. Nitration substitutes on the ring, not on a CH3 group. An –NH2 group (amine) is not formed by HNO3, and two –NO2 groups would need a second nitration.
x: Here the –NO<sub>2</sub> is on a CH<sub>3</sub> group, not on the ring. HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> replaces a ring H.
This has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Nitration attaches an N bonded to two O atoms; –NH<sub>2</sub> would need a separate reduction step.
This has two –NO<sub>2</sub> groups. One nitration replaces only one ring H.

q: Which reagents carry out the conversion shown?
h: The Cl replaced an H on the ring itself. Which conditions substitute on an aromatic ring?
w: Cl2 with an FeCl3 catalyst substitutes Cl for a ring H (HCl is the by-product). Cl2 with light substitutes on the CH3 groups, as it does with alkanes. HCl does not react with a benzene ring, and Br2/FeBr3 would add Br, not Cl.
x: With light, Cl<sub>2</sub> substitutes on the CH<sub>3</sub> groups, as it does with alkanes, not on the ring. Look at where the Cl ends up in the product.
HCl does not react with a benzene ring. Putting a halogen on an aromatic ring takes the halogen itself plus a catalyst.
Br<sub>2</sub> with FeBr<sub>3</sub> does substitute on aromatic rings, but it adds Br. The product shown has Cl.

q: 1,4-Dichlorobenzene is used in mothballs; its four ring H atoms are equivalent. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Nitration replaces a ring H with –NO2. The Cl atoms and the aromatic ring stay.
w: One ring H is replaced by –NO2: 1,4-dichloro-2-nitrobenzene + H2O. 4-Chloronitrobenzene has the –NO2 replacing a Cl instead of an H. –NH2 is not formed by nitration. Adding H–O and –NO2 across a ring double bond is addition, which the aromatic ring resists.
x: Here –NO<sub>2</sub> replaced one of the Cl atoms, so only one Cl is left. Nitration replaces a ring H, and both Cl atoms stay.
This has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Nitration attaches an N bonded to two O atoms; –NH<sub>2</sub> would need a separate reduction step.
Here –OH and –NO<sub>2</sub> added across a ring double bond, leaving only two. The aromatic ring resists addition and does substitution instead.

q: 1,2,4,5-Tetramethylbenzene has two equivalent ring H atoms. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: With FeCl<sub>3</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub> substitutes on the aromatic ring; HCl is the by-product.
w: Cl replaces one ring H and the ring stays aromatic: 3-chloro-1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene + HCl. Adding Cl2 across a ring C=C is alkene behavior. Cl on a CH3 group needs light instead of FeCl3, and replacing both ring H atoms needs a second Cl2.
x: Here Cl<sub>2</sub> added across a ring double bond, leaving only two. That is alkene behavior; the aromatic ring does substitution instead.
Here Cl replaced an H on a CH<sub>3</sub> group. That happens with Cl<sub>2</sub> and light, not with an FeCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
Both ring H atoms were replaced here. One Cl<sub>2</sub> replaces only one; this product would need a second Cl<sub>2</sub>.

q: Is the aldohexose shown a D-sugar or an L-sugar, and why?
c: L, because the –OH on C5 points to the left
D, because the –OH on C2 points to the right
D, because the –OH on C4 points to the right
L, because the –OH on C3 points to the right
h: Find the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O (just above the bottom CH<sub>2</sub>OH).
w: D or L is decided only by the bottom chiral carbon (C5 in a hexose). Here its –OH is on the left, so this is an L-sugar (it is L-galactose). The C2, C3 and C4 positions do not decide D or L.
x: Look again: the C2 –OH points left. In any case, C2 does not decide D or L; only the bottom chiral carbon does.
The C4 –OH does point right, but C4 does not decide D or L. Check the chiral carbon just above the CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
L is the right label, but C3 is not the reason. D or L is decided by only one chiral carbon: the one farthest from the C=O.

q: How is the monosaccharide shown classified?
h: Count every carbon, look for –CHO at the top vs. C=O inside the chain, then check the bottom chiral carbon.
w: Five carbons (pent-ose), a C=O on C2 (keto-), and the –OH on the bottom chiral carbon (C4) points right (D): a D-ketopentose (D-xylulose). Count every carbon, including both CH2OH ends: there are 5, not 6, so it is not a hexose.
x: The bottom chiral carbon (the one just above the CH<sub>2</sub>OH) has its –OH on the right. Which label does that give?
An aldose has –CHO at the top. This sugar has CH<sub>2</sub>OH at the top and the C=O on carbon 2.
Count every carbon, including both CH<sub>2</sub>OH ends and the C=O carbon. There are not six.

q: Glyceraldehyde is the reference sugar for the D/L system. How is the molecule shown classified?
h: Three carbons = triose. A –CHO at the top makes it an aldose. The –OH side on the chiral carbon gives D or L.
w: It has 3 carbons and an aldehyde (–CHO), so it is an aldotriose. The only chiral carbon has its –OH on the left, so it is L-glyceraldehyde, an L-aldotriose.
x: In this drawing the –OH on the chiral carbon points to the left. Which label does that give?
Glyceraldehyde has –CHO at the top, which is an aldehyde, not a ketone.
Both parts are off: the top carbon is –CHO (an aldehyde), and the –OH on the chiral carbon points left.

q: For the sugar shown, which description is correct?
h: Only carbons bonded to H and OH on the sides are chiral. The CHO and CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbons are not.
w: Four carbons with a –CHO: an aldotetrose. The two middle carbons each carry H, OH and two different chain groups, so there are 2 chiral carbons. The bottom chiral carbon has –OH on the right: D (D-erythrose).
x: The –CHO and –CH<sub>2</sub>OH end carbons are not chiral. Count only the carbons with H and OH on the sides.
The bottom chiral carbon has its –OH on the right. Which label does that give?
The top group is –CHO, so this is an aldose, not a ketose. Also count the chiral carbons again: the ends are not chiral.

q: Which Fischer projection shows D-glucose?
h: Recall the left/right pattern of the –OH groups on C2–C5 of D-glucose. The bottom chiral carbon must have its –OH on the right.
w: D-glucose has –OH groups right, left, right, right on C2–C5, the pattern in structure III. The mirror image (all reversed) is L-glucose; changing only C2 gives D-mannose; changing only C4 gives D-galactose.
x: Structure IV has every –OH reversed from D-glucose (left, right, left, left). Its bottom –OH points left, so it is an L-sugar.
Structure II has the C2 –OH on the left (left, left, right, right). That pattern is D-mannose.
Structure I has the C4 –OH on the left (right, left, left, right). That pattern is D-galactose.

q: Galactose is one of the two sugars released when lactase digests milk sugar (lactose). Which Fischer projection shows D-galactose?
h: D-galactose is the C4 epimer of D-glucose (right, left, right, right).
w: D-galactose differs from D-glucose only at C4: right, left, left, right, structure II. One structure is D-glucose, one is L-galactose (every –OH reversed), and one is D-talose (C2 also changed).
x: Structure III is right, left, right, right: D-glucose itself. Galactose differs from it at one carbon.
Structure I is left, right, right, left: every –OH reversed, so its bottom –OH points left. That is an L-sugar.
Structure IV is left, left, left, right. It differs from D-glucose at C2 as well as C4, so it is a different sugar (D-talose).

q: Which Fischer projection shows D-fructose, the sugar in honey and fruit?
h: Fructose is a ketohexose (C=O on C2). Its C3–C5 –OH groups match C3–C5 of D-glucose.
w: D-fructose has its C=O on C2 and –OH groups left, right, right on C3–C5 (same as C3–C5 of D-glucose): structure IV. One ketose is L-fructose (all reversed), one is D-sorbose (C3 and C4 swapped), and the aldose is D-glucose.
x: Structure III is a ketose with C3–C5 right, left, left. Every –OH is reversed, and the bottom –OH points left, so it is an L-sugar.
Structure I has –CHO at the top, so it is an aldose (D-glucose). Fructose has its C=O on C2.
Structure II is a D-ketose, but its C3–C5 pattern (right, left, right) does not match C3–C5 of D-glucose. It is D-sorbose.

q: Name the sugar shown. (D-glucose has its –OH groups right, left, right, right on C2–C5; D-mannose differs from D-glucose only at C2, and D-galactose only at C4.)
h: Compare carbon by carbon with D-glucose. Which carbon is different? Then check the bottom chiral carbon for D/L.
w: Compared with D-glucose, only the C2 –OH is moved (to the left), so this is the C2 epimer, D-mannose. The bottom –OH still points right, so it is D, not L. D-galactose would differ at C4.
x: D-galactose would differ from D-glucose at C4. Here the C4 –OH points right, just as in glucose.
The bottom chiral carbon has its –OH on the right, so this is a D-sugar, not L.
L-glucose has every –OH reversed (left, right, left, left). Here only one carbon differs from D-glucose, and the bottom –OH points right.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the open-chain sugar shown?
h: A chiral carbon has four different groups. The C=O carbon and the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbons cannot be chiral.
w: D-fructose has 6 carbons, but C1 and C6 are CH2OH and C2 is the C=O carbon. Only C3, C4 and C5 carry four different groups: 3 chiral carbons. Answering 4 counts the C=O carbon as in an aldohexose.
x: 4 is the count for an aldohexose. Here C2 is a C=O carbon, which cannot be chiral.
5 counts too many: the two CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbons and the C=O carbon cannot have four different groups.
2 misses one. Check each carbon that carries an H and an OH on its sides.

q: How many chiral carbons are in the ring form of glucose shown?
h: Ring closure makes C1 a new chiral carbon. Check C1 through C5; C6 is a CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
w: In the open chain, glucose has 4 chiral carbons (C2–C5). Closing the ring turns C1 into the anomeric carbon with four different groups (ring O, OH, H, C2), so the ring form has 5. C6 (CH2OH) is not chiral.
x: 4 is the count for open-chain glucose. In the ring, C1 now has four different groups (ring O, OH, H and C2).
6 counts C6 as well, but C6 is a –CH<sub>2</sub>OH with two H atoms, so it is not chiral.
3 misses some ring carbons. Check C1 through C5 one at a time for four different groups.

q: The Haworth projection shows a form of D-glucose. Which anomer is it?
c: β, because the C1 –OH points up, on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH
α, because the C1 –OH points up, on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH
β, because the C2 –OH points down
α, because the C4 –OH points down
h: Look only at the anomeric carbon (C1, next to the ring O). Compare its –OH with the CH<sub>2</sub>OH on C5.
w: For D-sugars, the anomeric –OH up (cis to the CH2OH on C5) is β; down (trans) is α. Here the C1 –OH points up, so this is β-D-glucose. The –OH groups on C2–C4 do not decide α or β.
x: The C1 –OH does point up on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH, but that position is not α for a D-sugar.
β is right, but the C2 –OH does not decide α or β. Only the anomeric carbon's –OH matters.
The C4 –OH does not decide α or β. Look only at the anomeric carbon next to the ring oxygen.

q: The five-membered ring shown is a form of D-fructose. What is its full name?
h: Count the ring atoms (5 = furanose). For fructose the anomeric carbon is C2; check whether its –OH points down or up.
w: The ring has 4 C + 1 O, a furanose. At the anomeric carbon (C2) the –OH points down, opposite the CH2OH on C5, so it is α: α-D-fructofuranose. A pyranose has a six-membered ring.
x: β would need the C2 –OH on the same side as the CH<sub>2</sub>OH on C5. Check which way the C2 –OH points in this drawing.
Pyranose means a six-membered ring. Count the ring atoms here: four carbons and one oxygen.
The question says this is a form of D-fructose, and its anomeric carbon is C2, as in a ketose. Glucose is an aldose.

q: Name the sugar shown.
h: Decide α/β at C1 first. Then compare C2–C4 with glucose (C2 –OH down, C3 up, C4 down).
w: The C1 –OH is up (β). The C4 –OH points up, while glucose has it down; that single change at C4 makes this β-D-galactopyranose. Mannose would differ at C2 instead.
x: For a D-sugar, α means the C1 –OH points down. In this drawing the C1 –OH points up.
In β-D-glucose the C4 –OH points down. Compare C2–C4 here with glucose: one of them points the other way.
Mannose differs from glucose at C2 (C2 –OH up). Here the C2 –OH points down, as in glucose.

q: The ring sugar on top forms when an open-chain sugar cyclizes. Which Fischer projection (I–IV) is that open-chain sugar?
h: For a D-sugar: an –OH pointing DOWN in the Haworth ring was on the RIGHT in the Fischer projection; UP was on the LEFT.
w: In the ring, C2 –OH is up (left), C3 up (left), C4 down (right), and the CH2OH on C5 is up (a D-sugar, C5 –OH right). Left, left, right, right is D-mannose, structure IV. The anomeric C1 is the former –CHO, so α or β does not matter.
x: Structure III is right, left, right, right: D-glucose. In the ring, the C2 and C3 –OH groups both point up, so both were on the left.
Structure I has C4 and C5 –OH groups on the left, so it is an L-sugar. The CH<sub>2</sub>OH pointing up in the ring tells you it is D.
Structure II has C4 on the left (left, left, left, right). In the ring the C4 –OH points down, which means right in the Fischer projection.

q: Which open-chain sugar cyclized to form the ring shown?
h: Count the carbons (four in the ring plus the CH<sub>2</sub>OH). Check whether C2 has an –OH.
w: The ring has C1–C4 plus a CH2OH (C5): a pentose. C2 and C3 both have –OH pointing down (right in Fischer), like D-ribose (right, right, right). It has an –OH on C2, so it is D-ribose (the sugar of RNA and ATP), not deoxyribose; D-xylose would have its C3 –OH up, and fructose would carry a CH2OH on the anomeric carbon.
x: Deoxyribose has no –OH on C2 (just two H). In this ring, C2 still carries an –OH.
Fructose is a hexose, and its anomeric carbon would also carry a CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Count the carbons here: four in the ring plus one CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
D-xylose would have its C3 –OH pointing up in the ring (left in Fischer). Here both the C2 and C3 –OH groups point down.

q: Which labeled carbon is the anomeric carbon?
h: The anomeric carbon was the C=O carbon of the open chain. It is bonded to the ring O and to an –OH.
w: Carbon a (C1) is bonded to two oxygens: the ring O and the –OH. It was the aldehyde carbon before the ring closed, and its –OH sets α or β. Carbon d (C5) is also next to the ring O, but it carries the CH2OH, not a second O.
x: Carbon b (C2) carries only an H and an –OH; it is not bonded to the ring oxygen.
Carbon c (C4) carries only an H and an –OH. The anomeric carbon is bonded to two oxygens.
Carbon d (C5) is next to the ring O, but its other group is the CH<sub>2</sub>OH, not an –OH. It was not the C=O carbon.

q: In this form of fructose, which labeled atom is the anomeric carbon?
h: In a ketose, the ring closes at the former C=O carbon, C2. Look for the carbon bonded to the ring O and an –OH.
w: Fructose is a ketose: its C=O was on C2, so the anomeric carbon is C2, atom a, bonded to the ring O, an –OH and the C1 CH2OH. Atom d is the ring oxygen, not a carbon; atoms b and c (C3, C4) carry only H and OH.
x: Atom b carries only H and –OH and is not bonded to the ring oxygen. The anomeric carbon was the C=O carbon of the ketose.
Atom c carries only H and –OH. Look for the carbon bonded to both the ring O and an –OH.
Atom d is the ring oxygen, not a carbon. The anomeric carbon is one of the carbons next to it.

q: Maltose, formed when amylase digests starch, is shown. What type of glycosidic bond joins the two glucose units?
h: Find which carbon of each ring the bridging O joins. Then check whether the left ring's C1 bond to that O points down or up.
w: The bridging O joins C1 of the left glucose to C4 of the right glucose: (1→4). At C1 the bond points down, so it is α(1→4), the same bond as in starch. β(1→4) would point up, as in cellulose.
x: For β the C1 bond to the bridging O would point up. Check which way it points at C1 of the left ring.
α(1→6) would connect to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon (C6) of the right ring. Here the O connects to a ring carbon.
α,β(1→2) is the sucrose bond, which joins glucose to C2 of fructose. Both rings here are glucose; check which right-ring carbon the O joins.

q: Lactose, the sugar in milk, is shown. What type of glycosidic bond joins its two rings?
h: Number the carbons from the ring O. The bridge starts at C1 of the left ring; is that bond up or down?
w: The bond leaves C1 of the left ring (galactose) pointing up (β) and reaches C4 of the right ring (glucose): a β(1→4) glycosidic bond. Lactase is the enzyme that breaks it.
x: α would mean the bond at C1 of the left ring points down. Here it points up.
(1→6) would link to the CH<sub>2</sub>OH carbon (C6). Here the bridging O attaches directly to a ring carbon of the right sugar.
α,β(1→2) is the sucrose bond to C2 of fructose. Both rings here are six-membered aldoses, and the O reaches a different carbon.

q: Sucrose (table sugar) is shown. Which glycosidic bond joins glucose (left) and fructose (right)?
h: Look at which carbon of each ring the O bridges. The fructose anomeric carbon is C2.
w: The O joins C1 of α-glucose (bond down) to C2 of β-fructose. Both anomeric carbons are used, so the link is α,β(1→2) (also written α(1→2)β).
x: α(1→4) joins two glucose units, as in maltose. Here the right ring is fructose, and the O reaches its anomeric carbon.
β(1→4) is the lactose and cellulose bond. The glucose C1 bond here points down, and the O does not reach C4 of fructose.
The α,β part fits, but check the fructose end: the O joins fructose at its anomeric carbon, which is not C4.

q: Which polysaccharide is built from the same kind of glycosidic bond as the disaccharide shown?
h: Identify the bond: which carbons, and does the C1 bond point up (β) or down (α)?
w: The C1 bond of the left glucose points up, and the O joins it to C4: a β(1→4) bond (this disaccharide is cellobiose, released when cellulose is partly hydrolyzed). Cellulose is a chain of β(1→4) glucose. Amylose uses α(1→4); glycogen and amylopectin add α(1→6) branches.
x: Amylose uses α(1→4) bonds, with the C1 bond pointing down. In this drawing the C1 bond points up.
Glycogen has α linkages, with α(1→6) branches. The C1 bond in this drawing points up, which is not α.
Amylopectin has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches. The C1 bond in this drawing points up, which is not α.

q: Is the disaccharide shown (sucrose) a reducing sugar?
c: No: both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond
Yes: the glucose ring has a free hemiacetal –OH group at C1
Yes: fructose is a ketose, and every ketose is reducing
No: a disaccharide can never be a reducing sugar at all
h: A reducing sugar needs one anomeric carbon that still has a free –OH (a hemiacetal that can open to C=O).
w: The bridging O uses C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose, the two anomeric carbons. Neither ring has a free hemiacetal, so neither can open, and sucrose gives a negative Benedict's test. Maltose and lactose are disaccharides that are reducing.
x: Glucose C1 is the carbon bonded to the bridging O, so it has no free hemiacetal –OH.
Free fructose is a reducing sugar, but only because its anomeric C2 has a free –OH that lets the ring open. In sucrose, fructose C2 is tied up in the glycosidic bond.
"No" is right, but the reason is not: maltose and lactose are disaccharides that are reducing. Look at what is special about this glycosidic bond.

q: Maltose (shown) gives a positive Benedict's test. Which labeled carbon is responsible?
h: Look for an anomeric carbon (bonded to a ring O) that still has a free –OH instead of the bridging O.
w: Carbon a is C1 of the right glucose: it is bonded to the ring O and a free –OH, a hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde and reduce Cu2+. Carbon b is the other anomeric carbon, but it is locked in the α(1→4) glycosidic bond (an acetal). Carbons c and d (C2 and C3) are not anomeric.
x: Carbon b is an anomeric carbon, but it is locked in the α(1→4) glycosidic bond as an acetal, so its ring cannot open.
Carbon c is C2 of a ring; it is not bonded to the ring oxygen, so it is not anomeric.
Carbon d is C3 of a ring, carrying only H and –OH. A reducing sugar needs a free hemiacetal carbon.

q: The disaccharide shown is completely hydrolyzed. Which two monosaccharides form?
h: Compare the left ring with glucose at C4. Hydrolysis just adds water across the glycosidic bond.
w: Both rings are six-membered aldohexoses. The right ring matches glucose; the left ring has its C4 –OH up, which makes it galactose. Adding H2O across the β(1→4) bond gives galactose + glucose. This disaccharide is lactose; people with lactose intolerance lack lactase, the enzyme for this step.
x: Compare the left ring with glucose at C4: its C4 –OH points up, while glucose's points down. So the two rings are not both glucose.
Fructose would appear as a five-membered ring. Both rings here are six-membered aldose rings.
Fructose would appear as a five-membered ring with a CH<sub>2</sub>OH on its anomeric carbon. Both rings here are six-membered aldoses.

q: Which Haworth projection shows α-D-galactopyranose?
h: α: C1 –OH down. Galactose differs from glucose only at C4 (–OH up).
w: α-D-galactopyranose has its anomeric (C1) –OH down and its C4 –OH up: structure II. The β form has C1 –OH up, α-glucose has C4 –OH down, and α-mannose differs at C2.
x: Structure III has its C1 –OH pointing up, which is β for a D-sugar.
Structure IV has its C4 –OH pointing down, as in glucose. Galactose differs from glucose at C4.
Structure I has its C2 –OH pointing up, which makes it mannose. Galactose differs from glucose at C4, not C2.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain is –CH2OH. The –OH can hydrogen bond with water but carries no charge, so serine is polar neutral.
x: Nonpolar side chains contain only C and H. This side chain, –CH<sub>2</sub>OH, has an O–H group.
An acidic side chain has a –COO<sup>−</sup> group. This side chain has an –OH, which does not lose H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.
A basic side chain has an extra amine nitrogen that carries a + charge. This side chain contains no nitrogen.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in a carboxylate (–COO−), which is negatively charged at pH 7.4, so aspartate is acidic. The backbone COO− does not count; every amino acid has one.
x: A nonpolar side chain has only C and H. This side chain ends in a charged –COO<sup>−</sup> group.
Polar neutral side chains carry no charge. This side chain's –COO<sup>−</sup> is negatively charged at pH 7.4.
Basic side chains carry a + charge on nitrogen. This side chain ends in a negatively charged carboxylate.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in an –NH+3 group, positively charged at pH 7.4, so lysine is basic. The backbone H3N+ is on every amino acid.
x: A nonpolar side chain has only C and H. This side chain ends in a charged –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group.
Polar neutral side chains carry no charge. This side chain's –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> is positively charged at pH 7.4.
Acidic side chains end in –COO<sup>−</sup>. This side chain ends in a positively charged nitrogen group; the backbone –COO<sup>−</sup> does not count.

q: Phenylalanine must be limited in the diet of people with PKU. How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain is a benzyl group (–CH2–C6H5) of only C and H, so phenylalanine is nonpolar and tends to be buried inside folded proteins.
x: Polar side chains contain O, N or S groups such as –OH or amides. This side chain is a –CH<sub>2</sub>– plus a benzene ring.
Acidic side chains have a –COO<sup>−</sup> group. This side chain has none; ignore the backbone carboxylate.
Basic side chains have an extra nitrogen that carries a + charge. This side chain has no nitrogen.

q: How is the side chain of the amino acid shown (as it exists at pH 7.4) classified?
h: Ignore the H3N+–CH–COO− backbone. Look only at the side chain: charged –COO−, charged –NH+3, –OH/–SH/amide, or only C and H?
w: The side chain ends in an amide (–CONH2). Amides are polar but neither acidic nor basic at pH 7.4, so glutamine is polar neutral. Students often confuse it with glutamate, whose –COO− side chain is acidic.
x: Nonpolar side chains contain only C and H. This side chain ends in a –CONH<sub>2</sub> group with polar C=O and N–H bonds.
This is not a –COO<sup>−</sup> group: the C=O carbon carries –NH<sub>2</sub>, making an amide. Amides do not lose H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.
The nitrogen here is part of an amide (bonded to C=O), and amide nitrogens are not basic. It does not pick up H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Which amino acid has a nonpolar side chain?
h: A nonpolar side chain contains only carbon and hydrogen.
w: The correct structure is valine: its side chain is an isopropyl group, –CH(CH3)2, only C and H, so it is nonpolar. Serine (–CH2OH) is polar neutral, aspartate (–COO−) acidic and lysine (–NH+3) basic.
x: This side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The –OH group makes it polar.
This side chain ends in –COO<sup>−</sup>, a negatively charged acidic group.
This side chain ends in –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, a positively charged basic group.

q: The dipeptide Ala–Gly is shown. The peptide bond joins which two labeled atoms?
h: A peptide bond is an amide bond: the carbonyl carbon of one amino acid bonded to the nitrogen of the next.
w: The peptide (amide) bond links the C=O carbon of alanine (b) to the N–H nitrogen of glycine (c). Atoms a and d are the α-carbons; the a–b and c–d bonds are ordinary C–C and N–C bonds inside each residue.
x: a and b are the α-carbon and carbonyl carbon of the same residue (alanine). That C–C bond is inside one amino acid.
c and d are the nitrogen and α-carbon of the same residue (glycine). That N–C bond is part of glycine itself.
a and d are the two α-carbons. They are not bonded directly to each other.

q: The –COOH group of glycine (first structure) reacts with the –NH<sub>2</sub> group of alanine (second structure), releasing H<sub>2</sub>O. Which product forms?
h: A peptide bond is an amide: C(=O)–NH. Glycine's carboxyl carbon bonds to alanine's nitrogen.
w: Condensation joins glycine's C=O carbon to alanine's N, giving the amide (peptide) bond of Gly–Ala; the free –NH2 stays on glycine and the free –COOH on alanine. The reversed dipeptide is Ala–Gly; the C(=O)–O–C(=O) structure is an anhydride, and the N–CH2 link has no C=O, so it is an amine, not an amide.
x: This is the reversed dipeptide: alanine's C=O is bonded to glycine's N. That would come from alanine's –COOH reacting with glycine's –NH<sub>2</sub>.
This structure joins two C=O groups through an O, a C(=O)–O–C(=O) anhydride link. A peptide bond needs a nitrogen.
This structure links the two residues through N–CH<sub>2</sub> with no C=O next to the N. That is an amine, not an amide (peptide) bond.

q: Which structure shows alanine as it mainly exists in blood plasma (pH 7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4 the carboxyl group has lost H<sup>+</sup> and the amino group has gained H<sup>+</sup>.
w: At physiological pH alanine is a zwitterion: –NH+3 and –COO−, net charge 0. The uncharged form is not actually present in water; –NH+3/–COOH is the low-pH form, and –NH2/–COO− is the high-pH form.
x: This is the uncharged form, with –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH. In water this form is almost never present.
This form has –COOH and –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, net +1. That is the main form at low pH, far below the pI.
This form has –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COO<sup>−</sup>, net −1. That is the main form at high pH, far above the pI.

q: Glycine is dissolved in stomach acid, at a pH far below its pI. Which structure is the main form present?
h: Far below the pI there is a lot of H<sup>+</sup>: every basic group is protonated and every acidic group keeps its H.
w: Far below the pI both groups carry H: –NH+3 and –COOH, net charge +1. The zwitterion (net 0) dominates at the pI (about 6), and –NH2/–COO− (net −1) far above the pI.
x: This is the zwitterion (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and –COO<sup>−</sup>), the main form near the pI. Far below the pI there is extra H<sup>+</sup> to pick up.
This form has –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COO<sup>−</sup>, net −1. That form is found far above the pI, in basic solution.
This is the uncharged form, which is almost never present in water. In strong acid, think about what extra H<sup>+</sup> does.

q: Lysine is shown in its uncharged form. What is its net charge in a strongly acidic solution, at a pH far below its pI?
h: Far below the pI, protonate every amino group and leave the carboxyl group as –COOH.
w: Far below the pI both –NH2 groups (backbone and side chain) gain H+ to become –NH+3, and the –COOH stays neutral: net charge +2. Answering +1 forgets the side-chain amino group.
x: +1 protonates only the backbone amino group. Lysine also has a second amino group at the end of its side chain.
0 would be a zwitterion-type balance of charges. Far below the pI the carboxyl stays as –COOH, so it is not negative.
A negative charge needs an ionized –COO<sup>−</sup>, which happens at high pH. In strong acid the carboxyl keeps its H.

q: Aspartic acid is shown in its uncharged form. What is its net charge in a strongly basic solution, at a pH far above its pI?
h: Far above the pI every –COOH loses H+ and every –NH+3 loses H+ (becomes neutral –NH2).
w: Far above the pI both carboxyl groups become –COO− and the amino group is neutral –NH2: net charge −2. Answering −1 forgets the side-chain carboxyl.
x: −1 counts only one carboxylate. Aspartic acid has a second –COOH in its side chain.
0 balances one + and one − charge, as near the pI. Far above the pI the amino group is neutral –NH<sub>2</sub>.
A positive charge needs –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, which is lost at high pH. In strong base the groups lose H<sup>+</sup>.

q: Hair proteins (keratin) are held in shape by disulfide bridges, –S–S–. Which amino acid forms them?
h: A disulfide forms when two thiol (–SH) groups are oxidized and join.
w: The correct structure is cysteine: its side chain ends in a thiol, –SH. Oxidizing two cysteine –SH groups forms an –S–S– bridge (tertiary structure). Methionine has sulfur but as a thioether (–S–CH3) with no S–H; serine and threonine have –OH.
x: This amino acid has sulfur, but as a thioether (–CH<sub>2</sub>–S–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no S–H bond. Without an –SH group it cannot form a disulfide.
This side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. It has an –OH group and no sulfur, so it cannot form –S–S– bridges.
This side chain is –CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>. It contains oxygen, not sulfur, so no disulfide is possible.

q: Oleic acid, the main fatty acid in olive oil, is shown. How is it classified?
h: Count the C=C double bonds. For the omega number, count carbons from the CH<sub>3</sub> end (not the COOH end) to the first double-bond carbon.
w: There is one C=C, so it is monounsaturated. Counting from the methyl end, the double bond starts at carbon 9: omega-9. (For oleic acid the count from the COOH carbon, Δ9, happens to be 9 as well.) Omega-7 is a miscount, omega-6 needs two or more C=C, and a saturated acid has no C=C.
x: Omega-7 is a miscount. Starting at the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon as 1, count to the first carbon of the C=C.
Polyunsaturated means two or more C=C. Count the double bonds in this chain.
Saturated means no C=C at all. This chain has a double bond.

q: Linoleic acid, an essential fatty acid, is shown. What is its omega number?
h: Start counting at the CH<sub>3</sub> end of the chain. Stop at the first carbon of the first C=C you reach.
w: From the methyl carbon (carbon 1 on the omega scale), the first double bond begins at carbon 6, so linoleic acid is an omega-6 fatty acid. Omega-9 and omega-12 come from counting from the carboxyl end (Δ9 and Δ12).
x: Omega-9 is the Δ9 position, counted from the carboxyl end. Omega counting starts from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
Omega-3 is too close to the CH<sub>3</sub> end. Count again, starting with CH<sub>3</sub> as carbon 1.
Omega-12 is the Δ12 position, counted from the carboxyl end. Omega counting starts from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.

q: α-Linolenic acid, found in flaxseed oil, is shown. Which description is correct?
c: Three cis double bonds; an omega-3 fatty acid
Three trans double bonds; an omega-3 fatty acid
Three cis double bonds; an omega-9 fatty acid
Two cis double bonds; an omega-6 fatty acid
h: Look at each C=C: are the two chain parts on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans)? Count the omega number from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
w: All three C=C bonds have the chain continuing on the same side (cis), which puts kinks in the chain. The first double bond is at carbon 3 from the methyl end: omega-3. Omega-9 counts from the wrong end (Δ9).
x: Look at each C=C in the drawing: the chain continues on the same side of each double bond, which is not trans.
Omega-9 comes from counting from the –COOH end (Δ9). The omega number counts from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
Count the C=C bonds again: there are more than two. Then count from the CH3 carbon as 1 to the first carbon of the nearest C=C.

q: The fatty acid shown forms during partial hydrogenation of vegetable oil. Which description is correct?
c: Trans; its nearly straight chain packs like a saturated fat
Cis; the C=C puts a sharp kink in the chain, so it packs poorly
Saturated; it has no C=C double bond, so it packs closely
Omega-3; the first C=C is three carbons from the CH<sub>3</sub> end
h: At the C=C, are the two chain parts on the same side or on opposite sides? Count the omega number from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.
w: The two chain parts leave the C=C on opposite sides (and so do the two H atoms), so this is a trans fatty acid (elaidic acid). Trans chains are nearly straight, pack closely like saturated chains, and raise LDL cholesterol. CH3(CH2)7CH= puts the C=C at carbon 9 from the methyl end: omega-9, not omega-3.
x: Check the C=C: the two chain parts leave it on opposite sides, and so do the two H atoms. That is not cis.
The drawing shows a C=C double bond in the middle of the chain, so this fatty acid is not saturated.
CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>7</sub>– puts eight carbons before the C=C on the methyl side, so the double bond is far from carbon 3.

q: Oleic acid (shown) is completely hydrogenated with H<sub>2</sub> and a Ni catalyst. What is the product?
c: Elaidic acid, the trans isomer of oleic acid
Linoleic acid, with one more C=C double bond
h: Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> across each C=C. Does the number of carbons change?
w: H2 adds across the one C=C, giving the saturated 18-carbon acid stearic acid (C18H36O2), which melts higher; this is how oils become solid margarine. Trans isomers form only as a side product of partial hydrogenation; the carbon count does not change, and hydrogenation removes C=C bonds rather than adding them.
x: Elaidic acid still has a C=C; it forms only as a side product of partial hydrogenation. Complete hydrogenation removes the double bond.
Hydrogenation does not remove carbons. Oleic acid has 18 carbons, so the product does too.
Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> across a C=C and removes it; it never creates a new double bond.

q: The triglyceride shown (in "MCT oil" supplements) is heated with NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
h: Saponification is ester hydrolysis in strong base. Each ester gives an alcohol and the salt of a carboxylic acid.
w: NaOH cleaves all three ester bonds: the alcohol part is glycerol and each acyl group becomes a carboxylate salt, 3 sodium octanoate (a soap). In base, the free acid is not left behind; it is deprotonated to the Na+ salt.
x: Free octanoic acid would form in acid hydrolysis. In NaOH, each acid is deprotonated to its sodium salt.
Excess NaOH and heat break all three ester bonds, not just one.
The acyl parts keep their C=O and become carboxylates, not alcohols. The only alcohol produced is glycerol.

q: A triglyceride with the structure shown is most likely found as which, at room temperature?
c: A liquid oil: cis double bonds kink the chains, so they pack poorly
A solid fat: the double bonds make the chains straight and rigid
A solid fat: triglycerides with ester bonds are always solid
A liquid oil: it has no ester bonds to hold the molecules together
h: Look at the C=C bonds in each fatty acid chain. Straight chains pack tightly; kinked chains do not.
w: Each chain has a cis double bond, which bends it. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly, so the dispersion forces between molecules are weaker and the melting point is low: a liquid oil. Saturated (or trans) chains pack well, giving solid fats.
x: Cis double bonds bend chains, they do not straighten them. Bent chains pack poorly.
Many triglycerides are liquid oils, so ester bonds alone do not make a fat solid. The shape of the chains decides.
This molecule does have three ester bonds joining the chains to glycerol. Its physical state depends on how the chains pack.

q: Glycerol (first structure) reacts with three molecules of the fatty acid shown (second structure). What forms?
c: A triglyceride with three ester bonds, plus 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
A triglyceride with three ether bonds, plus 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
A triglyceride with three ester bonds, plus 1 H<sub>2</sub>O
A phospholipid with three amide bonds, plus 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water. Glycerol has three –OH groups.
w: Each of glycerol's three –OH groups condenses with the –COOH of a fatty acid, forming one ester bond and releasing one H2O: 3 ester bonds and 3 H2O (esterification). Ethers and amides do not form from an acid and an alcohol.
x: An acid plus an alcohol makes an ester (–COO–), not an ether (–O–). The C=O of each fatty acid stays in the product.
Each of the three ester bonds releases its own water molecule, so more than one H<sub>2</sub>O forms.
No phosphate or amine is involved, so no phospholipid or amide bonds form. Glycerol's –OH groups react with the –COOH groups.

q: Which lipid has the steroid ring system?
h: A steroid has four fused rings: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring.
w: The correct structure is testosterone: four fused rings (6-6-6-5), the steroid nucleus. Retinol (vitamin A) has only one ring; the prostaglandin has one five-membered ring with two chains; the fatty acid has no ring.
x: This is retinol (vitamin A): one six-membered ring with a long chain of alternating double bonds, not four fused rings.
This is a prostaglandin: one five-membered ring with two side chains, made from a 20-carbon fatty acid.
This is a straight-chain fatty acid (12 carbons) with no ring at all.

q: The lipid shown is made in the liver and found in cell membranes. To which class of lipids does it belong?
h: Look at the ring system. Are there ester bonds or a phosphate anywhere?
w: The molecule (cholesterol) has four fused rings (three 6-membered, one 5-membered), the mark of a steroid. It has no ester bonds (triglyceride, wax) and no phosphate group (phospholipid).
x: A triglyceride has three ester bonds to a glycerol backbone. This molecule has no ester group.
A phospholipid has a phosphate group. This molecule has no phosphorus, only one –OH group.
A wax is a long-chain ester. This molecule has no ester group; look at its ring system instead.

q: The sugar shown is part of a nucleotide. In which nucleic acid is it found, and why?
c: DNA, because C2′ has no –OH (it is deoxyribose)
RNA, because C2′ has no –OH (it is ribose)
DNA, because the ring has five atoms
h: Compare C2′ of the ring: ribose has –OH there; deoxyribose has only H.
w: C2′ carries two H atoms and no –OH, so this is 2-deoxyribose (C5H10O4), the sugar of DNA. Ribose (RNA) is also a five-membered ring with a C3′ –OH; the difference is only at C2′.
x: Ribose has an –OH on C2′. A sugar with no –OH at C2′ is not ribose.
Both ribose and deoxyribose have five-membered rings, so ring size cannot tell them apart.
Both ribose and deoxyribose have an –OH on C3′, so it cannot tell them apart. Look at C2′.

q: In the ribose ring shown, which labeled carbon would lose its –OH to make the sugar of DNA?
h: Deoxyribose is "2′-deoxy": the oxygen is missing next to the anomeric carbon.
w: Carbon a is C1′ (anomeric, bonds to the base). Carbon b is C2′; removing its –OH gives 2′-deoxyribose, the DNA sugar. C3′ (c) keeps its –OH to form the phosphodiester bond, and C4′ (d) carries the C5′ CH2OH.
x: Carbon a is C1′, the anomeric carbon that bonds to the base. Its –OH is replaced by the base, not removed to make deoxyribose.
Carbon c is C3′. Its –OH is kept in DNA because it forms the phosphodiester bond to the next nucleotide.
Carbon d is C4′, which carries the CH<sub>2</sub>OH (C5′) group and has no –OH of its own on the ring.

q: The nitrogen base shown is part of ATP. How is it classified?
c: A purine: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
A pyrimidine: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
A purine: a single six-membered ring
A pyrimidine: a single six-membered ring
h: Purines (A, G) have two fused rings. Pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one ring.
w: This is adenine. It has a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, the purine ring system (as in guanine). Pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have only one six-membered ring.
x: Pyrimidines have only one six-membered ring. Two fused rings is a different ring system.
Purines have two fused rings, not a single ring. Look again at the drawing: how many rings share an edge?
This base has two rings sharing an edge, not just one six-membered ring.

q: In double-stranded DNA, which base pairs with the base shown, and how many hydrogen bonds hold the pair together?
h: Identify the base: one ring with an –NH<sub>2</sub> group and one C=O. A pyrimidine always pairs with a purine.
w: The base is cytosine (a pyrimidine with –NH2 and C=O). It pairs with the purine guanine through 3 hydrogen bonds. A–T pairs use 2 hydrogen bonds, which is why G–C-rich DNA is harder to separate.
x: Recount the hydrogen bonds in the pair this base forms, and recall which pair in DNA is held by more of them.
Adenine pairs with thymine or uracil. The base shown has an –NH<sub>2</sub> and one C=O, which is not thymine.
Thymine is a pyrimidine, like the base shown. Two pyrimidines do not pair; each pair needs one purine.

q: The base shown is found in DNA but not in RNA. Which base pairs with it, and with how many hydrogen bonds?
h: One ring with a –CH<sub>3</sub> group and two C=O groups: which pyrimidine is that?
w: The ring with a methyl group and two C=O groups is thymine. It pairs with adenine through 2 hydrogen bonds. In RNA, uracil (no methyl group) takes thymine's place; uracil does not pair with thymine.
x: Three hydrogen bonds hold the G–C pair. Recount the hydrogen bonds in the pair this base forms.
Guanine pairs with cytosine. The base shown has a methyl group and two C=O groups, so it is not cytosine.
Uracil is a pyrimidine, like the base shown. Two pyrimidines do not pair, and uracil is found only in RNA.

q: An mRNA codon contains the base shown. In standard (Watson–Crick) base pairing, which base on the tRNA anticodon pairs with it?
h: Identify the base (one ring, two C=O, no methyl). In RNA, which purine pairs with it?
w: One ring, two C=O groups and no –CH3: this is uracil, found in RNA in place of thymine. In standard base pairing it pairs with adenine (2 H bonds). Thymine pairs with adenine in DNA; it is not a partner for uracil, and U–U and U–C are not standard pairs.
x: Uracil does not pair with itself. A pyrimidine pairs with a purine.
Thymine is found in DNA, not tRNA, and it is a pyrimidine like the base shown, so they do not pair.
Cytosine pairs with guanine. It is a pyrimidine, so it does not pair with the single-ring base shown.

q: Benzene is drawn below in one of its forms. How many equivalent resonance structures does benzene have?
h: Keep all six carbons in place. In how many ways can the three double bonds alternate around the ring?
w: The three double bonds can sit on either set of alternating ring bonds, giving 2 equivalent structures. That is why benzene is often drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. 3 counts double bonds; 6 counts carbons.
x: Three is the number of double bonds in each drawing, not the number of resonance structures. In how many ways can three double bonds sit on alternating ring bonds?
One structure would mean the double bonds are fixed in place. Shift every double bond one position around the ring: you get a different but equivalent drawing.
Six is the number of ring carbons. Shifting the double bonds around the ring gives only a few distinct drawings; count them.

q: The acetate ion forms when acetic acid (vinegar) loses H<sup>+</sup>. One Lewis structure is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures does the acetate ion have?
h: Only the –COO<sup>−</sup> part has electrons that can move. Which atoms could share the C=O double bond?
w: The C=O double bond and the −1 charge can be on either oxygen, giving 2 equivalent structures. The CH3 carbon has no lone pairs or double bonds to move, so it adds none.
x: The drawn structure is only one way to place the double bond. Could the C=O double bond be drawn to the other oxygen instead?
The CH3 carbon has no double bond or lone pair to move, so it cannot hold the double bond. Count only the atoms that can.
Count only arrangements that move the C=O double bond and charge between atoms. The C–H bonds and CH<sub>3</sub> carbon do not take part.

q: Sodium benzoate, a food preservative, contains the benzoate ion drawn below. In the real ion, the two carbon–oxygen bonds of the –COO<sup>−</sup> group are the same length. Why?
c: Resonance spreads the double bond and − charge over both O atoms.
Both oxygens form single bonds and each carries a full − charge.
The two oxygens rapidly pass an H<sup>+</sup> back and forth between them.
Both bonds are full C=O double bonds, so neither O is charged.
h: Draw a second structure that moves only electrons. Where can the double bond go?
w: The double bond can be drawn to either oxygen, so the real ion is an average of two equivalent structures: each C–O bond is between single and double, and the − charge is spread over both oxygens. Benzoate has no H on oxygen to trade, and it has only one negative charge.
x: The ion has only one negative charge, not two. If both C–O bonds were single, the carbon would be missing a bond.
Benzoate has no H on either oxygen to pass around; it already lost its H<sup>+</sup>. The equal bonds come from electrons, not protons, moving.
Two full C=O bonds would give the carbon five bonds, and the ion does carry a − charge. The real bonds are neither fully single nor fully double.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Compare each chiral carbon. Are both wedges/dashes switched, or only one? Then ask whether the molecule has an internal mirror plane.
w: Both wedge/dash bonds are switched, so II is the mirror image of I. This form of 2,3-butanediol has no internal mirror plane, so the mirror image is not superimposable: enantiomers.
x: Diastereomers differ at only some chiral carbons. Here both wedge/dash bonds are switched between I and II.
Identical would require II to be superimposable on I. Ask whether this form of 2,3-butanediol has an internal mirror plane.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Picture turning drawing I like a steering wheel, keeping it flat on the page. Do wedges stay wedges?
w: II is just I turned 180° in the plane of the page. Turning a drawing on the page never changes a wedge into a dash, so every group keeps its front/back position: identical (same compound). Students who see the groups on "opposite sides" often call these enantiomers.
x: The groups only look like they are on opposite sides. Turning a drawing in the plane of the page keeps wedges as wedges, so check whether II is just I rotated.
Diastereomers differ at some chiral carbons. Rotate II on the page: does any wedge turn into a dash compared with I?
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Imagine a mirror standing between I and II. Is II exactly the reflection of I? Then ask: is I superimposable on its reflection?
w: II is the reflection of I in a vertical mirror: the left–right layout is reversed and the wedges stay wedges. This form of 2,3-dibromobutane has no internal mirror plane, so the reflection is not superimposable: enantiomers.
x: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. II is the reflection of I, with the left–right layout reversed and wedges kept.
II is the mirror image of I. This form of 2,3-dibromobutane has no internal mirror plane, so check whether the reflection can be superimposed.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Count how many chiral carbons are switched. If every one is switched, you have drawn the mirror image.
w: Both wedge/dash bonds are switched, which gives the mirror image. 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane is chiral, so its mirror image is not superimposable: enantiomers.
x: Diastereomers differ at only some chiral carbons. Here both wedge/dash bonds are switched between I and II.
Identical would mean the mirror image is superimposable, but this molecule is chiral, so its mirror image is a different compound.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Check the carbon with Br, then the carbon with Cl. Which ones changed between wedge and dash?
w: The carbon bearing Br is the same in both drawings; only the carbon bearing Cl is switched. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a stereoisomer that is not a mirror image: diastereomers.
x: Enantiomers need every chiral carbon switched. Compare the two chiral carbons one at a time: only one of them differs between I and II.
I and II are not the same: the carbon bearing Cl has a wedge in one drawing and a dash in the other.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: What is the relationship between molecules I and II?
h: Flipping a molecule over like a pancake reverses left–right AND turns every wedge into a dash. Does II match I after a flip?
w: II looks like a mirror image because left and right are reversed, but every wedge has also become a dash. That is exactly what you see after turning the molecule over (a 180° turn out of the page), so I and II are identical (same compound). A true mirror image would reverse the layout but keep the wedges.
x: II looks reversed left to right, but every wedge has also become a dash. A true mirror image keeps the wedges; ask what flipping I over would look like.
Diastereomers differ at only some chiral carbons. Try turning I over like a pancake and compare it with II at both carbons.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: First turn II by 180° in the page so the OH carbon is on the same side as in I. Then compare each chiral carbon.
w: Turn II 180° in the plane (wedges stay wedges) so it lines up with I. The carbon with OH now matches, but the carbon with Cl has the opposite wedge/dash. One of two chiral carbons is different: diastereomers.
x: Turn II 180° in the page to line it up with I. Then only one chiral carbon has the opposite wedge/dash; enantiomers need both switched.
Line II up with I by turning it 180° in the page. The carbon bearing Cl still has the opposite wedge/dash, so they are not the same.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Both methyls change between wedge and dash. Is this ring compound cis or trans, and does it have an internal mirror plane?
w: In I one methyl is a wedge and one is a dash (trans); in II both are switched. The trans isomer has no internal mirror plane, so switching both chiral carbons gives a non-superimposable mirror image: enantiomers.
x: Diastereomers differ at only some chiral carbons. Here both methyls switch between wedge and dash.
This trans compound has no internal mirror plane, so switching both chiral carbons gives a different 3-D arrangement, not the same molecule.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Decide whether each drawing has the methyls on the same side of the ring or on opposite sides. Then count how many chiral carbons differ.
w: I is cis (both wedges) and II is trans (one wedge, one dash). Cis and trans ring isomers have the same connections but are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers (they even have different boiling points).
x: Enantiomers would both have to be cis or both trans with every chiral carbon switched. Here one drawing is cis and the other is trans.
Look at each drawing: in one the methyls are on the same side of the ring, and in the other they are on opposite sides. Those are different compounds.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Before looking at wedges, check where the methyl groups are attached. Are they on neighboring ring carbons in both?
w: Both are C8H16, but in I the methyls are on neighboring ring carbons (1,2) and in II they are separated by one CH2 (1,3). Different connections make them constitutional isomers; the matching wedges do not matter.
x: Enantiomers have identical connections. Check where the methyl groups are attached in each ring.
Diastereomers have identical connections and differ only in 3-D arrangement. Check where the methyl groups are attached.
Look at the ring carbons holding the methyls: neighboring in one, separated by a CH<sub>2</sub> in the other. That is not the same compound.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Turn II in the plane so its OH groups line up with I. Then compare wedges: is each one switched, or only one?
w: Both are trans (one OH wedge, one dash). After turning II 180° in the page, each OH sits where it does in I but with the opposite wedge/dash. Both chiral carbons are switched and trans-1,2-cyclopentanediol has no mirror plane, so they are enantiomers.
x: Turn II 180° in the page to line it up with I. Both OH carbons then have the opposite wedge/dash, not just one.
Both are trans, and trans-1,2-cyclopentanediol has no internal mirror plane. After lining them up, every wedge/dash is opposite, so they are not superimposable.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: How are structures I and II related?
h: Find which ring carbons carry the OH groups in each drawing before thinking about wedges and dashes.
w: Both are C5H10O2. In I the OH groups are on neighboring ring carbons (1,2); in II a CH2 separates them (1,3). Different connections means constitutional isomers; stereo terms only apply when the connections match.
x: Enantiomers need identical connections. Check which ring carbons carry the OH groups in each drawing.
Diastereomers need identical connections and differ only in 3-D arrangement. Check which ring carbons carry the OH groups.
In one drawing the OH groups are on neighboring carbons; in the other a CH<sub>2</sub> separates them. That is not the same compound.

q: Structure I is threonine, an amino acid found in proteins. How are I and II related?
h: Compare the carbon bearing NH<sub>2</sub> and the carbon bearing OH separately. How many changed?
w: The carbon with NH2 is the same in I and II; only the carbon with OH is switched. One of two chiral carbons different means diastereomers. (I is threonine, the amino acid in proteins; II is allothreonine.)
x: Enantiomers need every chiral carbon switched. Compare the two chiral carbons one at a time: only one of them differs between I and II.
I and II are not the same: the carbon bearing OH has a wedge in one drawing and a dash in the other.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Molecules I and II are drawn with wedge and dash bonds. How are they related?
h: Turn II 180° on the page so COOH points the same way as in I. Then compare both chiral carbons.
w: After turning II 180° in the plane (wedges stay wedges), it lines up atom for atom with I, but both the NH2 and the OH have the opposite wedge/dash. Both chiral carbons switched, no mirror plane: enantiomers. II is the mirror-image form of threonine, which the body cannot use in proteins.
