x: Turn II 180° in the page so COOH points the same way as in I. Diastereomers would differ at one carbon; here check both the NH<sub>2</sub> and the OH carbons.
After lining II up with I, the NH<sub>2</sub> and OH groups have the opposite wedge/dash, so II is not superimposable on I.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Ephedrine (I) and pseudoephedrine (II, the decongestant in Sudafed) are shown. How are they related?
h: Both drugs have two chiral carbons. Compare the carbon with OH and the carbon with the N group one at a time.
w: The carbon with the NHCH3 group is the same in both; only the carbon with OH is switched. One of two chiral carbons different: diastereomers. That is why the two drugs have different melting points and different effects in the body.
x: Enantiomers would differ at every chiral carbon. In these two drugs the carbon with the NHCH<sub>3</sub> group is the same; only the OH carbon differs.
Ephedrine and pseudoephedrine are different drugs: the carbon bearing OH has the opposite wedge/dash in the two drawings.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Two four-carbon sugars, I and II, are drawn as zig-zag chains. How are they related?
h: These four-carbon sugars have two chiral carbons. Compare the OH next to the CHO, then the other OH.
w: Only the OH on the carbon next to the CHO is switched; the other chiral carbon is unchanged. One of two chiral carbons different: diastereomers (I is erythrose, II is threose). For enantiomers, both OH groups would have to switch.
x: Enantiomers would have both OH groups switched. Here only the OH next to the CHO is different; the other chiral carbon is unchanged.
I and II are different sugars: the OH on the carbon next to the CHO has the opposite wedge/dash.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. I and II have the same atoms bonded the same way; only wedges and dashes differ.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer has both chiral carbons switched (each wedge ↔ dash, same layout). Switching only one gives a diastereomer. The drawing turned 180° on the page is the same compound, and the one with Br on the end carbon is a constitutional isomer.
x: In this drawing only the Cl carbon is switched; the Br carbon still has a wedge. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a diastereomer.
This is the original molecule turned 180° on the page. Rotating in the plane keeps wedges as wedges, so it is the same compound.
Here Br is on the end carbon instead of C2, so the atoms are connected differently. That makes it a constitutional isomer, not a stereoisomer.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: Imagine a mirror beside the molecule: the reflection reverses left and right but keeps wedges as wedges.
w: A mirror beside the molecule reverses left and right but keeps wedges as wedges: that reflection is the enantiomer. The tempting choice that is reversed left–right AND has every wedge switched is just the molecule flipped over, so it is the same compound. Switching one center gives a diastereomer; moving Cl to the end carbon gives a constitutional isomer.
x: Here only the Cl carbon is switched; the OH carbon is unchanged. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a diastereomer.
This drawing is reversed left to right AND has every wedge changed to a dash. That is just the molecule flipped over, so it is the same compound.
Here Cl is on the end carbon, so the atoms are connected differently. That makes it a constitutional isomer, not a stereoisomer.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer keeps the trans arrangement but switches both methyls (wedge ↔ dash). The cis drawing (both wedges) is a diastereomer; the drawing turned 180° on the page is the same compound; and the 1,3-dimethyl ring is a constitutional isomer.
x: Both methyls are wedges here, so this is the cis isomer. Changing trans to cis switches only one chiral carbon, giving a diastereomer.
This is the original molecule turned 180° on the page. Wedges stay wedges and dashes stay dashes, so it is the same compound.
Here the methyls are on carbons 1 and 3 of the ring, not neighboring carbons. Different connections make it a constitutional isomer.

q: Threonine, an amino acid, is shown. Which structure is its enantiomer?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: Turn each choice so COOH points the same way as in threonine. The enantiomer (drawn turned 180°) has both NH2 and OH switched. The one with only OH switched is a diastereomer (allothreonine). The left–right reversed drawing with all wedges switched is threonine flipped over; swapping where NH2 and OH are attached gives a constitutional isomer.
x: Here only the OH carbon is switched; the NH<sub>2</sub> carbon is unchanged. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a diastereomer (allothreonine).
This drawing is reversed left to right AND has every wedge changed to a dash. That is threonine flipped over, so it is the same compound.
Here the NH<sub>2</sub> and OH have traded carbons, so the atoms are connected differently. That makes it a constitutional isomer.

q: Which structure is the enantiomer of the molecule shown?
h: The enantiomer is the mirror reflection. Check that the ring compound stays trans and the OH groups stay on neighboring carbons.
w: Reflecting the molecule in a vertical mirror reverses left and right and keeps each wedge or dash: that is the enantiomer (still trans). The cis diol is a diastereomer, the drawing turned 180° on the page is the same compound, and the 1,3-diol is a constitutional isomer.
x: Both OH groups are wedges here, so this is the cis diol. Changing trans to cis switches only one chiral carbon, giving a diastereomer.
This is the original molecule turned 180° on the page. Wedges stay wedges and dashes stay dashes, so it is the same compound.
Here the OH groups are on carbons 1 and 3, not neighboring carbons. Different connections make it a constitutional isomer.

q: Ephedrine, a drug used to raise blood pressure, is shown. Which structure is its enantiomer?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer has both chiral carbons switched (OH and the CH3/NH group). Switching only the OH carbon gives pseudoephedrine, a diastereomer. The drawing turned 180° on the page is ephedrine itself; swapping where OH and NHCH3 are attached is a constitutional isomer.
x: Here only the OH carbon is switched; the carbon with the NH group still has a dash. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a diastereomer (pseudoephedrine).
This is ephedrine turned 180° on the page. Rotating in the plane keeps wedges as wedges, so it is the same compound.
Here the OH and the NHCH<sub>3</sub> group have traded carbons, so the atoms are connected differently. That makes it a constitutional isomer.

q: The sugar erythrose is shown. Which structure is its enantiomer?
h: An enantiomer is the non-superimposable mirror image: EVERY chiral carbon must be switched. Watch for drawings that are only turned around.
w: The enantiomer switches both OH groups on the chiral carbons. Switching just one gives threose, a diastereomer. The 180°-turned drawing is erythrose itself, and the ketone (C=O in the middle) is erythrulose, a constitutional isomer.
x: Here only the OH next to the CHO is switched; the other OH is unchanged. Changing one of two chiral carbons gives a diastereomer (threose).
This is erythrose turned 180° on the page. Rotating in the plane keeps wedges as wedges, so it is the same compound.
This one has its C=O in the middle of the chain (a ketone), so the atoms are connected differently. That makes it a constitutional isomer.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, shown?
h: Count the chiral carbons and use 2<sup>n</sup>.
w: 2 chiral carbons give 22 = 4 stereoisomers (two pairs of enantiomers).
x: Use 2n: with 2 chiral carbons the maximum is 22 = 4, not 3.
2 counts only one pair of enantiomers. With two chiral carbons, use 2<sup>n</sup> to find the total.
8 is 2<sup>3</sup>, for three chiral carbons. This molecule has only two: the carbon with Cl and the carbon with Br.

q: Threonine, an essential amino acid, is shown. How many stereoisomers of threonine are possible?
h: Find every carbon with four different groups, then use 2<sup>n</sup>.
w: Threonine has 2 chiral carbons (the one with NH2 and the one with OH), so 22 = 4. The four are two pairs of enantiomers, and only one is used in proteins.
x: 2 counts only one pair of enantiomers. Threonine has two chiral carbons, so use 2<sup>n</sup>.
Use 2n: with 2 chiral carbons the maximum is 22 = 4, not 3.
8 is 2<sup>3</sup>, for three chiral carbons. In threonine the CH<sub>3</sub> and –COOH carbons cannot be chiral, so count again.

q: Carvone I smells like spearmint, and its mirror image II smells like caraway (rye bread). Which property is different for I and II?
c: The direction they rotate plane-polarized light
Their boiling points at the same pressure
Their densities as pure liquids at 25 °C
h: I and II are enantiomers. Which properties depend only on the atoms and bonds, and which need something with handedness to detect?
w: I and II are mirror images (enantiomers). Enantiomers have identical boiling points, densities and solubility in ordinary solvents, but they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions (by the same amount). They also smell different because the smell receptors in your nose are chiral.
x: Enantiomers have identical boiling points. Their intermolecular forces are the same because they have the same atoms and bonds.
Enantiomers dissolve equally well in water, which is not a chiral solvent. Think about what can sense handedness.
Enantiomers have the same density as pure liquids. Only something chiral, or polarized light, can tell them apart.

q: A pure sample of the caraway form of carvone rotates plane-polarized light by +61°. Measured the same way (same concentration and tube), what rotation does the pure spearmint form, its enantiomer, give?
h: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by the same amount but in opposite directions.
w: Enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions, so the spearmint form gives −61°. 0° would be a 50:50 (racemic) mixture of the two, and +61° would mean the sample is the caraway form itself.
x: +61° is the rotation of the caraway form itself. Its mirror image rotates light the same amount but the other way.
0° is what a 50:50 (racemic) mixture of the two forms gives. A pure single enantiomer does rotate light.
Enantiomers rotate light by the same amount, not double. The size stays the same; only the direction changes.

q: The two enantiomers of the pain reliever ibuprofen, I and II, are shown. Which property is the same for pure I and pure II?
c: Direction of rotation of plane-polarized light
How well each fits the pain-related enzyme it blocks
h: Enantiomers behave alike toward anything that is not chiral, but differently toward polarized light and chiral enzymes.
w: Enantiomers have identical physical properties such as melting point, boiling point and solubility. They rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions, and because enzymes are chiral, only one form (the active one) fits the enzyme well, so their pain-relieving power differs.
x: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. That is one of the few ways to tell them apart.
The enzyme is chiral, like a glove, so it fits one enantiomer better than the other. This property differs.
Pain relief depends on fitting a chiral enzyme, and only one form fits well. So the two enantiomers differ in strength.

q: The two mirror-image forms of thalidomide cannot be separated by distillation or by dissolving one in water. Why not?
c: Enantiomers have identical boiling points and identical solubility in water.
Enantiomers have different boiling points, but both decompose when heated.
Diastereomers like these always form a racemic mixture.
The two forms are constitutional isomers with the same molecular mass.
h: Distillation separates by boiling point; dissolving separates by solubility. How do these properties compare for mirror-image molecules?
w: Mirror-image forms (enantiomers) have identical boiling points and solubility in ordinary (achiral) solvents, so distillation and simple dissolving cannot separate them. Separating enantiomers needs something chiral, such as a chiral column. The two forms are enantiomers, not diastereomers or constitutional isomers.
x: Enantiomers do not have different boiling points. Their boiling points are identical, which is why distillation fails.
These mirror-image forms are not diastereomers, and a racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of enantiomers, not diastereomers.
The two forms have the same bonding, so they are not constitutional isomers. They differ only in 3-D arrangement.

q: L-DOPA, shown, treats Parkinson's disease; its enantiomer, D-DOPA, does not work in the body. A pharmacist has a pure sample of each. Which measurement can tell them apart?
c: The direction each rotates plane-polarized light
The melting point of each pure solid sample
The solubility of each in water at 25 °C
The molar mass of each, from its formula
h: Enantiomers share nearly every physical property. Which measurement uses something "handed" that can sense the difference?
w: L- and D-DOPA are enantiomers: same melting point, same solubility, same molar mass. A polarimeter tells them apart because the two forms rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. The body also tells them apart, because its enzymes are chiral.
x: Enantiomers have identical melting points, so this measurement would give the same value for both.
Enantiomers dissolve equally well in water, which is not chiral. This measurement cannot tell them apart.
Enantiomers have the same molecular formula, so their molar masses are identical.

q: Ephedrine (I) and pseudoephedrine (II) melt at very different temperatures. Which statement explains this?
c: They are diastereomers, and diastereomers can have different physical properties.
They are enantiomers, and enantiomers have different melting points.
They are constitutional isomers with different molecular formulas.
They are the same compound, so the difference must come from impurities.
h: Compare the two chiral carbons. Are both switched, or only one? Then recall which kind of stereoisomer has different physical properties.
w: Only the carbon with OH is switched, so I and II are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers. Diastereomers have different shapes overall, so their melting points, boiling points and solubilities differ. Enantiomers would have identical melting points; constitutional isomers have the same formula, not different ones.
x: Enantiomers have identical melting points, and these two are not enantiomers: only one of their two chiral carbons is switched.
I and II have the same molecular formula; only the arrangement at one carbon differs. They are not constitutional isomers.
I and II are not the same compound: the carbon bearing OH has the opposite wedge/dash in the two drawings.

q: In the drawing of 2-butanol shown, the OH is attached by a solid wedge. What does the wedge tell you about the OH?
c: It points toward the viewer, out of the page.
It points away from the viewer, behind the page.
It lies flat in the plane of the page.
It is joined by a stronger bond than a plain line.
h: Plain lines lie in the page. One kind of stereo bond comes toward you; the other goes behind the page.
w: A solid wedge means the group points toward the viewer, out of the page (the wide end is nearer to you). A hashed (dashed) wedge means the group points away, behind the page. Plain lines lie in the plane of the page. The wedge says nothing about bond strength.
x: Pointing away, behind the page, is what a dashed (hashed) bond shows. A solid wedge means the opposite.
Plain lines lie in the plane of the page. Wedges and dashes are used for bonds that leave the plane, toward you or away from you.
A wedge shows direction in space, not bond strength. It is still an ordinary single bond.

q: In the 2-bromobutane drawing shown, the Br is on a dashed bond (behind the page). If you redraw it with the Br on a solid wedge and change nothing else, what do you get?
c: A constitutional isomer of the original
h: The molecule has only one chiral carbon. What does switching the only chiral carbon do?
w: Moving Br from behind the page to in front switches the only chiral carbon, which produces the non-superimposable mirror image: the enantiomer. With only one chiral carbon, a diastereomer is impossible; diastereomers need at least two chiral carbons.
x: For a molecule like this, a diastereomer needs at least two chiral carbons. 2-Bromobutane has only one.
Moving Br from behind the page to the front changes the 3-D arrangement at the chiral carbon, so the new drawing cannot be superimposed on the old one.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. Switching a wedge and dash changes only 3-D arrangement, never which atoms are bonded.

q: 3-Chloro-2-butanol is shown. If you switch the wedge/dash on the carbon bearing Cl only, and leave the OH carbon unchanged, what is the new structure?
c: A constitutional isomer of the original
h: The molecule has two chiral carbons. An enantiomer needs every chiral carbon switched. How many did you switch?
w: Switching one of the two chiral carbons gives a stereoisomer that is not the mirror image: a diastereomer. To get the enantiomer you would have to switch both the Cl carbon and the OH carbon. Connections are unchanged, so it is not a constitutional isomer.
x: An enantiomer needs every chiral carbon switched. Here the OH carbon is left unchanged.
Switching the Cl carbon changes the 3-D arrangement there, so the new structure cannot be superimposed on the original.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. Switching a wedge and dash changes only 3-D arrangement, never which atoms are bonded.

q: The drawing of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane shown is turned 180° in the plane of the page (like turning a steering wheel). The turned drawing shows
h: When a drawing turns flat on the page, does a group in front of the page end up behind it?
w: Turning a drawing within the plane of the page moves groups around on the page but never moves anything from front to back, so every wedge stays a wedge and every dash a dash: the same compound. Only a reflection, or switching every wedge and dash, gives the enantiomer.
x: Turning a drawing flat on the page never moves a group from front to back. An enantiomer needs every wedge and dash switched or a true reflection.
A diastereomer needs some chiral carbons switched. Turning flat on the page keeps every wedge as a wedge and every dash as a dash.
Turning a drawing does not change which atoms are bonded to which, so it cannot make a constitutional isomer.

q: Curve 1 shows the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction with no inhibitor. Curve 2 was measured with the same amount of enzyme after an inhibitor was added. What type of inhibitor is it?
h: Compare the two curves at very high substrate concentration. Can enough substrate overcome the inhibitor?
w: With the inhibitor (curve 2) the rate is lower at low [substrate], but at high [substrate] the two curves approach the same maximum rate. Extra substrate outcompetes the inhibitor for the active site, so it is a competitive inhibitor. A noncompetitive inhibitor would lower the maximum rate at every [substrate]; an irreversible inhibitor would not be reversed by substrate.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate at every substrate concentration. Look at where the two curves end up at high [substrate].
Substrate cannot overcome an irreversible inhibitor, so the maximum rate would stay lower. Compare the curves at high [substrate].
An activator would make curve 2 faster than curve 1. Curve 2 is slower, at least at low [substrate].

q: Curve 1 is an enzyme working without inhibitor; curve 2 is the same enzyme with an inhibitor present. What does the graph show about the inhibitor?
c: It is noncompetitive; adding more substrate does not restore the maximum rate
It is competitive; adding more substrate restores the maximum rate
It is competitive; it lowers the maximum rate the enzyme can reach
It is noncompetitive; adding more substrate fully overcomes it
h: Look at the plateau of each curve. A plateau that stays lower no matter how much substrate is added means substrate cannot displace the inhibitor.
w: Curve 2 levels off at a lower maximum rate even when substrate is in large excess, so the inhibitor is not displaced by substrate: it binds somewhere other than the active site, a noncompetitive inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor would give a curve that eventually reaches the same plateau as curve 1.
x: If more substrate restored the maximum rate, the two curves would reach the same plateau. Check whether curve 2 catches up.
A competitive inhibitor does not lower the maximum rate; enough substrate can outcompete it. The type does not fit what the graph shows.
If more substrate fully overcame the inhibitor, curve 2 would eventually reach curve 1's plateau. Look at the two plateaus.

q: The graph shows reaction rate versus substrate concentration for a fixed amount of enzyme. Which change would significantly increase the rate at point c?
h: At point c the curve is flat. Ask what is limiting the rate there: the amount of substrate or the number of active sites?
w: At point c the enzyme is saturated: essentially every active site is occupied, so the curve has leveled off and the rate no longer depends on [substrate]. Only more enzyme (more active sites) raises the rate there. Adding substrate helps only where the curve is still rising, as at points a and b.
x: At point c the curve is flat, so more substrate barely changes the rate. Ask what is limiting the rate there.
A competitive inhibitor slows the enzyme; it cannot increase the rate.
At point c the enzyme is saturated, so removing some substrate would not raise the rate. It could only stay the same or drop.

q: The curves show the activity of three digestive enzymes as a function of pH. Which assignment is correct?
h: Match each optimum pH to the pH of the organ where the enzyme works: stomach acid is near pH 2; the small intestine is slightly basic.
w: Curve 1 peaks near pH 2, the pH of stomach acid, so it is pepsin; curve 3 peaks near pH 8, the slightly basic small intestine, so it is trypsin. Curve 2 (optimum near pH 7) fits salivary amylase. Reversing 1 and 3 is the common slip: trypsin is destroyed, not activated, by stomach acid.
x: This reverses the two. Curve 1 peaks near pH 2; ask which enzyme works in stomach acid.
Curve 2 peaks near pH 7, not pH 2, so it does not fit the stomach. Match each peak to the pH of each organ.
Curve 3 peaks near pH 8, which is too basic for the stomach. Match each peak to the pH of each organ.

q: The pH profile of an enzyme is shown. In which location would this enzyme most likely do its job?
h: Read the pH of maximum activity, then match it to the body compartment with that pH.
w: Activity peaks at about pH 8 and is nearly zero below pH 5, so the enzyme is built for a slightly basic environment: the small intestine, where pancreatic enzymes such as trypsin work. At blood pH (7.4) the enzyme would still be partly active, but its optimum is clearly higher.
x: This enzyme is almost inactive at pH 2. Read the pH where the curve peaks.
At pH 5 this enzyme has almost no activity. Read the pH where the curve peaks.
The enzyme is partly active at pH 7.4, but its peak is at a higher pH. Match the peak to a body location.

q: The graph shows the rate of a reaction catalyzed by a human enzyme at different temperatures. Why does the rate fall so sharply above about 40 °C?
c: The enzyme denatures, so its active site loses its shape
Molecules collide less often at higher temperature
The substrate is used up faster at higher temperature
Higher temperature turns the enzyme into a competitive inhibitor
h: Below the optimum, heat speeds collisions. Above it, heat does something to the protein itself.
w: Up to about 37–40 °C the rate rises because molecules move faster and collide more often. Above that, heat breaks the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the protein's tertiary structure, so the enzyme denatures and the active site no longer fits the substrate. Collisions do not become rarer with heat; that answer reverses the kinetics.
x: Higher temperature makes molecules move faster and collide more often, not less. The drop comes from a change in the enzyme itself.
The steep drop happens even with plenty of substrate. Think about what heat does to a protein's shape.
Heat does not turn an enzyme into an inhibitor. Think about what heat does to the weak interactions that hold a protein's shape.

q: Curves 1 and 2 are temperature profiles of two enzymes that catalyze the same reaction: one from a human and one from a bacterium living in a hot spring. Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: Curve 1 is the human enzyme; it is denatured at the optimum temperature of enzyme 2
Curve 2 is the human enzyme; it is denatured at the optimum temperature of enzyme 1
Curve 1 is the human enzyme; the two enzymes share the same optimum temperature
Curve 2 is the human enzyme; it works fastest at about 75 °C
h: Human enzymes are tuned to body temperature, about 37 °C. Check what each curve does at the other curve's peak.
w: Curve 1 peaks near 37 °C (body temperature), so it is the human enzyme; curve 2 peaks near 75 °C, the hot-spring enzyme. At 75 °C curve 1 has dropped to zero: the human enzyme is denatured. The bacterial enzyme is simply slow, not denatured, at 37 °C.
x: Human enzymes work best near body temperature, 37 °C. Check which curve peaks near 37 °C.
The two curves peak at clearly different temperatures. Read the temperature at each peak.
Human enzymes work best near 37 °C, not 75 °C. Read which curve peaks near body temperature.

q: The energy diagram shows the same reaction with (curve 2) and without (curve 1) an enzyme. What does the enzyme change?
c: It lowers the activation energy; ΔH stays the same
It lowers ΔH; the activation energy stays the same
It makes ΔH more negative, releasing more energy
It raises the energy of the reactants to speed them up
h: Compare the two peaks, then compare where the two curves start and end.
w: Both curves start at the same reactant energy and end at the same product energy, so ΔH is unchanged (−20 kJ mol−1 either way). The enzyme provides a path with a lower peak: it lowers the activation energy. A catalyst never changes the energy of reactants or products, so it cannot make a reaction more exothermic.
x: Both curves start and end at the same energies, so ΔH is unchanged. Compare the heights of the two peaks instead.
A catalyst cannot change the energies of reactants or products, so the reaction does not become more exothermic.
Both curves start at the same reactant energy. The enzyme changes the pathway, not the energy of the reactants.

q: Use the energy diagram for a reaction run without enzyme (curve 1) and with enzyme (curve 2). By how much does the enzyme lower the activation energy?
h: Activation energy is measured from the reactants up to each peak. Subtract the two activation energies.
w: Ea(no enzyme) = 90 − 30 = 60 kJ mol−1; Ea(enzyme) = 55 − 30 = 25 kJ mol−1. The decrease is 60 − 25 = 35 kJ mol−1. 60 and 25 are the two activation energies themselves, not the difference; 45 comes from measuring the catalyzed peak from the products instead of the reactants.
x: 60 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is the activation energy without the enzyme. The question asks how much the enzyme lowers it.
25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is the activation energy with the enzyme. Subtract it from the uncatalyzed activation energy.
This measures the catalyzed peak from the products instead of the reactants. Activation energy is measured from the reactants up to the peak.

q: Four descriptions of how an enzyme binds its substrate are listed in the table. Which one describes the induced-fit model?
h: Induced fit says the active site is flexible: binding the substrate changes the shape of the active site slightly.
w: In the induced-fit model the active site is not a rigid mold; it adjusts its shape as the substrate binds, so description II is correct. Description I is the older lock-and-key model (rigid, exact fit). III would change the primary structure, which binding never does; IV describes a non-specific enzyme, which contradicts enzyme specificity.

head: Description
rows: The active site is rigid and matches the substrate exactly, like a key in a lock
The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, improving the fit
Binding the substrate changes the sequence of amino acids in the enzyme
Any molecule of about the right size can bind and be converted to product

x: A rigid active site that matches exactly, like a key in a lock, is the older lock-and-key model.
Substrate binding never changes the amino acid sequence (primary structure) of an enzyme.
Letting any molecule of about the right size bind goes against enzyme specificity. Neither model says this.

q: The table matches B vitamins to the coenzymes made from them. Which coenzyme belongs in the blank?
h: Which coenzyme carries acetyl and other acyl groups (as in acetyl CoA) and has pantothenic acid built into it?
w: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is part of coenzyme A, the carrier of acyl groups such as the acetyl group in acetyl CoA. NADP+ and FMN are hydrogen carriers made from niacin and riboflavin, and pyridoxal phosphate (from vitamin B6) carries amino groups in transamination.
x: NADP<sup>+</sup> is a hydrogen carrier made from niacin. The blank needs a coenzyme that carries acyl groups.
FMN is a hydrogen carrier made from riboflavin. The blank needs a coenzyme that carries acyl groups.
Pyridoxal phosphate comes from vitamin B<sub>6</sub> and carries amino groups. Think about which coenzyme carries acetyl groups.

q: The table lists four enzymes and the helper each one needs to be active. Which two helpers are coenzymes made from vitamins?
h: Cofactors can be metal ions or small organic molecules. Only the organic ones (coenzymes) come from vitamins.
w: NAD+ (from niacin) and biotin (vitamin B7) are small organic molecules, so they are coenzymes derived from vitamins. Zn2+ and Mg2+ are inorganic metal-ion cofactors that come from minerals in the diet, not vitamins.
x: Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup> are metal ions. Inorganic cofactors come from minerals, not vitamins.
NAD<sup>+</sup> is a vitamin-derived coenzyme, but Zn<sup>2+</sup> is an inorganic metal ion from minerals.
Biotin is a vitamin-derived coenzyme, but Mg<sup>2+</sup> is an inorganic metal ion from minerals.

q: In the pathway shown, the final product E binds to an allosteric site on enzyme 1 when E accumulates. Which statement describes this control?
c: Feedback inhibition: E slows enzyme 1, so less B, C and D are made
Competitive inhibition: E competes with A for the active site of enzyme 1
Feedback inhibition: E slows enzyme 4, the enzyme that makes E
Activation: E speeds up enzyme 1 so the cell makes more product
h: The end product regulates the FIRST enzyme, and it binds away from the active site (allosteric). What happens to everything downstream?
w: The end product binding an allosteric site on the first enzyme is feedback (end-product) inhibition: enzyme 1 slows, so B, C and D are all produced more slowly and the cell stops making E it does not need. Because E binds an allosteric site, not the active site, it is not competing with A. Inhibiting enzyme 4 would waste the intermediates already made.
x: E binds an allosteric site, not the active site, so it is not competing with A.
The end product regulates the first enzyme of the pathway. Slowing only the last step would waste the intermediates already made.
When the product accumulates, the cell needs less of it, not more. This control slows the pathway down.

q: A drug irreversibly inhibits enzyme 3 of the pathway shown. Which change in the concentrations of the intermediates is expected?
c: Z builds up and W is no longer made
W builds up and Z is no longer made
X builds up and Y, Z fall
Y builds up and Z, W rise
h: Find the step enzyme 3 catalyzes. Its substrate piles up; everything after it stops.
w: Enzyme 3 converts Z into W. Blocking it means Z accumulates (it is still made from Y but no longer used up) and W is no longer formed. Choosing W is the common mistake: the product of the blocked step disappears, it does not build up.
x: W is the product of the blocked step, so it disappears rather than building up. Z is still made, so think about what happens to it.
X and Y are made before enzyme 3, so the block does not stop their steps. Find the substrate of enzyme 3.
Blocking enzyme 3 stops W from forming, so W cannot rise. Find the step enzyme 3 catalyzes.

q: The table shows how each DNA base pairs with a base in DNA and with a base in RNA. Which base fills the blank?
h: RNA has no thymine. Which base takes thymine's place when pairing with adenine?
w: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine; in RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U), which also forms two hydrogen bonds with adenine. Choosing T forgets that RNA contains uracil instead of thymine.
x: T is the partner in DNA. RNA does not contain thymine.
Adenine does not pair with another adenine. A purine like A needs a single-ring pyrimidine partner.
Guanine pairs with cytosine, not with adenine. Both A and G are purines, and two purines do not pair.

q: Translate the mRNA below with the codon table. Which peptide is produced?
h: Read the mRNA 5′→3′ in groups of three, starting at AUG. Translation ends at a stop codon; nothing after it is read.
w: AUG = Met, GCU = Ala, UGG = Trp, then UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends: Met–Ala–Trp. The final GGC (Gly) is never read because it comes after the stop codon. Dropping Met forgets that the start codon also codes for methionine.
x: Gly comes from the codon after UAA. UAA is a stop codon, so nothing after it is read.
This drops Met. The start codon AUG also codes for an amino acid, and Gly comes after the stop codon.
This reads past the stop codon, and no codon in this mRNA is AAG (Lys). Translation ends at UAA.

q: A single-base substitution in a gene produces the mutated mRNA shown below the original. Using the codon table, what happens to the protein?
c: No change: both codons code for alanine (a silent mutation)
Alanine is replaced by a different amino acid (a missense mutation)
The protein is cut short at the second codon (a nonsense mutation)
Every codon after the change is read in a new frame (a frameshift)
h: Compare the codons one by one. One base changed, but check the table: did the amino acid change?
w: Only the second codon differs: GCU → GCC. The table shows both code for alanine, so the protein is identical: a silent mutation. A substitution keeps the reading frame (no frameshift); a frameshift needs a base inserted or deleted.

f.text:
original: 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAG-3′
mutated: 5′-AUG GCC UGG AAG-3′

x: Compare the changed codon in the table: GCC and GCU code for the same amino acid, so no different amino acid appears.
A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon. GCC is not a stop codon in the table.
A frameshift needs a base inserted or deleted. Here one base was swapped, so both mRNAs have the same length.

q: Two nitrogen bases found in DNA are drawn. Which one is a purine, and which DNA base pairs with it?
h: Purines have two fused rings. Then recall the Watson–Crick pairs: A–T and G–C.
w: Structure I has two fused rings (a six- and a five-membered ring), so it is a purine; its –NH2 and ring pattern make it adenine, which pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds. Structure II is the single-ring pyrimidine cytosine. Pairing I with cytosine confuses adenine with guanine.
x: Adenine pairs with a pyrimidine, but not cytosine; cytosine pairs with guanine.
II has only one ring, so it is a pyrimidine, not a purine.
II is a single-ring pyrimidine, so it is not the purine the question asks about.

q: Structures I–IV are nitrogen bases from nucleic acids. Which one appears only in RNA, never in DNA?
h: Two of these pyrimidines differ by a single methyl group. The one WITHOUT the methyl is the RNA-only base.
w: Structure II is uracil: a pyrimidine with two C=O groups and no methyl group, found only in RNA. Structure I is thymine (uracil plus a –CH3), found only in DNA; III is cytosine and IV is guanine, both present in DNA and RNA.
x: I has a methyl (–CH<sub>3</sub>) group on the ring: that is thymine, found in DNA.
III has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group and one C=O: that is cytosine, found in both DNA and RNA.
IV has two fused rings with –NH<sub>2</sub> and C=O: that is guanine, found in both DNA and RNA.

q: Four nitrogen bases are drawn. Which two are purines?
h: Count the rings: purines have a fused double-ring system; pyrimidines have one six-membered ring.
w: Structures II (adenine) and IV (guanine) each contain two fused rings, the purine skeleton. I (cytosine) and III (thymine) are single-ring pyrimidines. A handy check: in DNA each base pair is one purine plus one pyrimidine (A–T, G–C).
x: I and III each have a single six-membered ring, so both are pyrimidines.
II has two fused rings, but I has only one ring, making it a pyrimidine.
IV has two fused rings, but III has only one ring and a methyl group: a pyrimidine.

q: The nucleotide shown is a monomer of DNA. Which labeled group is removed when the nucleotide is hydrolyzed to a nucleoside?
h: Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate. Find the phosphate group in the drawing.
w: A nucleoside is just the base joined to the sugar; the nucleotide also carries a phosphate on the 5′ carbon. Removing the phosphate group at a leaves the nucleoside (deoxyadenosine). Position b is on the base, which stays attached to the sugar in a nucleoside.
x: b is a carbon in the base. The base stays attached to the sugar in a nucleoside.
c is the 2′ carbon of the sugar. The sugar stays in the nucleoside; only one group is removed.
d is the 3′ –OH of the sugar, which stays in place. Look for the group a nucleotide has but a nucleoside lacks.

q: In a DNA strand, the phosphate of the next nucleotide forms a phosphodiester bond with this nucleotide. Which labeled position bonds to that phosphate?
h: The sugar–phosphate backbone links the 5′-phosphate of one nucleotide to a free hydroxyl group on the sugar of the previous one.
w: The backbone of DNA runs 5′ → 3′: the phosphate on the 5′ carbon of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the 3′-hydroxyl group (d) of the growing strand. Position a is this nucleotide's own 5′-phosphate; c is the 2′ carbon, which in DNA has no –OH to bond with.
x: a is this nucleotide's own 5′ phosphate. The incoming phosphate bonds to a hydroxyl group on this sugar.
b is a carbon in the base. Bases pair with each other but are not part of the backbone.
c is the 2′ carbon, which in DNA has only H atoms and no –OH to bond with.

q: Which labeled position in the nucleotide shown proves that it belongs to DNA rather than RNA?
h: Compare ribose and deoxyribose: the difference is at one specific carbon of the sugar ring.
w: Position c is the 2′ carbon of the sugar, and it carries only hydrogens: no –OH. That makes the sugar 2′-deoxyribose, found only in DNA. Position d is the 3′-OH, present in both DNA and RNA; the phosphate (a) and the base (b) are also common to both.
x: The phosphate (a) is found in both DNA and RNA nucleotides, so it cannot tell them apart.
b is on adenine, a base found in both DNA and RNA.
d is the 3′ –OH, which both ribose and deoxyribose have. It is needed to link nucleotides in both.

q: The flow of genetic information in a cell is shown. Which names belong to steps 1 and 2?
h: Transcribing copies the message into the same "language" (nucleic acid); translating changes language (bases → amino acids).
w: Step 1 copies a gene's DNA into mRNA: transcription (DNA → RNA, in the nucleus). Step 2 uses the mRNA codons to build a polypeptide at the ribosome: translation. Replication (DNA → DNA) is not shown in this diagram.
x: This reverses the two steps. The step from DNA to mRNA keeps the nucleic acid 'language', and the step to the polypeptide changes it.
Replication copies DNA into DNA. Step 1 makes mRNA from DNA, and step 2 makes a polypeptide.
Replication makes new DNA. Step 1 produces mRNA, not DNA.

q: The diagram shows the steps from a gene to a protein in a human cell. Which step removes the introns, and where does it happen?
h: Introns are cut out of the first RNA copy before it leaves the nucleus; the trimmed mRNA is what gets translated.
w: Step 1 is transcription, which makes pre-mRNA containing introns and exons. Step 2 is splicing: introns are removed and exons joined, producing mature mRNA; this happens in the nucleus before the mRNA is exported. Step 3 (translation at the ribosome) only reads the already-spliced mRNA.
x: Step 1 makes pre-mRNA from DNA (transcription). The introns are still present at the end of that step.
Step 3 is translation, which reads mRNA that has already had its introns removed.
Splicing happens before the mRNA is exported. Think about where the pre-mRNA is when introns are cut out.

q: Heating separates the two strands of DNA. The graph shows the percentage of strands separated for samples 1 and 2 as they were warmed. Which sample has the higher G–C content, and why?
c: Sample 2; G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, so more heat is needed to separate them
Sample 1; A–T pairs have three hydrogen bonds, so more heat is needed to separate them
Sample 1; G–C pairs have two hydrogen bonds, so the strands separate at a lower temperature
Sample 2; G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds, which break at higher temperature
h: Find which curve needs the higher temperature to reach 50% separated, then recall how many hydrogen bonds each base pair has.
w: Sample 2 reaches 50% separation at about 88 °C versus about 76 °C for sample 1, so sample 2 is harder to pull apart. G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds (A–T by only two), so the sample with more G–C pairs, sample 2, has the higher melting temperature. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
x: A–T pairs have two hydrogen bonds, not three. Also check which curve needs the higher temperature.
G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, not two. Check which curve reaches 50% separated at the higher temperature.
The two strands are held by hydrogen bonds between bases, not covalent bonds. Compare hydrogen bonds per pair, and check which curve reaches 50% at the higher temperature.

q: Structures I and II are fatty acids with the same number of carbons. Which melts at the lower temperature, and why?
c: II; its cis double bond bends the chain, so molecules pack together poorly
I; its straight chain cannot pack closely with its neighbors
II; it has fewer carbon atoms, so its dispersion forces are weaker
I; a saturated chain has weaker dispersion forces than an unsaturated one
h: Both chains have 18 carbons. Look for a C=C and the kink it puts in the chain; kinks weaken packing between molecules.
w: Structure II (oleic acid) has a cis double bond that puts a kink in the chain; kinked chains cannot stack as closely, so the dispersion forces between molecules are weaker and the melting point is lower (oleic 13 °C vs stearic 70 °C). Both acids have 18 carbons, so chain length is not the reason.
x: I's straight chain is what lets it pack closely, so it melts higher, not lower.
Count again: I and II both have 18 carbons. The difference is the C=C in II.
Straight saturated chains pack more closely, so their dispersion forces are stronger, not weaker.

q: Fish-oil supplements contain the fatty acid drawn below (EPA). Which classification is correct?
h: Count the C=C bonds, then count carbons from the methyl (omega) end to the FIRST double bond.
w: The chain has five C=C double bonds, so it is polyunsaturated. Counting from the CH3 (omega) end, the first double bond starts at carbon 3, so EPA is an omega-3 fatty acid. "Omega-5" comes from counting the number of double bonds instead of the position of the first one.
x: Omega-6 is a miscount. Start at the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon as 1 and count to the first carbon of the nearest C=C.
Monounsaturated means only one C=C. Count the double bonds in EPA again.
Omega-5 is the number of double bonds, not the position. The omega number tells where the first C=C starts from the CH<sub>3</sub> end.

q: Structures I and II are both 18-carbon fatty acids with one double bond. Which statement about them is correct?
c: They are cis–trans isomers, and II has the higher melting point
They are cis–trans isomers, and I has the higher melting point
They are constitutional isomers, and II has the higher melting point
They are the same compound drawn in two different ways
h: Check the two groups on the double bond: same side or opposite sides? Straighter chains pack better and melt higher.
w: The chains are attached on the same side of the C=C in I (cis, oleic acid) and on opposite sides in II (trans, elaidic acid), so they are cis–trans isomers, not the same compound. The trans chain is nearly straight and packs like a saturated acid, so II has the higher melting point (45 °C vs 13 °C).
x: They are cis–trans isomers, but check which one has the kinked chain. A kinked chain packs poorly and melts lower.
Constitutional isomers have atoms connected in a different order. Here the connections are the same; only the arrangement around the C=C differs.
Look at the C=C in each drawing: in one the chain continues on the same side, in the other on opposite sides. These cannot be interconverted without breaking the double bond.

q: Complete hydrolysis breaks every ester bond in the triacylglycerol drawn below. What forms?
c: Glycerol plus three fatty acid molecules of two different kinds
Glycerol plus three identical fatty acid molecules
Glycerol plus three fatty acid molecules of three different kinds
A monoacylglycerol plus two identical fatty acid molecules
h: Lipase hydrolyzes every ester bond. Count the carbons in each acyl chain to see how many kinds of fatty acid there are.
w: All three ester bonds are hydrolyzed, giving glycerol and three fatty acids. Two of the chains have 4 carbons (butanoic acid) and one has 6 carbons (hexanoic acid), so there are two different fatty acids. Complete hydrolysis leaves no acyl group on the glycerol.
x: Count the carbons in each acyl chain. They are not all the same length.
Count the carbons in each acyl chain carefully. Two of the chains have the same length.
Every ester bond breaks here, so no acyl group stays on glycerol. Glycerol is released free, along with all three fatty acids.

q: The triacylglycerol drawn below is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub> over a Ni catalyst until it is fully saturated. What amount of H<sub>2</sub> is consumed per mole of triacylglycerol?
h: One H<sub>2</sub> adds to each C=C. Count all the carbon–carbon double bonds in the three chains; ester C=O groups do not react.
w: One end chain has 1 C=C, the other end chain has 2 and the chain on the middle carbon of glycerol is saturated: 1 + 2 + 0 = 3 mol H2. Counting the three C=O groups of the esters (6) is wrong; carbonyl groups are not hydrogenated under these conditions.
x: 2 mol counts the double bonds in only one chain. Check every chain for C=C bonds.
1 mol counts only one C=C. Look at each of the three chains, since more than one of them may have C=C bonds.
6 mol counts the three ester C=O groups as well. Carbonyl groups are not hydrogenated under these conditions.

q: The membrane lipid shown is drawn with four labeled positions. In a cell-membrane bilayer, which labeled position lies in the nonpolar interior, away from water?
h: Phospholipids have a polar head (phosphate and charged group) and two nonpolar hydrocarbon tails. Which label is on a tail?
w: Position c is the end of a long hydrocarbon tail: nonpolar, so it points into the interior of the bilayer, away from water. Positions a (the choline group with its charged N+) and d (the charged phosphate) form the polar head that faces water; b is the glycerol backbone that joins head and tails.
x: Position a is on the choline group next to the charged N<sup>+</sup>. It is part of the polar head that faces water.
Position b is the glycerol backbone carbon that joins the head to the tails. It sits at the water interface, not deep in the nonpolar interior.
Position d is an oxygen on the charged phosphate group, part of the polar head that faces water.

q: Complete hydrolysis of the lipid shown gives which set of products?
c: Glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphate and choline
Sphingosine, one fatty acid, phosphate and choline
Glycerol, two fatty acids, phosphate and glucose
h: Find the backbone (three-carbon glycerol or sphingosine), count the acyl chains, and identify what is attached to the phosphate.
w: The three-carbon glycerol backbone carries two fatty acid esters and a phosphate that is also esterified to choline (the –CH2CH2N+(CH3)3 group). This is a glycerophospholipid (phosphatidylcholine). Three fatty acids would make it a triacylglycerol with no phosphate.
x: Glycerol plus three fatty acids is a triacylglycerol. This molecule has only two acyl chains, and a phosphate on the third carbon.
The backbone here is a three-carbon glycerol unit with two ester-linked chains, not sphingosine with one amide-linked chain.
The group attached to the phosphate is –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>N<sup>+</sup>(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, a nitrogen-containing alcohol, not a sugar.

q: The ring system shown is found in cholesterol, estrogen, testosterone and cortisol. Which description fits it?
c: A steroid nucleus: three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring
A steroid nucleus: four fused six-membered rings and no five-membered ring
A steroid nucleus: two six-membered and two five-membered rings
A triacylglycerol core: three fatty acid chains on glycerol
h: Count the atoms in each fused ring. Steroids share one specific four-ring pattern.
w: Counting the corners of each fused ring gives 6, 6, 6 and 5: the steroid nucleus has three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring (17 carbons). Steroids are not built from fatty acids and glycerol, so they have no ester bonds and are not saponifiable.
x: Count the atoms around each ring again. One of the four rings has only five corners.
Count the corners of each ring: only one of the four rings is five-membered.
This drawing has four fused rings and no glycerol or ester groups, so it is not a triacylglycerol.

q: Melting points of five fatty acids are listed. Which conclusion is supported by the table?
c: For a fixed chain length, each added cis double bond lowers the melting point
For saturated acids, a longer chain gives a lower melting point
Double bonds raise the melting point by strengthening the dispersion forces between chains
Melting point depends only on the number of carbons, not on double bonds
h: Compare the three 18-carbon acids with each other, then compare the three saturated acids with each other.
w: Among the 18-carbon acids, melting point drops from 70 °C (0 C=C) to 13 °C (1 cis C=C) to −5 °C (2 cis C=C): each cis double bond lowers the melting point because the kinks weaken packing. Among saturated acids, a longer chain melts higher (44 → 63 → 70 °C), so the claim that a longer saturated chain melts lower reverses the trend.
x: The table shows the opposite: lauric (12 C) 44 °C, palmitic (16 C) 63 °C, stearic (18 C) 70 °C. Longer saturated chains melt higher.
Compare the 18-carbon acids: the melting point drops as C=C bonds are added, so double bonds do not raise it.
Stearic, oleic and linoleic acids all have 18 carbons but very different melting points, so double bonds clearly matter.

q: Four blood lipoproteins are described in the table (composition in % by mass). Which one is HDL, the "good cholesterol" that carries cholesterol back to the liver?
h: High-density lipoprotein is named for its density. Protein is denser than lipid, so the one richest in protein is densest.
w: HDL has the highest density and the highest protein content (about 50%), so it is IV: protein is denser than lipid, so more protein means a denser particle. Row III (25% protein, cholesterol-rich) is LDL, the "bad" cholesterol; row I, almost entirely lipid (triacylglycerol), is a chylomicron from the intestine; row II is VLDL.
x: Row III is LDL: 25% protein. HDL is named for the highest density, which comes from the most protein.
Row II (10% protein) is VLDL, a low-density particle that carries mostly triacylglycerol from the liver.
Row I is almost all lipid with the lowest density: that is a chylomicron from the intestine.

q: The fatty acid composition of four dietary fats is shown. Which fat is most likely a liquid oil at room temperature?
h: Oils are rich in unsaturated fatty acids, whose cis double bonds keep the triacylglycerols from packing into a solid.
w: Fat II is only 14% saturated and 84% unsaturated (mostly monounsaturated), so its kinked chains pack poorly and it is a liquid: these are the numbers for olive oil. Fat IV (87% saturated, coconut oil) and fat I (63% saturated, butter) are solids; III (lard) is a soft solid.

head: Fat
Sat. (%)
Mono (%)
Poly (%)
f.cap: Sat. = saturated, Mono = monounsaturated, Poly = polyunsaturated fatty acids

x: Fat IV is 87% saturated (like coconut oil). Straight saturated chains pack well, so it is a solid.
Fat I is 63% saturated (like butter), so it is solid at room temperature.
Fat III is 39% saturated (like lard), enough straight chains to make it a soft solid. Look for the fat with the least saturated fat.

q: The compound shown is made in the body from arachidonic acid, and aspirin works by blocking its synthesis. To which lipid class does it belong?
h: Count the carbons (20) and notice the five-membered ring in the middle of a fatty-acid-like chain.
w: A 20-carbon carboxylic acid with a five-membered ring and hydroxyl groups is a prostaglandin, one of the eicosanoids. Steroids have a four-ring nucleus with no carboxylic acid chain; sphingolipids contain an amide-linked fatty acid on sphingosine; waxes are simple esters of long-chain alcohols.
x: Steroids have four fused rings and are made from cholesterol. This molecule has one five-membered ring and a –COOH chain.
Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine with an amide-linked fatty acid. This molecule has no nitrogen.
Waxes are esters of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol. This molecule has a free –COOH and a ring, not an ester.

q: Four amino acids are drawn as they exist at pH 7.4. Which one is most likely found buried in the interior of a water-soluble, globular protein?
h: Ignore the common backbone. Look at each side chain: is it hydrocarbon only, or does it carry –OH, a charge, or N/O that attracts water?
w: Structure I is valine: its side chain, –CH(CH3)2, is pure hydrocarbon (nonpolar, hydrophobic), so it avoids water and is tucked inside the folded protein. II (threonine, –OH), III (glutamate, –COO−) and IV (arginine, charged guanidinium) are polar or charged and stay on the water-exposed surface.
x: II's side chain has an –OH group, which hydrogen bonds with water. Polar side chains tend to stay on the surface.
III's side chain ends in a negatively charged –COO<sup>−</sup> group. Charged groups attract water and stay on the protein surface.
IV's side chain carries a positively charged nitrogen group. Charged side chains prefer water and stay on the surface.

q: Four amino acids are drawn at pH 7.4. Which one can link to another copy of itself through a disulfide bond in a protein?
h: A disulfide bond forms when two –SH groups are oxidized. Two structures contain sulfur; only one has an –SH.
w: Structure II is cysteine, whose side chain ends in a thiol (–SH). Two cysteine –SH groups are oxidized to a –S–S– disulfide bridge, which stabilizes tertiary structure. Structure IV (methionine) also contains sulfur, but as a thioether (–S–CH3) that cannot form a disulfide; I (serine) and III (threonine) have –OH groups.
x: I's side chain is –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. It has oxygen but no sulfur, so it cannot form a disulfide.
III's side chain is –CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>, with an –OH and no sulfur. Disulfides need sulfur atoms.
IV contains sulfur, but as a thioether (C–S–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no S–H bond. A disulfide needs two –SH groups.

q: Glutamic acid has an acidic side chain, –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, in addition to its α-carboxyl and α-amino groups. What is its net charge at physiological pH (7.4)?
h: At pH 7.4 every –COOH loses H<sup>+</sup> (−1 each) and the –NH<sub>2</sub> gains H<sup>+</sup> (+1). Count both carboxyl groups.
w: At pH 7.4 both carboxyl groups are deprotonated to –COO− (−1 each) and the amino group is –NH+3 (+1): −1 − 1 + 1 = −1. “0” treats glutamic acid like a neutral amino acid and forgets the acidic side chain; −2 forgets the positive amino group.
x: 0 treats glutamic acid like a neutral amino acid. Its side-chain –COOH is also ionized at pH 7.4.
−2 counts both carboxylates but forgets the α-amino group, which is –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4.
A positive net charge would need more + groups than − groups. Glutamic acid has two carboxyl groups and only one amino group.

q: Glutamic acid (side chain –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH) has a pI of 3.2. One sample is placed in an electrophoresis buffer at a pH equal to its pI, and another in a buffer at physiological pH (7.4). How does it move in each?
c: At the pI it does not move; at pH 7.4 it moves toward the + electrode
At the pI it moves toward the − electrode; at pH 7.4 it does not move
It moves toward the + electrode in both of the two buffers
At the pI it does not move; at pH 7.4 it moves toward the − electrode
h: At pH = pI the net charge is zero. When the pH is above the pI, is the net charge positive or negative?
w: At its pI the amino acid has zero net charge, so it does not move. pH 7.4 is above the pI, so glutamate is net negative (two –COO− and one –NH+3, net −1) and moves toward the positive electrode.
x: At pH = pI the net charge is zero, so the amino acid does not move. And pH 7.4 is far from its pI of 3.2.
At the pI the net charge is zero, so there is no movement in that buffer.
The first part is right, but check the second. pH 7.4 is above the pI, so think about whether the net charge is positive or negative.

q: The dipeptide shown is drawn as it exists at pH 7.4. What is its name, written from the N-terminal end?
h: The N-terminus is the residue with the free –NH+3. Identify each side chain: –CH2OH is serine, –CH3 is alanine.
w: The residue with the free –NH+3 has a –CH2OH side chain: serine is the N-terminal residue. The residue with the free –COO− has a –CH3 side chain: alanine. Written N → C, the dipeptide is Ser–Ala. "Ala–Ser" reads the structure from the wrong end; threonine would need a –CH(OH)CH3 side chain.
x: This reads the dipeptide from the wrong end. Start with the residue that has the free –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group.
Threonine's side chain is –CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>. The residue drawn here has –CH<sub>2</sub>OH, with no extra methyl group.
Glycine's side chain is just H. The C-terminal residue here has a –CH<sub>3</sub> side chain on its α-carbon.

q: Which structure is a dipeptide, two amino acids joined by a peptide bond?
h: A peptide bond is an amide: the –COOH of one amino acid joined to the α-amino group of another. Check each structure for two α-carbons and an amide between them.
w: Structure I has two α-carbons (each with its own N) connected through a –C(=O)–NH– amide: it is the dipeptide Gly–Ala. II (asparagine) contains an amide, but in its side chain; it is a single amino acid. III joins glycine to serine through an ester (–C(=O)–O–), not a peptide bond. IV (lysine) has two amino groups but no amide at all.
x: II contains an amide, but it is in the side chain (–CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>). There is only one α-carbon, so it is a single amino acid.
III joins two amino acid units through C(=O)–O, an ester link. A peptide bond needs C(=O)–NH.
IV is a single amino acid with an amino group on its side chain. It has two amino groups but no C(=O)–NH amide anywhere.

q: The table lists denaturing treatments and the interactions each one disrupts. Which level of protein structure survives every treatment in the table?
h: Which level is held together by covalent peptide bonds? None of the listed treatments is hydrolysis.
w: Every interaction in the table (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, salt bridges, disulfide bonds) is part of the secondary, tertiary or quaternary structure. None of the treatments breaks the peptide bonds, so the primary structure (the amino acid sequence) survives denaturation. Only hydrolysis (digestion) breaks primary structure.
x: Secondary structure is held by backbone hydrogen bonds, which are disrupted by treatments that break H bonds.
Tertiary structure depends on side-chain interactions like salt bridges, hydrophobic interactions and disulfides, which these treatments disrupt.
Quaternary structure is held by the same weak interactions between chains, so denaturing treatments disrupt it too.

q: Two regular folding patterns of a polypeptide backbone are compared in the table. Which identification is correct?
c: I = α-helix, II = β-pleated sheet; both are secondary structure
I = β-pleated sheet, II = α-helix; both are secondary structure
I = α-helix, II = β-pleated sheet; both are tertiary structure
h: Match each shape to its name. Then ask what holds each pattern together: backbone C=O and N–H groups, or side chains?
w: A coiled spiral with hydrogen bonds along one chain is the α-helix (I); strands lying side by side held by hydrogen bonds between them form the β-pleated sheet (II). Both are stabilized by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds, so both are secondary structure. Tertiary structure involves side-chain interactions, not the backbone pattern.

head: Feature
I
II
rows: zig-zag strands lying side by side
within one chain, between C=O and N–H four residues apart

x: This swaps the two. The coiled spiral along one chain and the side-by-side strands are different patterns; match each to its name.
Tertiary structure comes from side-chain interactions. These patterns come from hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups.
Both patterns are held by the same kind of backbone hydrogen bonds, so they belong to the same structural level.

q: Lysine has a basic side chain, so its pI is high (about 9.7). At physiological pH (7.4), which is below its pI, what is lysine’s net charge?
h: Below the pI an amino acid carries extra H<sup>+</sup>. Which groups are charged at pH 7.4?
w: At pH 7.4 the α-carboxyl is –COO− (−1), the α-amino group is –NH+3 (+1), and the side-chain amino group is also protonated (+1): −1 + 1 + 1 = +1. Below its pI an amino acid is positive overall. “0” is the charge only at the pI; +2 forgets the negative carboxylate.
x: 0 is the net charge at the pI. At pH 7.4, below the pI, lysine carries extra H<sup>+</sup>.
A negative charge is expected above the pI. pH 7.4 is below lysine's pI.
+2 counts both amino groups but forgets the α-carboxyl, which is –COO<sup>−</sup> at pH 7.4.

q: Aspartic acid has a pI of about 2.8, glycine about 6.0, and lysine about 9.7. Which statement best explains the difference?
c: An acidic side chain lowers the pI; a basic side chain raises it
A larger side chain always gives a higher pI, whatever its group
Polar side chains lower the pI, and nonpolar side chains raise it
The pI depends only on the number of carbon atoms in the side chain
h: Aspartic acid has an extra –COOH in its side chain; lysine has an extra –NH<sub>2</sub>. What does each do to the charge?
w: Aspartic acid’s side chain is acidic (–COOH), so it takes a lower pH to keep it neutral overall: a low pI. Lysine’s side chain is basic (–NH2), so it stays positive until the pH is high: a high pI. Glycine (R = H) sits in between. Size, polarity and carbon count don’t set the pI.
x: Size does not set the pI. Lysine and aspartic acid differ in the type of group on their side chains, not just in size.
Polarity alone does not set the pI; serine is polar but has a pI close to glycine's. What matters is whether the side chain gains or loses H<sup>+</sup>.
Carbon count does not set the pI. Look at which functional group is in each side chain and whether it is acidic or basic.

q: Curve 1 is the normal oxygen-binding curve of hemoglobin in blood at pH 7.4. Curve 2 was measured in blood from an actively exercising muscle, which contains more CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sup>+</sup> (a lower pH). What does the shift from curve 1 to curve 2 show?
c: At the lower pH, hemoglobin holds O<sub>2</sub> less tightly and releases more to the muscle
At the lower pH, hemoglobin holds O<sub>2</sub> more tightly and keeps it in the blood
At the lower pH, hemoglobin is fully denatured and can bind no O<sub>2</sub> at all
At the lower pH, hemoglobin binds O<sub>2</sub> exactly the same as at pH 7.4
h: At the same O<sub>2</sub> pressure, which curve shows less of the hemoglobin carrying O<sub>2</sub>?
w: Curve 2 lies to the right: at any O2 pressure hemoglobin is less saturated, so it holds O2 less tightly and unloads it more readily where CO2 and H+ are high (the Bohr effect), delivering O2 where it is needed. Curve 2 still reaches high saturation at high O2 pressure, so hemoglobin is not denatured.
x: A curve shifted to the right shows less saturation at each O<sub>2</sub> pressure, which means O<sub>2</sub> is held less tightly, not more.
Curve 2 still reaches high saturation at high O<sub>2</sub> pressure, so hemoglobin still binds O<sub>2</sub> and is not denatured.
The two curves are not the same; curve 2 is shifted. Compare their % saturation at the same O<sub>2</sub> pressure.

q: Use the oxygen-binding curve of hemoglobin. Blood leaves the lungs at an O<sub>2</sub> pressure of 100 mmHg and reaches resting tissue where the O<sub>2</sub> pressure is 40 mmHg. About what percentage of the hemoglobin's O<sub>2</sub>-binding sites unload their O<sub>2</sub> in the tissue?
h: Read the % saturation at 100 mmHg and at 40 mmHg from the curve. The difference is what was delivered.
w: From the curve, saturation is about 98% at 100 mmHg (lungs) and about 77% at 40 mmHg (tissue). The difference, roughly 98 − 77 ≈ 21%, or about 20%, is the fraction of sites that released O2. "75%" is the saturation remaining in the tissue, not the amount unloaded; the sigmoid shape means most of the O2 stays bound until the pressure falls further, as in exercising muscle.
x: About 75% is the saturation still remaining at 40 mmHg. The amount unloaded is the difference between the lung and tissue values.
About 98% is the saturation at 100 mmHg in the lungs. Subtract the tissue saturation to find how much was released.
50% would mean saturation drops to about half. Read the curve at 40 mmHg; it is still well above 50%.

q: The cartoons show an enzyme interacting with a substrate (yellow) and an inhibitor (red). Which panel shows competitive inhibition?
h: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the same spot on the enzyme. Find the panel where the red molecule occupies that spot.
w: In panel III the red inhibitor sits in the active site and the yellow substrate is locked out, so inhibitor and substrate are competing for the same site: competitive inhibition. Panel IV is the tempting wrong pick: there the inhibitor is bound on the side of the enzyme and the active site is distorted (noncompetitive).
x: In panel IV the inhibitor is bound on the side of the enzyme, away from the active site, and warps the site. That is noncompetitive inhibition.
Panel II shows the substrate fitting in the active site with no inhibitor bound. Look for the red molecule.
Panel I shows the enzyme with no inhibitor bound. Look for the panel where the red molecule sits in the substrate's spot.

q: In each panel a red inhibitor molecule or a yellow substrate molecule approaches the same enzyme. Which panel shows noncompetitive inhibition?
h: A noncompetitive inhibitor never enters the active site. Look for an inhibitor bound elsewhere that has changed the shape of the site.
w: In panel II the red inhibitor is attached away from the active site, and the site has become warped so the substrate can no longer fit: noncompetitive inhibition. In panel I the inhibitor is inside the active site itself, which is competitive inhibition. Panels III and IV contain no inhibitor at all.
x: In panel I the inhibitor sits inside the active site, competing with the substrate. That is competitive inhibition.
Panel III shows a substrate fitting in the active site, with no inhibitor present.
Panel IV shows a substrate that does not fit the active site, with no inhibitor present.

q: Each panel is a snapshot of the same enzyme with a yellow molecule nearby. Which panel best illustrates the induced-fit model of enzyme action?
h: In induced fit the active site is flexible: binding the substrate makes the site change shape and close around it.
w: In panel IV the walls of the active site have tilted inward to hug the substrate: the site changed shape when the substrate bound, which is induced fit. Panel II is the common wrong choice: the substrate fits a rigid, unchanged site, which is the lock-and-key picture. Panel III shows a substrate that cannot bind at all.
x: In panel II the substrate fits a rigid, unchanged active site. That is the lock-and-key picture.
Panel I shows the enzyme with no substrate bound, so it cannot show the site changing shape around one.
Panel III shows a substrate that does not bind at all. Look for a site that has closed around its substrate.

q: The yellow shape is the substrate and the red shape is an inhibitor. Which panel shows an enzyme–substrate complex?
h: An enzyme–substrate complex forms when the substrate itself is bound in the active site, before any product is made.
w: Panel III shows the yellow substrate bound in the active site: the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex. Panel II looks similar but the red molecule in the site is an inhibitor, so it is an enzyme–inhibitor complex. Panel IV shows the products leaving after the reaction, and panel I is the free enzyme.
x: Panel II looks similar, but the molecule in the active site is the red inhibitor. That is an enzyme–inhibitor complex.
Panel I shows the free enzyme with nothing bound in the active site.
Panel IV shows products leaving after the reaction is over. Look for the substrate itself sitting in the active site.

q: Lettered labels mark parts of the drawings. Which label marks the active site of the enzyme?
c: a, the pocket in the top of the enzyme
b, the yellow molecule outside the enzyme
c, the red molecule sitting in the pocket
the entire blue body of the enzyme
h: The active site is a small region of the enzyme, not a separate molecule and not the whole protein.
w: The active site is the pocket (a) on the enzyme where the substrate binds. The yellow molecule (b) is the substrate and the red molecule (c) is an inhibitor, both separate molecules. A common misconception is that the whole enzyme is the active site; the site is only a small part of the large protein.
x: Label b is the yellow substrate, a separate molecule that binds to the enzyme. The active site is part of the enzyme itself.
Label c is the red inhibitor, a separate molecule. The active site is a region of the enzyme, not a molecule sitting in it.
The active site is only a small region of the large protein, not the whole enzyme.

q: In panel III, the red molecule is an inhibitor. It competes with…
c: the substrate, for the active site
the substrate, for a site away from the active site
the enzyme, for the substrate molecule
the product, for release from the enzyme
h: Look at where the red molecule is sitting and what the yellow molecule is waiting to do.
w: In panel III the inhibitor occupies the active site, the spot where the substrate (yellow) must bind, so inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site. Choosing "a site away from the active site" describes panel IV (noncompetitive). An inhibitor does not compete with the enzyme or with the product.
x: Binding at a site away from the active site describes noncompetitive inhibition (panel IV). Look at where the red molecule sits in panel III.
Inhibitors compete with something for a spot on the enzyme. They do not compete with the enzyme itself.
The product is released after the reaction; it is not what the inhibitor is competing with. Look at what the yellow molecule is waiting to do.

q: Two inhibited enzymes are drawn in panels II and III. Adding a large excess of substrate would restore the reaction rate in which panel, and why?
c: II, because substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site, so extra substrate wins the site more often
III, because the extra substrate crowds the inhibitor off its separate side site and frees the enzyme
II, because the extra substrate changes the shape of the inhibitor so it no longer fits the active site
III, because the extra substrate forces the distorted active site back into its original shape
h: Which inhibitor can be outcompeted? Substrate can only displace an inhibitor that is bound where the substrate itself binds.
w: In panel II the inhibitor is in the active site, competing with substrate; flooding the enzyme with substrate means the site is occupied by substrate most of the time, so the rate recovers (competitive inhibition is reversed by excess substrate). In panel III the inhibitor sits on a separate site and warps the active site; substrate cannot bind to the warped site at any concentration, so excess substrate does not help.
x: In panel III the inhibitor is on a separate site, so substrate cannot push it off. Substrate only displaces an inhibitor bound where substrate binds.
Substrate does not change the shape of the inhibitor. Think about why extra substrate helps when both molecules want the same site.
Substrate cannot bind a warped active site, so it cannot force the site back into shape. Adding substrate does not help in panel III.

q: Each enzyme catalyzes only one reaction or one type of reaction. Which panel illustrates the reason for this specificity?
h: Specificity means molecules of the wrong shape are rejected. Which panel shows a molecule that cannot enter the active site?
w: In panel I a triangular molecule is near the active site but its shape does not match the pocket, so it cannot bind and cannot react: the shape of the active site determines which substrate the enzyme accepts. Panels II and IV show the correct substrate binding and reacting, and panel III shows an empty enzyme. Picking II confuses binding of the right substrate with rejection of the wrong one.
x: Panel II shows the right substrate binding. Specificity is best shown by a molecule of the wrong shape being turned away.
Panel III shows an empty enzyme, so it does not show any molecule being accepted or rejected.
Panel IV shows products being released after the reaction. Look for a molecule that cannot fit the active site.

q: Panel I shows an enzyme at 37 °C with its substrate (yellow) bound. Panel II shows the same enzyme after it was heated to 80 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled. What happened to the enzyme in panel II?
c: Denaturation: heat broke the weak interactions holding the protein's folded shape
Noncompetitive inhibition: heat produced an inhibitor that bound to a side site
Saturation: the heat made the enzyme bind substrate too tightly to release it
Hydrolysis: heat broke the peptide bonds of the primary structure
h: Compare the shape of the protein in the two panels. Heat disrupts the weak interactions that hold the folded shape, not the covalent peptide backbone.
w: In panel II the protein chain has unfolded: there is no longer a pocket with the right shape, so the substrate cannot bind at all. Heat broke the hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions that hold the tertiary structure, which is denaturation; for most enzymes it is not reversed by cooling. The peptide (covalent) bonds survive, so the primary structure is intact and this is not hydrolysis. No inhibitor molecule is present, so it is not inhibition.
x: No inhibitor molecule is present in panel II. Compare the overall shape of the protein in the two panels.
Saturation means all active sites are filled with substrate. In panel II the substrate cannot bind at all.
Heat at 80 °C breaks weak interactions, not the covalent peptide bonds. The primary structure stays intact, so this is not hydrolysis.

q: Of the four enzyme cartoons, which statement describes what is happening in panel IV?
c: The inhibitor occupies the active site, so the substrate cannot bind there
The inhibitor has bound outside the active site and changed the site's shape
The substrate is bound in the active site and is being converted to product
The enzyme has been permanently denatured by the inhibitor
h: Notice which molecule is inside the active site in panel IV and which one is waiting outside.
w: In panel IV the red inhibitor fills the active site and the yellow substrate is left outside, which is competitive inhibition. The statement about binding outside the site and reshaping it describes panel III (noncompetitive). Nothing in the drawing shows the enzyme unfolded, and a competitive inhibitor is usually reversible, so the enzyme is not permanently denatured.
x: Binding outside the active site and reshaping it describes panel III. Look at which molecule is inside the active site in panel IV.
In panel IV the substrate is outside the enzyme, not bound in the active site.
Nothing in panel IV shows the protein unfolded. The enzyme still has its shape; something is simply sitting in the active site.

q: A regulator molecule binds to an enzyme at a site that is not the active site. Binding changes the enzyme's shape so that the substrate no longer fits, slowing the reaction. Which panel shows this kind of regulation?
h: Find the panel where the regulating molecule is attached somewhere other than the active site, and the site itself has been distorted.
w: Panel III shows a molecule bound at a separate (allosteric) site, with the active site warped so the substrate cannot bind: this is allosteric regulation, the way many pathway end products shut off their own first enzyme. Panel I is the usual wrong choice, but there the molecule is inside the active site, which is competitive inhibition, not binding at a separate site.
x: In panel I the molecule sits inside the active site. The question describes binding at a site that is not the active site.
Panel II shows the substrate fitting in the active site, with no regulator bound.
Panel IV shows a substrate that does not fit, with no regulator bound. Look for a molecule attached away from the active site.
