q: The panels show stages of enzyme action in scrambled order. Starting from the free enzyme, which order of panels shows one complete catalytic cycle?
h: An enzyme binds its substrate, converts it to product, releases the product, and is free to start again. An inhibitor is not part of this cycle.
w: The cycle is free enzyme (IV) → enzyme–substrate complex (I) → products released (III), after which the enzyme is free again. Panel II shows an inhibitor blocking the active site, which is not a step in catalysis, so any order including II is wrong. IV → III → I puts the products before the substrate has even bound.
x: Panel II shows an inhibitor blocking the active site, which is not a step in catalysis.
This order shows products released before the substrate has bound. Substrate binding must come first.
A cycle that starts from the free enzyme must begin with the panel where nothing is bound. Find that panel first.

q: A lab measures the rate of an enzyme reaction while the amount of enzyme is increased and the substrate is kept in large excess. Which curve shows the expected result?
h: With substrate in excess every enzyme molecule is kept busy. Twice the enzyme means twice as many active sites working.
w: With excess substrate each added enzyme molecule immediately finds substrate, so the rate is directly proportional to the enzyme amount: a straight line through the origin, curve I. Curve II is the tempting mix-up: it is the shape of rate versus substrate concentration, where the enzyme (not the substrate) becomes the limit. Curve IV is the shape of a temperature or pH profile.
x: Curve II levels off, which is the shape of rate versus substrate concentration. Here substrate is in excess, so nothing runs out.
Curve III is flat, meaning adding enzyme would not change the rate at all. With excess substrate, more enzyme means more active sites working.
Curve IV is bell-shaped, the shape of a temperature or pH profile. Adding enzyme does not have an optimum amount.

q: The graph shows the rate of an enzyme reaction versus substrate concentration for a fixed amount of enzyme; the dashed line is the maximum rate. Why does the rate rise much less between 16 and 20 mM substrate than between 0 and 4 mM?
c: At high substrate most active sites are already filled, so extra substrate adds little
At high substrate the extra substrate begins to denature the enzyme molecules
At high substrate the substrate starts to act as a competitive inhibitor
At high substrate the enzyme is used up as it is converted into product
h: With a fixed amount of enzyme there is a fixed number of active sites. What happens when nearly all of them are busy?
w: From 0 to 4 mM the rate jumps from 0 to about 40 μmol min−1, but from 16 to 20 mM it only creeps from about 64 to 67 as it approaches the dashed maximum. At high substrate most active sites are already occupied, so the enzyme is nearly saturated and extra substrate adds little. Only more enzyme would raise the maximum. Enzymes are not used up or denatured by their substrate.
x: Substrate does not denature enzymes; heat and extreme pH do. Think about how many active sites are free at high substrate.
The substrate is what the enzyme acts on, not an inhibitor. Think about the fixed number of active sites.
Enzymes are catalysts and are not used up. The limit comes from how many active sites are already busy.

q: Curve 1 is an enzyme with no inhibitor. Curve 2 was run with an inhibitor, and curve 3 with twice as much of the same inhibitor. Which conclusion do the curves support?
c: Competitive: more inhibitor means more substrate is needed to reach a given rate, but the same maximum is still approached
Noncompetitive: more inhibitor lowers the maximum rate the enzyme can reach, in proportion to the amount added
Irreversible: at the higher level used for curve 3 the enzyme molecules have been permanently destroyed
Competitive: the inhibitor lowers the maximum rate the enzyme can reach, and more inhibitor lowers it further
h: Compare where the three curves are heading at high substrate concentration, and how far each is shifted to the right at low concentration.
w: All three curves climb toward the same dashed maximum rate at high substrate concentration; the inhibitor only shifts the curve to the right, and doubling the inhibitor (curve 3) shifts it further than curve 2. Because a large excess of substrate overcomes the inhibitor, it is competitive. A noncompetitive inhibitor would give lower plateaus, and an irreversible inhibitor would not be overcome by added substrate.
x: If the inhibitor were noncompetitive, curves 2 and 3 would level off at lower plateaus. Look at where all three curves are heading.
An irreversible inhibitor could not be overcome by adding substrate. Check whether curve 3 still approaches the same maximum.
A competitive inhibitor does not lower the maximum rate. Look at the plateaus of the three curves at high substrate.

q: Lysosomes are acidic compartments inside cells (pH about 5) that break down worn-out cell parts. The graph shows pH profiles of four enzymes. Which curve most likely belongs to a lysosomal enzyme?
h: Each enzyme works fastest at the pH of the place where it normally acts. Find the curve whose peak sits at about pH 5.
w: A lysosomal enzyme is most active at the lysosome's pH, so its peak should be near pH 5: curve 2. Curve 1 (peak near pH 2) fits a stomach enzyme such as pepsin; curve 3 (near 7.4) fits an enzyme of blood or cytoplasm; curve 4 (near 9.5) fits an enzyme that works in strongly basic conditions. Students who assume "acidic" means the most acidic curve pick 1, but pH 2 is far more acidic than a lysosome.
x: Curve 1 peaks near pH 2, which fits the stomach. A lysosome, at pH about 5, is much less acidic than that.
Curve 3 peaks near pH 7.4, which fits blood or cytoplasm. Find the curve that peaks near pH 5.
Curve 4 peaks near pH 9.5, which is basic. A lysosome is acidic, at about pH 5.

q: Curve 1 is a human enzyme and curve 2 is the matching enzyme from a cold-water fish. At which temperature are both enzymes working at more than half of their maximum rate?
h: Follow the 50 % line across the graph and note where each curve lies above it. Only one of the listed temperatures is inside both ranges.
w: At 25 °C curve 1 (human) is at about 75 % and curve 2 (fish) at about 70 %, so both are above half-maximum. At 15 °C the fish enzyme is near its peak but the human enzyme is below 40 %; at 35 °C the human enzyme is near its maximum but the fish enzyme has already denatured and is close to zero; at 45 °C the human enzyme is collapsing and the fish enzyme is completely inactive.
x: At 15 °C the fish enzyme is near its peak, but the human enzyme is below half its maximum.
At 35 °C the human enzyme is near its maximum, but the fish enzyme has already denatured and is close to zero.
At 45 °C the human enzyme is already falling, and the fish enzyme is completely inactive.

q: A sample of a human enzyme is held at 60 °C for 15 minutes, cooled back to 37 °C, and then its rate is measured. Using the temperature profile shown, what rate is expected, and why?
c: Far below the value shown at 37 °C, because heat unfolded the protein and cooling does not refold it
The value shown at 37 °C, because the drop at 60 °C was only molecules moving too fast to bind and cooling reverses it
Above the value shown at 37 °C, because the enzyme stored extra heat energy that speeds up catalysis
The value shown at 60 °C, because an enzyme's rate is fixed by the highest temperature it has ever reached
h: The sharp collapse above the optimum is denaturation, a change in the protein's shape. Ask whether that change undoes itself on cooling.
w: The steep fall above about 40 °C is denaturation: the heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the active site's shape, and for most enzymes this unfolding is not reversed by cooling, so the sample stays nearly inactive at 37 °C. The tempting wrong answer treats the drop like the slow rates at low temperature, which are reversible because the enzyme is still folded. Enzymes do not store heat energy.
x: The steep drop above the optimum is not from molecules moving too fast; it is a change in the protein's shape. Ask whether cooling undoes that.
Enzymes do not store heat energy. Think about what high heat does to the protein's folded shape.
A rate is not fixed by the highest temperature reached. What matters is whether the protein still has its folded shape.

q: The graph shows the amount of product formed over time in an enzyme-catalyzed reaction that started with 40 μmol of substrate. What is the initial rate of the reaction?
h: Rate = slope of the product-versus-time line. Use the straight early part of the curve, before the substrate runs low.
w: During the first few minutes the line is straight: about 20 μmol of product form in the first 4 min, so the initial rate is 20 μmol / 4 min = 5 μmol min−1. The curve is straight at first because the enzyme is saturated with substrate; it flattens later because the substrate is used up. Dividing the final 40 μmol by 20 min (2 μmol min−1) averages over the time when the reaction had already slowed; 20 μmol min−1 reads the product at 4 min as if it were a rate.
x: This divides the final 40 μmol by 20 min, averaging in the time when the reaction had already slowed. Use the straight early part of the curve.
20 μmol is an amount of product read from the graph, not a rate. A rate has units of μmol per minute.
40 μmol is the total substrate, not a rate. Find the slope of the straight early part of the curve.

q: Reaction 1 and reaction 2 convert the same substrate to the same product. What does the shape of curve 2 indicate about reaction 2?
c: It is not catalyzed by an enzyme; with no active sites to fill, the rate just rises with the number of substrate collisions
It is catalyzed by an enzyme with a larger maximum rate than the enzyme in reaction 1
It is catalyzed by an enzyme that reaches half of its maximum rate at a lower substrate concentration than the enzyme in reaction 1
It is catalyzed by the same enzyme as reaction 1 but with a competitive inhibitor present
h: Every enzyme has a limited number of active sites, so an enzyme-catalyzed rate must eventually level off. What kind of reaction never saturates?
w: An enzyme has a fixed number of active sites, so at high substrate concentration they are all occupied and the rate levels off (curve 1). Curve 2 is a straight line that never levels off, so there is no saturable catalyst: reaction 2 is an uncatalyzed reaction whose rate simply grows with the collision frequency. A faster enzyme or one that is half-saturated at lower substrate would still give a curve that bends toward a plateau, and a competitive inhibitor would make curve 2 lie below curve 1 at low substrate but still level off.
x: Any enzyme, however fast, would still give a curve that bends toward a plateau once its active sites fill. Curve 2 never levels off.
An enzyme that is half-saturated at lower substrate would still bend toward a plateau. Curve 2 is a straight line.
With a competitive inhibitor, the enzyme would still level off at high substrate. Curve 2 never bends.

q: A purified enzyme was treated to remove any bound metal ions, then its activity was measured alone and after adding different ions. What do the results show?
c: Mg<sup>2+</sup> is a required cofactor of the enzyme, and the other ions cannot take its place
Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> are inhibitors that shut the enzyme down
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is a coenzyme that the enzyme uses as a source of energy
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is the substrate of the enzyme, so adding it raises the rate
h: Compare the metal-free bar with each added-ion bar. Only one ion changes the activity. Is a metal ion a cofactor or a coenzyme?
w: Without any ion the enzyme is almost inactive; adding Mg2+ restores full activity while Zn2+ and Ca2+ leave it as low as the metal-free control, so Mg2+ is a required cofactor and the other ions cannot substitute for it. They are not inhibitors because they did not lower activity below the control. A metal ion is a cofactor, not a coenzyme; coenzymes are organic molecules made from vitamins.
x: Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> did not lower activity below the metal-free control, so they are not acting as inhibitors.
A metal ion is a cofactor, not a coenzyme; coenzymes are organic molecules made from vitamins. Mg<sup>2+</sup> is also not an energy source.
The enzyme was nearly inactive without any metal ion. That points to a helper the enzyme needs, not a substrate that gets converted.

q: The graph follows the activity of an enzyme solution over time. Hg<sup>2+</sup> ions were added at 2 min, and at 6 min the solution was dialyzed, which removed all free Hg<sup>2+</sup>. What type of inhibition does the graph show?
c: Irreversible (noncompetitive) inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> bonds to –SH groups of cysteine side chains and permanently changes the enzyme's shape
Competitive inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> resembles the substrate and occupies the active site until it is removed
Reversible inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> binds loosely to a side site and leaves when its concentration drops
Feedback inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> is the end product of the pathway and signals the enzyme to stop
h: A reversible inhibitor leaves the enzyme once it is removed from the solution. Check whether the activity came back after dialysis.
w: Activity drops when Hg2+ is added and stays near zero after dialysis removes the free Hg2+, so the inhibitor remains bonded to the enzyme: it is held by strong covalent bonds, typically to the –SH groups of cysteine, which is irreversible inhibition. Hg2+ does not compete with the substrate for the active site, so heavy metals are also classed as noncompetitive inhibitors. A reversibly bound inhibitor would release the enzyme, so the activity would climb back after dialysis. Heavy-metal ions are not pathway products, so this is not feedback inhibition.
x: Hg<sup>2+</sup> does not look like the substrate, and a competitive inhibitor comes off when it is removed, so activity would have recovered after dialysis.
If Hg<sup>2+</sup> were only loosely bound, dialysis would have pulled it off and activity would have climbed back. It stayed near zero.
Feedback inhibition is a pathway's own end product switching off an early enzyme. Hg<sup>2+</sup> is a toxic metal ion, not a product of the pathway.

q: Capsaicin, shown, is the compound that makes chili peppers hot and is used in pain-relief creams. Besides the benzene ring, which functional groups does it contain?
c: an amide, an ether, a phenol and an alkene
an ester, an ether, an alcohol and an alkene
an amide, a ketone, a phenol and an alkyne
an amine, an ether, a phenol and an alkene
h: Look at each heteroatom: a C=O bonded to N is an amide; O between two carbons is an ether; OH on the ring is a phenol.
w: The N–H next to a C=O makes an amide (not an amine or ester); the –OCH3 on the ring is an ether; the –OH on the ring is a phenol; and the C=C in the chain is an alkene. There is no isolated ketone and no triple bond.
x: An ester needs an O next to the C=O, but here the C=O is bonded to N–H. And –OH directly on a benzene ring is a phenol, not an alcohol.
The only C=O is bonded to an N, so it is not a ketone. The chain has a C=C double bond, not a triple bond.
An amine has N with no C=O next to it. Here the N–H is bonded directly to the C=O carbon.

q: Veterinarians and emergency physicians use ketamine, drawn here, as an anesthetic. Ignoring the benzene ring, what three functional groups does the drawing contain?
c: a ketone, a secondary (2°) amine and a halogen
an aldehyde, a primary (1°) amine and a halogen
a ketone, an amide and a halogen
an ester, a secondary (2°) amine and an alcohol
h: Where is the C=O? Count the carbons on the N. Is the Cl on a carbon?
w: The C=O is inside the ring bonded to two carbons, so it is a ketone (an aldehyde would need an H on the C=O). The N bonds to two carbons (CH3 and the ring carbon) and is not bonded to the C=O carbon, so it is a 2° amine, not an amide. The Cl on the ring is a halogen (organohalide) group.
x: An aldehyde needs an H on the C=O carbon, but here the C=O is inside the ring, between two carbons. The N also has two carbons on it, not one.
An amide needs N bonded directly to the C=O carbon. Here the N is on a neighboring ring carbon, not on the C=O carbon.
An ester needs an O next to the C=O, and an alcohol needs an –OH. The drawing has neither; Cl and O are the only non-carbon atoms besides N.

q: Four nitrogen- or oxygen-containing compounds are drawn. Pick the one that is an amide.
h: An amide has a nitrogen bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon (C=O).
w: Only one structure has N bonded to a C=O carbon: it is N-methylpropanamide. The compound with N but no C=O is an amine; the one with –O– next to C=O is an ester; the C=O flanked by two carbons is a ketone.
x: This one has an N but no C=O, so it is an amine.
Here the C=O carbon is bonded to an –O–CH<sub>3</sub>, which makes an ester.
Here the C=O is between two carbons, which makes a ketone. There is no nitrogen.

q: Compounds I and II both have the formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> and the same polar C–Cl bonds. Which statement about their polarity is correct?
c: I is nonpolar because its two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel; II is polar.
II is nonpolar because its two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel; I is polar.
I and II are equally nonpolar, because they contain exactly the same bonds.
I and II are equally polar, because every C–Cl bond is polar.
h: Bond polarity is not enough: the molecular shape decides whether the bond dipoles add up or cancel.
w: In the trans isomer (I) the two Cl atoms sit on opposite sides of the flat molecule, so the C–Cl dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel: I is nonpolar. In the cis isomer (II) both Cl atoms are on the same side, the dipoles add, and II is polar. Having identical bonds does not make molecules identical in polarity; shape matters.
x: This reverses the two drawings. Look at which one has the two Cl atoms on opposite sides of the C=C and which has them on the same side.
Same bonds do not mean same polarity. Shape decides whether the C–Cl dipoles cancel or add up.
Polar bonds can still cancel if they point in opposite directions. Check whether the two Cl atoms are on the same side or opposite sides.

q: This aldehyde also carries an OH group. Give its IUPAC name.
h: The aldehyde carbon is C1 and sets the name; the OH is a "hydroxy" prefix with its own number.
w: The –CHO carbon must be C1 (an aldehyde is always at the chain end). Counting from it, the OH is on C3: 3-hydroxybutanal. "2-hydroxy" counts from the CH3 end, "4-hydroxy" would put the OH on the end carbon, "butanone" would need a ketone C=O in the middle of the chain.
x: Count from the –CHO carbon as C1. The –OH is not on the carbon right next to it; one CH<sub>2</sub> lies in between.
The -one ending is for a ketone, with C=O between two carbons. Here the C=O is at the end of the chain with an H: an aldehyde.
4-Hydroxybutanal has the OH on the last carbon of the chain, the far end from the –CHO. Here the OH is on the carbon next to the CH3, not on the end carbon.

q: The drawn compound is a beta-amino acid used to make some drugs. Name it by IUPAC rules.
h: The –COOH carbon is C1. Number toward the NH<sub>2</sub> and name it as an "amino" prefix.
w: The carboxylic acid carbon is C1, so the chain is numbered from it: C2 is the CH2, and the NH2 is on C3, giving 3-aminobutanoic acid. 4-Aminobutanoic acid (GABA) would have the NH2 on the last carbon; "butanal" would require an aldehyde instead of the acid.
x: 2-Amino would place the NH<sub>2</sub> on the carbon right next to the –COOH carbon. Here a CH<sub>2</sub> sits between them.
4-Amino would put the NH<sub>2</sub> on the last carbon, at the far end of the chain (as in GABA). Here a CH<sub>3</sub> is still beyond the NH<sub>2</sub> carbon.
The -al ending means an aldehyde (–CHO). This compound has a –COOH group.

q: Name the branched alcohol drawn below, choosing the parent chain correctly.
h: Pick the longest chain that includes the OH carbon, then number from the end that gives the OH the lower number.
w: The longest chain through the OH carbon has five carbons; numbering from the right puts the OH on C3 and the methyl on C2: 2-methyl-3-pentanol. Numbering from the other end gives 4-methyl-3-pentanol (same OH locant, but the substituent gets the higher number, so it is wrong). 3-Ethyl-2-butanol uses a shorter chain, and "hexanol" counts six carbons that are not there.
x: This numbers from the wrong end. The –OH gets C3 either way, so the tie is broken by giving the methyl the lower number.
This uses a four-carbon chain. A longer chain through the C–OH carbon is possible if you follow the branch.
Hexanol needs six carbons in the chain, but the molecule has only six carbons in all, including a branch. Count the longest chain again.

q: Chemists call water amphoteric. Which statement explains the term?
c: It can act as either a proton donor (acid) or a proton acceptor (base), depending on its partner.
It is a strong acid and a strong base at the same time, so it neutralizes itself completely.
It can neither donate nor accept protons, so any solution made with it stays exactly neutral.
It dissolves polar and nonpolar substances equally well, so it is called a universal solvent.
h: Think about what water does with HCl versus what it does with an amine.
w: With an acid such as HCl, water accepts H+ (acts as a base, forming H3O+); with a base such as CH3NH2, water donates H+ (acts as an acid, forming OH−). Either role, depending on the partner, is what amphoteric means. Water is a weak acid and a weak base, not strong, and its solvent behavior is a separate idea.
x: Water is a very weak acid and a very weak base, not a strong one. Amphoteric is about being able to play either role.
Water does donate and accept protons: it gives H<sup>+</sup> to amines and takes H<sup>+</sup> from HCl.
That describes water as a solvent, which is a separate idea, and water does not dissolve nonpolar substances well.

q: Propanoic acid ionizes in water as written below. What role does water play here?
c: a base, because it accepts a proton from the carboxylic acid
an acid, because it donates a proton to the carboxylic acid
a base, because it donates a proton to the carboxylic acid
an acid, because it accepts a proton from the carboxylic acid
h: Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: whatever gains it is the base; whatever loses it is the acid.
w: Propanoic acid loses H+ (acid → propanoate ion) and water gains it, becoming H3O+. A species that accepts a proton is a base, so here water is the base. Bases never donate protons, and water accepting a proton makes it a base, not an acid.
x: Water does not donate a proton here. Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: water ends up as H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.
A base accepts protons; it does not donate them. Also, here water gains an H<sup>+</sup> rather than losing one.
Accepting a proton makes a species a base, not an acid. Acids give protons away.

q: One of the following acids ionizes completely in water (a strong acid). Which one?
h: Only a short list of inorganic acids ionize completely. Carboxylic acids never do.
w: HBr (like HCl, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4) ionizes essentially 100% in water, so it is strong. Propanoic acid and benzoic acid are carboxylic acids: carboxylic acids are weak. HF is the tempting one: it is a hydrogen halide, but it is a weak acid, unlike HCl, HBr and HI.
x: Propanoic acid is a carboxylic acid. Carboxylic acids ionize only slightly in water, so they are weak.
HF is a hydrogen halide, but unlike HCl, HBr and HI it ionizes only partly: it is a weak acid.
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH (benzoic acid) is a carboxylic acid, and carboxylic acids are weak acids.

q: Three of these bases dissociate completely in water; one does not. Which is the weak base?
h: Metal hydroxides of Groups 1 and 2 dissociate completely. What kind of base is an amine?
w: Ethylamine is an organic base: it accepts H+ from water only partly (CH3CH2NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2NH+3 + OH−), so it is weak. NaOH, KOH and Ca(OH)2 are ionic hydroxides that dissociate completely: strong bases.
x: NaOH is a Group 1 metal hydroxide, an ionic compound that dissociates completely: a strong base.
KOH is a Group 1 metal hydroxide that dissociates completely in water: a strong base.
Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> is a Group 2 hydroxide. The part that dissolves dissociates completely, so it counts as a strong base.

q: Each drawn compound has a six-carbon chain, so their dispersion forces are about equal. Which one melts at the highest temperature?
h: Same size means similar dispersion forces, so compare the other forces: which compound can form the most hydrogen bonds?
w: Hexanoic acid has an O–H donor and two oxygens; its molecules pair up through two hydrogen bonds each, giving the strongest attractions and the highest melting point (about −3 °C). 1-Hexanol can hydrogen bond, but only one O–H per molecule (−47 °C); hexanal has a polar C=O but no O–H (−56 °C); hexane has only dispersion forces (−95 °C). The same ranking applies to boiling points.
x: 1-Hexanol hydrogen bonds, but each molecule has only one O–H and one O. Look for a group that lets pairs of molecules form two hydrogen bonds.
Hexanal has a polar C=O but no O–H, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. It adds dipole–dipole forces to dispersion, which is weaker than hydrogen bonding.
Hexane has only dispersion forces, the weakest attractions here, so it melts lowest.

q: Oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate), drawn below, gives muscle rubs their warming smell. Count its atoms and use the table to find the molar mass.
h: Each corner or line end is a carbon with enough H to make four bonds. Count C, H and O, then multiply by the atomic masses.
w: The formula is C8H8O3: 8(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 96.08 + 8.06 + 48.00 = 152.14 g mol−1. Forgetting the four hidden H atoms on the ring gives 148.11; missing one oxygen gives 136.14; doubling the H count gives 160.21.
x: 148.11 is four H short, from forgetting the hidden H atoms on the ring carbons. Each ring corner with no group carries one H.
160.21 counts too many H atoms. Recount: each ring corner with no group carries one H, then add the H atoms on the methyl and hydroxyl groups.
136.14 counts only two O atoms. Count the O in the –OH and both O atoms in the ester group.

q: When each drawn compound is dissolved in water, only one releases H<sup>+</sup> and lowers the pH. Which is that organic acid?
h: Of the common oxygen- and nitrogen-containing groups, only one donates a proton to water.
w: The –COOH group of butanoic acid loses its O–H proton to water (CH3CH2CH2COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2CH2COO− + H3O+). Butylamine is a base (it accepts H+). The alcohol has an O–H, but it is essentially neutral in water; the aldehyde has no acidic H at all.
x: This is an amine. Amines are bases: they accept H<sup>+</sup> from water and raise the pH.
This is an alcohol. Its O–H is about as weakly acidic as water, so it does not noticeably lower the pH.
This is an aldehyde. It has no O–H and does not release H<sup>+</sup> in water.

q: Which compound acts as a base in water, raising the pH of the solution?
h: A base accepts a proton. Which atom here has a lone pair that readily picks up H<sup>+</sup> from water?
w: The nitrogen of cyclohexylamine accepts H+ from water, leaving OH− behind and raising the pH: amines are the organic bases. The carboxylic acid lowers the pH; the alcohol and the ketone are neutral, since their oxygens do not take protons from water to any useful extent.
x: This is a carboxylic acid: it donates H<sup>+</sup> to water and lowers the pH.
This is an alcohol, cyclohexanol. Its oxygen does not take protons from water to any useful extent, so the solution stays neutral.
This is a ketone, cyclohexanone. Its oxygen does not take protons from water to a useful extent, so it is neutral.

q: Propanoic acid and ethylamine are simply mixed at room temperature; nothing is heated. Which pair of products forms?
h: Acid + base at room temperature is a proton transfer, not a condensation. The acid gives H<sup>+</sup>; the amine takes it.
w: The carboxylic acid donates H+ to the amine nitrogen, giving the propanoate ion and the ethylammonium ion (a salt). The amide forms only when the mixture is heated so water is driven off. Propanoate paired with a neutral amine is unbalanced: the proton must land on the N. The ester would require an alcohol, not an amine.
x: This amide forms only when the mixture is heated and water is driven off. At room temperature there is just a fast proton transfer.
This shows the acid losing H<sup>+</sup>, but the H<sup>+</sup> has to go somewhere. The amine is the base that takes it.
This is an ester, ethyl propanoate, which needs an alcohol. Ethylamine is an amine, not an alcohol.

q: A hydrocarbon is labeled saturated. What must be true of its structure?
c: It contains only C–C and C–H single bonds, so it cannot add H<sub>2</sub>.
It contains at least one C=C double bond, so it can add H<sub>2</sub>.
It contains as many double bonds as the carbon skeleton allows.
It is a hydrocarbon that dissolves readily in water.
h: "Saturated" means the molecule is already full of hydrogen: no more can be added.
w: A saturated hydrocarbon (an alkane or cycloalkane) has only single bonds; every carbon already holds the maximum number of H atoms, so it cannot undergo addition. Compounds with C=C or C≡C are unsaturated and can add H2. Solubility in water has nothing to do with saturation; hydrocarbons of both kinds are insoluble.
x: A C=C double bond makes a hydrocarbon unsaturated, able to add H<sub>2</sub>. Saturated means the opposite.
Many double bonds would make it highly unsaturated. Saturated means it already holds all the H it can.
Saturation describes bonding, not solubility. Hydrocarbons, saturated or not, are nonpolar and insoluble in water.

q: Only one of the drawn hydrocarbons is saturated. Pick it.
h: Saturated = no double or triple bonds anywhere, ring or chain.
w: Methylcyclopentane has only single bonds, so it is saturated; a ring by itself does not count as unsaturation in this sense. 1-Pentene (C=C), 2-pentyne (C≡C) and benzene (alternating double bonds) are all unsaturated and can take up H2.
x: This chain has a C=C double bond, so it is unsaturated and can add H<sub>2</sub>.
This chain has a C≡C triple bond, so it is unsaturated and can add H<sub>2</sub>.
This is benzene, drawn with alternating double bonds, so it is unsaturated. Look for a structure with only single bonds.

q: Cyclohexene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, reacts with H<sub>2</sub> over a platinum catalyst. What is the product?
h: Hydrogenation adds one H<sub>2</sub> across each C=C. Does the ring open?
w: H2 adds across the one C=C, giving the saturated ring cyclohexane, C6H12. The ring stays closed.
x: Benzene has fewer H atoms than cyclohexene. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen; it does not remove it.
Hexane is an open chain. Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> to the C=C but does not break the ring.
Cyclohexanol would come from adding H<sub>2</sub>O (hydration), not H<sub>2</sub>.

q: Which alkene gives 2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH, as the major product when it reacts with H<sub>2</sub>O and an acid catalyst?
h: Work backward. The –OH is on a carbon bonded to three CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Which alkene has that branched skeleton?
w: Hydration does not change the carbon skeleton. Only 2-methylpropene has the branched four-carbon skeleton, and by Markovnikov's rule the H adds to the CH2 and the –OH goes to the carbon with the two CH3 groups, giving (CH3)3COH.
x: 1-Butene has an unbranched chain. Its major hydration product is 2-butanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
2-Butene is unbranched and gives 2-butanol. The product here has a branched skeleton.
Propene has only three carbons and gives 2-propanol. The product here has four carbons.

q: Which alkene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> to give 2,3-dibromobutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: In halogenation of an alkene, the two Br atoms add to the two carbons that were joined by the C=C.
w: The Br atoms end up on C2 and C3, so the C=C was between C2 and C3: 2-butene. Addition of Br2 is the reaction behind the bromine test, in which the red-brown color disappears.
x: 1-Butene has its C=C between C1 and C2, so it gives 1,2-dibromobutane.
Butane has no C=C, so Br<sub>2</sub> cannot add to it. In light it would undergo substitution and give a single Br plus HBr.
2-Methylpropene has a branched skeleton and gives 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane, not an unbranched product.

q: Which of the following reactions is a substitution?
h: In a substitution, one atom or group replaces another, so there are two products.
w: In the reaction of ethane with Br2, a Br atom replaces an H atom on ethane and HBr is released: the halogenation of an alkane, a substitution. The HBr and H2 reactions add to a C=C (addition), and the ethanol reaction removes water to form a C=C (elimination, dehydration).
x: Here HBr adds across a C=C and only one product forms. That is an addition (hydrohalogenation).
Here an alcohol loses H<sub>2</sub>O and a C=C forms. That is an elimination (dehydration).
Here H<sub>2</sub> adds across a C=C. That is an addition (hydrogenation).

q: A cyclohexane ring carries a sec-butyl group. Which drawing shows this compound, sec-butylcyclohexane?
h: A sec-butyl group attaches to the ring through a carbon that is bonded to two other carbons (one CH<sub>3</sub> and one CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>).
w: In sec-butyl the ring attaches to an inner carbon of the butyl chain (a secondary carbon in butane), so that carbon carries one methyl and one ethyl group, –CH(CH3)CH2CH3. The straight four-carbon chain is butyl; the Y-shaped group attached through a CH2 is isobutyl; the carbon bearing three methyls is tert-butyl.
x: This is butyl, the straight four-carbon chain attached through its end carbon. Sec-butyl attaches through an inner carbon.
This is isobutyl: attached through a CH<sub>2</sub> that leads to a Y-shaped CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. The attachment carbon here is bonded to only one other carbon in the group.
This is tert-butyl: the attachment carbon carries three CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Sec-butyl's attachment carbon is bonded to two carbons in the group.

q: Isopropylbenzene (cumene) is the starting material for making phenol and acetone. Which structure is isopropylbenzene?
h: An isopropyl group is Y-shaped: the ring is attached to the middle carbon of a three-carbon group.
w: Isopropylbenzene has a three-carbon group bonded to the ring through its middle carbon, –CH(CH3)2. Propylbenzene attaches through the end carbon of a straight chain; 1-ethyl-2-methylbenzene has the same formula but two separate groups; tert-butylbenzene has four carbons in its substituent.
x: This is propylbenzene: the ring is bonded to the end carbon of a straight three-carbon chain. An isopropyl group attaches through its middle carbon.
This has two separate groups on the ring, ethyl and methyl (1-ethyl-2-methylbenzene). Isopropylbenzene has a single three-carbon substituent.
This substituent has four carbons, a central carbon holding three CH3 groups (tert-butyl). An isopropyl group has three carbons.

q: meta-Xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene) is a solvent in some paints. Pick its drawing.
h: Meta = the two groups have exactly one ring carbon between them (positions 1 and 3).
w: In meta-xylene the two CH3 groups sit on carbons 1 and 3, with one unsubstituted ring carbon between them. Adjacent methyls (1,2) are ortho-xylene; methyls directly across the ring (1,4) are para-xylene. Ethylbenzene is an isomer with a single two-carbon group.
x: Here the two CH3 groups are on neighboring carbons (1,2). That is ortho-xylene.
Here the two CH3 groups are directly across the ring (1,4). That is para-xylene.
This is ethylbenzene, with one two-carbon group. Xylenes have two separate CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the ring.

q: How many different compounds with the formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> exist, if cis and trans forms are counted separately?
h: Put both Cl on one carbon, or one on each. If one on each, can they be on the same side or opposite sides?
w: 1,1-Dichloroethene (both Cl on the same carbon), cis-1,2-dichloroethene and trans-1,2-dichloroethene: 3. Forgetting that 1,2-dichloroethene has cis and trans forms gives 2; 1,1-dichloroethene has no cis/trans forms because one double-bond carbon carries two identical groups (H, H).
x: This forgets that one of the structures has a cis and a trans form, which count separately here.
This counts too many. When both Cl atoms are on the same carbon, the other carbon holds two H, so there is only one form.
There is more than one way to place two Cl atoms on a C=C. They can be on the same carbon or on different carbons.

q: Thiols give skunk spray and natural gas their warning odors. Which of these drawings is a thiol?
h: A thiol is the sulfur analog of an alcohol: –SH on a carbon.
w: Only one structure has an –SH group (1-butanethiol, a skunk-like odorant). The –OH compound is an alcohol; the C–S–C compound is a sulfide (thioether); the S–S compound is a disulfide, the product of oxidizing two thiols.
x: This has an –OH group, so it is an alcohol (1-butanol). A thiol has S in place of that O.
Here the S is between two carbons with no H on it, so this is a sulfide.
This has two S atoms bonded together, so it is a disulfide, the product of oxidizing two thiols.

q: Linalool, shown, gives lavender and coriander their scent. How is the alcohol group at carbon a classified?
c: tertiary (3°): the OH carbon is bonded to three other carbons
secondary (2°): the OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons
primary (1°): the OH carbon is bonded to one other carbon
it is a phenol, because the molecule contains double bonds
h: Go to the carbon that holds the OH and count the C–C bonds it makes; ignore the rest of the molecule.
w: Carbon a is bonded to a methyl group, a vinyl (CH=CH2) group and the long chain: three carbons, so it is a 3° alcohol (and would not be oxidized). The double bonds elsewhere do not change the classification, and a phenol needs the OH on a benzene ring, which linalool does not have.
x: Count again: carbon a is bonded to a CH3, the CH=CH2 group and the long chain. Each counts as a carbon neighbor.
Carbon a is bonded to more than one carbon. Count every carbon attached directly to it, including the small groups.
A phenol needs the –OH on a benzene ring. C=C double bonds in a chain do not make a compound a phenol.

q: Methanethiol condenses with propanoic acid when the two are heated, losing water. Which drawing is the sulfur-containing product?
h: Treat the thiol like an alcohol: the acid loses –OH, the thiol loses its H, and C(=O)–S forms. Sulfur stays in the product.
w: Condensation of a carboxylic acid with a thiol gives a thioester, CH3CH2C(=O)–S–CH3: the C=O side comes from the acid and the S from the thiol. The ester (C(=O)–O–CH3) is the product with an alcohol, not a thiol. The thioester with the groups swapped would have to come from acetic acid and ethanethiol. A sulfide (C–S–C with no C=O) requires losing the carbonyl, which does not happen.
x: This is an ordinary ester with C(=O)–O–CH<sub>3</sub>. That forms with methanol; here the reactant is a thiol, so S should be in the product.
This thioester has a two-carbon acyl group and an ethyl on S, which is reversed. The C=O side should keep propanoic acid's three carbons.
This is a sulfide with no C=O. Condensation keeps the acid's carbonyl group.

q: A thioester is formed when a thiol condenses with a carboxylic acid. How does a thioester differ structurally from an ordinary ester?
c: A sulfur atom replaces the single-bonded oxygen between the C=O carbon and the alkyl group.
A sulfur atom replaces the double-bonded oxygen of the C=O group, giving a C=S double bond.
A sulfur atom replaces the carbonyl carbon itself, so the group becomes O=S bonded to oxygen.
An –SH group is added to the carbonyl carbon alongside the –OR group, with no atoms removed.
h: Where does the sulfur of the thiol end up? The thiol loses only its H.
w: The thiol R–SH plays the role of the alcohol R–OH, so its S ends up where the ester's single-bonded O would be: R–C(=O)–S–R′. The C=O group is unchanged (it comes from the acid). Acetyl-CoA, the key thioester of metabolism, has exactly this C(=O)–S linkage.
x: A C=S group is a thiocarbonyl, not a thioester. The C=O comes from the acid and stays unchanged.
The carbonyl carbon stays; it comes from the acid. Sulfur from the thiol does not replace a carbon atom.
A condensation always loses a small molecule (water here). Nothing is simply added without atoms removed.

q: Butanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, and butanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, are each reduced with [H] (a reducing agent). Which pair of products forms?
c: butanal → butanoic acid; butanone → no reaction
h: Reduction turns the C=O into CH–OH on the same carbon. Where is the C=O in each compound?
w: Reduction adds two H atoms across the C=O, so the –OH ends up on the carbon that held the C=O. The aldehyde carbon is at the end of the chain, giving a 1° alcohol; the ketone carbon is in the chain, giving a 2° alcohol: 1-butanol and 2-butanol.
x: This swaps the two. The aldehyde's C=O is on the end carbon, so it gives the 1° alcohol.
Butanone's C=O is on carbon 2, so its –OH ends up on carbon 2 as well, giving 2-butanol.
That describes oxidation with a mild oxidizing agent. [H] reduces both aldehydes and ketones.

q: Which alcohol is formed by reducing an aldehyde?
h: Reduction of a C=O puts an H on the carbonyl carbon. An aldehyde's C=O carbon already has one H, so the product carbon has two H.
w: An aldehyde carbon has one H and one R group; adding H to it gives R–CH2–OH, a primary alcohol such as 1-pentanol. 2-Pentanol and cyclopentanol are secondary alcohols and come from ketones. 2-Methyl-2-butanol is a tertiary alcohol, which cannot be made by reducing any carbonyl compound.
x: This drawing is 2-pentanol: its C–OH carbon has two carbon groups, a 2° alcohol. That comes from reducing a ketone.
This drawing is a 3° alcohol: its C–OH carbon has three carbons and no H. No carbonyl compound reduces to that.
This drawing is cyclopentanol: its C–OH carbon has two ring carbons, a 2° alcohol. That comes from reducing a ketone.

q: The compound shown is a cyclic protecting group used in drug synthesis. Carbon a is bonded to two oxygen atoms. Which term describes it?
c: an acetal carbon: two –OR groups and one H, from an aldehyde
a ketal carbon: two –OR groups and two carbons, from a ketone
a hemiacetal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from an aldehyde
a hemiketal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from a ketone
h: Find the carbon bonded to two O atoms. Does either O carry an H? How many carbons are attached to that carbon?
w: Carbon a carries two ring –O–C groups (both are –OR; neither is an –OH), so it is a full acetal/ketal, not a hemi-. It is bonded to only one other carbon (the CH3) plus an H, so it came from an aldehyde (ethanal): an acetal. A ketal carbon would have two carbon groups and no H.
x: A ketal carbon has two carbon groups and no H. Carbon a is bonded to only one carbon (the CH<sub>3</sub>) and carries an H.
A hemiacetal has an –OH. Both oxygens on carbon a are ring –O–C groups; neither has an H.
A hemiketal needs an –OH and two carbon groups on that carbon. Carbon a has neither.

q: In the five-membered ring below, carbon a holds both an OH and a ring oxygen. What kind of carbon is it?
c: a hemiketal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from a ketone
a hemiacetal carbon: one –OH and one –OR, from an aldehyde
a ketal carbon: two –OR groups, from a ketone
an acetal carbon: two –OR groups, from an aldehyde
h: One of the two oxygens is an OH, so it is a "hemi". Count the carbons on carbon a to decide aldehyde or ketone origin.
w: Carbon a has one –OH and one ring –O–C (an –OR), so it is a hemi- compound; the OH has not yet been replaced. It is bonded to two carbons (the CH3 and the ring CH2) and has no H, so its parent was a ketone: a hemiketal. A hemiacetal carbon would carry an H; acetals and ketals have two –OR groups and no –OH.
x: A hemiacetal carbon keeps the aldehyde's H. Carbon a has no H; count the carbons bonded to it.
A ketal carbon has two –OR groups and no –OH. Carbon a still has an –OH.
An acetal has two –OR groups and no –OH. Carbon a still has an –OH.

q: Which combination of reactants produces a ketal?
c: a ketone and two molecules of alcohol, with loss of water
an aldehyde and two molecules of alcohol, with loss of water
a ketone and one molecule of alcohol
a carboxylic acid and one molecule of alcohol, with loss of water
h: Ketal comes from "ketone"; the "hemi" versions stop after one alcohol.
w: A ketone plus two alcohols (acid catalyst, water removed) gives a ketal: the carbonyl carbon ends up with two –OR groups and two carbon groups. An aldehyde with two alcohols gives an acetal; a ketone with only one alcohol stops at the hemiketal; an acid plus an alcohol gives an ester.
x: An aldehyde plus two alcohols gives an acetal, whose carbon keeps the aldehyde H. The "ket-" in the name points to a different parent.
With only one alcohol, the reaction stops at the hemi- stage, which still has an –OH.
A carboxylic acid plus an alcohol gives an ester, which keeps its C=O.

q: An ester is hydrolyzed once with aqueous acid and once with aqueous NaOH. How do the organic products differ?
c: Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid; base hydrolysis gives its carboxylate salt. The alcohol released is the same.
Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt; base hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid. The alcohol released is the same.
Acid hydrolysis gives an alcohol; base hydrolysis gives an aldehyde instead.
The products are identical; only the reaction rate differs.
h: In base, any carboxylic acid that forms is immediately neutralized by the OH<sup>−</sup> present.
w: Both reactions cut the ester at the C–O single bond, releasing the alcohol. In acid the carbonyl piece is the free carboxylic acid; in NaOH the acid is neutralized to the sodium carboxylate salt (saponification). No aldehyde forms in either case, and the products are not identical because the salt is ionic.
x: This has the two cases reversed. Think about which conditions have extra OH<sup>−</sup> around to neutralize the acid as it forms.
Hydrolysis does not reduce anything, so no aldehyde forms. Both reactions split the ester into the same two pieces; only one piece's form differs.
The products are not identical. In one set of conditions the acid piece is neutralized by the reagent.

q: Methyl butanoate smells like apples. Which drawing matches this ester name?
h: In an ester name, the first word is the alkyl group on the single-bonded O; the "-oate" part contains the C=O.
w: "Butanoate" means a four-carbon chain that includes the C=O carbon, and "methyl" is the one-carbon group on the other oxygen: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(=O)–O–CH<sub>3</sub>. Butyl methanoate has the same formula but the groups swapped (the C=O is in the one-carbon part). Methyl propanoate has one carbon too few in the acid part; ethyl propanoate puts two carbons on the oxygen.
x: This is butyl methanoate: the C=O is on the one-carbon side and the four-carbon chain is on the O. In methyl butanoate the four carbons include the C=O carbon.
This is methyl propanoate: the C=O side has only three carbons. Butanoate needs four, counting the C=O carbon.
This is ethyl propanoate: two carbons on the O and three on the C=O side. Methyl means one carbon on the O.

q: Exactly one of the drawn nitrogen compounds is a tertiary (3°) amine. Which one?
h: Count the carbons bonded directly to N, and make sure the N is not attached to a C=O.
w: In N-methylpiperidine the nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and the CH3) and to no C=O: a 3° amine. Piperidine (N–H, two ring carbons) is a 2° amine and cyclohexylamine (NH2) is 1°. N,N-dimethylacetamide also has three carbons on N, but one of them is a C=O carbon, which makes it an amide, not an amine.
x: This is piperidine: its N has an H and only two ring carbons, so it is a 2° amine.
This is cyclohexylamine: its N is an –NH<sub>2</sub> with one carbon, so it is a 1° amine.
This N has three carbons, but one of them is a C=O carbon. An N bonded to a carbonyl carbon is an amide, not an amine.

q: Pyrrolidine, a cyclic secondary amine, condenses with acetic acid on heating (water is lost). Which drawing is the amide formed?
h: Acid –OH plus amine N–H leave as water; the new bond is C(=O)–N. A 2° amine gives an amide with no N–H.
w: The acid's –OH and the amine's only N–H are lost as water, joining the C=O carbon to the ring nitrogen: N-acetylpyrrolidine, an amide whose N carries two ring carbons and the acetyl group. The N-cyclopentyl amide has the N outside the ring (that would require cyclopentylamine). The ammonium acetate ion pair is what forms without heating. The structure with a C–OH in place of the C=O is not an amide: amidation keeps the acid's C=O and removes its –OH.
x: This drawing puts the N–H outside the ring on a cyclopentyl group; that would need cyclopentylamine. Pyrrolidine's N is part of the ring.
This acetate and pyrrolidinium ion pair is the acid–base salt that forms without heating. Heating drives off water and forms a new bond.
This drawing has a C–OH where the carbonyl should be. Amidation keeps the acid's C=O and removes its –OH.

q: Four small biological molecules are drawn. Which one is a carbohydrate (a monosaccharide)?
h: A monosaccharide is a polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone: look for a C=O (aldehyde or ketone) plus –OH on the other carbons.
w: The correct structure is glyceraldehyde: an aldehyde carbon (–CHO) and an –OH on each remaining carbon, so it is an aldotriose. Glycerol has three –OH groups but no carbonyl (it is a sugar alcohol, not a sugar); lactic acid has a carboxylic acid, not an aldehyde or ketone; alanine has an amino group and a carboxyl group, so it is an amino acid.
x: This is glycerol: three –OH groups but no C=O. Without an aldehyde or ketone it is a sugar alcohol, not a sugar.
This is lactic acid. Its C=O is part of a carboxylic acid (–COOH), not an aldehyde or ketone.
This is alanine, an amino acid: it has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group and a –COOH group, and no polyhydroxy chain.

q: Which of the structures drawn is an amino acid of the kind found in proteins?
h: A protein amino acid has an amino group AND a carboxylic acid group attached to the same (alpha) carbon.
w: The correct structure is alanine: an –NH<sub>2</sub> and a –COOH are both bonded to the same carbon, the α carbon, which also carries the side chain –CH<sub>3</sub>. Lactic acid has –OH and –COOH (a hydroxy acid, no nitrogen); 2-aminoethanol has an amine and an alcohol but no carboxyl group; propanamide contains an amide group but no free amine or carboxylic acid.
x: This structure has an –OH and a –COOH (a hydroxy acid) but no nitrogen, so it has no amino group.
This structure has an amine and an alcohol, but no carboxylic acid group.
This structure has a C=O bonded to –NH<sub>2</sub>, which is an amide. It has neither a free amino group nor a carboxylic acid.

q: A biological polymer is hydrolyzed by dilute acid and gives only glucose. The bonds that held the monomers together are best described as which functional group?
h: Think about what forms when the hemiacetal –OH of one sugar ring reacts with an –OH of the next sugar.
w: A polymer of glucose is a polysaccharide (starch, glycogen or cellulose). Each glycosidic bond forms when the hemiacetal carbon of one glucose bonds through oxygen to an –OH of the next unit, giving an acetal (two –OR groups on one carbon). Esters link fatty acids in lipids, amides link amino acids in proteins and phosphodiesters link nucleotides.
x: Ester linkages join fatty acids to glycerol in fats. A polymer that gives only glucose is linked through sugar–O–sugar bonds.
Amide (peptide) bonds join amino acids in proteins. Hydrolysis here gives only glucose, not amino acids.
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides in DNA and RNA. Hydrolysis here gives only glucose, with no phosphate.

q: Which class of biomolecule contains phosphodiester linkages in its backbone and nitrogen-containing amines in its monomers?
h: Which polymer has a sugar–phosphate backbone with nitrogen bases hanging off it?
w: In DNA and RNA the phosphate group forms ester bonds to two different sugars (a phosphodiester), and the bases are heterocyclic amines, so nucleic acids fit both clues. Proteins contain amide bonds and amines but no phosphodiesters; triacylglycerols are esters; polysaccharides are acetals.
x: Proteins have amide (peptide) bonds in their backbone, not phosphodiester links.
Triacylglycerols contain ester bonds but no phosphate and no nitrogen.
Polysaccharides are linked by glycosidic bonds and contain no phosphate or nitrogen bases.

q: Lipids are grouped together as a class not by a shared functional group but by a shared property. Which property defines a lipid?
c: Insoluble in water but soluble in nonpolar solvents
Soluble in water because of its many polar –OH groups
Made of repeating amino acid units joined in a chain
Always contains a phosphate group in its structure
h: Fats, oils, waxes, steroids and phospholipids have very different structures. What do they all do in water?
w: A lipid is defined as a biomolecule that is insoluble in water and soluble in nonpolar solvents such as hexane or ether, because most of its structure is hydrocarbon. Carbohydrates are the water-soluble polyhydroxy compounds; only phospholipids contain phosphate, and proteins are the amino acid polymers.
x: Many –OH groups and water solubility describe carbohydrates. Most of a lipid's structure is hydrocarbon.
Repeating amino acid units make proteins, not lipids.
Only phospholipids contain phosphate. Fats, waxes and steroids have none, yet they are all lipids.

q: A liver cell is making glycogen from glucose and proteins from amino acids. Which statement correctly describes these anabolic pathways?
c: They build larger molecules from smaller ones and generally require ATP
They break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy
They oxidize fuels to CO<sub>2</sub> and reduce NAD<sup>+</sup> to NADH
They occur only in the mitochondria during fasting
h: Ana- = building up; cata- = breaking down. Building bonds costs energy.
w: Anabolism is biosynthesis: small molecules are joined into larger ones (glucose → glycogen, amino acids → protein, acetyl CoA → fatty acids), which requires energy from ATP and usually reducing power (NADPH). Breaking fuels down to CO2 while making NADH describes catabolism.
x: Breaking large molecules down and releasing energy describes catabolism. Making glycogen and proteins builds things up.
Oxidizing fuels to CO<sub>2</sub> while making NADH is catabolism. Building pathways usually use reducing power and ATP instead.
Building pathways like glycogen and protein synthesis run in many places, mostly when fuel is plentiful (after a meal), not only during fasting.

q: D-Arabinose, an aldopentose found in plant gums, is drawn at the top. Which of structures I–IV is the enantiomer (mirror image) of D-arabinose?
h: An enantiomer is the complete mirror image: every chiral carbon must have its H and OH swapped, not just one of them.
w: The mirror image of D-arabinose reverses all three chiral carbons: C2 right, C3 left, C4 left, which is structure I (L-arabinose). Structure III swaps only C4, so it is L but not the mirror image (a diastereomer); II (D-ribose) differs at only one carbon (an epimer) and IV (D-xylose) at two.
x: Structure II is right, right, right: D-ribose. It differs from D-arabinose at just one carbon (C2), so it is an epimer, not a mirror image.
Structure III reverses only C4 (left, right, left). It is an L-sugar, but a mirror image must reverse every chiral carbon.
Structure IV (right, left, right) differs from D-arabinose at C2 and C3 but not C4. It is still a D-sugar, so not the mirror image.

q: Glucose gives a positive Benedict's test (a reducing sugar) but sucrose does not. Which structural feature makes glucose a reducing sugar?
c: Its ring can open to a free aldehyde, since C1 is not locked in a glycosidic bond
It has five –OH groups, and Benedict’s reagent oxidizes these alcohol groups
Its ring oxygen has lone pairs that can pass electrons to Cu<sup>2+</sup>
It contains an acetal carbon that is oxidized to a carboxylic acid
h: Benedict's reagent oxidizes aldehydes. Which carbon of glucose can become an aldehyde in solution, and why can't sucrose do the same?
w: In solution the cyclic hemiacetal of glucose opens to the free aldehyde, which Cu2+ oxidizes to a carboxylate (red Cu2O forms), so a free hemiacetal/aldehyde makes a sugar reducing. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up as an acetal and a ketal, so no aldehyde can form. The alcohol –OH groups are not oxidized by Benedict's reagent.
x: The alcohol –OH groups are not oxidized by Benedict's reagent, and sucrose has many –OH groups too but tests negative.
The ring oxygen is not what reacts with Cu<sup>2+</sup>; sucrose has ring oxygens too and tests negative. Think about what the ring can open into.
An acetal carbon is locked and cannot open, which is why sucrose is non-reducing. Glucose on its own has no acetal carbon.

q: In its five-membered ring form, fructose has an –OH group and the ring oxygen both attached to carbon 2, which also bears two carbon groups. What functional group is at C2?
h: C2 of fructose is a ketone carbon in the open chain. What forms when an –OH adds to a ketone?
w: When the C5 –OH adds to the C2 ketone, the carbon ends up with –OH, –OR (the ring O) and two carbon substituents: a hemiketal. A hemiacetal would have an H on that carbon (from an aldose such as glucose); a ketal needs two –OR groups and forms only when the sugar makes a glycosidic bond.
x: A hemiacetal has an H on that carbon and comes from an aldehyde. Here C2 has two carbon groups because it came from a ketone.
A ketal has two –OR groups on the carbon. Here C2 still has one free –OH.
A ketone has a C=O. Once the ring closes, C2 no longer has a double bond to oxygen.

q: Each row of the table names a glucose polysaccharide and describes its linkages, branching and digestibility. Which row describes its polysaccharide correctly?
h: All four are glucose polymers. Sort them by α or β linkages, branching, and whether human enzymes can digest them.
w: Glycogen is the highly branched α(1→4)/α(1→6) glucose polymer that animals store in liver and muscle, so row II is correct. Row I is wrong because cellulose is β(1→4) and not digestible by humans; row III is wrong because amylose is unbranched; row IV is wrong because amylopectin is a plant starch, not a fructose polymer.

head: Polysaccharide
Description
rows: α(1→4) glucose; unbranched; digested by human amylase
α(1→4) glucose with α(1→6) branches; stored in liver and muscle
β(1→4) glucose; highly branched; in plant starch
α(1→6) fructose; unbranched; in animal muscle

x: Row I is wrong about cellulose: cellulose has β(1→4) linkages, which human amylase cannot digest.
Row III is wrong about amylose: amylose has α(1→4) linkages and is unbranched.
Row IV is wrong about amylopectin: it is a branched glucose polymer in plant starch, not a fructose polymer in muscle.

q: Octanoic acid, a fatty acid in coconut and goat's milk fat, is drawn with four carbons lettered. Which letter marks the β carbon?
h: Greek letters start next to the carboxyl group: the carbon bonded to the –COOH carbon is α, the next one is β.
w: Counting from the carboxyl carbon (C1): the first carbon attached to it (b) is the α carbon (C2) and the next one, c, is the β carbon (C3), the carbon oxidized in β-oxidation. Letter a is the γ carbon (C4), and the far-end methyl carbon (d) is the omega (ω) carbon.
x: Carbon b is bonded directly to the –COOH carbon, so it is the α carbon. β is the next one along the chain.
Carbon a is one carbon too far from the carboxyl group: it is the γ carbon.
Carbon d is the methyl carbon at the far end of the chain: the ω (omega) carbon, not β.

q: In the octanoic acid drawn, which lettered carbon is the omega (ω) carbon, the one used for naming omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids?
h: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet. Which carbon is farthest from the carboxyl group?
w: The omega carbon is the methyl carbon at the end of the chain farthest from –COOH, letter d. Counting from the carboxyl carbon, b is the α carbon (C2), c is the β carbon (C3) and a is the γ carbon (C4). In an omega-3 acid the first C=C begins three carbons in from carbon d.
x: Carbon a is near the carboxyl end (the γ carbon). Omega is the last Greek letter, so look at the far end.
Carbon b is bonded directly to the –COOH carbon, making it the α carbon, the first Greek letter.
Carbon c is the β carbon, the one oxidized in β-oxidation. The omega carbon is at the opposite end.

q: Cholesterol is the starting material for several hormones. Which hormone is NOT made from cholesterol?
h: Steroid hormones keep the four-ring steroid nucleus of cholesterol. Which hormone is a protein instead?
w: Insulin is a small protein (51 amino acids) made in the pancreas, not a steroid. Testosterone, estradiol (sex hormones) and cortisol (an adrenal corticosteroid) are all steroids synthesized from cholesterol, as are aldosterone, bile salts and vitamin D.
x: Testosterone is a steroid sex hormone with cholesterol's four-ring nucleus, so it is made from cholesterol.
Cortisol is an adrenal corticosteroid with the four-ring nucleus, so it is made from cholesterol.
Estradiol is a steroid sex hormone with the four-ring nucleus, so it is made from cholesterol.

q: Two students break down samples of the same vegetable oil (a triacylglycerol): one uses hot water with an H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst, the other uses aqueous NaOH. Compare the products of the two experiments.
c: Both give glycerol; acid gives fatty acids, and NaOH gives fatty acid salts (soaps)
Acid gives glycerol and fatty acids; NaOH gives glycerol and three alcohols
Acid gives three new esters; NaOH gives glycerol and free fatty acids
Fatty acid salts form in each case, but only the NaOH reaction releases glycerol
h: Both reactions break the same three ester bonds. Think about what a carboxylic acid becomes in a strongly basic solution.
w: Either way the three ester bonds are hydrolyzed and the alcohol portion, glycerol, is released. In acid the carboxylic acids are freed as RCOOH; in NaOH the base neutralizes them to RCOO−Na+, the salts we call soap. Fatty acids are the acid part of the ester, so they are never released as alcohols.
x: Fatty acids are the acid part of each ester, so they are never released as alcohols. The only alcohol produced is glycerol.
Hydrolysis breaks esters; it does not make new ones. And in NaOH the acids do not stay as free RCOOH.
Both reactions break the same three ester bonds, so both release glycerol. Salts form only where a strong base is present.

q: Phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes, but triacylglycerols do not; they collect as droplets inside fat cells. Why?
c: A triacylglycerol has no polar, charged head group; it is nonpolar throughout
A triacylglycerol has only one fatty acid tail, too few to line up in a bilayer
Triacylglycerols are too water soluble to stay in a membrane
Triacylglycerols contain a steroid ring that is too rigid to fit in a bilayer
h: A bilayer needs molecules with a polar head facing water and nonpolar tails facing inward. Compare the "head" of each lipid.
w: In a phospholipid one ester is replaced by a charged phosphate–amino alcohol head, so the molecule is amphipathic and lines up with heads toward water. In a triacylglycerol all three glycerol –OH groups are esterified to fatty acids, leaving no polar head; the whole molecule is nonpolar, so it simply clumps into oily droplets.
x: A triacylglycerol has three fatty acid tails, one on each glycerol –OH.
Triacylglycerols are insoluble in water, not too soluble. The problem is that no part of the molecule is attracted to water.
Triacylglycerols contain no steroid ring; that describes cholesterol, which is actually found in membranes.

q: Four examples of substances crossing a cell membrane are described in the table. Which process is facilitated transport?
h: Facilitated transport uses a protein channel or carrier but no ATP, and moves the substance from high to low concentration.
w: Row II moves glucose down its concentration gradient through a carrier protein without ATP: facilitated transport. Rows I and IV are simple diffusion (small O2 and CO2 molecules slip directly through the bilayer), and row III is active transport (ATP is spent to pump K+ against its gradient).
x: Row I is O<sub>2</sub> moving with no protein: small nonpolar molecules slip straight through the bilayer by simple diffusion.
Row III uses a pump and ATP to move K<sup>+</sup> from low to high concentration. That is active transport.
Row IV is CO<sub>2</sub> crossing with no protein: small molecules like this pass by simple diffusion.

q: Two side chains lie next to each other in the tertiary structure of an enzyme. For which pair is hydrogen bonding the main attraction holding them together?
h: Hydrogen bonds need an O–H or N–H plus an O or N. Charged pairs make salt bridges; hydrocarbon pairs are hydrophobic; two –SH groups make a disulfide.
w: Both serine and threonine side chains have an –OH, so one O–H can hydrogen-bond to the oxygen of the other: hydrogen bonding. Leucine/valine are hydrocarbons (hydrophobic interaction), lysine/glutamate carry opposite charges (salt bridge), and two cysteines are joined by a covalent disulfide bond.
x: Leucine and valine side chains are hydrocarbons with no O–H or N–H. They attract by hydrophobic interactions.
Lysine is positively charged and glutamate negatively charged, so their main attraction is an ionic salt bridge.
Two cysteine –SH groups are oxidized to a covalent disulfide bond, not held mainly by hydrogen bonds.

q: A chemist makes an alanine solution strongly basic with NaOH, to a pH far above its pI. Which of the structures drawn is the predominant form of alanine?
h: Far above the pI, OH<sup>−</sup> removes H<sup>+</sup> from acidic groups. Which groups on alanine can give up an H<sup>+</sup>?
w: Far above the pI the carboxyl group is deprotonated (–COO−) and the base has also pulled the proton off the –NH+3, leaving a neutral –NH2: the anion H2N–CH(CH3)–COO−, net charge −1. The zwitterion is the main form at the pI and the cation far below it; the fully uncharged –NH2/–COOH molecule is not the major form at any pH.
x: This is the zwitterion (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and –COO<sup>−</sup>), the main form at the pI. In strong base OH<sup>−</sup> removes another H<sup>+</sup>.
This form has –COOH and –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, net +1. That is the main form in strong acid, far below the pI.
This is the uncharged form, which is not the major form at any pH in water.

q: The tripeptide drawn (uncharged form) is completely hydrolyzed by digestive enzymes. What are the products?
c: Glycine, alanine and serine, using 2 H<sub>2</sub>O
Glycine, alanine and serine, using 3 H<sub>2</sub>O
One amino acid and one dipeptide, using 1 H<sub>2</sub>O
Three different carboxylic acids and NH<sub>3</sub>
h: Count the peptide (amide) bonds: each one hydrolyzed consumes one water and separates two amino acids.
w: A tripeptide has two peptide bonds, so complete hydrolysis uses 2 H2O and releases the three free amino acids: glycine (H side chain), alanine (–CH3) and serine (–CH2OH). "3 H2O" counts amino acids instead of bonds. Hydrolysis breaks only the amide bonds; the α-amino groups stay on their amino acids as NH+3, not as free NH3.
x: 3 H<sub>2</sub>O counts the amino acids instead of the peptide bonds. Each water breaks one peptide bond.
Complete hydrolysis breaks every peptide bond, not just one. Count how many amide bonds the tripeptide has.
Hydrolysis breaks only the peptide (amide) bonds. Each amino group stays attached to its own amino acid; none is released as NH<sub>3</sub>.

q: A nursing student says that enzymes are "used up" by the reactions they speed up. Which statement about enzymes is actually correct?
c: They are proteins that speed up a reaction without being used up
They are carbohydrates that supply energy to a reaction
They shift the equilibrium so that more product forms
They are consumed in the reaction, so more must be eaten daily
h: Enzymes are biological catalysts. What is a catalyst made of in the body, and what does a catalyst do and not do?
w: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as catalysts: they lower the activation energy and are released unchanged, so one enzyme molecule can be reused thousands of times. A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the energy difference between reactants and products, only how fast equilibrium is reached. Vitamins, not enzymes, must be eaten.
x: Enzymes are proteins, not carbohydrates, and they do not supply energy to the reaction.
A catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not shift the equilibrium.
This repeats the student's misconception. Catalysts come out of the reaction unchanged and can be reused.

q: Four digestive enzymes are matched in the table with the bond each one hydrolyzes and the nutrient it digests. Which enzyme replaces the question mark?
h: Match the name to the substrate: -ase added to the thing it works on, or a name based on protein, fat, starch or nucleic acid.
w: Peptide (amide) bonds between amino acids are hydrolyzed by proteases such as pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin. Lipases hydrolyze the ester bonds of fats, amylase hydrolyzes the α(1→4) bonds of starch, and nucleases hydrolyze the phosphodiester bonds of DNA and RNA.
x: Lipases hydrolyze ester bonds in fats; that row already has an enzyme. The blank row hydrolyzes peptide bonds.
Amylase hydrolyzes glycosidic bonds in starch. The blank row hydrolyzes peptide (amide) bonds.
Nucleases hydrolyze phosphodiester bonds in DNA and RNA. The blank row hydrolyzes the bonds in proteins.

q: Lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme measured in blood tests for tissue damage, catalyzes the reaction drawn. To which class of enzymes does it belong?
h: Look at what happens to the –OH carbon: it becomes C=O while NAD<sup>+</sup> picks up the hydrogen.
w: A secondary alcohol (–CH(OH)–) is converted to a ketone (C=O) and the hydrogens are transferred to NAD+, so the reaction is an oxidation–reduction and the enzyme is an oxidoreductase (dehydrogenases belong here). Nothing is rearranged within one molecule (isomerase), no water is used to split a bond (hydrolase) and no group is removed to form a double bond (lyase).
x: An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule without changing its formula. Here H is removed and given to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. No water is used and the molecule is not split.
A lyase removes a group to form a C=C or adds one to it. Here a C–OH becomes C=O, with hydrogen going to NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: A liver esterase breaks down the ester shown (a food flavoring) in the reaction drawn. In which of the six enzyme classes is this esterase placed?
h: The reagent over the arrow is water, and the ester splits into two pieces. Which enzyme class uses water to break bonds?
w: The ester bond is split by water into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, which is hydrolysis, so the enzyme is a hydrolase (lipases, proteases and amylases are also hydrolases). A ligase joins two molecules using ATP, a transferase moves a group from one molecule to another and an oxidoreductase changes oxidation state.
x: A ligase joins two molecules using ATP. Here one molecule is split into two by water.
A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Look at the reagent over the arrow: water splits the ester.
An oxidoreductase changes oxidation state, usually with NAD<sup>+</sup> or FAD. No redox coenzyme is involved here.

q: Rickets is a childhood disease in which bones stay soft and bend because too little calcium is deposited in them. A deficiency of which vitamin causes rickets, and what is that vitamin’s role?
c: Vitamin D; it is needed to absorb calcium and phosphate for bone
Vitamin A; it is needed to make the visual pigment in the retina
Vitamin K; it is needed to make blood-clotting proteins
Vitamin B<sub>1</sub>; it is converted to a coenzyme for decarboxylation
h: Which fat-soluble vitamin is made in skin exposed to sunlight and controls blood calcium?
w: Rickets (soft, bending bones) is caused by a lack of vitamin D, which the body needs to absorb Ca2+ and phosphate from the intestine and deposit them in bone. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, and B vitamins are water-soluble coenzyme precursors.
x: Vitamin A is needed for vision; a deficiency causes night blindness, not soft bones.
Vitamin K is needed for clotting; a deficiency causes bleeding, not soft bones.
Thiamine (B<sub>1</sub>) is a water-soluble coenzyme precursor. Rickets involves calcium and bone, which points to a fat-soluble vitamin.

q: A nutrition handout pairs four vitamins with a claimed function (table). Which pairing is correct?
h: A, D, E and K are fat-soluble with specific jobs (vision, bone, clotting); the B vitamins become coenzymes.
w: Row II is correct: vitamin K is required to make the clotting factors, so a deficiency causes bleeding. Row I has the roles of A and D reversed (A is for vision, D for calcium and bone); row III is wrong because niacin (B3) is the precursor of NAD+, not of FAD (that is riboflavin, B2); row IV is wrong because vitamin D is fat-soluble and is stored.

head: Row
Vitamin
Function stated
rows: absorption of calcium for strong bones
water-soluble; excess is lost in urine daily

x: Row I gives vitamin A the job of vitamin D. Vitamin A is needed for vision.
Niacin (B<sub>3</sub>) is the precursor of NAD<sup>+</sup>. FAD comes from riboflavin (B<sub>2</sub>).
Vitamin D is fat-soluble and can be stored in the body, so excess is not lost in urine each day.

q: A student made the comparison chart of DNA and RNA shown. One row contains an error. Which one?
h: Check each row against what you know: sugar, bases, number of strands and where each is found.
w: Row III is wrong: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine, so RNA has A, G, C and U, while DNA has A, G, C and T. The other rows are correct: DNA has deoxyribose and RNA has ribose (I), DNA is a double helix and RNA is mostly single-stranded (II), and DNA stays in the nucleus while mRNA travels to ribosomes in the cytoplasm (IV).
x: Row I is correct: DNA contains deoxyribose and RNA contains ribose.
Row II is correct: DNA is a double helix, and RNA is mostly single-stranded.
Row IV is correct: DNA stays in the nucleus, and RNA is found in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.

q: A liver cell needs the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, so it first copies that gene into mRNA (transcription). In which part of the cell is this mRNA made?
c: In the nucleus, where the DNA is
In the cytoplasm, on the ribosomes
Outside the nucleus, in the endoplasmic reticulum
h: RNA polymerase must read the DNA template. Where is the cell's DNA kept?
w: In eukaryotic cells the DNA never leaves the nucleus, so RNA polymerase makes mRNA in the nucleus; the finished mRNA is then exported through the nuclear envelope to ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where translation occurs. Replication also happens in the nucleus. A common mix-up is to place transcription with translation in the cytoplasm.
x: Ribosomes in the cytoplasm carry out translation, not transcription. RNA polymerase must read the DNA template.
Mitochondria hold only a small amount of their own DNA. Genes like this enzyme's are in the cell's main DNA store.
The endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes for making proteins, but no chromosomal DNA to transcribe.

q: During DNA replication, which enzyme unwinds the double helix and separates the two parent strands so they can serve as templates?
h: The name of the enzyme describes its job on the helix.
w: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and unwinds the helix, forming the replication fork. DNA polymerase then adds complementary nucleotides to each template (5′→3′), DNA ligase seals gaps between fragments, and RNA polymerase is used for transcription, not replication.
x: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to each new strand. It needs the helix already opened.
DNA ligase seals gaps between DNA fragments. It does not unwind the helix.
RNA polymerase makes RNA during transcription. It is not the replication enzyme that opens the helix.

q: In translation, a tRNA is attached to its amino acid and also pairs with a codon on the mRNA. Which statement correctly compares the two attachments?
c: The amino acid is held by a covalent ester bond; the codon by hydrogen bonds
The amino acid and the codon are each held by hydrogen bonds between bases
The amino acid is held by hydrogen bonds; the codon by a covalent bond
The amino acid and the codon are each held by covalent peptide bonds
h: Codon–anticodon pairing must be easy to break after the amino acid is delivered. The amino acid must stay firmly attached until then.
w: The amino acid is joined to the 3′ end of its tRNA through a covalent ester bond (aminoacyl-tRNA), while the anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon only through hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A–U, G–C), which let the tRNA detach once the peptide bond has formed.
x: Amino acids have no bases, so they cannot be held by base pairing. The amino acid needs a firmer link.
This reverses the two. The codon pairing must be easy to break, and the amino acid must stay firmly attached.
Peptide bonds join amino acids to each other. Codon–anticodon pairing is a weaker, temporary attraction.

q: Which metabolic term means "the synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate molecules such as lactate or amino acids"?
h: Break the word apart: gluco- (glucose), neo- (new), -genesis (creation).
w: Gluconeogenesis = "new glucose creation", mainly in the liver during fasting. Glycogenolysis is the splitting (-lysis) of glycogen into glucose, glycolysis is the splitting of glucose into pyruvate and glycogenesis is making glycogen from glucose.
x: Glycogenolysis is the splitting (-lysis) of glycogen into glucose units. That starts from a stored carbohydrate, not from lactate or amino acids.
Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate. It breaks glucose down rather than making new glucose.
Glycogenesis makes glycogen from glucose. It does not create new glucose from non-carbohydrate molecules.

q: After a large meal, the liver converts excess glucose into glycogen for storage. Which term names this process, and is it anabolic or catabolic?
h: -genesis means making; -lysis means splitting. Making a polymer from monomers builds up, so which category is that?
w: Joining glucose units into the polymer glycogen is glycogenesis, a building (anabolic) process that uses ATP. Glycogenolysis is the reverse breakdown; glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate; gluconeogenesis is anabolic but makes glucose, not glycogen.
x: Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen down into glucose: the opposite of storing excess glucose.
