Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate for energy. The liver here is storing glucose as a polymer.
Gluconeogenesis is anabolic, but it makes new glucose from non-carbohydrates. Here glucose is being turned into a storage polymer.

q: The last step of the citric acid cycle, malate → oxaloacetate, is drawn. Which coenzyme is required, and what happens to it?
c: NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
FAD, which is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
NADH, which is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
Coenzyme A, which accepts the acetyl group
h: An alcohol is being oxidized to a ketone. Which coenzyme picks up hydrogen from an alcohol or aldehyde, and which from a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group?
w: The secondary alcohol –CH(OH)– loses two hydrogens to become a C=O: an oxidation. Oxidations of alcohols and aldehydes use NAD+, which is reduced to NADH (later worth about 2.5 ATP). FAD is reserved for oxidizing a C–C single bond to a C=C double bond, as in succinate → fumarate.
x: FAD handles C–C single bond → C=C double bond oxidations, like succinate → fumarate. Here an alcohol becomes a ketone.
Malate is losing hydrogens here (oxidized), so the coenzyme must gain them. NADH being oxidized would mean hydrogens are added to the substrate.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups and accepts no hydrogen. This step is an oxidation of an alcohol to a ketone.

q: After alcohol is consumed, the liver converts acetaldehyde to acetate as drawn. Which description of this step is correct?
c: Oxidation of an aldehyde; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
Reduction of an aldehyde; NADH is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
h: Compare the carbon in question: an aldehyde carbon becomes a carboxylate carbon. Does it gain oxygen or hydrogen?
w: The –CHO carbon gains an oxygen (and loses its H) to become –COO−, so acetaldehyde is oxidized; the electrons and hydrogen go to NAD+, forming NADH. This is why heavy drinking floods the liver with NADH. No CO2 leaves and no bond is split by water.
x: The aldehyde carbon gains an oxygen to become a carboxylate, which is oxidation, not reduction. Check which way the coenzyme changes too.
Hydrolysis splits a molecule into two pieces using water. Both structures here have two carbons; only the end carbon changed.
Decarboxylation removes a carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>. Both molecules have two carbons, so no carbon was lost.

q: In the step of the citric acid cycle drawn, succinate loses two hydrogen atoms to become fumarate. Which coenzyme picks up those hydrogen atoms?
h: Look at what changed: a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– became a –CH=CH–. One specific coenzyme handles this kind of oxidation.
w: Oxidizing a saturated C–C bond to a C=C double bond (removing 2 H) is the job of FAD, which is reduced to FADH2 (later worth about 1.5 ATP). NAD+ handles alcohol → carbonyl oxidations. Coenzyme A carries acyl groups and ATP transfers phosphate; neither accepts hydrogen.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> usually oxidizes alcohols and aldehydes to C=O groups. Here a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– became a C=C double bond.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups such as acetyl; it does not accept hydrogen atoms from the substrate.
ATP transfers phosphate groups and does not accept hydrogen atoms. Also, ATP → ADP is a phosphate change, not a reduction.

q: Liver cells attach a phosphate group to glycerol, as drawn, before building triacylglycerols. Which coenzyme change goes along with this phosphorylation?
h: A phosphate group was added to the molecule. Where does a cell get a phosphate group it can donate?
w: Adding a phosphate group to a molecule (phosphorylation) uses ATP as the phosphate donor, leaving ADP. "ADP → ATP" is the reverse: it describes a step that makes ATP by removing a phosphate from a substrate. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD+ and FAD are not involved.
x: ADP → ATP happens when a phosphate is removed from a substrate. Here the glycerol gains a phosphate, so the donor loses one.
NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH goes with an oxidation (hydrogen removed). Glycerol keeps all its hydrogens and simply gains a phosphate.
FAD → FADH<sub>2</sub> goes with forming a C=C double bond. No hydrogen is removed here; a phosphate group is added.

q: A sprinter's oxygen-starved leg muscle carries out the reaction drawn, turning pyruvate into lactate. Which label describes what happens to pyruvate?
c: Reduction; NADH is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
Oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
Hydration; H<sub>2</sub>O adds to the C=O
Decarboxylation; a carbon is lost as CO<sub>2</sub>
h: Compare the middle carbon: a ketone C=O becomes –CH(OH)–. Did the molecule gain or lose hydrogen?
w: The ketone gains two hydrogen atoms to become a secondary alcohol, so pyruvate is reduced; the hydrogens come from NADH, which is oxidized back to NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Both molecules keep three carbons, so there is no decarboxylation, and no water is added.
x: Compare the middle carbon: the C=O becomes –CH(OH)–, so pyruvate gains hydrogen. The arrow also shows NADH turning into NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Hydration would add H<sub>2</sub>O. Here two hydrogen atoms come from a coenzyme, as shown over the arrow.
Decarboxylation would lose a carbon. Both pyruvate and lactate have three carbons.

q: In yeast, pyruvate is converted to acetaldehyde as drawn (the step before ethanol forms). How is this reaction labeled?
c: Oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
h: Count carbons on each side. Three became two: the small molecule written over the arrow left.
w: Pyruvate (3 C) loses its carboxylate carbon as CO2, leaving acetaldehyde (2 C): a decarboxylation. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD+ is not reduced here (it is NADH that then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol). Water is neither removed nor added.
x: An oxidation removes hydrogen or adds oxygen. Here no hydrogen is removed; count the carbons and look at what is written over the arrow.
Dehydration removes H<sub>2</sub>O. The small molecule over the arrow is CO<sub>2</sub>, and a carbon was lost.
Hydrolysis uses water to split a bond. No water is added here; a carbon leaves as a gas.

q: Which coenzyme carries the two-carbon acetyl group from pyruvate (or from β-oxidation) into the citric acid cycle?
h: The acetyl group is attached through a thioester bond to a coenzyme made from vitamin B<sub>5</sub>.
w: Coenzyme A (HS–CoA) bonds to the acetyl group through its –SH, forming acetyl CoA, which delivers the two carbons to oxaloacetate to make citrate. NAD+ and FAD carry hydrogen (electrons); ATP carries phosphate groups.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> carries hydrogen (electrons), not carbon groups. The acetyl carrier links to the acetyl group through a sulfur atom.
FAD carries hydrogen (electrons), not carbon groups. Think of a coenzyme that forms a thioester with the acetyl group.
ATP carries phosphate groups and energy, not acetyl groups. The carrier you want is made from vitamin B5.

q: NADH delivers its electrons to complex I of the electron transport chain. In this step NADH is ____ and complex I is ____.
h: LEO says GER: Losing Electrons is Oxidation; Gaining Electrons is Reduction. NADH gives electrons away.
w: NADH loses two electrons (and H+) and becomes NAD+, so it is oxidized; complex I gains those electrons, so it is reduced. The electrons then pass down the chain to O2, each carrier being reduced then re-oxidized. Students often reverse this because NADH is "the reduced coenzyme", but it gets oxidized when it unloads.
x: NADH is the reduced form, but here it gives its electrons away. Losing electrons is oxidation, and whatever gains them is reduced.
Electrons cannot just disappear: if NADH loses them, complex I must gain them. Both cannot be oxidized.
NADH loses electrons in this step, so it cannot be the one being reduced. Use LEO says GER.

q: Glycolysis produces 2 NADH per glucose in the cytosol. What must happen to these NADH before their energy appears as ATP?
c: Their electrons must be shuttled into the mitochondria to the electron transport chain
They are hydrolyzed in the cytosol, releasing their stored energy directly as ATP
They donate their hydrogen atoms to pyruvate, converting it into acetyl CoA
They diffuse out of the muscle cell and are excreted in the urine unchanged
h: Where is the electron transport chain located? NADH is only "worth" ATP when O<sub>2</sub> takes its electrons.
w: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner mitochondrial membrane, so cytosolic NADH must pass its electrons (via a shuttle) into the mitochondria, where NADH is oxidized to NAD+ and the energy drives ATP synthesis (about 2.5 ATP each). NADH cannot be hydrolyzed for ATP, and pyruvate → acetyl CoA produces NADH rather than using it.
x: NADH is not hydrolyzed like ATP. Its energy is released only when its electrons are passed along a chain to O<sub>2</sub>.
Pyruvate → acetyl CoA actually produces NADH; it does not use it. Think about where the electron transport chain is located.
NADH is a recycled coenzyme, not a waste product. Its electrons are used to make ATP inside the cell.

q: When a cyclist pedals, ATP made from the oxidation of glucose is used by muscle proteins. Which energy conversion best describes muscle contraction?
c: Chemical energy in ATP → mechanical energy of movement
Mechanical energy → chemical energy stored in glycogen
Light energy → chemical energy stored in ATP
Electrical energy of the nerve → chemical energy in NADH
h: The energy was stored in chemical bonds of food, then of ATP. What form does it take when a muscle shortens?
w: Hydrolysis of ATP releases chemical energy, which myosin converts into mechanical work as the muscle fibers slide, with much of the rest lost as heat (why exercise warms you). Storing glycogen is chemical → chemical; light → chemical is photosynthesis.
x: This is backward. During contraction, energy stored in ATP is spent to move the muscle, not stored in glycogen.
Light → chemical energy happens in photosynthesis in plants. Muscle runs on ATP made from food.
Muscle contraction does not make NADH. The energy in ATP is used to produce movement and heat.

q: In the citric acid cycle drawn, one intermediate has been replaced by a question mark. Which compound is missing?
h: The hidden compound has 5 carbons: it forms when isocitrate (6 C) loses CO<sub>2</sub>, and it loses another CO<sub>2</sub> to give succinyl CoA (4 C).
w: Isocitrate (6 C) undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to α-ketoglutarate (5 C), which is then decarboxylated again to succinyl CoA (4 C); the two CO2 on the arrows confirm it. Pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA before the cycle, acetoacetate is a ketone body and glucose 6-phosphate belongs to glycolysis, so none of them is an intermediate of the cycle.
x: Pyruvate is changed to acetyl CoA before the cycle starts, so it is not a cycle intermediate. The missing compound has 5 carbons.
Acetoacetate is a ketone body made in the liver during fasting. It is not one of the citric acid cycle intermediates.
Glucose 6-phosphate belongs to glycolysis (and glycogen metabolism). The missing cycle intermediate has 5 carbons.

q: Before a fatty acid can be oxidized it is "activated" by attaching coenzyme A, a step in which ATP is converted to AMP and two phosphates. What is the energy cost of activation?
c: No ATP; the step releases energy
h: ATP → AMP breaks two phosphate bonds, not one. Count how many ATP it takes to rebuild ATP from AMP.
w: Activation hydrolyzes ATP to AMP + PPi, breaking two high-energy phosphate bonds; restoring AMP to ATP costs two phosphorylations, so the cost is counted as 2 ATP. This is why the total ATP from a fatty acid is reduced by 2 (for example 108 − 2 = 106 for palmitic acid). A hexokinase-type phosphorylation (ATP → ADP) would cost only 1.
x: Activation uses one ATP molecule, but it goes all the way to AMP, breaking two phosphate bonds. Count how much it costs to rebuild ATP from AMP.
This double-counts. Check how many high-energy phosphate bonds are actually broken when one ATP becomes AMP; it is fewer than four.
Activation costs energy: ATP is broken down to AMP to attach coenzyme A. That is why the fatty acid's total ATP yield is reduced.

q: Each turn of the β-oxidation spiral shown produces one NADH and one FADH2 (plus an acetyl CoA that enters the citric acid cycle separately). Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, how many ATP come from the coenzymes of one turn?
h: Count the coenzymes one turn makes, then give each one its ATP value from the question.
w: One turn: 1 NADH × 2.5 + 1 FADH2 × 1.5 = 4 ATP. "2.5" counts only the NADH, "5" uses the old value of 2 ATP per FADH2 plus 3 per NADH, and "14" adds the 10 ATP from the acetyl CoA going through the citric acid cycle.
x: That counts only the NADH. One turn also produces an FADH<sub>2</sub>, which is worth ATP too.
This uses the old values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 as stated in the question.
This adds the 10 ATP from the acetyl CoA going through the citric acid cycle. The question asks only about the coenzymes from the spiral itself.

q: Palmitoyl CoA (16 carbons) goes completely through the β-oxidation spiral shown. Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, how many ATP are produced from the NADH and FADH2 of the spiral itself (not counting the acetyl CoA or the activation cost)?
h: Find the number of turns first (one fewer than the number of acetyl CoA), then multiply by the ATP from one turn's NADH + FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 16 C gives 8 acetyl CoA in 16/2 − 1 = 7 turns. Each turn yields 1 NADH (2.5) + 1 FADH2 (1.5) = 4 ATP, so 7 × 4 = 28 ATP. "32" uses 8 turns, "20" counts only the NADH and uses 8 turns (8 × 2.5), and "106" is the total yield including the 8 acetyl CoA minus activation.
x: This uses 8 turns. A 16-carbon chain gives 8 acetyl CoA in only 7 turns, because the last turn splits a 4-carbon piece into two acetyl CoA.
This counts only the NADH (and uses 8 turns). Each turn also makes an FADH<sub>2</sub>, worth 1.5 ATP.
106 is the total ATP for palmitate, including the acetyl CoA and the activation cost. The question asks only about NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> from the spiral.

q: A disaccharide is hydrolyzed to two D-glucose molecules. Benedict's test on the intact disaccharide is positive, and the enzyme that digests it in humans is maltase, not lactase or cellulase. Which linkage joins the two rings?
c: α(1→4), with one free hemiacetal carbon
β(1→4), with one free hemiacetal carbon
α,β(1→2), with no free hemiacetal carbon
α(1→6), with the two anomeric carbons used
h: Positive Benedict's test → a hemiacetal is still free. Maltase digests one specific kind of glucose–glucose bond.
w: Maltose is the glucose–glucose disaccharide hydrolyzed by maltase, joined α(1→4); its second ring keeps a free hemiacetal at C1, which opens to an aldehyde and reduces Cu2+. A β(1→4) glucose pair is cellobiose (from cellulose, not digestible); α,β(1→2) is sucrose, which is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are used.
x: A β(1→4) glucose pair is cellobiose, from cellulose. Maltase does not break this β bond, and humans cannot digest cellulose.
α,β(1→2) uses both anomeric carbons, as in sucrose, so it would test negative with Benedict's. This sugar tests positive and has no fructose.
If both anomeric carbons were used, no hemiacetal would be free and Benedict's test would be negative. Also, α(1→6) is the branch-point link, not maltose's.

q: A water-soluble enzyme is placed in a nonpolar solvent such as hexane. Which change in its structure is most likely, and why does activity fall?
c: Hydrophobic side chains turn outward and polar ones inward, so the active site is lost
The peptide bonds hydrolyze, so the primary structure and with it the active site are destroyed
New disulfide bonds form between all of the cysteine residues, locking the active site shut
The α-helices convert into β-sheets, but the shape of the active site itself is unchanged
h: In water, hydrophobic R groups hide inside and polar R groups face out. What happens when the solvent itself is nonpolar?
w: In hexane the driving force reverses: hydrophobic side chains are now happiest facing the solvent and polar side chains cluster inside, so the protein refolds or unfolds and the precisely shaped active site is lost: denaturation of tertiary structure. The covalent peptide bonds are not broken by a solvent (that needs hydrolysis), and disulfide formation requires an oxidizing agent.
x: A solvent like hexane does not hydrolyze peptide bonds; that needs water plus an enzyme or strong acid. The change here is to folding.
Disulfide bonds form only by oxidation of –SH groups, which a nonpolar solvent does not cause. Think about where nonpolar side chains would now prefer to be.
Any change in folding also changes the active site, whose shape depends on the folded protein. Think about which side chains now prefer to face outward.

q: A DNA template strand segment reads 3′-TAC GGA ATT-5′. Use the codon table given. What peptide is made?
h: Transcribe the template into mRNA (A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C) written 5′→3′, then read codons from the table.
w: Complementary mRNA (5′→3′): AUG CCU UAA. From the table AUG = Met, CCU = Pro and UAA = stop, so translation gives Met–Pro and then stops. "Tyr–Gly–Ile" comes from reading the DNA letters as if they were codons; "Met–Pro–Asn" treats UAA as an amino acid codon; "Asn–Pro–Met" lists the amino acids in the wrong direction (and treats UAA as Asn).
x: This treats UAA as a codon for an amino acid. In the table UAA is a stop codon.
This reads the DNA letters directly as codons. First transcribe the template into mRNA.
This lists the amino acids from the wrong end and adds an amino acid where translation should stop.

q: A patient takes a drug that is a competitive inhibitor of an enzyme. After a meal, the concentration of the enzyme's natural substrate rises sharply. What happens to the degree of inhibition, and why?
c: It decreases, because substrate outcompetes the drug for the active site
It increases, because more substrate means more enzyme–inhibitor complexes
It is unchanged, because the drug binds at an allosteric site
It becomes permanent, because the substrate traps the drug in the active site
h: Competitive inhibitors and substrate fight for the same spot. Which wins when the substrate concentration is much higher?
w: Substrate and a competitive inhibitor bind the same active site, so raising [substrate] shifts the competition toward enzyme–substrate complexes and the inhibition decreases (the maximum rate can still be reached). Inhibition unaffected by substrate describes a noncompetitive (allosteric-site) inhibitor; permanent loss describes an irreversible inhibitor.
x: More substrate means more enzyme–substrate complexes, not more enzyme–inhibitor complexes. Both are competing for the same site.
A competitive inhibitor binds the active site, not an allosteric site. Binding there means substrate concentration matters.
Substrate does not trap a competitive inhibitor; competitive binding is reversible. Permanent loss would describe an irreversible inhibitor.

q: A food company hydrogenates 2.0 mol of a cooking oil whose triacylglycerol contains one palmitic acid (16:0), one oleic acid (18:1) and one linoleic acid (18:2). What amount of H<sub>2</sub> is consumed, and how does the melting point change?
c: 2.0 mol H<sub>2</sub>; melting point is unchanged
h: Count the C=C bonds in one molecule (the number after the colon), then scale to 2.0 mol. Saturated chains pack better.
w: One molecule has 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 C=C bonds, so 1 mol of fat needs 3 mol H2 and 2.0 mol needs 6.0 mol H2. Removing the cis kinks lets the chains pack tightly, so the melting point rises (an oil becomes a solid fat). "3.0 mol" forgets the 2.0 mol of fat.
x: 3.0 mol H<sub>2</sub> is right for 1 mol of fat, but the company hydrogenates 2.0 mol.
The H<sub>2</sub> amount fits, but removing cis kinks lets chains pack better. What does that do to the melting point?
2.0 mol H₂ gives only one H₂ per molecule. Count the C=C bonds in each chain, and remember that adding H₂ changes how the chains pack.

q: An unknown white solid dissolves in 5% NaHCO<sub>3</sub>(aq) with bubbles of CO<sub>2</sub>. Which compound could it be?
h: Only one class of organic compound is acidic enough to react with sodium bicarbonate. Which one?
w: Carboxylic acids are the only common organic acids strong enough to react with NaHCO3: RCOOH + NaHCO3 → RCOO−Na+ + H2O + CO2. The bubbles point to benzoic acid, which dissolves as sodium benzoate.
x: Phenol is a weak acid that dissolves in NaOH, but it is not acidic enough to react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, so there are no bubbles.
Alcohols are about as weakly acidic as water. Cyclohexanol does not react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub> or NaOH.
Naphthalene is a hydrocarbon with no acidic H. It does not react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>.

q: Cream of tartar, a by-product of making wine from Valley grapes, is potassium hydrogen tartrate: tartaric acid with one –COOH still present. Baking powder mixes it with baking soda (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>). When water is added, CO<sub>2</sub> bubbles form. Which part of the cream of tartar causes this?
c: its remaining –COOH group, which is acidic enough to react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>
its two alcohol –OH groups, which react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>
the K<sup>+</sup> ion, which reacts with water to give CO<sub>2</sub>
its C–H bonds, which are oxidized by NaHCO<sub>3</sub>
h: Bubbles of CO<sub>2</sub> with sodium bicarbonate are the test for which functional group?
w: Only a carboxylic acid group reacts with NaHCO3 to release CO2: –COOH + HCO3− → –COO− + H2O + CO2. The remaining –COOH group of the hydrogen tartrate supplies the H+, and the gas makes the batter rise.
x: Alcohol –OH groups are about as weakly acidic as water and do not react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>.
K<sup>+</sup> is a spectator ion. It has no carbon, so it cannot be the source of CO<sub>2</sub>; the CO<sub>2</sub> comes from the bicarbonate.
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> is a weak base, not an oxidizing agent. The reaction is an acid–base reaction.

q: Dehydration of cyclohexanol to cyclohexene with an acid catalyst is reversible. In the lab, cyclohexene (bp 83 °C) is distilled out of the flask as it forms, while cyclohexanol (bp 161 °C) stays behind. Why does this increase the yield of cyclohexene?
c: Removing a product shifts the equilibrium toward more products (Le Chatelier's principle)
Distilling makes the acid catalyst stronger
Removing cyclohexene makes the reaction release more heat
Cyclohexanol boils away first, leaving the product behind
h: cyclohexanol ⇌ cyclohexene + H<sub>2</sub>O. What does an equilibrium do when one product is taken away?
w: The reaction is an equilibrium, cyclohexanol ⇌ cyclohexene + H2O. Removing cyclohexene as it forms keeps the reverse reaction (hydration) from catching up, so the equilibrium shifts toward products (Le Chatelier's principle).
x: A catalyst speeds up both directions equally and is not changed by distillation. The yield increases because the product is removed.
Removing a product does not change how much heat the reaction releases. It changes the position of the equilibrium.
Cyclohexanol boils at 161 °C, much higher than cyclohexene (83 °C), so it stays in the flask. Only the product distills out.

q: Hydration of an alkene and dehydration of an alcohol are the same reaction run in opposite directions: alkene + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ alcohol, with an acid catalyst. Which conditions favor making the ALCOHOL?
c: a large excess of water with dilute acid
removing water from the flask as it forms
distilling the alkene out of the flask as it forms
h: Le Chatelier's principle: adding a reactant pushes an equilibrium toward the products. Which side is water on?
w: Water is a reactant in hydration, so a large excess of water with dilute acid pushes the equilibrium toward the alcohol. Concentrated acid and heat, or removing water or alkene, push it the other way, toward dehydration.
x: Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and heat are the conditions for dehydration, which makes the alkene.
Removing water takes away a reactant of hydration, which shifts the equilibrium toward the alkene.
Distilling out the alkene removes a reactant of hydration, so less alcohol forms, not more.

q: 4-Methylphenol (p-cresol) is only slightly soluble in water but dissolves completely in NaOH(aq). It does not react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>(aq). 1-Hexanol dissolves in neither base. What do these tests show?
c: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols but less acidic than carboxylic acids
Phenols are bases, which is why they react with NaOH
Phenols are more acidic than carboxylic acids such as acetic acid
1-Hexanol is more acidic than 4-methylphenol, so it stays undissolved
h: NaOH reacts with any acid stronger than water; NaHCO<sub>3</sub> reacts only with carboxylic acids. Which tests did the phenol pass?
w: NaOH turns the phenol into its water-soluble sodium salt, so the phenol is acidic; the alcohol does not react, so it is less acidic. NaHCO3 does not react, so the phenol is weaker than a carboxylic acid. Ranking: carboxylic acid > phenol > alcohol.
x: NaOH is a base. A compound that reacts with it and dissolves as a salt is acting as an acid, not a base.
Carboxylic acids react with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, and this phenol does not, so the phenol is the weaker acid.
The alcohol does not react even with NaOH, so it is less acidic than the phenol, not more.

q: Which statement best describes a neurotransmitter?
c: a chemical that carries a signal from a nerve cell across a synapse
a hormone carried by the blood to organs far from where it is made
an enzyme that breaks down nerve signals in the brain and spinal cord
the electrical signal that travels along a nerve fiber to its end
h: Think about how a signal gets across the tiny gap between two nerve cells.
w: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger released by a nerve cell. It crosses the synapse, binds to receptors on the next cell, and is then removed or broken down. Many neurotransmitters are amines, such as dopamine and serotonin.
x: A hormone travels through the blood to distant tissues. A neurotransmitter acts across the short gap between two cells.
Enzymes such as acetylcholinesterase break neurotransmitters down, but the enzyme is not the messenger itself.
The electrical signal travels along the nerve fiber. At the synapse a chemical messenger carries the signal to the next cell.

q: Dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine are neurotransmitters made from amino acids. Each carries a positive charge in body fluids (pH about 7.4). Which functional group do all four share, and why is it charged?
c: An amine, which accepts H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4
An amide, which accepts H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4
An amine, which gives up H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4
A carboxylic acid, which gives up H<sup>+</sup> at pH 7.4
h: They are made from amino acids by removing the –COOH group. Which group is left, and is it an acid or a base?
w: All four keep the amine nitrogen of their parent amino acid (the –COOH is removed). Amines are weak bases, so at pH 7.4 the nitrogen accepts H+ and becomes –NH3+ (or –NH2+–), giving the positive charge. Amides are not basic, and a group that gives up H+ (like –COOH) becomes negative.
x: An amide N is bonded to a C=O, which pulls its lone pair into resonance, so amides are neutral, not basic. These four molecules have N bonded only to C and H.

The group is an amine, but amines are weak bases: they gain H<sup>+</sup> (becoming –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), which is what makes them positive. Losing H<sup>+</sup> would not give a positive charge.
A carboxylic acid that gives up H<sup>+</sup> becomes –COO<sup>−</sup>, a negative charge. These molecules are made by removing the –COOH group, and they are positive.

q: SSRI antidepressants such as fluoxetine (Prozac) block the reuptake of serotonin, the step in which the sending nerve cell takes serotonin back in from the synapse. What is the effect?
c: Serotonin stays in the synapse longer, so its signal lasts longer
The body stops making serotonin in the sending nerve cell
Serotonin is broken down faster by enzymes in the synapse
Serotonin can no longer bind to its receptors on the next cell
h: If the sending cell cannot take serotonin back in, where does the serotonin stay?
w: Reuptake normally clears serotonin from the synapse and ends its signal. Blocking it means serotonin stays in the synapse longer and keeps acting on the receptors of the next cell.
x: An SSRI acts on the reuptake protein. It does not stop the body from making serotonin.
Blocking reuptake leaves more serotonin in the synapse, not less. Faster breakdown would weaken the signal.
That would describe a receptor blocker. SSRIs leave the receptors free, and more serotonin is available to bind them.

q: Ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) from dairies and fertilizer reacts in Valley air with nitric acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>) from vehicle exhaust, forming tiny particles of ammonium nitrate, NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>. In this reaction, ammonia acts as
c: a base that accepts H<sup>+</sup> to form the ammonium ion
an acid that donates H<sup>+</sup> to the nitrate ion
an oxidizing agent that takes electrons from HNO<sub>3</sub>
a catalyst that speeds the reaction but is not changed
h: Amines and ammonia have a lone pair on nitrogen. What do they do with H<sup>+</sup>?
w: Like an amine, ammonia uses its nitrogen lone pair to accept H+ from the acid, forming NH4+. The product, ammonium nitrate, is an ammonium salt, just like the salt formed when an amine reacts with HCl.
x: Nitric acid donates the H<sup>+</sup>. Ammonia gains it.
This is an acid–base reaction. No electrons are transferred between the reactants.
Ammonia is used up and becomes part of the product, so it is not a catalyst.

q: Rank benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), toluene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and phenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: Which compound can hydrogen bond to itself? Of the two hydrocarbons, which is bigger?
w: Phenol's O–H lets its molecules hydrogen bond to each other, so it boils highest (about 182 °C). Toluene is larger than benzene and has stronger dispersion forces (about 111 °C vs 80 °C). Order: phenol > toluene > benzene.
x: Toluene has only dispersion forces. Phenol's molecules hydrogen bond to one another, which takes more energy to overcome.
This reverses the order. Hydrogen bonding and larger size both raise the boiling point.
Phenol is right at the top, but benzene is smaller than toluene, so benzene has weaker dispersion forces and boils lower.

q: Of these four benzene derivatives, which is the most soluble in water?
h: Which compound has a group that can hydrogen bond with water?
w: Only phenol has an –OH group, which hydrogen bonds with water, so it is moderately soluble. Benzene, toluene and chlorobenzene are almost insoluble because they cannot hydrogen bond with water.
x: Benzene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon. It cannot hydrogen bond with water, so it barely dissolves.
Toluene is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with only dispersion forces, so it is almost insoluble in water.
The C–Cl bond is polar, but chlorobenzene has no H on O or N and cannot donate a hydrogen bond. It is almost insoluble.

q: Naphthalene (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, two fused benzene rings, once used in mothballs) is a solid at room temperature, while benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) is a liquid. What best explains the difference?
c: Naphthalene is a larger molecule, so its dispersion forces are stronger
Naphthalene molecules hydrogen bond to each other
Benzene is more polar than naphthalene
h: Both are hydrocarbons with only C and H. Which intermolecular force do they have, and what makes it stronger?
w: Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons with only dispersion forces. Naphthalene has more atoms and electrons and a larger flat surface, so its dispersion forces are stronger, and it melts higher (about 80 °C vs about 6 °C for benzene).
x: Hydrogen bonding needs an H on O, N or F. Naphthalene has only C–H bonds.
Naphthalene is a covalent molecule made of C and H only. It contains no ions.
Both are nonpolar hydrocarbons. Polarity does not explain the difference; size does.

q: Wildfire smoke that drifts into the Valley contains formaldehyde (methanal, HCHO). Formaldehyde is a gas at room temperature. What best explains its very low boiling point?
c: It is small and has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself
It is completely nonpolar, with no dipole
Its molecules hydrogen bond strongly to each other
h: Look for an H bonded to O in HCHO. How big is the molecule?
w: Formaldehyde has a polar C=O, so it has dipole–dipole attractions, but its H atoms are on carbon, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself, and with only four atoms its dispersion forces are weak. Its attractions are weak, so it boils far below room temperature (about −19 °C).
x: Formaldehyde is a covalent molecule, not an ionic compound. Ionic compounds are solids with very high melting points.
The C=O bond is polar, so formaldehyde does have a dipole. Look at how big the molecule is and at what its H atoms are bonded to.
A hydrogen bond needs an H on O, N or F. Formaldehyde's H atoms are on carbon.

q: Warm nitric acid, a strong oxidizing agent, oxidizes both C1 (the aldehyde) and C6 (the –CH<sub>2</sub>OH) of glucose to –COOH. What is the product?
h: Aldonic: only C1 oxidized. Uronic: only the last carbon. Which name means both ends?
w: When both ends become –COOH, the product is a dicarboxylic acid called an aldaric acid: glucaric acid. Oxidizing only C1 gives gluconic acid (aldonic), and oxidizing only C6 gives glucuronic acid (uronic).
x: Gluconic acid forms when only C1 is oxidized, as in the Benedict's test. Here C6 is oxidized too.
Glucuronic acid has only C6 oxidized, while C1 stays an aldehyde. Here both ends are oxidized.
Sorbitol forms by reduction of the aldehyde, not oxidation. It has no –COOH group.

q: The liver attaches glucuronic acid to many drugs and to bilirubin (glucuronidation). Glucuronic acid is a uronic acid made from glucose. Which carbon(s) of glucose have been oxidized to –COOH in glucuronic acid?
c: only C6; C1 stays an aldehyde
both C1 and C6, giving a diacid
only C2; C1 and C6 are unchanged
h: Uronic acids are the "other end" acids: C1 is protected in a ring while the enzyme works.
w: In a uronic (alduronic) acid, only the last carbon, C6, is oxidized to –COOH. C1 is untouched, so glucuronic acid is still a reducing sugar.
x: Oxidizing only C1 gives gluconic acid, an aldonic acid.
Oxidizing both ends gives glucaric acid, an aldaric acid.
C2 of glucose carries a secondary –OH. Uronic acids are named for oxidation at the last carbon, not C2.

q: Glucuronidation helps the kidneys excrete a drug in urine. Attaching glucuronic acid has this effect mainly because it
c: adds polar –OH and ionized –COO<sup>−</sup> groups, making the drug water soluble
makes the drug more nonpolar, so it moves out of the blood into body fat
breaks the drug down completely into CO<sub>2</sub> and water for exhalation
turns the drug into a polysaccharide that is stored in the liver
h: Urine is mostly water. What kind of molecule dissolves well in water?
w: Glucuronic acid has several –OH groups and a –COOH that is ionized (–COO−) at body pH. Attaching it makes the drug much more polar and water soluble, so the kidneys can excrete it in urine.
x: More nonpolar compounds stay in fat and are harder to excrete. Glucuronidation does the opposite.
Glucuronidation adds a group; it does not burn the drug to CO<sub>2</sub> and water.
Only one sugar acid is attached, not a polysaccharide, and the product is excreted, not stored.

q: The A1C test measures hemoglobin A1C, which forms when glucose attaches, without any enzyme, to an –NH<sub>2</sub> group of hemoglobin. Which group of glucose reacts with the –NH<sub>2</sub>?
c: the aldehyde C=O of the open-chain form
a glycosidic bond at the anomeric carbon
the oxygen atom inside the closed ring
h: Amines react with carbonyl groups. Where is the carbonyl group in glucose?
w: In its open-chain form, glucose has an aldehyde (C=O) at C1. This carbonyl reacts with an amino group on hemoglobin. The more glucose in the blood, the more hemoglobin becomes glycated.
x: The –OH on C6 is a primary alcohol. It is not the reactive carbonyl group.
Free glucose is a monosaccharide and has no glycosidic bond.
The ring oxygen is part of a hemiacetal. The ring must open to show the reactive aldehyde.

q: Why does an A1C result reflect a patient's average blood glucose over the past 2–3 months instead of only today's level?
c: Glucose stays bound to hemoglobin for the life of the red blood cell
Hemoglobin is made only once every three months, in a single batch
Glucose needs about three months to cross into red blood cells
The A1C test measures glycogen that the liver stored over those months
h: How long does a red blood cell, and the hemoglobin inside it, last?
w: Once glucose is attached to hemoglobin, it stays there for the rest of the red blood cell's life, about 120 days. So the percentage of glycated hemoglobin builds up in step with average blood glucose over the past few months.
x: Red blood cells, and their hemoglobin, are made continuously. The time window comes from how long each cell lasts.
Glucose enters red blood cells quickly. The A1C reflects how long the attached glucose remains.
A1C is measured on hemoglobin in red blood cells, not on liver glycogen.

q: Lactose-free milk from Valley dairies is made by adding the enzyme lactase to milk. It tastes slightly sweeter than regular milk, even though no sugar is added. Why?
c: Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose, which taste sweeter together
Lactase converts lactose into sucrose, a sweeter disaccharide
Lactase polymerizes the lactose into short starch chains
Removing lactose leaves only the milk proteins, which are sweet
h: What are the products when lactase hydrolyzes lactose?
w: Lactase breaks the β(1→4) glycosidic bond, giving glucose and galactose. Together these monosaccharides taste sweeter than the same amount of lactose, and people who make little lactase can absorb them.
x: Sucrose is glucose bonded to fructose. Lactose contains galactose, not fructose, and lactase only breaks bonds.
Lactase is a hydrolase; it breaks glycosidic bonds rather than making polymers. Starch is a glucose polymer that plants make.
The sugar is not removed; it is split into smaller sugars. Milk proteins are not what makes it taste sweeter.

q: Many people with lactose intolerance can eat yogurt or aged cheese with fewer symptoms than milk causes. What is the main reason?
c: Bacteria have already fermented much of the lactose into lactic acid
The proteins in cheese block lactose from being digested
Yogurt contains more lactose than milk, which trains the body to make lactase
h: Yogurt and cheese are made with bacteria. What do the bacteria use for food?
w: During fermentation, bacteria break down much of the milk's lactose and turn it into lactic acid (which makes yogurt tangy). In cheese, more lactose also leaves with the whey. Less lactose remains, so less reaches the colon undigested.
x: Cheese proteins do not block lactose. The difference is how much lactose is left after fermentation.
Neither yogurt nor cheese is made by turning lactose into cellulose, and humans cannot digest cellulose anyway.
Yogurt has less lactose than the milk it is made from, not more.

q: The pancreas makes the protein-digesting enzyme trypsin as an inactive zymogen, trypsinogen, which is switched on only in the small intestine. Why is this important?
c: It keeps trypsin from digesting the proteins of the pancreas itself
Trypsinogen digests proteins faster than trypsin
It allows trypsin to work in the acid of the stomach
Zymogens can pass through cell membranes, but enzymes cannot
h: Trypsin hydrolyzes peptide bonds. What else is made of proteins besides food?
w: An active protease made in the pancreas would hydrolyze the pancreas's own proteins. Making it as an inactive zymogen and activating it only in the small intestine protects the pancreas. Activation cuts off a piece of the chain (hydrolysis of a peptide bond).
x: A zymogen is inactive. It must be activated before it can digest anything.
Trypsin works in the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, not in the acid of the stomach.
Zymogens are secreted from cells like other proteins. The point is that they are inactive until they reach the right place.

q: Glycogen phosphorylase is switched on when a kinase attaches a phosphate group to a serine side chain of the enzyme, and switched off when a phosphatase removes the phosphate. This type of regulation is called
c: allosteric control by a regulator that binds without forming a covalent bond
feedback inhibition by the end product of the pathway
h: Is a covalent bond formed to the enzyme, and can the change be undone?
w: Adding or removing a phosphate group through a covalent bond is covalent modification. Phosphorylation is reversible: a kinase adds the phosphate, and a phosphatase takes it off.
x: An allosteric regulator binds reversibly through weak attractions at a regulatory site. Here a phosphate group is covalently bonded to the enzyme.
In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway binds to an earlier enzyme. Here a phosphate is attached by another enzyme.
Zymogen activation cuts a peptide bond and cannot be undone. Phosphorylation can be reversed by a phosphatase.

q: Which statement correctly compares zymogen activation with phosphorylation as ways of turning enzymes on?
c: Zymogen activation cuts a peptide bond and cannot be reversed; phosphorylation can be reversed by a phosphatase
Both can be reversed easily within seconds
Zymogen activation adds a phosphate group; phosphorylation cuts a peptide bond
Neither involves forming or breaking a covalent bond
h: What happens to the protein chain in each case, and can it be put back?
w: Activating a zymogen hydrolyzes a peptide bond and removes a piece of the chain, so it is one-way. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate that a phosphatase can remove, so it is reversible. Zymogen activation is permanent; phosphorylation is reversible.
x: Once the blocking piece of a zymogen is cut off, it cannot be reattached, so zymogen activation is not reversible.
This swaps the two. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate group; zymogen activation cuts a peptide bond.
Both are covalent changes: one breaks a peptide bond and the other forms a phosphate ester bond.

q: Some California workers who mix and apply organophosphate pesticides have the cholinesterase activity of their blood checked. After a spraying season, a worker's result is well below the worker's own starting value. What does this most likely mean?
c: The pesticide has bonded covalently to the enzyme's active site and inhibited it
The worker's body has made extra cholinesterase to protect itself
The worker's blood is low in acetylcholine
The pesticide has been hydrolyzed by the enzyme and is now harmless
h: Organophosphates bond to a serine –OH in the active site of cholinesterase. What does that do to enzyme activity?
w: Organophosphates form a covalent bond to the active-site serine of cholinesterase, which is irreversible inhibition, so measured activity drops. A fall from the worker's own starting value is a warning of exposure, even before symptoms appear.
x: Making more enzyme would raise the activity, not lower it.
The test measures the enzyme's activity. When the enzyme is blocked, acetylcholine tends to build up rather than fall.
The organophosphate stays bonded to the enzyme and blocks it. A lower activity means the enzyme is inhibited.

q: Acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that organophosphate pesticides block, normally adds water to break the ester bond of acetylcholine, giving choline and acetic acid. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Which class of enzyme uses water to split a bond?
w: Breaking a bond by adding water is hydrolysis, so acetylcholinesterase is a hydrolase. When it is blocked, acetylcholine is not broken down, and nerves keep firing.
x: Oxidoreductases move electrons or hydrogen, as dehydrogenases do. Hydrolysis of an ester is not a redox reaction.
A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here water splits one molecule into two.
A ligase joins two molecules using ATP. Acetylcholinesterase splits a molecule.

q: Fluconazole treats Valley fever by binding to a fungal enzyme in the pathway that makes ergosterol. Why does it harm the fungus much more than the patient?
c: It binds the fungal enzyme far more tightly than the matching human enzyme
Human cells have no membranes for the drug to attack
It denatures every protein it touches, fungal or human
Humans need ergosterol in their diet, so the drug is harmless
h: Enzymes are specific: a drug fits the active site of one enzyme better than another.
w: Enzyme action depends on the shape of the active site. The fungal enzyme and its human counterpart differ in shape, so fluconazole binds the fungal enzyme far more tightly. That specificity is what makes it a useful drug.
x: Human cells have membranes too; they use cholesterol instead of ergosterol.
A drug that denatured all proteins would harm the patient as much as the fungus.
Humans do not use ergosterol in their membranes. The selectivity comes from the drug binding the fungal enzyme.

q: In 2-methylbutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, how is carbon 2 (the carbon that carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch) classified?
h: Count how many other carbon atoms are bonded directly to carbon 2.
w: Carbon 2 is bonded to C1, C3 and the CH3 branch: three other carbons, so it is tertiary (3°). A carbon's class counts carbon neighbors only; the H atoms do not count.
x: A secondary carbon is bonded to two other carbons. Carbon 2 also carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch, so count again.
A primary carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, like the CH<sub>3</sub> groups at the ends of the chain. Carbon 2 is in the middle and is branched.
A quaternary carbon is bonded to four other carbons and has no H. Carbon 2 still has one H.

q: Which alkane contains a quaternary (4°) carbon?
h: A quaternary carbon is bonded to four other carbons, so it has no H atoms at all. Look for a C with two branches on it.
w: In 2,2-dimethylbutane, carbon 2 carries two CH3 branches and is also bonded to C1 and C3: four carbons, no H. So 2,2-dimethylbutane has a quaternary carbon. All four compounds are C6H14 isomers.
x: Carbon 2 of 2-methylpentane has one branch and one H, so it is bonded to three carbons: tertiary, not quaternary.
Carbon 3 of 3-methylpentane has one branch and one H, so it is tertiary. A quaternary carbon needs two branches on the same carbon.
Hexane is unbranched. Its end carbons are primary and its inner carbons are secondary; none is bonded to four carbons.

q: How many secondary (2°) carbons are in 3-methylhexane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: A secondary carbon is bonded to exactly two other carbons. In an alkane, that is every CH<sub>2</sub> in the chain.
w: Classify each carbon: the three CH3 groups are 1°, the CH carrying the branch (C3) is 3°, and the three CH2 groups (C2, C4, C5) are 2°. There are 3 secondary carbons.
x: Two misses one of the CH<sub>2</sub> groups. There are CH<sub>2</sub> groups at C2, C4 and C5.
Four counts C3 as secondary, but C3 is bonded to C2, C4 and the CH<sub>3</sub> branch: three carbons, so it is tertiary.
One counts only a single CH<sub>2</sub>. Every CH<sub>2</sub> inside the chain is bonded to two carbons.

q: Under which conditions does an alkane such as methane react with Cl<sub>2</sub>?
c: when the mixture is heated or exposed to light (UV)
in the dark at room temperature, with no catalyst
with H<sub>2</sub> and a platinum catalyst
with water and an acid catalyst
h: Alkanes are unreactive. What energy source starts their reaction with a halogen?
w: Alkanes have only strong, nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds, so a halogen reacts with them only when heat or light supplies energy. A Cl atom then replaces an H (a substitution), and HCl forms.
x: In the dark at room temperature an alkane and Cl<sub>2</sub> do not react. That is why the reaction needs a source of energy.
H<sub>2</sub> with a Pt catalyst is the condition for hydrogenating an alkene. An alkane has no C=C to add H<sub>2</sub> to.
Water and an acid catalyst hydrate an alkene. Alkanes do not react with water.

q: When methane reacts with excess Cl<sub>2</sub> in light, the products include CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, CHCl<sub>3</sub> (chloroform, once used as an anesthetic) and CCl<sub>4</sub>, not just CH<sub>3</sub>Cl. Why do these more highly chlorinated products form?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl still has C–H bonds, so a Cl can replace another H, and then another
Cl<sub>2</sub> adds across a C=C that forms in methane
CCl<sub>4</sub> forms first and then loses Cl atoms one at a time
Methane molecules join into a polymer that contains chlorine
h: Halogenation is a substitution: one Cl replaces one H. How many H atoms does CH<sub>3</sub>Cl still have?
w: Each substitution replaces one H with one Cl and releases HCl. CH3Cl still has three C–H bonds, so with excess Cl2 further substitutions give CH2Cl2, then CHCl3, then CCl4.
x: Methane is an alkane and has no C=C. Halogenation of an alkane is a substitution, not an addition.
The reaction goes the other way: H atoms are replaced by Cl one at a time, starting from CH<sub>4</sub>.
Halogenation does not link methane molecules together. Each product still has only one carbon.

q: Propane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> in light. Counting only products with ONE Cl, how many different compounds can form?
h: Replace one H with Cl at each different kind of carbon. Are the two end carbons different from each other?
w: Cl can replace an H on an end carbon (1-chloropropane, CH3CH2CH2Cl) or on the middle carbon (2-chloropropane, CH3CHClCH3). The two end carbons are equivalent, so there are 2 monochlorinated products.
x: One counts only a single position. The middle CH<sub>2</sub> is different from the two end CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
Three counts each carbon separately, but C1 and C3 are equivalent: putting Cl on either end gives the same compound, 1-chloropropane.
Eight counts every H atom. Many H atoms are equivalent, and replacing equivalent H atoms gives the same compound.

q: Ethylene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>, is the plant hormone that Valley packing houses use to ripen fruit. It is also the monomer of polyethylene, used in plastic bags and squeeze bottles. How does polyethylene form?
c: Addition polymerization: each C=C opens and the monomers join into a long chain of –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– units
Condensation polymerization: each pair of monomers joins and gives off a water molecule
Substitution: a Cl atom replaces an H atom on each ethylene molecule
Combustion: ethylene reacts with O<sub>2</sub> to give a long chain
h: Ethylene has a C=C and no O or N atoms. Which kind of reaction lets alkenes link to each other without losing any atoms?
w: In addition polymerization, the double bond of each alkene monomer opens and the carbons bond to the next monomer, giving a chain of repeating –CH2–CH2– units. No atoms are lost, so the polymer has the same formula ratio as the monomer.
x: Condensation polymers such as nylon and polyesters form from monomers with –COOH, –OH or –NH<sub>2</sub> groups, which lose water. Ethylene has no such groups.
Replacing H with Cl would be a substitution and would not link monomers together. PVC is made from a monomer that already contains Cl.
Combustion breaks a hydrocarbon down to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. It does not build chains.

q: Polypropylene is the plastic in most disposable syringe barrels. Which monomer is used to make it?
h: An addition polymer is named after its monomer, and the monomer must have a C=C.
w: Polypropylene is made by addition polymerization of propene, CH2=CHCH3. Each C=C opens, and the CH3 groups hang off every other carbon of the chain.
x: Propane has no C=C, so it cannot undergo addition polymerization.
Ethene is the monomer of polyethylene. Polypropylene has a CH<sub>3</sub> branch on every other carbon, so its monomer has three carbons.
Chloroethene (vinyl chloride) is the monomer of PVC, the plastic in IV bags. Polypropylene contains no chlorine.

q: Teflon, the nonstick coating, is the addition polymer of tetrafluoroethene, CF<sub>2</sub>=CF<sub>2</sub>. Which is its repeating unit?
h: In addition polymerization the C=C becomes a single bond, and every atom of the monomer stays in the polymer.
w: The double bond opens to link monomers, so the repeating unit is –CF2–CF2–, with only single bonds and all four F atoms kept.
x: A carbon with a C=C and two F atoms could not also bond to the next unit. The C=C becomes a single bond as the chain forms.
This unit has H atoms, but the monomer has none. Each carbon keeps its two F atoms.
A CF<sub>3</sub> carbon has only one bond left, so it could end a chain but cannot be a repeating unit in the middle.

q: On cold Valley nights, a gas wall heater or a generator burning fuel with too little air produces a deadly, odorless gas. Incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms which product that complete combustion does not?
h: Complete combustion gives CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. What forms when there is not enough O<sub>2</sub> to finish the job?
w: With too little O2, some carbon is only partly oxidized and leaves as carbon monoxide, CO. CO binds the iron in hemoglobin far more tightly than O2 does, which is why fuel-burning devices must never be run indoors.
x: CO<sub>2</sub> is the product of complete combustion.
Water forms in both complete and incomplete combustion.
O<sub>2</sub> is a reactant in combustion, not a product.

q: After a heart attack, patients are often told to take low-dose aspirin, which lowers thromboxane production in platelets. What do thromboxanes normally do?
c: promote platelet clumping and narrow blood vessels
constrict the smooth muscle of the airways during an asthma attack
carry cholesterol in the blood from the liver out to the tissues
store energy in fat cells as long-chain fatty acid esters
h: Aspirin is given to prevent clots. Which eicosanoid is made in platelets?
w: Thromboxanes are eicosanoids made in platelets. They promote platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Aspirin blocks the COX enzymes that make them, so clots are less likely to form.
x: Constricting the airways in asthma is a job of leukotrienes, which COX inhibitors like aspirin do not block.
LDL, a lipoprotein, carries cholesterol to the tissues. Thromboxanes are local signaling molecules.
Triacylglycerols store energy in fat cells. Thromboxanes are signals made in tiny amounts.

q: Montelukast (Singulair), a daily asthma medicine, blocks the action of the eicosanoids that constrict the airways and increase mucus. Which eicosanoids are they?
h: Which eicosanoids are made by lipoxygenase in white blood cells and act on the airways?
w: Leukotrienes are made from arachidonic acid by lipoxygenase. In asthma they constrict airway smooth muscle and increase mucus, so blocking them helps prevent attacks.
x: Prostaglandins cause pain, fever and inflammation; they are the target of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen.
Thromboxanes act on platelets and blood vessels during clotting, not on the airways.
Cortisol is a steroid hormone, not an eicosanoid. Eicosanoids are made from a 20-carbon fatty acid.

q: Prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes are all made from the same starting material. What is it?
c: cholesterol, a steroid with four fused rings
h: The name "eicosanoid" comes from the Greek word for twenty.
w: All eicosanoids come from arachidonic acid, a 20-carbon fatty acid with four cis C=C bonds that is cut out of membrane phospholipids when needed.
x: Cholesterol is the starting material for steroid hormones and bile salts, not eicosanoids.
Glycerol is the backbone of triacylglycerols and glycerophospholipids. It has only 3 carbons.
Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids. Eicosanoids are 20-carbon fatty acid derivatives.

q: Flaxseed oil turns rancid by reacting with O<sub>2</sub> in the air much faster than coconut oil does. What is the best explanation?
c: Flaxseed oil has many C=C bonds that O<sub>2</sub> attacks; coconut oil is mostly saturated
Flaxseed oil has more ester bonds per molecule, and O<sub>2</sub> attacks ester bonds
Saturated fats react with O<sub>2</sub> faster, and flaxseed oil is the more saturated oil
Coconut oil contains no carbon–hydrogen bonds for O<sub>2</sub> to attack
h: Oxidative rancidity starts at a particular part of a fatty acid chain. Which kind of fat has more of it?
w: Oxygen attacks fatty acid chains at and next to their C=C bonds. Flaxseed oil is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids with many C=C bonds, while coconut oil is mostly saturated, so flaxseed oil oxidizes and turns rancid faster.
x: Both oils are triacylglycerols with three ester bonds per molecule. Oxidative rancidity depends on the C=C bonds, not the esters.
This is reversed. Saturated chains have no C=C bonds and are the most resistant to oxidation.
Coconut oil is made of hydrocarbon chains full of C–H bonds. Its chains have few C=C bonds, which is why it resists oxidation.

q: Butter left out too long smells sour and "cheesy" because butyric acid (a 4-carbon fatty acid) is released. Which reaction releases it?
c: hydrolysis of the ester bonds of triacylglycerols
hydrogenation of the C=C double bonds in the fat’s chains
saponification of the fat with NaOH
dehydration of the glycerol backbone, which splits off the chains
h: Butyric acid is attached to glycerol by an ester bond. Which reaction breaks an ester bond with water?
w: This is hydrolytic rancidity: lipase enzymes from microorganisms hydrolyze the ester bonds of butterfat, releasing free short-chain fatty acids such as butyric acid, which are volatile and smell bad.
x: Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> to C=C bonds. It does not release fatty acids.
Saponification uses a strong base like NaOH and gives soap (carboxylate salts). Butter on the counter is not treated with NaOH.
Dehydration removes water. Releasing a fatty acid from an ester needs water to be added.

q: Valley citrus packing houses coat lemons and oranges with a thin layer of food-grade wax (such as carnauba wax) to reduce water loss. Why is a wax good at keeping water in?
c: A wax is an ester with long nonpolar chains on both sides, so it repels water
A wax is very polar, so it hydrogen bonds strongly to water and holds it in
A wax is a triacylglycerol, with three polar ester groups that hold water
A wax is a steroid with an –OH group that traps water inside the fruit
h: Waxes are esters of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol. What do the long chains do?
w: A wax is an ester of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol. Except for one small ester group, it is all long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains, so it repels water and forms a waterproof barrier, like the natural wax on fruit peel.
x: Waxes are mostly nonpolar. A very polar coating would attract water instead of sealing it in.
A triacylglycerol is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids. A wax has one ester bond between a fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol.
Steroids have four fused rings. Waxes are long-chain esters.

q: A handful of Valley almonds supplies a good share of the day's vitamin E (α-tocopherol), an antioxidant that protects the polyunsaturated fatty acid chains in cell membranes. Which part of vitamin E gives up an H atom to stop the oxidation?
c: the phenol –OH group on its ring
an ester group on its side chain
h: Vitamin E has a ring with one –OH group on it, plus a long nonpolar tail.
w: Vitamin E gives up the H of its phenol –OH to a reactive oxygen species, stopping the chain of oxidation before it spreads through the membrane's fatty acid chains.
x: The long tail anchors vitamin E in the nonpolar interior of the membrane. Its C–H bonds are not the ones that stop oxidation.
α-Tocopherol itself has no ester group. (Some supplements sell it as an acetate ester, which the body must hydrolyze first.)
Vitamin E has no carboxylic acid group. Its acidic –OH is a phenol.

q: Vitamin E from almonds ends up mostly in cell membranes rather than in the watery cytosol. Why?
c: Its long nonpolar tail dissolves in the nonpolar interior of the lipid bilayer
It is a very polar molecule that is attracted to the phosphate heads
It is a protein that is built into the membrane and anchored there
It is water soluble and is pumped into the membrane by active transport
h: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin. Where does a fat-soluble molecule dissolve in a cell?
w: Except for a ring that holds an –OH and an ether oxygen, vitamin E is a large hydrocarbon, so it is fat soluble. Its nonpolar tail dissolves among the fatty acid chains of the bilayer, right next to the polyunsaturated chains it protects.
x: Vitamin E is mostly nonpolar. A very polar molecule would stay in water, not in the membrane interior.
Vitamin E is a small lipid, not a protein.
Vitamin E is fat soluble, not water soluble. It dissolves into the membrane without being pumped.

q: Fluconazole, a drug used to treat Valley fever (coccidioidomycosis), blocks a fungal enzyme needed to make ergosterol, the four-ring lipid that fungal cell membranes use in place of cholesterol. To which lipid class does ergosterol belong?
h: Ergosterol plays the role of cholesterol and has four fused rings.
w: Four fused carbon rings (three six-membered and one five-membered) define a steroid. Ergosterol is the fungal steroid that does the job cholesterol does in human membranes, so blocking its synthesis damages the fungal membrane.
x: A triacylglycerol is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids. It is a storage fat with no ring system.
A glycerophospholipid has glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group. It has no fused rings.
A wax is an ester of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol. It has no fused rings.

q: Complete oxidation of stearic acid (18 carbons, saturated) gives 120 ATP. Oleic acid also has 18 carbons but one C=C. In this course, each C=C that is already present skips one FAD step of β-oxidation (1.5 ATP). How many ATP does oleic acid give?
h: Same number of carbons means the same acetyl CoA. Subtract one FADH<sub>2</sub> for the double bond.
w: Oleic acid gives the same 9 acetyl CoA and 8 NADH as stearic acid, but one fewer FADH2 because its C=C is already there. 120 − 1.5 = 118.5 ATP.
x: 120 is the value for saturated stearic acid. The C=C in oleic acid means one FADH<sub>2</sub> is not made.
117.5 subtracts 2.5, the value for NADH. The step that is skipped is the FAD step, worth 1.5 ATP.
An existing double bond lowers the yield; it does not raise it. Less oxidation happens, so less ATP is made.

q: Linoleic acid (18 carbons, two C=C bonds) and stearic acid (18 carbons, saturated) are both oxidized completely. Compared with stearic acid, β-oxidation of linoleic acid produces
c: two fewer FADH<sub>2</sub> but the same number of acetyl CoA (9)
two fewer acetyl CoA and the same FADH<sub>2</sub>
two fewer NADH but the same number of FADH<sub>2</sub>
exactly the same products in the same amounts
h: The number of acetyl CoA depends on the number of carbons. Which step does a double bond that is already present skip?
w: Both fatty acids have 18 carbons, so both give 9 acetyl CoA. Each existing C=C skips the FAD step once, so linoleic acid gives two fewer FADH2 and therefore less ATP.
x: Acetyl CoA comes from the carbon chain two carbons at a time. Both acids have 18 carbons.
The step that is skipped is the one that forms a C=C, which uses FAD, not NAD<sup>+</sup>.
The double bonds already present change the count of one reduced coenzyme, so the products are not identical.

q: Fatty acids are activated as fatty acyl CoA in the cytosol, but β-oxidation happens in the mitochondrial matrix. Which molecule carries the fatty acyl group across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
h: This carrier gives its name to the "shuttle" that moves fatty acyl groups into the mitochondria.
w: Fatty acyl CoA cannot cross the inner membrane. The acyl group is moved onto carnitine, carried across, and then moved back onto CoA inside the matrix (the carnitine shuttle).
x: Coenzyme A carries the acyl group on each side of the membrane, but acyl CoA cannot cross the inner membrane itself.
Albumin carries free fatty acids in the blood, not across the mitochondrial membrane.
Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the intestine through the lymph and blood. They do not enter mitochondria.

q: Which is NOT a source of amino acids for the body's amino acid pool?
c: fatty acids released from stored fat
breakdown of the body's own proteins (protein turnover)
synthesis of nonessential amino acids in the liver
h: Amino acids contain nitrogen. Which choice has no nitrogen to give?
w: The amino acid pool is fed by dietary protein, by protein turnover, and by synthesis of nonessential amino acids. Fatty acids contain no nitrogen, so they cannot be made into amino acids.
x: Digested dietary protein is the main source of new amino acids for the pool.
Body proteins are constantly broken down, and their amino acids return to the pool.
The liver makes nonessential amino acids, for example by transamination, and adds them to the pool.

q: What does protein turnover mean?
c: Body proteins are constantly broken down and rebuilt
Dietary protein is digested only in the stomach by pepsin
Proteins are converted into stored fat when eaten in excess
Amino acids are excreted unchanged in the urine each day
h: Turnover is the same idea as staff turnover at a job: the old ones leave and new ones replace them.
w: Protein turnover is the ongoing breakdown of body proteins into amino acids and the building of new proteins from the amino acid pool. It lets cells replace damaged proteins and adjust enzyme levels.
x: Protein digestion starts in the stomach and finishes in the small intestine. Turnover is about the body's own proteins.
Excess amino acids can end up as fat after their nitrogen is removed, but that is not what turnover means.
Healthy kidneys excrete very few free amino acids. Excess nitrogen leaves as urea.

q: The body has no storage form for amino acids. What happens to amino acids in the pool that are not needed for making proteins and other nitrogen compounds?
c: Their amino groups become urea, and their carbon skeletons are burned or made into glucose or fat
They are stored as a reserve protein in muscle, the way glucose is stored as glycogen
They are excreted unchanged in the urine, along with the extra water
They are converted into essential amino acids for use later on
h: Think about transamination, deamination and the urea cycle.
w: Extra amino acids are not stored. Their nitrogen is removed (transamination and oxidative deamination) and excreted as urea, and the carbon skeletons enter pathways that give energy, glucose or fat.
x: Muscle proteins all have jobs to do; there is no storage protein comparable to glycogen.
Healthy kidneys excrete very few amino acids. Extra nitrogen leaves the body as urea.
The body cannot make the carbon skeletons of essential amino acids, so extra amino acids cannot be turned into them.

q: A clinic patient has a fasting blood glucose of 132 mg/dL and an A1C of 7.1%. Using the usual cut-offs (fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, or A1C 6.5% or higher), how should these results be read?
h: Compare each result with its cut-off.
w: A fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher and an A1C of 6.5% or higher are both in the diabetes range, and this patient is above both (132 mg/dL and 7.1%).
x: Normal fasting glucose is 99 mg/dL or lower, and normal A1C is below 5.7%. Both results are higher.
Prediabetes is a fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL. 132 mg/dL is above that range.
Hypoglycemia means glucose is too low. These values are high.

q: To make human insulin in bacteria, the insulin gene is inserted into a plasmid. Which enzyme cuts the plasmid and the DNA containing the gene at specific base sequences?
h: This enzyme acts like a pair of molecular scissors and leaves "sticky ends."
w: A restriction enzyme recognizes a specific short base sequence and cuts (hydrolyzes) the DNA backbone there, leaving sticky ends that can pair with matching ends.
x: DNA ligase joins pieces of DNA by re-forming phosphodiester bonds. It seals; it does not cut.
RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template during transcription. It does not cut DNA.
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template, as HIV does. It does not cut DNA at specific sites.

q: After the sticky ends of the insulin gene pair with the sticky ends of the cut plasmid, which enzyme re-forms the phosphodiester bonds to seal the gene into the plasmid?
h: The same enzyme seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments during replication.
w: DNA ligase forms the phosphodiester bonds that join the DNA pieces, producing one continuous recombinant plasmid. The bacteria then copy the plasmid and make human insulin from the gene.
x: The restriction enzyme cut the DNA in the first place. Sealing the pieces back together needs a different enzyme.
Helicase unwinds the double helix during replication. It does not join DNA pieces.
RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template. It does not join DNA strands.

q: A PCR test for Valley fever copies a short stretch of DNA from the Coccidioides fungus many times. In every cycle the sample is heated to about 95 °C to separate the DNA strands. Why must the DNA polymerase used in PCR be heat-stable?
c: So it is not denatured by the repeated heating and keeps building new strands every cycle
Because heat makes the polymerase read RNA instead of DNA
So it can cut the fungal DNA at specific sequences
Because a heat-stable polymerase does not need nucleotides
h: Most enzymes are proteins that unfold when heated. What would happen to an ordinary polymerase at 95 °C?
w: Heating to about 95 °C would denature most enzymes. PCR uses a polymerase from a heat-loving microbe, so it survives every heating step and keeps copying the DNA cycle after cycle.
x: DNA polymerase copies a DNA template in PCR. Heat does not change which template it reads.
Cutting DNA at specific sequences is the job of restriction enzymes. A polymerase builds new strands.
Every polymerase needs nucleotides to build a new strand. Heat stability only keeps the enzyme from denaturing.

q: Aflatoxin, made by molds that can grow on poorly stored nuts, corn and grain, is changed by liver enzymes into a form that bonds to guanine in DNA. If the damaged G is copied wrongly during replication, one base pair is replaced by another. What kind of mutation is this?
c: a frameshift caused by an insertion
a frameshift caused by a deletion
a mutation that is always silent
h: One base pair is swapped for another; none are added or removed.
w: Replacing one base pair with another is a substitution, also called a point mutation. A chemical that causes mutations, like aflatoxin, is a mutagen; aflatoxin is also a known cause of liver cancer.
x: An insertion adds a base. Here a base is replaced, so the reading frame is not shifted.
A deletion removes a base. Here the number of bases stays the same.
A substitution can be silent, but it can also change an amino acid or create a stop codon. It is not always silent.

q: Which amino acid is matched with BOTH its correct three-letter and one-letter abbreviations?
h: Some one-letter codes are simply the first letter, but when two amino acids share a first letter, one gets a different letter.
w: Glycine is Gly, G. Lysine is Lys, K (L is leucine). Glutamine is Gln, Q; Glu is glutamic acid. Tryptophan is Trp, W (T is threonine).
x: Lys is right, but L is the one-letter code for leucine. Lysine is K.
Glu is glutamic acid, whose one-letter code is E. Glutamine is Gln, Q.
Trp is right, but T is threonine. Tryptophan is W.

q: A tripeptide is written in one-letter code as M-A-C (N-terminal end first). How is it written with three-letter abbreviations?
h: One-letter codes are not always the first letter of the name. Which amino acid is A, and which three-letter codes start with A?
w: M is methionine (Met), A is alanine (Ala), and C is cysteine (Cys): Met–Ala–Cys. The order stays the same, from the N-terminal to the C-terminal end.
x: Arg is arginine, whose one-letter code is R, not A.
Asn is asparagine, whose one-letter code is N, not A.
Lys is lysine (K). M stands for methionine.

q: Almost all of the amino acids in human proteins have the same configuration at the alpha carbon. Which one?
c: equal amounts of D and L (racemic)
none, because amino acids are not chiral
h: The D/L system for amino acids works like the one for sugars. Which form do human enzymes build proteins from?
w: Nearly all amino acids in human proteins are L-amino acids. D-amino acids occur mainly in some bacterial cell walls and certain antibiotics. Glycine is the one amino acid with no chiral carbon, so it is neither D nor L.
x: D-amino acids are rare in human proteins. Some bacteria and antibiotics contain them.
Enzymes are specific for one enantiomer, so cells do not build proteins from a racemic mixture.
Every common amino acid except glycine has a chiral alpha carbon (H, –NH<sub>2</sub>, –COOH and R are four different groups).

q: In a Fischer projection of an amino acid with –COO<sup>−</sup> at the top and the side chain at the bottom, where is the –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> group in an L-amino acid?
h: Amino acids use the same D/L rule as sugars, where the side of the –OH on the last chiral carbon decides D or L. Recall which side goes with L.
w: For amino acids, the –NH3+ group on the alpha carbon is drawn on the left in the L form and on the right in the D form, just as the –OH on the last chiral carbon of a sugar decides D or L.
x: The side on which –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> appears decides D or L, just as the –OH does for sugars. Recall which side goes with L.
The top position holds the –COO<sup>−</sup> group in this Fischer projection.
The bottom position holds the side chain (R group).

q: Biuret reagent (blue Cu<sup>2+</sup>) turns violet when it reacts with two or more peptide bonds. Which sample gives a positive (violet) biuret test?
h: Which sample contains molecules with many peptide bonds?
w: The biuret test detects peptides and proteins with two or more peptide bonds. Egg albumin is a protein, so it turns violet. Free amino acids and sugars have no peptide bonds.
x: Glycine is a single amino acid with no peptide bonds, so the biuret reagent stays blue.
Glucose is a sugar and has no peptide bonds.
Alanine is a free amino acid with no peptide bonds, so the test is negative.

q: A student tests a solution of free alanine with ninhydrin and with biuret reagent. What results are expected?
c: ninhydrin turns purple; biuret stays blue
ninhydrin stays colorless; biuret turns violet
h: Ninhydrin needs a free amino group. Biuret needs two or more peptide bonds.
w: Ninhydrin reacts with the free –NH2 group of an α-amino acid to give a purple color, so it is positive. Alanine has no peptide bonds, so the biuret reagent stays blue: ninhydrin positive, biuret negative.
x: Biuret needs at least two peptide bonds. A single amino acid has none.
This is the pattern reversed. A free amino acid has a free amino group but no peptide bonds.
Ninhydrin reacts with the free amino group of an amino acid, so it is positive here.

q: Healthy kidneys keep proteins in the blood. A test on the urine of a patient with long-standing diabetes shows protein (proteinuria), a sign of kidney damage. A biuret test on this urine detects protein because the reagent reacts with
c: the peptide bonds of the protein
the urea that is always present in urine
the glucose spilled into the urine
h: What do all proteins contain that urea, glucose and fatty acids do not?
w: Biuret reagent forms a violet complex with peptide bonds (two or more in a row). Normal urine has only a trace of protein, so a positive result points to protein leaking through damaged kidneys.
x: Urea is always in urine but has no peptide bonds, so it does not give a positive biuret test.
Glucose in urine is detected by Benedict's test or a test strip, not by biuret.
Many molecules have –COOH groups. The biuret test needs peptide bonds.

q: A farmworker collapses on a very hot afternoon with a core body temperature above 40 °C (heat stroke). Rapid cooling is started at once. Why is cooling so urgent?
c: Hot enzymes keep unfolding, and many of them cannot fold back
Cooling quickly re-forms the peptide bonds that were broken by the heat
Cooling makes enzymes work faster than they do at 37 °C
Heat converts proteins into fats, and cooling reverses this
h: Heat breaks the weak attractions that hold a protein's shape. What happens to an unfolded enzyme's activity?
w: High temperature breaks the hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions that hold an enzyme's shape, so enzymes denature and can clump (aggregate). Peptide bonds survive, but many unfolded proteins do not refold, so every minute counts.
x: Denaturation by heat does not break peptide bonds. The primary structure stays intact; the folded shape is lost.
Enzymes have their highest activity near 37 °C. Cooling a patient back toward normal does not make enzymes faster than normal.
Heat changes a protein's shape. It does not turn protein into fat.

q: Nitrate from fertilizer and manure can seep into Valley well water. In the body some nitrate becomes nitrite, which converts the Fe<sup>2+</sup> in hemoglobin's heme to Fe<sup>3+</sup>, forming methemoglobin, which cannot carry O<sub>2</sub>. What has happened to the iron?
c: It has been oxidized: it lost an electron
It has been reduced: it gained an electron
It has been hydrolyzed by water
It has been removed from the heme
h: Going from Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>, did the iron gain or lose a negative electron?
w: Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e−: the iron lost an electron, so it was oxidized. Nitrite is the oxidizing agent. Fe3+ heme cannot bind O2, so less oxygen is delivered, which can make an infant's skin look bluish.
x: Gaining an electron would lower the charge, for example Fe<sup>3+</sup> to Fe<sup>2+</sup>. Here the charge rises.
Hydrolysis breaks a bond by adding water. A change in the charge of iron is a redox change.
The iron stays in the heme. Only its charge changes, which is why it can no longer carry O<sub>2</sub>.

q: How many valence electrons must appear in the Lewis structure of the ammonium ion, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>?
h: Add the valence electrons of every atom from the group numbers, then adjust for the charge. Does a positive charge mean an electron was gained or lost?
w: N brings 5 and the four H atoms bring 4, for 9. A 1+ charge means one electron has been lost, so the structure uses 8 electrons: four N–H bonds and no lone pairs.
x: 9 is the count for the neutral atoms (5 + 4). For a cation you must subtract one electron for each positive charge.
10 comes from adding an electron for the charge. Electrons are added for negative charges; a positive charge means one electron is missing.
11 uses nitrogen's atomic number (7) instead of its valence electrons. Only the outer-shell electrons count: 5 for N, a Group 5A element.

q: In the correct Lewis structure of carbon dioxide, O=C=O, how many lone pairs are there in the whole molecule?
h: CO<sub>2</sub> has 16 valence electrons. Work out how many are used in the two double bonds, then see what is left over and which atoms still need them.
